method: 20 agents, one per inventory cluster, each reading its sections AND searching the live Nerva repo for what exists. Every row cites a Nerva path or states 'none'. Raw entries rolled up to capability level (a thing a user or operator can do), roll-up ratio recorded per cluster. Decisions: keep / copy / update / skip — skip requires a product reason, never an effort reason.
adaptation_rule: Anything copied that performs a privileged effect must land BEHIND the Action Kernel, not beside it. Nerva is behind Hermes on breadth and ahead on governance; a ported feature that bypasses the kernel is a regression even if it works.

clusters.verdict: Nerva is not behind Hermes on CLI *capability* so much as it has no operator surface at all: 83 HTTP routers and a governed kernel exist behind a browser tab on 127.0.0.1, while the terminal offers `serve.py`, a 3-target Makefile, ~35 unrelated argparse scripts and a 47-line `input()` loop (agents/run.py) — so a headless or SSH install cannot be set up, inspected or recovered, and roughly half of Hermes' 73 commands map onto Nerva mechanisms that are already equal or better (import, estop, memory, pairing, peer/A2A, skills, curator, support bundle, insights). The single most valuable thing to build here is the unified `nerva` command whose every mutating verb calls the same in-process service the HTTP routers call, so it inherits kernel mediation for free — and the first three verbs to put on it are `doctor`, `kernel explain` (Hermes' `approvals test`, which finally makes Nerva's governance legible before it fires) and `prompt-size`.
clusters.biggest_miss: The unified `nerva` command itself. Everything else in this cluster is either already built behind HTTP or is one verb away from it — but with no CLI there is no way to configure, diagnose, back up, stop or update a Nerva install that has no browser in front of it, which is exactly the home-server/SSH deployment the product is aimed at. It is also the dependency for ~15 other rows here, and the reason `nerva doctor` sits as P0 #10 in the repo's own gap matrix while GAP-0 records 24,182 visitors and 0 converted partners: the failure is friction at install and operation, not capability. The close second is `approvals test` (row 20) — a read-only simulator that replays the real kernel gates and prints the trace — because Nerva's differentiator is governance and today it is invisible until it fires.

clusters.cluster: gateway (07-gw-slash.md + 08-gw-core.md — the always-on gateway process and its 57 slash handlers)
clusters.verdict: Nerva is behind Hermes on almost everything a person can *type* into a chat and level or ahead on almost everything the system *decides* — it has no chat command plane at all (agents/core/quickbar.py parses slashes for the desktop bar; agents/core/channels/telegram.py forwards every message straight to the orchestrator and intercepts only `/start <token>`), no busy-turn control, no per-session turn lease, no delivery ledger and no drain, while its approval queue, kernel mediation, audit chain, local-first fallback policy and governed work runs are genuinely better than Hermes's equivalents. The single most valuable thing to build here is the chat command plane with per-command access tiers on top of it — one shared registry serving chat, quickbar and HUD, with `/stop`, `/status`, `/pause` and `/sessions` first — because it is the dependency for eleven other rows and it is what turns Nerva's governance from something you can only see in a browser into something the owner can exercise from the phone in their pocket.
clusters.biggest_miss: The chat slash-command plane (gw-slash.command-grammar / alias-resolution / dispatch-order and the 57 handlers hanging off it). Its absence hurts most because Nerva's differentiator is currently unreachable from the surface owners actually use: the decision-inbox buttons work on Telegram, but there is no way to ask what is running, stop it, lift the e-stop, list or resume a session, or switch model without opening the HUD — and worse, because there is no command recognition there is also no `/stop` and no busy policy, so a second Telegram message during a turn starts a *concurrent* turn against the same session key with no lease (agents/core/orchestrator.py:1109-1176 has no lock), which is a transcript-corruption risk rather than merely a missing convenience. Every other buildable row in this cluster that a user can type — access tiers, session commands, quick commands, blueprints, maintenance verbs, plugin/skill commands — depends on it existing first.

clusters.verdict: Nerva is not behind Hermes on channel breadth so much as on channel *depth*: it has five-plus adapters but the deepest is 203 lines against Hermes' 11,296, and the shortfall is concentrated in things that are not optional — a Telegram reply path that 400s on unbalanced markdown and cannot send past 4096 characters, a Discord adapter that skips the pairing gate it is wired to and answers around the send contract, a Slack adapter that cannot receive, and a webhook ingress that verifies no provider signature while the whole governance stack keys off the sender identity it accepts. Against that, Nerva is genuinely superior where it counts most — pairing as an approval rather than an allowlist, A2A that cannot self-execute, Home Assistant actuation through the kernel with an idempotency ledger, and WhatsApp on the official API — and the single most valuable thing to build is the adapter descriptor plus base-adapter split (agents/core/channels/base.py grown from a four-method ABC into a capability-declaring contract that names each channel's kernel kind), because rendering, chunking, media, streaming, gating, threads and per-channel verbosity are all currently blocked on channels having no way to say what they can do.
clusters.biggest_miss: Inbound gating — the group decision ladder (`require_mention`, mention detection, per-chat/per-topic allowlists, observe mode, `_should_process_message`). A repo-wide ripgrep for every one of those terms returns zero hits outside the inventory: Nerva's entire gating vocabulary is one flat `allowed_user_ids` list at agents/core/channels/telegram.py:26. That means a Nerva bot placed in any group chat answers every message from every allowlisted member with no way to say "only when addressed" — so group deployment is unusable in practice, and worse, every message in that room becomes tainted inbound context the agent reasons and acts on. It hurts more than the flashier gaps (streaming, media, topics) because it is an authorization boundary rather than a feature: the pairing gate, the owner binding on approval cards and the audit trail all assume the agent only engages when it should, and nothing in the code enforces that. It is also the gap that most directly limits reach — Telegram and Discord are group-shaped platforms, and Nerva can only safely be used in a DM.

clusters.verdict: Nerva's HUD is not a smaller dashboard — it is a different and in places better artifact: a structured chat with provenance where Hermes mirrors ANSI, a command palette Hermes explicitly lacks, honesty-bearing status chrome (DEMO/OFFLINE/EMPTY/LIVE, EGRESS, %-local) with no Hermes analogue, and a signed+moderated skill supply chain against Hermes' paste-a-Git-URL. But it is behind on the boring operator surfaces that make a system livable: there is no file browser, no log viewer, no session search or transcript, no user-created scheduled jobs, no channel or MCP configuration UI, no login page, no restart/update path, and — most surprising for a single-page app of this size — no URL routing at all, so nothing in the cockpit has an address. The single most valuable thing to build here is the owner-created scheduled job: Nerva already parses "every weekday at 7am" into a cron expression and throws it away, and a scheduled job is the one capability where Nerva's governance stack (approval tiers, interrupt budget, kill switch, audit chain) is not overhead but the actual product.
clusters.biggest_miss: The Cron page — the ability for the owner to create, schedule, pause and trigger his own recurring job, with Hermes' typed blueprint gallery (morning brief, important-mail monitor, price watch, competitor watch) so it needs no cron syntax. Its absence hurts most because Nerva has every piece except the store and the screen: `POST /api/schedule/parse` already turns natural language into a cron expression in English and Romanian and then does nothing with it (agents/core/routers/tools.py:73, surfaced in a console panel at gap.tsx:1858 that displays the string and discards it); SchedulerService already runs eleven APScheduler jobs, all of them written by developers (agents/core/scheduler_service.py); the Decision Inbox, autonomy tiers, interrupt budget and kill switch that a scheduled action needs are all shipped. So the owner cannot ask for a single recurring thing — which is the daily-value engine of a house brain and the reason the autonomy stack exists. BACKLOG.md:1459 already names it as the one part of DRA-08 still owed and correctly identifies the blocker as a product decision (what may run unattended, at which tier), not a wiring problem. It is also the row where Nerva's governance stops being a tax and becomes the differentiator: Hermes schedules unattended work with no queue behind it, and Nerva is the only one of the two that could ship the same feature and still let the owner sleep.

clusters.verdict: Nerva is not behind Hermes on desktop — it does not have a desktop app at all: desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs is 22 lines with a comment where the tray menu should be, and desktop/README.md says the shell is deliberately never built in CI, so every one of Hermes's 777 desktop entries lands against a web console in a browser tab. The exceptions are real and worth defending — the approval/kernel model, the versioned SOUL editor, the governed canvas, the memory graph and host_probe's honest refusal vocabulary are all ahead of their Hermes counterparts — but they are ahead inside a surface the owner reaches by typing a localhost URL. The single most valuable thing to build here is the shell that owns its backend: a signed installer whose app starts, supervises, health-probes and reaps the Python runtime, because until that exists the HUD, quick entry, notifications, global hotkeys, keep-awake and deep links all have nowhere to live, and every other row in this ledger is blocked behind it.
clusters.biggest_miss: HUD mode — the chrome-free, always-on-top floating chat that sits over whatever the owner is actually doing. Nerva's own vision documents claim an AI OS and a house brain, and its answer today is a browser tab you switch to; Hermes's answer is a panel window that stays over your work while a turn streams, with a per-compositor capability object that handles Wayland/X11/Cocoa/win32 differences once instead of scattering platform checks. Everything else in this cluster is ergonomics on top of a product that already exists somewhere in the repo; this is the one absence that changes what Nerva *is* — an assistant you visit versus an operating layer that is present. It is also the row that makes Nerva's real advantages visible at the moment they matter: an approval card that floats over the app the agent is about to act in is a governance surface, while the same card in a background tab is a notification nobody read.

clusters.verdict: Nerva has no terminal surface at all — agents/run.py is a 47-line `input()` loop — so on the literal reading of this cluster Nerva is behind on all 475 entries; but most of those entries are Ink/Node/terminal craft (skins, kaomoji, mouse protocols, heap monitors, a widget loader) that a governed household AI should not carry, and the ~199 gateway RPC methods hiding inside this shard are a control plane Nerva largely already has as 458 HTTP routes. The single most valuable thing to build is a small Python terminal client over the existing HTTP+SSE API whose first job is answering the approval queue, because Nerva today ships a `headless` profile that keeps background autonomy on and gives a server install no way to complete its own governed loop without a browser.
clusters.biggest_miss: There is no way to answer Nerva's approval queue from a terminal. Approvals exist only as HTTP routes (agents/core/routers/actions.py:51, agents/core/routers/autonomy.py:211) consumed by the HUD (frontend/src/gap.tsx:2904) and mobile (mobile/src/screens/ApprovalsScreen.tsx); grep of scripts/ found no CLI that can decide one. That hurts most because it undercuts the differentiator on the exact install shape Nerva advertises for it: agents/core/system_profiles.py:53 ships a `headless` profile described as \"for a server / TUI / low-VRAM (8GB) box\" with `background_autonomy: True` — so a box that keeps producing ask-tier tasks has no front door to resolve them, and the profile's own description names a TUI that does not exist. Hermes' in-flow approval prompt (20-tui.md §4) shows the exact command and takes the answer where the user already is; Nerva needs the same, posting to the existing admin-guarded decide route with no local decision cache, no batch-approve, and explicitly no `/yolo` per-session auto-approval bypass.

clusters.verdict: Nerva's config plane is small but unusually well built — 131 typed, hand-labelled, server-validated settings with encrypted secret fields, a settings-change audit trail and boot guards that refuse to start on a malformed posture flag, all of which Hermes's 785 inferred-schema keys do not match on quality; where Nerva is genuinely behind is breadth (no operator-pinned scope, no profiles, no per-helper-task model assignment, 368 undocumented env vars) and, more seriously, resilience and self-governance. The single most valuable thing to build here is to make the config plane obey Nerva's own rules: a `config.write` kind in the Action Kernel with policy-, money- and retention-touching keys pinned to the irreversible tier, sitting on top of a layered resolution that survives a corrupt store with last-known-good instead of silently falling back to permissive defaults.
clusters.biggest_miss: The `hermes config` CLI family — `show|get|set|unset|path|env-path|check|migrate` (22-config-b.md §A2). Nerva has no command-line access to configuration at all: pyproject.toml declares no console script, and the only read or write path is `GET/PUT /api/admin/settings/{category}` behind admin_guard, which requires a booted server and a valid token. That is exactly the state a broken install is not in, and docs/OWNER_TASKS.md is explicit that nothing in this product has yet run on real hardware. The absence turns every first real-world failure — wrong model pinned, autonomy misconfigured, settings.db unreadable — into hand-editing SQLite over a screen-share, and it compounds the corrupt-store row: with no last-known-good and no CLI, a box that silently degrades to permissive defaults offers no way to see it or fix it from the outside.

clusters.verdict: Nerva is genuinely ahead of Hermes on what a credential *is* — encrypted at rest, held as a `{{secret:name}}` handle, injected just-in-time behind approval, and scrubbed default-deny out of every child process — and ahead again on posture hygiene, with one boolean parser, declared defaults, and a boot that refuses a malformed posture flag; but it is behind on everything an operator *does* with configuration, because it has no write path, no key registry, no stated precedence, no provenance, and 46 of its 158 environment names are documented nowhere. The single most valuable thing to build here is a declared key registry plus a kernel-mediated `config.write` action (a new kind in agents/core/kernel/registry.py, which today has none) so an owner can configure the product from the product — with the writer allowlist and the pinned managed layer landing in the same move, since a config writer without them is a remote-code-execution primitive.
clusters.biggest_miss: The configuration surface itself — Hermes' OPTIONAL_ENV_VARS registry (152 declared keys with prompt, category, and what each unlocks) feeding a setup wizard and a dashboard Keys page, backed by the one writer at hermes_cli/config.py:4544. Nerva has no equivalent: /api/admin/env (agents/core/routers/admin.py:167) reads masked and nothing writes; provider keys are read once at HybridRouter construction (agents/core/llm/hybrid_router.py:325) so even a hand-edit needs a restart; and docs/FLAGS.md covers 26 of the 158 JARVIS_*/NERVA_* names the code actually reads. This hurts most because it silently caps everything else: the one-command install ends at a text editor, a non-developer owner cannot add an API key at all, and each remaining gap in this ledger — proxy and CA trust, the language setting, per-channel allowlists, extra provider endpoints — would land as yet another undocumented variable rather than something the owner can see and set. It is also the row where Nerva can overtake rather than catch up: Hermes' own rebuild notes ask for per-key provenance and a capability-scoped writer, and Nerva is the only one of the two with a kernel to put that write behind.

clusters.cluster: tools — the agent-callable surface (83 tools / 62 toolsets / registry, budget and guardrail machinery)
clusters.verdict: Nerva is not behind Hermes on tool *machinery* — it is behind on tool *surface*, and by roughly seven to one: the model-directed loop is offered 7 tools (`echo`, `time`, `desktop_plan`, `operator_plan`, `desktop_run`, `terminal_run`, `osint_enrich`) plus 4 default-off file tools, against Hermes's 83, and almost every missing capability already exists in `agents/core/` as a working, kernel-mediated subsystem that simply nobody registered on the allowlist — browser control, web search, memory search, subagents, media generation, house control, the sandbox code-runner and every connected MCP server are all built and all unreachable from a turn. The single most valuable thing to build here is the toolset-profile layer (row 8) together with a bulk exposure wave behind it: profiles make least privilege real at the moment of *offering* rather than only at execution, and without them, wiring twenty subsystems into one flat allowlist would hand a Telegram-channel turn the same tools as the owner's HUD — the exposure gap and the scoping gap have to close together or not at all.
clusters.biggest_miss: Content search over files (`search_files`) — the ripgrep-backed regex-and-glob tool. Nerva has `file_read` and `file_list` but no way to search, so the model's only routes to finding anything are listing and reading files one at a time (which burns the context budget local models can least afford) or shelling out via `terminal_run` — which turns a read-only grep into a gated ask-tier task that wakes the owner for an approval decision. That is the worst possible outcome for both sides of Nerva's thesis: it degrades capability and it debases the approval queue by filling it with requests that carry no risk. The fix is small and self-contained (rooted ripgrep reusing `agents/core/file_tools.py`'s existing symlink/secret-name/byte-bound path resolution, ungated because it performs no effect), and it unblocks everything downstream — `execute_code` pipelines, code intelligence, `local_docs`, and any autonomous work over the owner's own files.

clusters.verdict: Nerva is ahead of Hermes on every question about whether a skill may run — signing with TOCTOU-safe snapshot imports, a default-on fail-closed quarantine for LLM-authored code, kernel-mediated marketplace installs with moderation and version rollback, a sandbox-only acquisition broker, and skills projected into a capability registry with real rollback contracts — and behind on every question about whether a skill can be found, chosen, or improved: there is no prompt index, no skills_list/skill_view, no security scanner worth the name (11 injection regexes against Hermes' 129 severity-scored patterns), no hub, no gating, no disable, and no in-session patch. The single most valuable thing to build here is the model-facing skill catalogue — an L0 index plus governed skill_view/skill_view(file) through ToolRPC — because it is the one change that converts every asset already built in this cluster from infrastructure into product.
clusters.biggest_miss: Progressive-disclosure skill discovery (`<available_skills>` index + `skills_list` + `skill_view`). Nerva's model has no idea skills exist: `agents/core/agent.py:124-128` builds a skills block from `context["skills"]`, and nothing in the repo ever sets that key — the only route from a user turn to a skill is exact regex command matching in `agents/core/skills/loader.py:785` plus eight hard-coded heartbeat names. That means the 78-entry Hermes pin, the signed marketplace, the curator, the usage telemetry and the acquisition broker are all machinery serving a library the agent cannot enumerate, so the owner's directive to "keep what is superior" is currently keeping a locked room. It also blocks the rest of the cluster: the hub, the optional catalog, the setup/readiness contract and skill patching are each worth little until something can list and load a skill by relevance — and Hermes' ~3k-token L0 index is exactly the shape a local model with a small context can afford, which makes this a differentiator for Nerva rather than a catch-up.

clusters.verdict: Nerva is far behind Hermes on provider breadth and, more damagingly, on wire depth: it reaches four backends in practice (LM Studio, Ollama, Gemini, Anthropic) against Hermes's 48 profiles, its declarative provider registry is documented as not affecting routing at all, and its Anthropic and Gemini clients are plain text-completion callers with no tools, no thinking control and no prompt caching — so the cloud escalation the owner depends on is exactly the path where Nerva stops being an agent. It is genuinely ahead on the things Hermes chose not to build — a spend cap enforced before provider selection, a per-call egress ledger that makes the local-first claim measurable, per-agent model allowlists with a code-enforced local-only floor, and real local-model lifecycle governed by the kernel. The single most valuable thing to build here is native tool-calling plus streaming on the Anthropic and Gemini wires against the existing provider-neutral tool_protocol, because it converts the cloud tier from a text oracle back into a governed agent and is the precondition for every other provider being worth adding.
clusters.biggest_miss: Native tool-calling on the cloud wires. `supports_tools = True` appears exactly once in the repo — on LMStudioBackend (agents/core/llm/base.py:443) — and agents/core/agent.py:171 gates the whole tool runtime on that flag, so the instant a heavy agent routes to Claude (the designed path in hybrid_router.py for CLAUDE_AGENTS and POLICY_CLAUDE) it silently drops to base.py's text fallback, which flattens the transcript into one prompt string and returns a ToolTurn with no tool calls. The owner's own constraint — local models cannot carry the context load — guarantees the important work lands on precisely the backend that cannot use tools. It also quietly hollows out the governance story: on a cloud-routed turn the Action Kernel authorises nothing, because nothing is ever attempted. Provider breadth is worth little until this is fixed; forty more provider logos would all inherit the same text-only ceiling.

clusters.verdict: Nerva is ahead of Hermes on the two things it claims — governed effects and honest compaction (kernel-mediated tool dispatch, spotlight/taint, a Merkle audit chain, and a two-tier compaction policy with image-first eviction and lineage rows that Hermes has no equivalent of) — but it is behind on almost everything that makes a turn survive contact with a weak local model: the tool loop never compacts its own message list, a truncated answer is discarded rather than continued, no guardrail notices a model repeating a failing call, failures reach the owner as bracketed strings, and the running turn cannot be steered or interrupted. The single most valuable thing to build here is verification: recipe detection plus a passive evidence ledger plus a verify-on-stop nudge, crossing terminal.exec, because it is the one capability that converts this repo's own "✅ means DELIVERED, not PROVEN" rule from a documentation discipline into a runtime one — and it is the precondition for the autonomous-developer lane the roadmap already assumes.
clusters.biggest_miss: Compaction inside the running turn (row 6). Everything else on this list degrades an experience; this one loses work. `agents/core/agent_runtime.py:137` appends an assistant message plus one tool result per call across up to 32 iterations and never measures the growing message list — it does not even import the compressor — while `agents/core/orchestrator.py:2305` compacts only the history assembled for the prompt, behind a default-off flag. Nerva ships an excellent compaction policy (`agents/core/context_compressor.py:116`, images dropped first, per-model 32k default window) and then never calls it on the one path that actually grows fast. A desktop-operator or coding turn that takes twenty screenshots or twenty file reads inside a single loop will exceed a 32k local window, and the provider — not Nerva — will do the truncating, from the tail: the half that says what is happening right now. Hermes fails closed here (`PreflightCompressionTimedOut` stops an oversized turn rather than sending it); Nerva has no gate at all. The policy exists, the trigger points do not, and the fix is calling code that is already written before each model call in the loop.

clusters.verdict: Nerva's "AHEAD on memory" rating is real but narrow: it is decisively ahead on the *semantics* of memory (bi-temporal facts, RRF fusion, ACT-R decay, consolidation planning, episodes, recall-admission trails, an eval harness Hermes has no counterpart for) and it is behind — structurally, not cosmetically — on the *substrate*: Hermes keeps every message of every conversation in one indexed SQLite store with FTS5 and hands the model a `session_search` tool, while Nerva writes one JSON blob per session, surfaces at most five of them, and has no full-text index anywhere in the repo. The single most valuable thing to build here is that substrate plus the tool on top of it: a real transcript store with FTS and a model-callable `session_search`, because auto-titling, export/import, prune/archive/pin, recap and lineage are all cheap once it exists and are all impossible until it does.
clusters.biggest_miss: `session_search` — the model being able to search and scroll its own past conversations (inventory `memory.tool-session-search`, over the `memory.session-fts5` index). Nerva has rich recall over *derived* facts (`/api/memory/search`, `search_memory` in `agents/core/memory/rag_tool.py`) but zero recall over what was actually said: `rg` for `fts5` across `agents/`, `scripts/`, `frontend/src` returns nothing, and `agents/core/memory/persistence.py::list_sessions()` caps discovery at the five most recent JSON snapshots. For an always-on house assistant this is the absence a user feels every day — "what did we decide about the boiler last month" has no answer path at all, and it cannot be reconstructed from the KG because the KG only holds what the extractor happened to promote. It also blocks four other rows (auto-titling, export/import, session management, recap), which is why it outranks the fail-closed pre-compress checkpoint despite that one being the more dangerous governance hole.

clusters.verdict: Nerva is decisively ahead of Hermes at exactly one thing in this cluster and behind almost everywhere else: its goal loop is governed end to end — a six-field contract that cannot be proposed half-filled (goal_contract.py), an owner approval that crosses `goal.approve` in the kernel, a verifier that refuses to treat a run's own claims as evidence (work_verifier.py), and a fail-closed judge where a model rubric can only withhold a pass (work_judge.py) — against Hermes' optional contract and fail-open judge; but Hermes' automation *surface* (an owner-createable cron table, an in-session /loop, a durable dependency-aware board) has no counterpart anywhere in the repo, and Nerva's own scheduling is entirely developer-authored in scheduler_service.py and HEARTBEAT.md files. The single most valuable thing to build is the owner-createable scheduled job on top of the existing queue and kernel — rows 2 through 10 of this ledger all hang off it, it is the trigger every autonomy component Nerva already shipped is waiting for, and it is what makes the "first governed morning brief in 30 minutes" activation story the gap matrix already committed to actually reachable.
clusters.biggest_miss: The user-createable scheduled job (`hermes cron`) — a durable job the owner arms in a sentence, that fires without anyone watching, remembers its last run, skips the model when nothing changed, and pauses itself with a stated reason when it cannot succeed. Its absence hurts most because it is not one feature but the *entry point*: Nerva has a task queue, a risk policy, a decision inbox, an approval kernel, a hash-chained audit log, presence-aware escalation and a morning-brief builder, and today none of it can be started by the owner without a developer editing agents/*/HEARTBEAT.md or scheduler_service.py and restarting the process. That turns a governance advantage into something the owner cannot exercise — the strongest audit chain in the field is worth nothing on automations the owner was never able to create. The runner-up is the durable dependency-aware board (row 18): company mode already has the goal, the ledger, the verifier and the judge, and the board is the missing shared unit of work that would let Nerva's cabinet of named agents claim from and hand off to each other instead of merely being routed to. Cron unlocks the single owner; the board unlocks the company.

clusters.verdict: Nerva is genuinely AHEAD on approval/safety and audit, and the "ahead" rating survives contact with the evidence: the Action Kernel mediates 25 classified action kinds with a CI-enforced registry snapshot, the approval queue is durable where Hermes' is in-memory, the audit chain is Merkle-hashed with optional off-box HMAC keying and external anchoring, SSRF does DNS pinning and rejects on any private record (the exact TOCTOU fix Hermes only lists as a wish), file access is an allowlist-of-roots with snapshot-backed reversible writes rather than a denylist race, and taint/quarantine/rag_guard fence untrusted content in ways Hermes has no equivalent for — but Nerva is genuinely BEHIND on three things it cannot keep calling defence-in-depth: there is no browser sign-in at all (a networked HUD is reachable only by a caller that can set a custom header), no secret redaction on the paths that write to disk (a terminal command that prints a token permanently commits it to the append-only audit chain and to the approval card the owner reads on a phone), and the hardline floor — the one control that is supposed to hold regardless of approval — matches a single lowercased shlex split with no de-obfuscation variants. The single most valuable thing to build here is that variant-normalization pipeline plus a risky-but-recoverable pattern tier on top of the existing terminal contract: it repairs the credibility of the floor Nerva's whole governance story rests on, it gives the approval card a real description instead of a bare argv, and it is the prerequisite for the guardian model and the policy simulator that would cut interrupt volume without weakening anything.
clusters.biggest_miss: The command normalization and de-obfuscation pipeline (`_command_detection_variants()`, tools/approval.py:2412) that Hermes runs every detector over — roughly fifteen passes producing NFKC-folded, backslash-stripped, quote-masked, `$()`/backtick-substituted, home-path-folded and interpreter-payload-extracted variants of the same command. Nerva's `agents/core/environments/terminal_contract.py::_normalize` does one shlex split, a lowercase and a whitespace squeeze, then matches nineteen regexes against that single string. Its hardline list is broader than Hermes' twelve rules and the governance around it is better in every respect — screened before authorize, before policy, before autonomy level, for every backend including docker, and unreachable without a durable human-accepted task. But the floor's entire promise is that it holds no matter who approved what, and a floor that can be stepped over by `sh -c 'mk'\''fs.ext4 /dev/sda'`, `$(printf mkfs).ext4 /dev/sda`, or a base64 pipe is not a floor — it is a speed bump with excellent paperwork. This matters more for Nerva than for Hermes precisely because Nerva sells governance: the owner is being asked to approve an argv they read once, on a phone, and the system's promise is that the catastrophic cases are refused underneath that decision. Every other gap in this cluster is a confidentiality leak, a missing convenience, or an unbuilt surface; this one is the load-bearing claim.

clusters.verdict: Nerva is dramatically ahead of Hermes on media *governance and presentation* — the Media Director's kernel-mediated present/restore with verified-not-asserted status and snapshot-as-undo, the room-aware Wyoming voice context, the searchable provenance-chained media catalog with an export bundler, the persona-voice consent gate and the dictation cleaner are all capabilities Hermes simply does not have — and dramatically behind on media *production and reach*: there is not one wired image or video backend in the repo (the only production `MediaGenManager()` is constructed with no backends), no chat attachment path, no way to serve a catalogued file to a client, no voice or photo delivery on any chat channel, no document extraction outside the memory indexer, and no media tool the model can actually call, since the agent's registered tool surface is desktop_run / terminal_run / desktop_plan / operator_plan / osint_enrich / echo / time plus file tools. The single most valuable thing to build here is a wired generation backend behind a shared media-provider seam — local diffusion by default through the existing VRAM-swap orchestrator, one cloud provider opt-in — landed on a new kernel-mediated `media.generate` kind rather than the plain `q.enqueue` media_gen uses today, because that one change turns five finished-but-inert Nerva subsystems into a working product and closes the governance hole that would otherwise ship with them.
clusters.biggest_miss: A working `image_generate` — a media generation backend that actually produces a file. Nerva has the complete governance frame around an empty socket: `media_gen.py` validates a contract and queues an ask-tier approval, `media_catalog.py` is a bounded searchable library, `media_export.py` zips a selection with a manifest, `creative/pipeline.py` plans script→prompts→render→assemble→export and builds per-platform export packs, `creative/video_pipeline.py` plans timelines and effect specs, and `media_director.py` even has a `catalog` content type that resolves a catalog item onto a real device. Every one of those consumes generated assets, and nothing in the repository can create one — `rg -i 'comfyui|fal|replicate|stable.?diffusion|dall-e|gpt-image|sdxl|flux'` over agents/, frontend/src/, mobile/src/ and scripts/ finds only an unrelated docstring, and the only place `backends={...}` is passed to MediaGenManager is a test fake and a hermetic reality pack. The absence hurts more than any single Hermes provider would help, because it is the keystone: the governance work is done and unproven, the planners plan into a void, the gallery lists files it cannot show, and the honest product claim today is that Nerva can approve an image it cannot make. It is also the row with the sharpest governance risk if built carelessly — `media.image` and `media.video` are absent from agents/core/kernel/registry.py, so a backend wired to the current code path would spend money on a plain `q.enqueue` that never crosses the kernel.

clusters.verdict: Nerva is genuinely ahead of Hermes on exactly one thing in this cluster and behind on nearly everything else: its MCP *server* is the only implementation in either product where an external client's write crosses an identity gate, a kernel decision and a mandatory audit row before the effect happens (agents/core/mcp/route_tools.py), while its MCP *client*, its A2A implementation and its entire extensibility story — no ACP, no plugin format, no hooks, no OpenAI-compatible front door — are either bespoke, minimal or absent, leaving a hub with 445 routes and 25 in-tree plugins that nobody outside the repo can extend or reach from the tools they already use. The single most valuable thing to build here is the outbound MCP authorization gate: generalising what agents/core/mcp/worldview_write.py already does for one server (plugin gate → Action Kernel → scoped capability → call) into a trust tier plus read/write classification plus a kernel hop on every external MCP tool call, because until that exists the product's central claim is false on the one path that connects it to the rest of the ecosystem.
clusters.biggest_miss: Hermes' `trust: untrusted` write gating on outbound MCP tool calls (acp-mcp-dev.mcp-key-trust) — a per-server trust tier plus a per-tool readOnlyHint classification that fails closed and routes every write-capable call from an untrusted server through the approval surface before it runs. Its absence hurts Nerva more than it hurts Hermes, because Nerva sells governance: agents/core/mcp/client.py `_tool_call_blocked` evaluates only an `mcp.tool_call` contract over name/args-key *shape* and transport, `rg 'kernel|authorize' agents/core/mcp/client.py` returns nothing, and agents/core/kernel/registry.py's `mcp.mutating` = KERNEL covers only the inbound server direction. So any MCP server the owner adds gets a tool surface that can send mail, move files or spend money without ever crossing kernel.authorize, the approval queue's reversible/irreversible split, or the hash-chained audit log — which makes "the Action Kernel mediates every privileged action" untrue precisely where Nerva meets the outside world. The fix is cheap and the pattern is already proven in-tree by agents/core/mcp/worldview_write.py. Runner-up, for reach rather than integrity: the ACP editor-agent surface, which is the cheapest distribution channel Nerva does not have and the best place to make the approval queue feel like a feature instead of a tax.

clusters.verdict: Measured against Hermes's own 52-page feature manual, Nerva is ahead exactly where it claims to be — memory (bitemporal KG, decay, per-turn strict-local distillation vs two Markdown files), governance of every privileged effect, the skill supply chain, sandboxed tool-RPC, desktop and browser operation behind a kernel, and a cockpit that shows governance state Hermes has no equivalent for — and it is behind almost everywhere a *user initiates* something: no user-creatable scheduled job, no in-session recurring instruction or loop, no @-file references, no attachment delivery, no pasted screenshots, no semantic diagnostics on writes and no OpenAI-compatible front door. The single most valuable thing to build here is a governed scheduled-job surface: a job the owner can create, name, pause, inspect and see the run history of, whose action scope is declared at creation the way goal_contract already declares a goal's, and whose every fired action crosses the kernel individually.
clusters.biggest_miss: User-creatable scheduled jobs (Hermes's cron, 44 of the 821 entries). Nerva's only scheduled work is per-agent HEARTBEAT.md frontmatter parsed at boot by agents/core/heartbeat.py with MIN_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL=3600 and no create/edit/list route (agents/core/routers/heartbeat.py exposes status/start/stop/run-now only) — so to make Nerva do something for him at 07:00 the owner must edit a Markdown file in the repo and restart, then get no run history, no failure incident, no delivery target and no way to ask what is scheduled. Everything an always-on assistant does between conversations is a scheduled job, so this single gap silently caps the product's core promise; and it hurts most because the ingredients are all already built and merely unassembled — a durable TaskQueue, a policy engine with night windows and do-not-disturb, an EN/RO natural-language→cron parser stranded behind a parse-only endpoint, and a kernel that could mediate job creation as the standing authorization it actually is.

clusters.cluster: rest-api (inventory shard 36-docs-rest.md — see cluster_verdict: this shard is "the REST of the docs", not a REST API surface)
clusters.verdict: First, an honest correction to the orientation: `36-docs-rest.md` is not Hermes' REST API — the shard's own header defines it as the *remaining* documentation cross-check (getting started, install/update, integrations & providers, the developer guide, the user-guide top level, and reference misc). I checked Nerva's 465-route surface anyway where it was relevant, and the most telling numbers from it are `grep update` → 0 routes, `grep provider` → 0 routes, `grep cron` → 0 routes, against 19 skill routes, 19 autonomy routes and 35 admin routes; Nerva's route surface is shaped around governance and memory, and has almost no lifecycle or extensibility surface at all. Across this cluster Nerva is superior on everything that touches trust — kernel-mediated actions, hash-chained audit, quarantined imports (scripts/nerva_import.py is strictly better than `hermes import-agent`), the secret broker, quarantine/taint, the signed skills marketplace, and hardware-tiered governed local-model setup — at parity on install ergonomics, diagnostics, MCP, subagents and contributor tooling, and behind on the entire lifecycle-and-extensibility half: no self-update, no third-party plugin loader, no swappable provider backends, ~6 model providers against 43, no project-file rollback, no user-authored schedules, and no published docs. The single most valuable thing to build here is the governed self-update path (check → plan → backup → apply → receipt → verify), because it is the only row that unblocks every other one: without it, everything else this ledger recommends is a feature the owner installs once and can never safely move forward from or back out of.
clusters.biggest_miss: The third-party plugin SDK (docs-rest.dev-plugins-guide + ~20 sibling entries) — a manifest, a `register(ctx)` entry point, lifecycle hooks, a `plugins doctor` that runs real discovery against a candidate, and a distribution channel. Self-update is the more urgent build, but the plugin loader is the more damaging absence, because it is a ceiling rather than a gap. agents/core/plugin_manager.py is twenty hardcoded `from .plugins.X import XPlugin` lines and the repo's own `jarvis-add-plugin` skill instructs a contributor to edit the core, so every integration, every messaging adapter, every provider backend and every capability implementation is a PR against Nerva — which is precisely why the counts are ~20 plugins, 5 channels, 6 providers and 12 skills while Hermes carries 20+ platforms, 43 providers and 137 optional skills. Nerva cannot close those counts by copying items one at a time; it closes them by growing a seam. And the adaptation is not a compromise but an upgrade: Nerva already owns the trust machinery Hermes never built — CDX-8 quarantine, signing, the pending-review approval queue, plugin_gate's network-scope/data-scope manifest, and the kernel kinds every plugin effect would have to cross. The port to build is Hermes' developer ergonomics on Nerva's trust model, gated by a new `plugin.load` kernel kind so that installing third-party code is itself an owner decision in the approval inbox rather than an import statement.

clusters.cluster: delta (37-delta-27-31.md — what changed between Hermes v2026.8.27 and v2026.8.31)
clusters.verdict: Nerva is architecturally ahead of Hermes on everything this delta touches that concerns authority — the kernel mediates what the room, the node, the tool and the subagent may do, ESTOP is already canonical and fail-safe, the audit chain is hash-chained, and Nerva's compressor and approval queue have better failure semantics than the ones Hermes shipped here — but it is behind on almost everything that concerns a session that does not end: the conversation does not know today's date, a compaction never picks up a config or skill change, context pressure is estimated rather than measured, code execution loses all state between calls, and there is no way to ask a question about a running conversation without interrupting it. The single most valuable thing to build here is the compaction commit boundary as a live-session migration point (rebuild the system prompt, re-resolve the tool schemas, refresh the date line, anchor context on provider-reported usage), because it is the one change that turns Nerva's forever-session from a liability into the thing it claims to be — and every other row in this cluster that matters on a 24/7 box either depends on it or gets cheaper once it exists.
clusters.biggest_miss: Session-persistent code kernels (tools/code_kernel.py + code_kernel_remote.py). Nerva's agents/core/sandbox.py spawns a fresh docker/wasm/subprocess run with a fresh mkdtemp per call, so every piece of analysis re-imports its libraries, re-loads its data and re-derives its intermediate state on every single tool call. That is a tax paid in tokens and seconds, and it is paid worst exactly where Nerva stakes its differentiation — a local model on the owner's own hardware, where a 32k window spent re-printing setup code is a task that does not finish. Two secondary consequences make it the biggest miss rather than merely the largest: it is why a long data or operator run degrades instead of compounding, and it is the reason the honest answer to "can Nerva actually do multi-step analytical work on this box" is currently no. The port is not a copy job — the hard and non-negotiable part is that each cell must re-cross the terminal.exec contract and kernel.authorize, because a long-lived interpreter that was authorized once and then accepts arbitrary later code is a kernel bypass wearing a performance improvement's clothes.

capabilities.name: Drive the whole product from one command (`nerva ...`) with a discoverable command tree
capabilities.hermes: A single `hermes` executable dispatches 73 sub-commands through one argparse tree, with a light 'top-level + chat' parser reused for fast paths, pre-argparse profile extraction, plugin-registered sub-commands, and int return codes as exit codes (01-cli-a.md cli-a.entrypoint, cli-a.startup-fast-paths, cli-a.relaunch-inherited-flags; the usage line enumerates all 73). Rebuild note in the inventory itself asks for a declarative command registry so help/completion/docs share one source of truth.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — `grep -rn 'console_scripts|[project.scripts]' pyproject.toml` returns nothing; /home/user/jarvis-hub/pyproject.toml carries only ruff/vulture config. The entry surfaces are /home/user/jarvis-hub/serve.py, /home/user/jarvis-hub/start.sh, /home/user/jarvis-hub/Makefile (3 targets) and ~35 independent argparse scripts under /home/user/jarvis-hub/scripts/
capabilities.rationale: This is not terminal-nativism — it is the only way to administer a headless install. Nerva's admin surface is real and rich (83 routers under agents/core/routers/) but reachable only from a browser on 127.0.0.1. An owner who installs Nerva on a home server over SSH today cannot configure it, check it, or recover it. It is also the dependency for ~15 other rows in this cluster; without it each becomes another one-off script.
capabilities.governance: The dispatcher is read-only. Every mutating verb must call the same in-process service the HTTP router calls, so it crosses kernel.authorize (agents/core/kernel/registry.py) rather than reaching brokers directly — a CLI that shells past the kernel is the exact regression the directive forbids.

capabilities.name: Run one scripted agent turn from a pipe and get a machine-readable cost report
capabilities.hermes: `hermes -z "prompt"` prints only the final assistant text on stdout, silences everything else, exits 0/1/2/130, and `--usage-file PATH` writes a JSON spend report (estimated_cost_usd, token counts, api_calls, model, provider, session_id, completed/failed) even when the run fails (01-cli-a.md cli-a.opt-oneshot, cli-a.opt-usage-file).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/run.py (47 lines, a bare `input("> ")` loop over orch.handle_input); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/cost_tracker.py exists but is not exposed per-run; no non-interactive single-turn entry point
capabilities.rationale: This is the primitive that makes an agent scriptable — cron entries, CI steps and shell pipelines all need one turn in, one answer out, with an exit code. Nerva has the orchestrator and the cost tracker already; only the wrapper is missing.
capabilities.governance: The turn itself is read-only, but the tools it calls are not. Do NOT copy Hermes' behaviour of setting HERMES_YOLO_MODE=1 and HERMES_ACCEPT_HOOKS=1 inside `-z` — auto-bypassing approvals because 'no user is watching' inverts Nerva's model. A one-shot run must QUEUE anything the kernel would queue interactively and exit non-zero with the pending-approval id.

capabilities.name: Talk to the agent in a terminal with editing, history, cancel, and a live tool feed
capabilities.hermes: prompt_toolkit REPL with banner, status bar, ~20 keybindings (Alt+Enter newline, Ctrl+P palette, Ctrl+S prompt stash, Ctrl+G external editor, Ctrl+V clipboard-image paste, Ctrl+B voice, Esc Esc discard draft), clarify overlay, inline model picker, `!` bang-shell, slash-command completer, thinking spinner, tool progress feed with preview truncation, bracketed paste/file drop, busy-input mode (01-cli-a.md, ~35 entries cli-a.repl*).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/run.py:35-42 (while True / input / handle_input, no readline, no cancel, no tool feed); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/quickbar.py is the closest analogue but it is the desktop floating-bar command service (plan-only, returns a plan, never executes)
capabilities.rationale: A 47-line input() loop is not a terminal surface — a Ctrl+C kills the process mid-turn and there is no way to see what a tool is doing. Worth a modest REPL (history, multiline, cancel-the-turn-not-the-process, streaming tool lines), not the full 35-entry Hermes shell. Skip the overlays and stash.
capabilities.governance: read-only — the REPL renders; actions still cross the kernel through the orchestrator

capabilities.name: Get shell tab-completion for the command tree
capabilities.hermes: `hermes completion {bash,zsh,fish}` prints a completion script generated by walking the live argparse tree, so it can never drift from the installed version (06-cli-f.md cli-f.completion, .bash, .zsh, .fish).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — `rg 'bash_completion|compgen'` over agents/, scripts/, frontend/src/ returns nothing
capabilities.rationale: Cheap and it is what makes a 40-verb CLI usable instead of a man-page exercise. Generate it from the parser tree so it cannot drift, exactly as the inventory's rebuild note says.
capabilities.governance: read-only

capabilities.name: Inspect, export, prune and repair the conversation/session store
capabilities.hermes: `hermes sessions` with 21 verbs — list, export (JSONL, --redact), delete, prune, prune --never-active, archive, optimize, clean-markers, optimize-storage, repair, repair-routing, recover, stats, rename, pin/unpin/pinned, retitle-skills, browse (curses picker), import — over a shared filter grammar (--older-than, --source, --max-tool-calls …) (06-cli-f.md, 24 entries cli-f.sessions*).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/routers/sessions.py — only GET /sessions (hardcoded limit=20) and POST /sessions/resume; /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/checkpoint.py (SQLite session/checkpoint store); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/data_export.py and data_purge.py behind POST /api/admin/export and /api/admin/forget (agents/core/routers/backup.py:82,99)
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already owns the store and has GDPR-grade export/forget, which Hermes lacks. What is missing is the operational half: no way to list past 20, no stats, no repair, no rename/pin, no per-session export. On a long-lived house hub the session DB is the thing that grows and corrupts.
capabilities.governance: delete/prune/repair are destructive to owner data — irreversible tier, must QUEUE in the approval path rather than execute on a flag; list/stats/export are read-only

capabilities.name: Read and change configuration without an editor, and validate/migrate it
capabilities.hermes: `hermes config` show / edit / get / set / unset / path / env-path / check (missing or outdated keys) / migrate (write new defaults into an existing file), plus `hermes migrate xai` for a vendor-specific retired-model rewrite (04-cli-d.md, 10 entries cli-d.config*; 01-cli-a.md cli-a.migrate-xai).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/settings_db.py (SQLite settings store seeded from agents.yaml); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/routers/admin.py:73-127 (GET/PUT /api/admin/settings, /reseed); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/env_config.py; /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/config.py; /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/config_preview.py; no `check`, no `migrate`, no CLI
capabilities.rationale: The store and the HTTP CRUD exist; a headless operator cannot use either. `config check` in particular is the thing that turns a silent misconfiguration into a named reason, which is this repo's whole style (see scripts/doctor.py's 'one named reason per check'). The xAI-retirement migrate is vendor-specific and folds into a generic `config migrate`.
capabilities.governance: Writes settings that change action posture (see docs/FLAGS.md — 20 flags, all default-off). A `config set` on a posture key is a privileged effect: it must go through the same admin_guard + kernel path as PUT /api/admin/settings, not write the DB directly.

capabilities.name: First-run setup: pick a model, a runtime, channels and tools without a browser
capabilities.hermes: `hermes setup` — a curses wizard with sections model / tts / terminal / agent / gateway / tools / telemetry, plus --quick (missing items only), --portal, Blank Slate install (minimal toolsets, minimised config), OpenClaw migration offer with a preview + high-impact warnings, a macOS Full Disk Access tip, and a closing Tool Availability table; `hermes setup <section>` re-runs one section (02-cli-b.md, ~40 entries cli-b.setup*).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/install.sh, install.ps1, INSTALL.bat; /home/user/jarvis-hub/scripts/bootstrap.py (stdlib-only, --unlocked/--skip-smoke/--json); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/routers/onboarding.py:358 (GET /api/onboarding/wizard) and :388 (command-center); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/routers/model_setup.py:81-88 (model-plan, model-pull)
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's one-command install plus a web wizard is the better shape for the target user and should stay the default. The gap is the headless case: install.sh ends with 'open http://127.0.0.1:8080/v2', which a server-over-SSH owner cannot do. Add a non-interactive/TTY `nerva setup [section]` that drives the same onboarding service the wizard route drives — not a second config writer.
capabilities.governance: Writes provider credentials and posture flags — same admin path as config set; never write a non-loopback bind (boot_guards.assert_safe_bind refuses one anyway)

capabilities.name: Diagnose a broken install and repair the fixable parts
capabilities.hermes: `hermes doctor` prints ~18 sections (Security Advisories, MCP Server Security, Python Environment, SSL/CA, Required Packages, Configuration Files, Auth Providers, Directory Structure, Gateway Service, s6, Command Installation, External Tools, API Connectivity, Tool Availability, Skills Hub, Memory Provider, Profiles), with `--fix` (auto-repair), `--live` (continuous re-run) and `--ack ADVISORY_ID` (04-cli-d.md, 20 entries cli-d.doctor*).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/scripts/doctor.py — 8 checks (python, venv, locks_in_sync, bind_is_loopback, data_root_writable, runtimes, readyz, smoke), --json, --smoke, exit 0/1; no --fix, no --live, no advisory acknowledgement
capabilities.rationale: The doctor already has the right discipline (one named reason per check, required vs advisory, stdlib-only so it runs in a broken install). It is missing the checks that matter once Nerva is actually configured: credentials/providers, MCP server reachability, channel tokens, kernel/flag posture, audit-chain integrity, desktop-driver host permissions. The gap matrix's own P0 #10 asks for `nerva doctor`, and OWNER_TASKS says none of this has run on real hardware.
capabilities.governance: read-only by default; `--fix` performs repairs (reinstall deps, recreate dirs) — each fix must be a named, reversible-tier action, and anything touching credentials or posture must QUEUE rather than auto-apply

capabilities.name: Produce a pasteable, non-sensitive diagnostic report for a support thread
capabilities.hermes: `hermes dump` prints a fixed-shape ~50-line block (version, OS, model, provider, terminal backend, which API keys are set, feature counts, non-default overrides). `hermes debug share` uploads a debug report to a paste service and prints a URL; `hermes debug delete` removes it (04-cli-d.md cli-d.dump, cli-d.debug, cli-d.debug-share, cli-d.debug-delete).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/support_bundle.py — safety by allow-list rather than redaction: meta, posture, capability readiness roll-ups, per-plugin egress tallies with a local-only proof, audit event counts by type plus hash-chain integrity, route count; exposed at GET /api/support/bundle (agents/core/routers/support.py:21, admin_guard)
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's bundle is strictly better than Hermes' dump: allow-list not redaction, and it carries the audit-chain integrity result, which is the product's own proof. Only the CLI shim is missing. `debug share`'s upload-to-a-paste-service is a deliberate non-copy — see the egress row's reasoning; the bundle is a file the owner attaches themselves.
capabilities.governance: read-only; the upload half would be an external-tier effect and is not being copied

capabilities.name: Back up and restore the whole install
capabilities.hermes: `hermes backup` writes a full zip of the Hermes home; `--quick` takes a state snapshot; `hermes import <zip>` restores it (04-cli-d.md cli-d.backup, cli-d.backup-quick, cli-d.import).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/backup.py; /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/routers/backup.py:33,39,56 (GET/POST /api/admin/backup, POST /api/admin/backup/verify); /home/user/jarvis-hub/scripts/backup-data.sh and backup-data.ps1
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already has this plus a verify step Hermes lacks. Add the CLI verb when the CLI lands; no new mechanism.
capabilities.governance: restore overwrites live state — irreversible tier, must QUEUE; backup and verify are read-only

capabilities.name: Roll back file edits an agent made, from a shadow checkpoint store
capabilities.hermes: `hermes checkpoints` status/list/prune/clear/clear-legacy manages `~/.hermes/checkpoints/` — a shadow git store that backs the `/rollback` slash command, with per-project size breakdown and orphan GC (04-cli-d.md, 6 entries cli-d.checkpoints*).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/checkpoint.py is *execution-state* checkpointing (SQLite agent state for crash recovery, promotion stats) — not a filesystem shadow store; `rg 'rollback'` finds prompt rollback (agents/core/routers/admin.py:358) and skill-marketplace rollback (routers/skills.py:208), but nothing that reverts agent file edits
capabilities.rationale: Nerva now ships desktop drivers, a terminal and file tools; an agent that edits the owner's files with no undo is the one place where 'reversible' stops being true. The approval queue's whole reversible/irreversible split assumes reversible actions can actually be reversed — without a file checkpoint store, a reversible-tier file edit is mislabelled. This is a correctness gap in the governance model, not a convenience.
capabilities.governance: Creating a checkpoint is read-only. Restoring one overwrites the working tree: reversible-tier at most inside a write-safe root, otherwise QUEUE. Prune/clear destroy the only undo record — irreversible tier.
capabilities.depends_on: file/terminal tool call sites to hook the pre-edit snapshot

capabilities.name: Migrate in from another agent (Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, Hermes)
capabilities.hermes: `hermes import-agent claude-code|codex` maps another agent's config, memory and instruction files into Hermes with documented per-source mappings; `hermes claw migrate` / `claw cleanup` does the OpenClaw case (04-cli-d.md cli-d.import-agent + 2 mapping entries; 06-cli-f.md cli-f.claw*).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/scripts/nerva_import.py — `--from hermes|openclaw|claude-code|all`, dry-run by default, `--apply` is the owner's explicit opt-in; skills land quarantined (PENDING_REVIEW, never exec'd until approved), persona files become a preview under data/imports/ and never overwrite SOUL.local.md, MEMORY.md facts are marked tainted and each crosses the kg.write kernel kind through an injected authorizer that only QUEUEs, tokens go to SecretStore masked, injection-flagged lines are denied at the contract
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's importer is the model for how everything else in this cluster should be ported: same capability, but every foreign artefact enters through a kernel kind with taint and a dry run. Hermes' importer just writes the files. Nothing to copy; if anything, extend the source list.
capabilities.governance: kg.write (memory), plus quarantine for skills — already wired; dry-run default

capabilities.name: Update the install itself, safely, with a plan and a rollback
capabilities.hermes: `hermes update` pulls new source, reinstalls deps, re-syncs bundled skills into every profile and restarts running services; `--check`, `--plan`, `--gateway`, `--backup/--no-backup`, `--yes`, `--keep-stash`, `--branch/--switch-branch`, `--force`, an in-progress lock file, per-run update receipts under logs/update_receipts/, and an admission contract that refuses to self-update image/package-managed installs (06-cli-f.md, 13 entries cli-f.update*).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/UPDATE.bat (Windows double-click: git pull, install deps, run tests); /home/user/jarvis-hub/scripts/update_thirdparty.py updates *vendored dependencies*, not the install; /home/user/jarvis-hub/update.json is a vendored-package record; no --check/--plan, no receipt, no lock, no admission contract
capabilities.rationale: A house hub that runs unattended has to be updatable without a human at the keyboard, and updates are the classic way a governed system silently loses its governance (a new default, a re-seeded config). capabilities.name: Source secrets from an external password manager instead of a .env file
capabilities.hermes: `hermes secrets bitwarden` setup / status / token / sync / disable / install (with a region picker) and `hermes secrets onepassword` setup / status / token / set <env_var> <reference> / remove / sync / disable — SecretSource adapters that resolve credentials from the owner's vault at runtime (01-cli-a.md, 17 entries cli-a.secrets*).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none for external managers — /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/vault.py and agents/core/security/secret_broker.py are Nerva's own stores; `rg -i '1password|onepassword'` over agents/, scripts/, frontend/src/ returns nothing outside research docs
capabilities.rationale: Every token an owner pastes into a .env is a credential that now lives in two places and expires in neither. secret_broker.py is already the seam — a Bitwarden/1Password SecretSource is an adapter behind it, not a new subsystem, and it is the cheapest real reduction in what a compromised Nerva install would leak. It also removes the worst step of onboarding for a security-conscious user.
capabilities.governance: Reading a secret is read-only, but *unlocking* the vault is an owner action that must never be automated — the adapter holds a session token with a TTL and refuses to prompt from a scheduled job; resolved secrets stay out of the audit payload (the broker's redact path already exists)

capabilities.name: Keep real credentials outside the sandbox: swap opaque tokens for real keys at the network boundary
capabilities.hermes: `hermes egress` install / setup / start / stop / restart / reload / status / disable / config runs a local TLS-intercepting proxy (iron-proxy) so a sandbox holds only opaque tokens; the proxy exchanges them for real provider credentials at egress, with a documented minted-mapping coverage table and a state-directory layout (01-cli-a.md, 14 entries cli-a.egress*).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/observability/egress_monitor.py (records every outbound attempt, allowed and blocked, per plugin and host); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/llm/egress.py (model-backend traffic under llm:<provider>); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/http_client.py (the choke point, plugin.egress KERNEL kind); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/security/ssrf.py — Nerva *observes and authorizes* egress but the real credential still travels with the caller
capabilities.rationale: This is the one Hermes security idea that is genuinely ahead of Nerva's, and it fits Nerva's thesis better than it fits Hermes'. Nerva is about to run agent work in docker and (per the roadmap) ssh targets; today that means shipping the real API key into the sandbox. Holding the credential at the boundary means a compromised sandbox leaks a revocable opaque token, not the owner's key — the containment story the audit chain is supposed to complete.
capabilities.governance: The proxy is itself a privileged component: minting a token mapping is a credential grant (irreversible tier, QUEUE), and every exchange must be recorded in the existing egress ledger so the local-only proof still counts what left. It must compose with plugin.egress, not replace it.
capabilities.depends_on: the execution-target transports (local/ssh/docker) and the secret broker

capabilities.name: Run several isolated instances of the product on one machine
capabilities.hermes: `hermes profile` list / use / create / delete / describe / show / alias / rename / export / import / install / update / info, each profile an isolated `~/.hermes/profiles/<name>` home selected pre-argparse by `-p`, with generated `~/.local/bin/<alias>` wrapper scripts, a profile.yaml and a distribution.yaml manifest (06-cli-f.md, 17 entries cli-f.profile*; 01-cli-a.md cli-a.opt-profile).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/system_profiles.py is *posture presets* (balanced / gaming / multimedia, JARVIS_SYSTEM_PROFILE) — not isolated homes; /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/data_spaces.py scopes what an agent may read; /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/identity_manifest.py; no per-instance home isolation anywhere
capabilities.rationale: Multiple isolated homes means multiple audit chains, multiple approval queues and multiple kill switches — the owner would lose the single tamper-evident record of what the system did, which is the entire product. Hermes needs profiles because it is a per-developer tool; Nerva is one governed hub per household. Re-open path: the real underlying need (several people, or a work/home split, on one hub) should be met as *identities inside one chain* — identity_manifest.py and data_spaces.py are already the seed — so the audit log stays whole and per-identity scoping does the isolating.
capabilities.governance: would fragment the audit chain and the kill switch — the reason for the skip

capabilities.name: Run a durable multi-worker task board: create work, claim it, track dependencies, review and complete it
capabilities.hermes: `hermes kanban` (50 entries) is a SQLite board with boards create/switch/export/import, task create / list / show / assign / set-model / claim (atomic) / reclaim / reassign / heartbeat / comment / attach / complete / edit / block / schedule / unblock / request-review / request-changes / reopen-review / promote / archive / link / unlink / tail / watch / stats / runs / log / context / assignees / dispatch / gc / repair, plus `swarm` (a task graph), `specify` and `decompose` (triage via an auxiliary LLM) and notify-subscribe. `hermes project` (15 entries) creates named multi-folder workspaces with a primary repo, deterministic branch names and a bound board (03-cli-c.md).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/routers/missions.py (GET/POST /api/missions, start/pause/resume/complete/cancel, steps/{idx}/finish); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/autonomy/ — queue.py, worker.py, work_runs.py, work_judge.py, work_verifier.py, company_planner.py, company_runtime.py, company_supervisor.py, missions.py, escalation.py; /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/routers/swarm.py; /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/subagents.py; no board, no atomic claim, no dependency links, no review verdicts, no worker heartbeat/reclaim
capabilities.rationale: This is the largest single block of the cluster (65 of 714 entries) and it maps directly onto Nerva's 'company mode'. Nerva has missions, a task queue, workers and a judge; what it lacks is the durable coordination layer that makes several workers safe on one goal — atomic claim so two workers cannot take the same task, heartbeat and reclaim so a dead worker's task returns, dependency links, review verdicts, and per-task attempt history. Absorb those semantics into the existing autonomy queue; do NOT port a second store — Nerva must not end up with a kanban.db beside its task queue.
capabilities.governance: Board reads are read-only. Every task the board *dispatches* runs as an autonomy action and keeps its own kind and tier — the board must not become a way for work to reach an executor without the tier it would have had interactively. Task-level decisions already flow through /autonomy/tasks/{id}/decision.
capabilities.depends_on: the autonomy queue and worker (exist); the execution-target transports for real multi-machine work

capabilities.name: Subscribe an external system's events to the agent via a webhook
capabilities.hermes: `hermes webhook` subscribe / list / remove / test (signed test POST), with a direct-delivery mode (`--deliver-only`, no agent turn) and a `--script` filter/transform hook, behind an enablement gate that prints a setup hint (03-cli-c.md, 9 entries cli-c.webhook*).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/routers/webhooks.py (GET/POST /api/webhooks, DELETE /api/webhooks/{id}, POST /api/webhooks/{id} to fire); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/webhooks.py; /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/channels/webhook_channels.py

capabilities.name: Sync the owner's own configuration and skills between their devices
capabilities.hermes: `hermes sync` status / pull / push / now / enable <skill> / disable / device (label this machine) / propose (submit a skill to the organisation) — a content-addressed sync plane for personal skills, plus org mirroring (03-cli-c.md, 9 entries cli-c.sync*).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/e2e_sync.py — H12.13 opt-in end-to-end encrypted device sync using Fernet (AES-128-CBC + HMAC-SHA256), so the transport only ever sees ciphertext and tampering is detected; skills are not yet a synced artefact and there is no CLI
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's sync is privacy-superior by construction — Hermes' plane sees the content, Nerva's sees ciphertext. The gap is coverage: e2e_sync exists but skills and configuration do not ride it, so a second machine is set up by hand. Extend the artefact list; keep the crypto. The org-sharing half is a separate matter and is not being copied — it moves the owner's skills off their devices to a third party, which is the opposite of what the E2E design is for.
capabilities.governance: Ciphertext-only transport is the guarantee; an incoming synced skill must still land quarantined and cross the owner-approval floor on the receiving machine rather than auto-installing because it 'came from me'

capabilities.name: Install the desktop-control driver and grant it the OS permissions it needs
capabilities.hermes: `hermes computer-use` install (fetch/repair the third-party cua-driver binary) / status / doctor, plus `computer-use permissions status` and `permissions grant` for the OS-level accessibility and screen-recording grants (05-cli-e.md, 7 entries cli-e.computer-use*).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/desktop_drivers/ (base.py, linux.py, macos.py, capture.py), desktop_host.py, host_probe.py, desktop_operator.py, desktop_control.py, screen_grounding.py, screen_locator.py, operator_router.py; /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/routers/host_probe.py; /home/user/jarvis-hub/scripts/operator_bench.py — Nerva builds its own governed drivers rather than shelling to a third-party binary, but there is no permission-grant UX
capabilities.rationale: Architecturally Nerva is ahead: no opaque third-party binary, and GovernedDesktop puts mutating steps behind approval. But on macOS the driver silently does nothing until the owner grants Accessibility and Screen Recording in System Settings, and on Wayland until a portal session is consented — and OWNER_TASKS records that none of this has run on real hardware. host_probe already computes the facts; what is missing is the command that says 'here is what is missing and here is exactly where to click'. Without it the flagship capability appears broken on first use.
capabilities.governance: The probe is read-only. Triggering an OS permission prompt is an owner action by design — the CLI reports and links, it must never attempt to grant on the owner's behalf, and it must refuse elevated/UIPI targets with a stable named reason.

capabilities.rationale: The need is real, the mechanism is wrong for Nerva. Hermes needs a hand-maintained allowlist because it has no authorization layer — its own rebuild note admits maintaining both an allow list and a deny list drifts. Building a second allowlist beside the kernel is precisely the 'ported feature that bypasses the kernel' regression. Re-open path: meet the same need by making the CLI's mutating verbs require a scoped capability token, so a restricted operator gets a narrow token instead of a narrow shell.

capabilities.name: Talking to a busy agent: queue / steer / interrupt, `/stop`, and the ack that says what happened
capabilities.hermes: `display.busy_input_mode` picks one of three semantics for a message that arrives mid-turn — redirect the active turn (default), queue it as the next full turn, or steer it into the running turn after the next tool call — with graceful downgrade between them. `/stop` is a hard kill that unlocks the session even if the agent thread is wedged; `/queue` is FIFO; `/steer` appends to the last tool result so role alternation never breaks. A debounced ack tells the user exactly which happened (six distinct strings). Protective demotions: a follow-up cannot interrupt a running subagent or an in-flight compression, near-simultaneous photos batch instead of interrupting once each, and a very fast Telegram follow-up is treated as the same intent. A pending-agent sentinel reserves the slot so a second message cannot spin up a duplicate agent. Every `CommandDef` carries a `busy_policy` of dispatch / reject / interrupt_then_dispatch. ~21 entries incl. gw-core.busy-input-mode / busy-ack / pending-sentinel / subagent-demotion / compression-demotion / photo-burst.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/subagents.py:482,504 has `steer()` / `stop()` — but for spawned children, not for the owner's own live turn. At the channel layer there is nothing: agents/core/orchestrator.py:1109 `channel_handler` binds a session key and calls `handle_input` with no lock, no sentinel and no busy branch, so two Telegram messages from the same chat run two concurrent turns against the same conversation. `rg 'asyncio.Lock|Semaphore' agents/core/orchestrator.py` returns nothing.
capabilities.rationale: Two reasons, and the second is the sharper one. First, an owner who cannot say 'stop' in chat has no brake on the surface they actually use — the HUD's estop route (agents/core/routers/ops.py:237) needs a browser. Second, the absence is not merely a missing feature: concurrent turns on one session key with no lease can interleave writes into the same transcript, which is a correctness bug in a product whose audit log is the differentiator. Take the three semantics and the demotions; the ack strings are cheap and prevent the 'did it hear me' failure mode.
capabilities.governance: `/stop` and interrupt are privileged control over a running agent, not read-only. Route them through the same origin binding as other operator actions (agents/core/action_origin.py) and record them in the audit chain; stopping a run must be recorded exactly like starting one.
