capabilities.name: Pluggable platform adapter contract (one descriptor per channel, one base class that owns the conversation runtime)
capabilities.hermes: `PlatformEntry` (gateway/platform_registry.py:63-230) is a ~25-field descriptor: adapter_factory, PASSIVE `check_fn` vs ACTIVE `ensure_deps_fn` (the split that fixed a desktop boot-loop and a Teams deadlock), is_connected, validate_config, allowed_users_env/allow_all_env, max_message_length, pii_safe, emoji, platform_hint, cron_deliver_env_var, standalone_sender_fn, parse_target_ref_fn/validate_target_ref_fn, send_message_handler, env_enablement_fn, apply_yaml_config_fn. `BasePlatformAdapter` (gateway/platforms/base.py:3031) owns session locking, interrupt/queue/debounce, typing heartbeats, media caching, `_send_with_retry`, and approval/clarify/picker rendering — the subclass supplies transport only. `MessageEvent` (base.py:2424) normalizes every inbound message; `SendResult` + `SEND_ERROR_KINDS` {too_long,bad_format,forbidden,not_found,rate_limited,transient,unknown} (base.py:2593-2744) give one failure vocabulary. platforms-b.contract-* (8 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/channels/base.py:12-33 (33-line ABC: start/stop/send/receive, `send` returns bool); agents/core/channels/manager.py:29-30 (`_SUPPORTED_SEND_CHANNELS`/`_SUPPORTED_REPLY_CHANNELS` hardcoded frozensets); agents/core/channels/gateway.py:41-116; agents/core/channels/session.py (SessionSource/DeliveryRouter is the one Hermes-shaped piece that exists)
capabilities.rationale: Nerva has a contract, but it is a four-method ABC with no capability information at all. Every fact Hermes puts in the descriptor — can this channel edit a message, what is its length cap, is it PII-safe, where does cron deliver, who is allowed — lives in Nerva as either a hardcoded frozenset or nowhere. Every other row in this ledger blocks on this: you cannot add media, streaming, chunking or gating per-channel until each channel can declare what it supports. Adapt rather than copy: the descriptor must additionally name the kernel action kind each adapter's outbound path emits, so the frozensets in manager.py become derived data instead of the security boundary.
capabilities.governance: Privileged: outbound send. Today `ChannelManager.send`/`send_channel_reply` are the seam and they gate on hardcoded channel names; the descriptor must carry the kernel kind (`channel.reply`, and new kinds for media) so a newly registered adapter cannot be reachable without declaring one.

capabilities.name: Add a new messenger without touching core code (platform plugin packages)
capabilities.hermes: `plugins/platforms/<name>/{plugin.yaml,__init__.py,adapter.py}`; a manifest with `kind: platform` plus `register(ctx)` is all it takes — "This requires zero changes to core Hermes code" (gateway/platforms/ADDING_A_PLATFORM.md:5-12). Discovery registers a *deferred loader* (platform_registry.py:255-268) because eagerly importing ~20 adapters' SDKs (lark_oapi, discord.py, slack_bolt…) added seconds to every CLI invocation. Manifests declare `requires_env`/`optional_env` with prompts, urls and `password: true`, plus `provides_tools`. Registrations are scoped per HERMES_HOME so profiles don't share them. platforms-b.contract-layout, contract-register-platform, platforms-a.discord-manifest-env, platform-telegram.plugin-manifest, .lazy-deps (~6 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/web.py:371-430 — every channel is an inline `if os.environ.get("X_TOKEN")` block in the lifespan; agents/core/channels/webhook_channels.py:262-268 (`_REGISTRY` hardcoded dict) is the only data-driven path, driven by `JARVIS_WEBHOOK_CHANNELS` (docs/FLAGS.md:84-111); agents/core/plugin_manager.py exists but manages tool plugins, not channels
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already proved the data-driven shape once with `channels_from_config`; it just stops at five hardcoded classes and every other channel is soldered into web.py's startup. Making channel registration manifest-driven is what lets the owner (or a design partner) add the one messenger they actually use without a core PR — and it is the only way the 'copy' decisions below stay affordable. Adapt: the manifest must declare the kernel kinds and ship default-off behind a flag, so a third-party manifest can never widen the action surface by itself.
capabilities.governance: Privileged: registration itself. A manifest that could register an adapter without naming its kernel kinds would be a way to smuggle an ungoverned egress path; manifest load must fail closed on an undeclared or unknown kind.

capabilities.name: Telegram as a full-fidelity surface (rich text, media, threads, buttons, resilience)
capabilities.hermes: An 11,296-line adapter (plugins/platforms/telegram/adapter.py) covering MarkdownV2 conversion with table normalization, 4096-char chunking, streaming edits, native drafts (`sendMessageDraft`) and Bot API 10.1 Rich Messages, albums, voice bubbles, stickers-with-vision, forum topics, inline keyboards, an inline command picker (`@botname <query>`), a command menu via `setMyCommands`, and roughly 30 entries of connection self-healing. Registered with `max_message_length=4096`, `emoji="✈️"`, `cron_deliver_env_var="TELEGRAM_HOME_CHANNEL"` (platform-telegram.register). 182 raw entries.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/channels/telegram.py (203 lines): long-poll `getUpdates`, text-only inbound (`if not text: continue`, :113), `sendMessage` with `parse_mode: "Markdown"` on raw model output (:57), `send_card` + `answerCallbackQuery` for decision cards, `sendChatAction` typing, `_maybe_pair_deeplink`. Media helpers exist but on a different object that never reaches ChannelManager: agents/core/plugins/telegram_bot.py:57-92 (send_photo/send_document).
capabilities.rationale: Telegram is Nerva's owner-facing channel — the decision inbox lives there (agents/core/autonomy_coordinator.py:103) and the gap matrix' P0 item 11 is 'pair in 60 seconds' on Telegram. It is therefore the one platform where being at ~2% of Hermes' depth is a product problem rather than a breadth problem. Two defects are live today: raw model text is posted with `parse_mode: "Markdown"`, so any unbalanced `*` or `_` returns 400 and the reply is silently lost; and there is no chunking, so any answer over 4096 characters fails outright. Those are not polish, they are the reply path not working.
capabilities.governance: Privileged: every outbound Telegram write. The existing `channel.reply` kernel kind covers text; media and edits need to extend that kind rather than reach Bot API directly the way telegram_bot.py does today.
capabilities.depends_on: adapter descriptor; per-platform rendering row; media rows

capabilities.name: Discord as a governed channel (server chat, threads, slash commands, roles)
capabilities.hermes: Full adapter with native slash commands including `/skill` with autocomplete, admin-vs-user command tiers and an unauthorized-slash admin alert, auto-threading and `/thread`, role-based access control, per-channel prompts and channel→skill bindings, forum channels, history and missed-message backfill, a gateway-WebSocket liveness watchdog, processing reactions 👀/✅/❌, exec-approval and clarify buttons, plus agent-facing `discord` and `discord_admin` tools. platforms-a.discord-* (42 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/channels/discord.py (78 lines): `on_message` calls `self.handler(message.content, channel="discord")` with **no `sender`** — so the H12.19 pairing gate in agents/core/channels/gateway.py:70-96 is skipped entirely for Discord — and replies go out via `await message.channel.send(response)` (:50), bypassing `ChannelManager.send` and its `channel.send` contract. `SUPPORTED_INBOX_CHANNELS` (agents/core/channel_inbox.py:20) excludes discord, so nothing it receives is ever recorded.
capabilities.rationale: This is the clearest governance regression in the cluster and it is Nerva's own code, not a Hermes port. Discord is wired to the governed gateway but passes no sender identity, so the pairing gate Nerva built specifically to hold unknown senders is a no-op there; and its reply path routes around the contract layer that manager.py exists to enforce. Fixing the wiring is a day's work and it has to happen before any Discord feature is worth adding. Only then does the Hermes feature set (mention gating, threads, reactions) become a sensible copy.
capabilities.governance: Privileged: outbound send, currently ungoverned. Must be routed through `ChannelManager.send` → `channel.reply`; inbound must thread `sender` so the pairing gate and the taint marking in gateway.py:159-166 both apply.
capabilities.depends_on: nothing (the wiring fix); adapter descriptor for the feature work

capabilities.name: Slack as a two-way channel (Socket Mode inbound, threads, workspace install)
capabilities.hermes: Socket Mode connection with a watchdog and connect-time diagnostics, app-manifest generation (`hermes slack manifest`), documented OAuth scopes and event subscriptions, native slash commands plus a `!command` bang prefix inside threads, ephemeral replies, thread/reply behaviour with watermark rehydration, six composable mention/trigger options, reaction triggers, `group_sessions_per_user` isolation, multi-workspace support, file upload/download, and interactive-click authorization. platforms-a.slack-* (46 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/channels/slack.py (65 lines) is **send-only**: `chat_postMessage` in an executor. `receive_event` is defined at :62 and has **zero callers** — `grep -rn receive_event` across the repo returns only its own definition. No Socket Mode, no Events API endpoint, no signature verification.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva ships a Slack channel that cannot hear anything. That is a truthfulness problem as much as a feature gap — `orch.channels` reports 'slack' as a live channel and the startup log says 'Slack channel wired'. Either give it a real inbound path (Socket Mode is ~150 lines with slack_bolt and needs no public URL, which suits a local-first hub) or stop registering it. Inbound is the whole capability; the Slack-native AI surfaces are a separate, skippable row below.
capabilities.governance: Privileged: outbound send (today bypasses nothing only because nothing triggers it). Inbound must thread `sender` (Slack user id) and `channel` through gateway.route so pairing + rate limit + injection detection apply.

capabilities.name: WhatsApp reach without account-ban risk
capabilities.hermes: A Baileys Node bridge (unofficial WhatsApp Web protocol) with QR pairing, session persistence, bridge supervision, LID↔phone allowlist matching, broadcast/status suppression, native polls, clarify-as-poll, location pins, read receipts and owner-message forwarding. platforms-a.whatsapp-* (28 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/channels/webhook_channels.py:127-155 — `WhatsAppChannel` uses the **official** Meta Graph Cloud API (`graph.facebook.com/v20.0/{phone_id}/messages`), inbound parsed from the webhook envelope with `sender` threaded so the pairing gate applies. Documented as a deliberate choice in docs/research/2026-09-06-hermes-and-field-gap-matrix.md:96 ('WhatsApp only via official Cloud API') and docs/FLAGS.md:84-111.
capabilities.rationale: Hermes' WhatsApp is richer and structurally riskier: the Baileys path is what got OpenClaw users' personal accounts banned (issue #4376, cited in the gap matrix). Nerva already made the right call and wrote down why. Keep the Cloud API path; the parts worth taking from the Hermes adapter are protocol-neutral and land in other rows (inbound media, dedup, batching). The one WhatsApp-specific idea worth stealing is clarify-as-poll — a native poll is a better approval widget than a text prompt — and that belongs in the in-chat approvals row.
capabilities.governance: Read-only for this decision; the existing outbound path already goes through the egress-gated PluginHTTPClient (webhook_channels.py:113) and the opt-in send rate limiter.

capabilities.name: Email as a conversational channel (authenticated senders, threading, attachments)
capabilities.hermes: IMAP polling with seen-UID tracking, **sender authentication via SPF/DKIM/DMARC**, automated-sender suppression (no-reply/bounce loops), allowlist access control, HTML stripping and body extraction, inbound attachment ingestion, RFC-correct reply threading (In-Reply-To/References), SMTP with IPv4 fallback, outbound attachments. platforms-a.email-* (14 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/channels/email.py (127 lines): IMAP `search(None, "UNSEEN")` poll every 60 s, text/plain body only, SMTP `MIMEText` send. No SPF/DKIM/DMARC check, no automated-sender suppression, no threading headers, no attachments. Nerva *is* ahead on governance: email is deliberately excluded from generic direct send (agents/core/channels/manager.py:26-30) and may only reach SMTP through the governed `channel.reply` executor.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's email governance posture is better than Hermes' and must be kept; what is missing is the part that makes inbound email safe to *act on*. Right now any sender who knows the address produces a tainted message in the inbox with no way to tell a forged From from a real one, and no automated-sender suppression means a single vacation autoresponder can loop. SPF/DKIM/DMARC verification is the highest-value single import in this row: it turns 'untrusted inbound' into 'untrusted inbound with a verified origin', which is exactly the signal the approval queue should be showing the owner on the card.
capabilities.governance: Privileged: SMTP send, already correctly behind `channel.reply` (agents/core/channel_reply.py). Sender-auth results should be attached to the inbound metadata alongside the existing taint marking so the decision card can display them.

capabilities.name: Governed webhook-class channels (Signal, Matrix, Teams, Google Chat) as real adapters
capabilities.hermes: Four full adapters: Matrix with E2EE modes, cross-signing, auto-join, room allowlists, `m.replace` edits, MSC3245 voice, bridge-loop protection and diagnostics; Teams with Adaptive Card approvals, Bot Framework token attachment download, and a service-URL allowlist + conversation-ID validation; Google Chat with Pub/Sub-pull and HTTP inbound, Card v2 clarify cards, per-user OAuth for native attachments, an attachment-download SSRF guard, retry/rate-limit handling and log redaction; Signal appears only via the WhatsApp-family bridges. platforms-a.matrix-*/teams-*/google-chat-* (~70 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/channels/webhook_channels.py:158-260 — each is a ~15-line `build_send`/`parse_inbound` pair (SignalChannel :158, MatrixChannel :183, TeamsChannel :213, GoogleChatChannel :240). Real strengths: dynamic egress-host registration (`_DYNAMIC_HOST_CONFIG_KEYS` → `register_dynamic_domain`, :40-46), sender threaded to the pairing gate, opt-in outbound rate limit. Inbound arrives at agents/core/routers/integrations.py:216-233, whose own docstring admits '(Provider signature verification is the host seam)'.
capabilities.rationale: The shape here is right and Nerva's version is genuinely better governed than a raw adapter — but four channels that can only send and receive plain text are not yet channels people would use. The specific gaps worth closing are the security ones, not the feature ones: Teams' service-URL allowlist and conversation-ID validation, and Google Chat's attachment-download SSRF guard, are both defences against a webhook endpoint being used as a confused deputy, and Nerva's endpoint is open to any authenticated caller today. Media in/out is the second tier. Matrix E2EE is deliberately excluded — see the separate row.
capabilities.governance: Privileged: outbound send (governed) and inbound ingestion (currently unauthenticated). Signature verification belongs in front of `/api/channels/{id}/inbound`, not inside each adapter.

capabilities.name: SMS as a channel (Twilio REST out, signed webhook in)
capabilities.hermes: `SmsAdapter` posts From/To/Body to the Twilio REST API and receives via a signed webhook with the full documented HMAC-SHA1 signature algorithm including a port-variant retry (`_validate_twilio_signature`, adapter.py:242-276), empty-TwiML responses, a 65,536-byte body cap enforced twice, echo-drop when From == TWILIO_PHONE_NUMBER, `redact_phone` in every log, `pii_safe=True`, `max_message_length=1600`, per-number multi-tenant sessions. Also: a reproducible defect — adapter.py never imports `re`, so `_strip_markdown_for_sms` (the only markdown path used by the cron/standalone sender) raises `NameError`, verified live. platforms-b.sms-* (4 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none as a channel. The only Twilio surface is agents/core/autonomy/call_broker.py:44-151 — *voice calls*, host-side seam, `_ALLOWED_HOSTS = {api.twilio.com, api.telnyx.com}`, already kernel-governed via `call.outbound`.
capabilities.rationale: SMS is the one channel that works when nothing else does — no app, no data, no account, and it reaches a phone that is on. For a house brain whose whole point is being reachable when something happens, that is a real capability rather than breadth for its own sake. The port is small and half-built already: call_broker.py has the Twilio credential resolution, host allowlist and kernel wiring; SMS adds a REST verb and a signed inbound webhook. Port the signature validation faithfully — including the port-variant retry — and do not reproduce the missing `import re`; use one shared plain-text renderer (see the rendering row) instead of a ninth private markdown stripper.
capabilities.governance: Privileged: outbound SMS costs money and reaches a third party. Must cross the kernel — reuse `call.outbound`'s tier or add a sibling kind; irreversible-tier, so it lands in the approval queue rather than auto-sending.

capabilities.name: Push notification to a phone without a bot or an account (ntfy)
capabilities.hermes: `NtfyAdapter` (plugins/platforms/ntfy/adapter.py:176) subscribes to a topic over a persistent HTTP stream (`/json?poll=false`, 90 s read timeout for ntfy's 55 s keepalive) and publishes replies with one POST; reconnect backoff [2,5,10,30,60] reset after 60 s of health; dedup by message id over a 300 s window; echo suppression via an `X-Tags: hermes-agent` header; explicit identity model — 'the topic name IS the user', and the publisher-controlled `title` is deliberately never used for authorization because 'it would let any publisher who knows the topic spoof an allowed user'. Self-hostable. platforms-b.ntfy-* (9 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — `grep -rni "ntfy|apns|fcm|push_notification" agents/` returns nothing
capabilities.rationale: This is the cheapest possible path from 'Nerva wants to tell you something' to a buzz on your phone: httpx only, no SDK, no daemon, no bot token, self-hostable so nothing leaves the LAN if the owner runs their own server. It fits the local-first thesis better than any other channel in this cluster, and it is the natural transport for approval prompts when the owner is away from the dashboard. Copy the identity discipline verbatim — topic-as-identity, never trust the publisher-supplied title — because a naive port would make the allowlist spoofable.
capabilities.governance: Privileged: outbound publish is egress to a (possibly third-party) server — route through `channel.reply` and the existing PluginHTTPClient egress gate. Inbound is untrusted: topic-as-identity means the pairing gate's sender is the topic, so the allowlist gates the whole channel.

capabilities.name: Connection self-healing (stay connected without an operator watching)
capabilities.hermes: Roughly thirty entries of hard-won resilience on Telegram alone: `deleteWebhook` before polling, polling generations with a progress verifier, a polling heartbeat that detects CLOSE-WAIT sockets, a pending-update probe for a wedged consumer, a stall watchdog, a 409-Conflict recovery ladder, a network-error reconnect ladder, connection-pool drains, transport error classifiers, fatal-error surfacing with retryable/non-retryable codes, graceful disconnect, a held-inbound queue that redispatches after reconnect, send-time reconnect wait with adapter replacement, and a wall-clock deadline helper. Discord adds a gateway-WebSocket liveness watchdog; Slack a Socket Mode watchdog; Mattermost a WS reconnect loop; ntfy a backoff ladder reset on health; Photon a presence watchdog. (~35 entries)
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/channels/telegram.py:180-199 — the entire recovery strategy is `except Exception: logger.warning(...); await asyncio.sleep(3)` in the poll loop. `grep -rn "backoff|jitter|reconnect|watchdog" agents/core/channels/` returns one *comment*, at telegram.py:196. Discord/Slack/webhook channels have none.
capabilities.rationale: A house brain that stops answering at 3am and does not notice is worse than one that was never installed, and this is the single area where Hermes' advantage is pure accumulated operational scar tissue rather than feature breadth. Nerva's flat 3-second retry cannot distinguish a transient network blip from a 409 (another process stole the bot token) or from a wedged consumer that is polling happily and delivering nothing — the second and third states look identical to a healthy loop from the outside. Copy the classifier + ladder + heartbeat trio; the exotic parts (fallback IPs) are excluded in their own row.
capabilities.governance: Read-only — this is transport health, no privileged effect. But fatal-error state should surface on the existing status/heartbeat surface so a dead channel is visible rather than silent.
capabilities.depends_on: adapter descriptor (fatal-error state and health belong on the descriptor)

capabilities.name: Alternative inbound transports and network placement (webhook mode, proxy, custom API host)
capabilities.hermes: Telegram supports webhook mode as an alternative to long polling with a documented comparison table, a custom Bot API base URL for a self-hosted telegram-bot-api server, `local_mode` to read Telegram files straight off disk (bypassing download), HTTP client pool/timeout tuning, TCP keepalive, and a Telegram-specific proxy. Matrix, Discord and Feishu each carry their own proxy support; Feishu has a full webhook mode with signature, rate limit and anomaly tracking. platform-telegram.webhook-mode/.base-url/.local-mode/.http-tuning/.proxy/.tcp-keepalive, platforms-a.discord-proxy/.matrix-proxy, platforms-b.feishu-webhook (~10 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: Webhook-style inbound exists but only for the five webhook_channels via agents/core/routers/integrations.py:216; Telegram is long-poll only (agents/core/channels/telegram.py:100). No proxy support and no custom API base anywhere in agents/core/channels/. Egress does go through agents/core/http_client.py (PluginHTTPClient) which is the natural place to hang proxy config.
capabilities.rationale: Two concrete product reasons, not completeness: a self-hosted telegram-bot-api server plus `local_mode` means inbound media never round-trips through Telegram's servers and lands as a local file path — that is the local-first thesis applied to the channel layer, and it is also the cheapest way to get large-file media working. Webhook mode matters for the always-on-box deployment the roadmap describes (gap matrix item 39), where a long-poll loop per channel is the wrong shape. Proxy support is a small config surface on an HTTP client Nerva already centralizes.
capabilities.governance: Read-only (transport config), but a custom API base URL is an egress-host change — it must register with the existing `plugin_gate.register_dynamic_domain` path the webhook channels already use (webhook_channels.py:40-46), not bypass it.

capabilities.name: DNS-over-HTTPS fallback-IP transport (reach the platform through a hostile network)
capabilities.hermes: `platform-telegram.fallback-ips` — direct-IP failover with DoH discovery when the platform's hostname is blocked or poisoned, one of the headline features in the plugin manifest's own description.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none
capabilities.rationale: This solves censorship circumvention, which is a different product from a governed house brain. It is also actively at odds with two Nerva invariants: the egress gate works on hostnames (agents/core/plugin_gate.py, webhook_channels.py:40-46), and connecting to a bare IP with a spoofed SNI is precisely the pattern that gate exists to refuse. Shipping it would mean building an exception to the egress allowlist for a scenario the owner is not in. Re-open if Nerva ever targets a market where the messenger host is blocked at the network level, and then as an explicit, separately-flagged transport that still registers its IPs with the egress gate.
capabilities.governance: Would be an egress-gate escape — the reason to refuse it.

capabilities.name: Per-platform outbound rendering (each channel gets text it can actually display)
capabilities.hermes: One renderer per dialect: Telegram MarkdownV2 with escaping and markdown-table normalization plus 4096-char chunking (platform-telegram.format-message/.tables/.send); Slack mrkdwn with table alignment; Matrix markdown→HTML with a sanitizer; WhatsApp markdown mapping and outbound sanitization; Mattermost formatting; LINE `strip_markdown_preserving_urls` + a bubble splitter; IRC/SMS/ntfy plain-text strippers. `max_message_length` on the descriptor drives smart chunking centrally; `SendResult.error_kind == "bad_format"` tells the gateway a plain-text retry is the fix. The inventory's own rebuild note: 'a better version would share one markdown stripper across every plain-text platform (IRC, SMS, ntfy all reimplement it)'. (~14 entries)
capabilities.nerva_evidence: `grep -rn "MarkdownV2|escape_markdown|mrkdwn|strip_markdown" agents/` returns nothing; `grep -rn "4096|chunk|truncate" agents/core/channels/ agents/core/channel_reply.py` returns nothing. agents/core/channels/telegram.py:57 posts raw model output with `parse_mode: "Markdown"`. The only cap anywhere is `_TEXT_CAP = 4_000` in agents/core/channel_reply.py:26, which truncates rather than splits and only covers the governed-reply path.
capabilities.rationale: This is where the Telegram channel is broken today rather than merely thin: a model reply containing an odd number of `*` or an unclosed code fence returns HTTP 400 from Telegram and `send()` returns False, so the owner sees nothing and the failure is a log line. A reply over 4096 characters fails the same way. Copy the mechanism but fix the flaw Hermes documented against itself — build one renderer registry keyed by dialect (markdownv2 / mrkdwn / html / plain) with one shared plain-text stripper, rather than nine private copies, and drive chunking from the descriptor's `max_message_length`.
capabilities.governance: Read-only transformation, but it sits inside the governed send path — the rendered form, not the raw form, is what should be hashed into the audit entry so the log matches what the user saw.

capabilities.name: Live/streaming replies in chat
capabilities.hermes: Three generations of it: edit-based streaming with saturated-preview dedup and oversized-edit splitting into continuation messages (platform-telegram.edit-message/.overflow-dedup/.overflow-split), native drafts (`sendMessageDraft`, Rich draft frames), and platform-native streaming APIs — Slack `chat.startStream`/`appendStream`/`stopStream` where the streamed message *is* the final message, with a one-shot capability latch and fallback to edit-based (platforms-a.slack-native-streaming); WeCom `msgtype: stream`; DingTalk AI Cards. Slack also renders live tool progress as native plan/task cards keyed by (team, channel, thread_ts) with per-tool rows. (~10 entries)
capabilities.nerva_evidence: No `editMessageText` anywhere (`grep -rn "editMessageText|edit_message" agents/` returns nothing). Nerva streams only on the web surface (frontend/src/api/live.ts). Chat channels get one final message.
capabilities.rationale: On a chat surface, a long silence and a crash look the same. Streaming edits are the difference between 'is it working?' and watching it work, and Nerva already has the token stream on the web path — this is plumbing it to a second consumer, not building it. Take only the edit-based tier: it works on Telegram, Discord, Slack, Matrix and Mattermost with one mechanism, and the platform-native tiers (Slack's stream API, DingTalk cards) are per-vendor bets that the capability descriptor can carry later.
capabilities.governance: Privileged: each edit is an outbound write. An edit stream must be one `channel.reply` decision, not one per frame — otherwise streaming would flood the approval queue and the audit chain. That is a real design constraint the port has to respect.

capabilities.name: Working-state feedback (typing, status lines, lifecycle reactions, read receipts)
capabilities.hermes: Typing indicator with per-chat cooldown and a typing heartbeat that survives long turns (platform-telegram.typing); status bubbles edited in place (`send_or_update_status`); message reactions as processing feedback — Telegram reactions, Discord 👀/✅/❌, Slack `:eyes:`/`:white_check_mark:` plus reaction *triggers* (react to a message to make the agent act on it), Matrix lifecycle reactions, Feishu Typing/CrossMark, DingTalk 🤔Thinking→🥳Done; Google Chat's 'Hermes is thinking…' marker; Slack's `typing_status_text` and per-tool `display.live_status`; WhatsApp read receipts and typing; Matrix presence/typing/read receipts; Photon tapbacks. (~16 entries)
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/channels/telegram.py:88-96 (`send_action`, typing) — that is the whole of it. No reactions, no status bubbles, no read receipts: `grep -rni "reaction" agents/core/channels/` returns nothing.
capabilities.rationale: Cheap, and disproportionately effective at making an agent feel alive rather than broken — but the one to prioritise is reactions-as-lifecycle, because on a governed system 👀→✅/❌ carries real information: seen, approved-and-done, refused. That maps directly onto Nerva's kernel outcomes and gives the owner a per-message record of what governance decided, without a second message. Reaction *triggers* (Slack) are the more interesting half: reacting to a message as a way to ask the agent to act on it is an approval gesture that costs one tap.
capabilities.governance: A reaction is an outbound write, but at read-only risk — it conveys state, it does not act. A reaction *trigger* is inbound and must go through the full gateway (sender, pairing, taint), not a shortcut path.

capabilities.name: In-chat approvals and interactive controls (approve, clarify, pick — from the phone)
capabilities.hermes: A full interactive layer per platform: exec-approval prompts with `✅ Allow Once / ✅ Session / ✅ Always / ❌ Deny` and tap handling with per-user authorization (`_is_callback_user_authorized`), slash-command confirmation, clarify prompts with numbered buttons and an `✏️ Other` free-text capture plus an expired-clarify notice, an interactive model picker with provider folding, pagination and an expensive-model confirmation, a generic choice picker, and Gmail-triage action buttons. Rendered natively per platform: Telegram inline keyboards, Discord buttons with approval mentions, Slack Block Kit buttons, Teams Adaptive Cards, Feishu approval cards, Matrix **reaction-based** approval/model/choice pickers, WhatsApp clarify-as-poll, Google Chat Card v2, LINE postback buttons. (~30 entries)
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/inbox.py:31-75 — `build_decision_card` renders four buttons (✅ Aprob / ✏️ Editez / ❌ Resping / 🕓 Amân) with a risk tier, rationale, expected result, **injection-taint warning** and a dry-run preview; agents/core/channels/telegram.py:167-186 parses the tap; agents/core/autonomy_coordinator.py:103-144 wires it to the queue. Telegram only — no other channel can approve anything. Authorization was a real hole: tests/test_sec_b3_telegram_owner_binding.py documents that `allowed_users` was empty so both guards were unreachable no-ops.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva is *ahead* here on the thing that matters and behind on everything around it. The Hermes buttons are a UI over an in-memory prompt; Nerva's card is a view onto a durable kernel-governed queue with a risk tier, a dry-run preview, an injection warning and a hash-chained audit entry — that is the product. What is missing is reach and vocabulary: only one channel can approve, there is no clarify/free-text-capture path, no 'always allow' scope that writes a real permission grant, and no fallback rendering for channels without buttons. Copy the *interaction vocabulary* (once/session/always/deny, numbered clarify with an Other escape, expiry notice) and the per-platform renderers; never copy the approval mechanism — it must stay the kernel queue. The Matrix reaction-picker and WhatsApp clarify-as-poll are the templates for channels with no button primitive.
capabilities.governance: This IS the governance surface. Every tap must resolve against the approval queue and the audit chain, and every renderer must verify the tapping identity against the owner binding (the SEC-B3 lesson). 'Always Allow' must mint a real entry in the permission ledger (`permission.grant`, a KERNEL kind), never a per-adapter cache.
capabilities.depends_on: adapter descriptor; per-platform button/reaction capability flags

capabilities.name: Sending media out (photos, albums, documents, video, voice notes, GIFs)
capabilities.hermes: A full outbound media surface per platform with fallbacks: `send_multiple_images` as native albums, `send_image_file` with document fallback, `send_document`, `send_video`, `send_image` from URL with upload fallback, `send_animation` for inline GIFs, `send_voice` as a native voice bubble with a duration probe, flood-control inline wait cap, a missing-media-path error with a Docker hint, and an inline `MEDIA:` tag protocol with a supported-extension list. Mattermost batches 5 images per post; LINE serves media from a tokenized endpoint; Discord/Slack upload files. (~20 entries)
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/plugins/telegram_bot.py:57-92 has `send_photo`/`send_document` — but on a *plugin* object, not the channel adapter, so it never passes `ChannelManager.send`, the `channel.send` contract, or `channel.reply`. The `ChannelAdapter` ABC (agents/core/channels/base.py:26) declares only `send(message: str)`. No album, video, voice or animation path anywhere.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva has media producers with nowhere to send them — the media director pillar, camera feeds (agents/core/house/camera_feed.py), report exports — and a chat layer that can only emit strings. 'Send me the snapshot from the front camera' is exactly the house-brain interaction the product is for, and it currently cannot be answered in the channel the owner is in. The important half of this is not the API calls, it is that the existing media helper bypasses the governed path entirely; consolidating onto one governed media send is the actual work.
capabilities.governance: Privileged and higher-risk than text: sending an image can exfiltrate a camera frame or a document. Needs its own kernel kind (a `channel.media` sibling to `channel.reply`) rather than riding the text kind, because the reviewer needs to see *what file* is leaving, and the existing `media.present` kind is about presentation, not egress.

capabilities.name: Receiving media in (photos, voice notes, documents, stickers, locations)
capabilities.hermes: Inbound handler covering photos, voice, audio, video and documents, cached into `~/.hermes/cache/{images,audio,video,documents}` as local paths the vision tools can open; photo-burst batching and media-group (album) debounce; sticker understanding via vision with a cache; location and venue pins; observed-group and replied-to media caching; a size guard and limits; download-failure surfacing; WhatsApp document-text injection; Discord arbitrary-attachment ingestion; Teams Bot-Framework-token attachment download; Google Chat per-user OAuth attachments with an SSRF guard; email attachment ingestion. (~20 entries)
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/channels/telegram.py:113 — `text = msg.get("text", ""); ... if not text: continue`. A photo, a voice note or a PDF sent to Nerva on Telegram is discarded silently. The webhook channels parse only `text` (webhook_channels.py:147, :172, :198). Nerva *has* the consumers: agents/core/routers/multimodal.py (VLM describe), the vision/OCR path, document ingestion.
capabilities.rationale: The most common thing a person does with a phone assistant is send it a photo of something and ask about it. Nerva has a VLM, an OCR path and a document pipeline, and the channel layer throws the input away before any of them see it — the capability exists and is unreachable. Copy the local-cache-then-hand-the-path pattern verbatim; it is exactly right for a local-first system and it is what lets the existing tools work unchanged. Voice-note→STT is the highest-value single case and is covered in its own row.
capabilities.governance: Inbound media is untrusted input and a bigger injection surface than text (a document's contents, an image's rendered text). It must carry the same taint marking the gateway already applies (agents/core/channels/gateway.py:159-166) and the size guard must be enforced before download, not after.

capabilities.name: Voice notes both ways on chat channels (speak to it, hear it back)
capabilities.hermes: Incoming voice → STT automatically on Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp and Matrix (native MSC3245 voice); outgoing TTS as a native voice bubble (Opus/OGG) with a duration probe; streaming TTS hooks on the base adapter; a per-platform auto-TTS set driven by `voice.auto_tts`. platform-telegram.stt-incoming/.tts-outgoing/.send-voice, platforms-a.discord-voice-messages/.slack-voice/.whatsapp-voice/.matrix-voice (~9 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: Nerva has the full voice stack — agents/core/channels/voice.py (VoiceChannel wrapping VoicePipeline: wake word → STT → TTS) and agents/core/voice/pipeline.py — but it is a **separate channel** bound to the local microphone. Nothing connects it to a chat channel: no `sendVoice` and no voice-note ingestion (`grep -rn "sendVoice|voice_note|sendAudio" agents/` returns nothing).
capabilities.rationale: This is the highest ratio of value to work in the whole cluster, because both halves already exist and have never been introduced to each other. Nerva's STT and TTS run locally with no API keys — which is a stronger position than Hermes on the *quality* axis — and the only missing piece is the adapter downloading an OGG and handing it to the pipeline, then handing a rendered OGG back. Sending a voice note while walking is how people actually use a phone assistant, and it is the interaction that makes the local-voice investment visible outside the house.
capabilities.governance: Outbound voice is a `channel.media`-class effect (see the media row). Inbound transcription is untrusted input — the transcript must inherit the inbound taint, which the decision card already knows how to display (agents/core/autonomy/inbox.py:56-60).

capabilities.name: Discord voice-channel presence (join a VC, listen, speak, ambient audio bed)
capabilities.hermes: The bot joins a Discord voice channel, listens and speaks, with audio effects — an ambient bed and verbal acknowledgements. platforms-a.discord-voice-channel/.discord-voice-fx (2 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none
capabilities.rationale: A live agent sitting in a Discord voice channel is a community/streaming product, not a house brain — the room it should be listening in is the owner's, and Nerva already does that natively through the local voice pipeline and the ambient runtime. Adding it would also put a continuous audio capture path behind a remote server's session, which cuts against the local-first privacy posture harder than any other item in this cluster. Re-open only if Nerva ever targets team/community deployments, and then as an explicit, separately-consented capture surface.
capabilities.governance: Would be a continuous remote audio-capture path — the reason to refuse it, not a detail.

capabilities.name: Inbound gating: who may talk to the agent, and when it should answer
capabilities.hermes: The deepest-layered part of the cluster. Per-platform allowlists (`*_ALLOWED_USERS` / `*_ALLOW_ALL_USERS` on the descriptor), plus a full group decision ladder: `require_mention`, entity-first bot-mention detection, `exclusive_bot_mentions` for deterministic multi-bot routing, `mention_patterns` regex wake words, `guest_mode`, `free_response_chats` / `free_response_topics`, `allowed_chats` / `group_allowed_chats` / `group_allow_from`, `allowed_topics`, `ignored_threads`, `observe_unmentioned_group_messages` (silent context with attribution), `ignore_root_dm`, own-message filter, trigger-text cleanup — all resolved by `_should_process_message()`. Mirrored per platform: Slack's six composable trigger options plus channel allowlist / ignored channels / `disable_dms` / `allow_bots`, Discord role-based access control, WhatsApp DM+group policy with LID↔number matching, Matrix room allowlists, Feishu 3-tier `group_rules`, WeCom dm_policy/group_policy, Photon mention gating. (~45 entries)
capabilities.nerva_evidence: `grep -rn "require_mention|mention_gat|allowed_chats|free_response|guest_mode|observe_unmentioned" --include=*.py --include=*.tsx .` returns **zero** results outside the inventory. Nerva has exactly one primitive: a flat `allowed_user_ids` list (agents/core/channels/telegram.py:26, populated from `TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_USER_IDS` per tests/test_sec_b3_telegram_owner_binding.py) — no concept of a group, a mention, or a channel-scoped rule.
capabilities.rationale: Not breadth — a correctness gap with a security edge. Put Nerva's Telegram bot in any group chat today and it answers every message from every allowlisted member, with no way to say 'only when addressed'. That makes group deployment unusable and, worse, it means every message in that group becomes tainted inbound context the agent acts on. Copy the ladder, but restructure it: Hermes has ~20 loose config keys resolved by one long function, and the rebuild note admits it. Model it as one ordered, testable policy chain evaluated in the Gateway (where sender, channel and taint already meet) so the same rules apply to every adapter instead of being reimplemented per platform.
capabilities.governance: This is an authorization boundary, so it belongs beside the pairing gate in agents/core/channels/gateway.py:70-96 — one place, fail-closed, not per-adapter. Its decisions should be auditable: 'ignored because unmentioned' is a fact worth recording.

capabilities.name: Pairing an unknown sender (first contact without editing a config file)
capabilities.hermes: Documented as a static allowlist workflow: find your numeric id via @userinfobot, paste it into `TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_USERS` in `~/.hermes/.env`, restart. The setup wizard warns '⚠️ Telegram has no user allowlist - anyone can use your bot!' and there is an unauthorized-DM pairing passthrough plus a DM-pairing flow that writes back into `TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_USERS`; SimpleX has its own DM pairing. Per the field research this is a static allowlist, not an approval flow (platform-telegram.pairing-allowlist/.pairing-passthrough, platforms-b.simplex-auth; ~5 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/channels/pairing.py (384 lines) — `SenderPairing`: unknown senders are **held pending owner approval** rather than dropped; optional rotating pairing code; single-use, minutes-TTL, constant-time-compared, never-logged deeplink tokens; per-(channel,sender) rate limit (5 per 10 min) and a bounded 200-entry pending list. Redeemed at agents/core/channels/telegram.py:128-165, gated in agents/core/channels/gateway.py:70-96 (fails **closed** on store error, with the reasoning written into the code). Tests: tests/test_h12_19_pairing.py, tests/test_telegram_deeplink_pairing.py, tests/test_channel_pairing.py; UI in frontend/src/test/pairing-deeplink.test.tsx.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva is straightforwardly better than Hermes here and better than the OpenClaw model the gap matrix cites, because pairing is an *approval*, not a code exchange, and the token semantics are right (one-use, short-lived, constant-time, never logged). Two things to finish rather than build: it is default-off behind `JARVIS_CHANNEL_PAIRING`, and Discord (no `sender` threaded) and Slack (no inbound) cannot use it at all. Turning it on by default for Telegram is the gap matrix' own P0 item 11 and costs nothing to ship.
capabilities.governance: Already the right shape — an inbound authorization gate that fails closed, feeding the same approval inbox as everything else. Extending it to Discord/Slack is part of those rows' wiring fixes.
capabilities.depends_on: Discord/Slack wiring fixes for full coverage

capabilities.name: Threads, topics and per-conversation sessions
capabilities.hermes: Telegram gets an entire forum-topic subsystem: operator-curated DM topics via `extra.dm_topics` with startup reconciliation, hot reload, creation/rename and `thread_id` write-back into config.yaml; a user-driven multi-session mode via `/topic` with a system topic that gets pinned, topic lanes and a root lobby with reminders, topic↔session bindings, lobby-shaped reply recovery, auto-rename from the session title, `/topic off`, and restore-a-session-into-a-topic. Elsewhere: Discord auto-threading and `/thread`, forum channels; Slack threading with watermark rehydration and `group_sessions_per_user` isolation; Google Chat per-thread sessions; Matrix `MATRIX_SESSION_SCOPE`; Mattermost thread reply mode with a broken-root fallback; SMS per-number sessions. (~30 entries)
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/channels/session.py — `SessionSource` carries `thread_id` and `build_session_key` derives a stable per-thread key from it; `DeliveryRouter` resolves a target with `thread_id`. The plumbing is right and **no adapter ever populates it**: `grep -rn "reply_to_message_id|message_thread_id|thread_ts|forum" agents/` returns nothing. Tests exist for the pure layer (tests/test_channel_sessions.py, tests/test_cross_channel_sessions.py).
capabilities.rationale: Nerva built the session-identity layer Hermes derives its topic features from, then never wired a thread id into it — so every conversation on a channel collapses into one session per sender. That is the difference between an assistant you can run three things with and one you have to finish a thought before starting another. The pragmatic slice is threads, not topics: reply-in-thread on Telegram/Discord/Slack/Matrix fills `SessionSource.thread_id` from data those platforms already send. Telegram's operator-curated DM-topics machinery (config write-back, startup reconciliation, hot reload) is a large, Telegram-shaped subsystem — defer it and see whether threads alone answer the need.
capabilities.governance: Read-only for identity; but the delivery target is part of the `channel.reply` payload, so a thread id has to be validated (the contract at agents/core/channel_reply.py:32-44 already checks reply-target shape per channel) rather than passed through.

capabilities.name: Per-channel personality, skills and verbosity
capabilities.hermes: `platform_hint` on the descriptor injects a system-prompt line per platform ('You are on IRC. Do not use markdown.'); per-channel and per-topic prompts on Telegram, Discord, Slack, Mattermost and Matrix; channel→skill bindings so a given channel auto-runs a skill (Discord, Slack, Telegram group topics); and four tiers of per-platform display defaults (`display.platforms.<name>.*`, gateway/display_config.py:120-192) controlling tool progress, reasoning display, streaming, interim messages and heartbeats — with in-source rationales (Buzz was moved to MEDIUM because every interim update became a permanent channel post; Photon is LOW because iMessage cannot edit messages). (~10 entries)
capabilities.nerva_evidence: `grep -rn "channel_prompt|platform_hint" agents/` returns nothing. Nerva has per-agent personas and `agents/core/product_posture.py`, but no per-channel prompt, no channel→skill binding, and no per-channel verbosity control.
capabilities.rationale: The display-tier idea is the valuable one and it generalizes past Hermes' use of it: a permanent-message channel like SMS or ntfy must not receive the same interim chatter as a chat window that can edit in place, and today Nerva has exactly one verbosity for every surface. Copy the tier resolver but take the inventory's own rebuild note — derive the tier from the descriptor's declared capabilities (can it edit? is it permanent? what is the cap?) instead of a hand-maintained name map that goes stale every time a platform is added. `platform_hint` is a two-line change with an outsized effect on output quality per channel.
capabilities.governance: Read-only. One caveat: a per-channel prompt is prompt content, so it must be operator-set configuration and never settable from inbound message content.

capabilities.name: Proactive delivery: home channel, scheduled output, and sending when no adapter is running
capabilities.hermes: Every platform declares `cron_deliver_env_var` (e.g. `TELEGRAM_HOME_CHANNEL`) making `deliver=<platform>` a valid cron target, with `/sethome` to set it from chat (Discord, Matrix, Yuanbao, Google Chat). Every platform also registers a `standalone_sender_fn` — an out-of-process async sender so a cron job can deliver without a live gateway; without one, 'a `deliver=<name>` cron job fires correctly but the actual send returns No live adapter'. Plus `parse_target_ref_fn`/`validate_target_ref_fn`/`send_message_handler` so an agent's `send_message` tool can address a chat on any platform. (~28 entries)
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/scheduler_service.py:570-579 — the daily digest reads `AUTONOMY_OWNER_CHAT_ID` and hardcodes `self._orch.channels.get("telegram")`; agents/core/autonomy_coordinator.py:103 does the same for decision cards. No home-channel concept, no per-channel delivery target, no out-of-process sender, and no agent-facing tool to send to a named channel (`grep -rn "def send_message" agents/` finds only the two plugin objects).
capabilities.rationale: Proactivity is the whole product — the morning brief, the approval prompt, the incident alert — and today all of it can only reach one hardcoded Telegram chat id read from an env var. That is both a reach limit (an owner who prefers Signal or ntfy gets nothing) and a robustness limit (if the channel is not registered in this process, the digest is silently dropped at a `if tg and owner` check). Generalize to a home-channel per platform plus a governed delivery target on the descriptor. The standalone sender matters less for Nerva, whose scheduler runs in-process, so port the concept only if a separate worker lands.
capabilities.governance: Privileged: proactive delivery is an outbound send with no user turn to attribute it to — arguably the case most needing an audit entry. Must go through `channel.reply` with the initiating task as the provenance, not a direct adapter call the way scheduler_service.py:576 does today.

capabilities.name: Catching up on what was missed while offline
capabilities.hermes: Discord history backfill and missed-message backfill on reconnect; Slack thread rehydration with per-thread watermarks; Matrix history fetch and serialization plus a startup grace filter for clock skew; Telegram's held-inbound queue that redispatches after a reconnect; the ntfy rebuild note calls out its own absence of a `since=` cursor as the fix. (~7 entries)
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/channel_inbox.py records only messages that arrive while the process is up (`record_inbound` is called from gateway.route). agents/core/channels/telegram.py keeps `self._offset` in memory only — a restart re-reads from Telegram's server-side queue by luck, not design, and every other channel loses the window entirely.
capabilities.rationale: An always-on house brain restarts — for an update, a power cut, a crash — and 'the agent silently ignored what you sent during the restart' is the failure mode that makes people stop trusting it. The Telegram offset happens to survive short gaps because Telegram queues server-side; Discord, Slack, Matrix and the webhook channels have nothing. Persist the per-channel watermark and backfill from it on connect. The clock-skew grace filter Matrix uses is worth taking with it — it is the guard against replaying old messages as new after a restart.
capabilities.governance: Backfilled messages are inbound and must re-enter through the full gateway path (taint, pairing, gating) — never a fast path that skips it because 'we already saw these'. Replay must not be able to re-trigger an action the owner already declined.
capabilities.depends_on: adapter descriptor; inbound gating (backfill must be gated identically)

capabilities.name: Message batching and debounce (treat a burst as one turn)
capabilities.hermes: Text batching for client-side splits (a long message Telegram broke into pieces becomes one turn), photo-burst batching, album/media-group debounce, Feishu burst batching with per-chat serialization, WhatsApp/Matrix/SimpleX/Discord text batching, WeCom's attachment+text merge window, and busy-text interrupt/debounce knobs on the base adapter (`_busy_text_debounce_seconds` 0.35, hard cap 1.0). (~10 entries)
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/channels/telegram.py:100-126 dispatches each update to `self.receive()` immediately, one turn per message. No debounce anywhere in agents/core/channels/.
capabilities.rationale: Small, self-contained, and it fixes a behaviour people notice within a minute of using the thing: send three lines of a thought as three messages and Nerva starts three turns, answers the first fragment, and races itself. It also costs real money and latency on every burst. This is one debounce window in the Gateway rather than per-adapter, which makes it cheaper for Nerva than it was for Hermes.
capabilities.governance: Read-only. One care point: batching merges messages before the injection scan in gateway.py:159-166, so the scan must run on the merged text, not per fragment.

capabilities.name: Guided setup for a channel (from 'I have nothing' to 'it replies')
capabilities.hermes: A per-platform `setup_fn` wizard for every platform: Telegram offers automatic QR-based bot creation through a hosted onboarding service (scan → tap 'Create Bot' → token fetched once, `hermes_cli/telegram_managed_bot.py`) or manual BotFather, with token-format validation (`^\d+:[A-Za-z0-9_-]{30,}$`), an allowlist prompt with the @userinfobot hint, and home-channel selection; Slack generates an app manifest and documents required scopes and event subscriptions; Google Chat walks GCP project/API/service-account/Pub-Sub/IAM setup; Teams registers a bot via the Teams CLI; Mattermost creates the bot account; Matrix handles login and cross-signing; DingTalk/Feishu/WeCom use QR scan-to-create. Plus troubleshooting matrices per platform. (~30 entries)
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/routers/onboarding.py has a real first-run wizard with ordered steps, completion tracking and an activation funnel (`/api/onboarding/wizard`, `_WIZARD_STEPS`, funnel events) — but `grep -rn "telegram" agents/core/routers/onboarding.py` returns nothing: there is no channel step. Channels are configured only by setting env vars before start (agents/web.py:371-430).
capabilities.rationale: Nerva has the wizard *frame* and it is measured (funnel events, time-to-first-action) — it just has no channel step, so the shortest path to a working Telegram bot is still 'read the docs, make a bot, edit .env, restart'. The gap matrix makes this a P0 (item 11, 'pair in 60 seconds') and the pieces are already built: the deeplink pairing token exists, the frontend test for it exists. Add one wizard step that takes a bot token, validates its format, calls `getMe` to confirm it and shows the bot's @username (the inventory's own rebuild note — Hermes writes the token before verifying it), then renders the pairing deeplink as a QR. Hermes' hosted QR bot-creation service is not portable to a local-first product with no hosted backend; skip that half.
capabilities.governance: Privileged: the wizard writes a bot token, which is a credential — it must go into the existing secret store (agents/core/routers/vault.py, secrets.py), never into a plaintext .env, and enabling a channel should be an explicit operator action, not a side effect of pasting a token.
capabilities.depends_on: adapter descriptor (required_env/prompts come from the manifest)

capabilities.name: Authenticating inbound webhooks (proving the message came from the platform)
capabilities.hermes: Per-provider verification: Twilio's full HMAC-SHA1 signature algorithm with a port-variant retry and constant-time byte comparison, refusing to start without `SMS_WEBHOOK_URL` unless an explicitly-named insecure flag is set (which logs 'Any client that can reach port %d can inject messages'); Feishu webhook signature with rate limiting and anomaly tracking; Teams service-URL allowlist plus conversation-ID validation; Google Chat attachment-download SSRF guard; A2A HMAC signing with an SSRF guard on push callbacks; WeCom callback crypto (WXBizMsgCrypt). (~8 entries)
capabilities.nerva_evidence: Nerva has HMAC webhook verification for its **own** triggers — agents/core/routers/webhooks.py:31 (`signed: bool` → `X-Signature-256`, H16.4) — and for A2A peers (agents/core/a2a.py, constant-time HMAC over the raw body). But the channel ingress at agents/core/routers/integrations.py:216-233 has none, and says so: 'Provider signature verification is the host seam — front this with the H16.4 signed-webhook path in production.'
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already owns the primitive and applies it correctly in two other places; the channel door is the one it was left off. Anyone who can authenticate to the API can currently POST a payload to `/api/channels/whatsapp/inbound` that the pairing gate will treat as coming from whatever `from` id they type — which means the sender identity the gate depends on is attacker-chosen. Wiring the existing signed-webhook path in front of channel ingress, per provider, closes it. This is a security fix ahead of every feature in this cluster.
capabilities.governance: Directly load-bearing for the whole governance stack: the pairing gate, the approval-card owner binding and the audit trail all key off `sender`, and an unverified webhook lets a caller forge it.

capabilities.name: Not answering itself: echo, duplicate and loop guards
capabilities.hermes: Own-message filters on every adapter ('adapters must filter their own outbound echoes to prevent reply loops', ADDING_A_PLATFORM.md); ntfy's `X-Tags: hermes-agent` echo tag plus a 300 s/1000-entry dedup window; Feishu message and card-action dedup; SMS drops inbound whose From equals its own number; Matrix bridge/appservice loop protection; WhatsApp broadcast/status/channel suppression; Telegram's delayed-delivery drop guard; Slack `allow_bots` gating messages from other bots. (~10 entries)
capabilities.nerva_evidence: Discord filters its own user (agents/core/channels/discord.py:47, `if message.author == self._client.user`). Telegram relies on the Bot API not echoing. The five webhook channels have **no** dedup and no echo guard: `parse_inbound` accepts any payload with text+sender (webhook_channels.py:147-260), so a Matrix room where the bot's own `m.room.message` is delivered back, or a retried provider webhook, is processed as a fresh user turn.
capabilities.rationale: Unglamorous and load-bearing: on Matrix and Signal in particular, a bot that reads its own messages back is a loop that runs until a rate limit or a bill stops it — and Nerva's outbound rate limiter is off by default (agents/core/channels/send_rate_limit.py). Provider webhook retries are the quieter version of the same bug: the same message approved twice. Copy the id-dedup window and the own-message filter as shared Gateway behaviour rather than per-adapter, and prefer a dedicated origin header over ntfy's user-visible tag (its own rebuild note).
capabilities.governance: A duplicate inbound can produce a duplicate approval request or a duplicate approved action — so dedup belongs upstream of the approval queue, and the queue should be idempotent on a message id regardless.

capabilities.name: Agent-to-agent as a channel (be callable by another agent; call peers)
capabilities.hermes:
A2A is a platform: an inbound adapter with an Agent Card advertising skills, a JSON-RPC task lifecycle with error codes, push notifications with HMAC-signed callbacks and an SSRF guard, authentication/trust/rate limiting, inbound prompt-injection framing and outbound redaction, plus five agent-facing tools (`a2a_discover`, `a2a_call`, `a2a_list`, `a2a_history`, `a2a_orchestrate`) gated per surface by `hermes tools enable a2a --platform

`, where enabling it for `--platform a2a` permits agent chaining. platforms-b.a2a-* (~13 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/a2a.py — off unless `JARVIS_A2A_ENABLED`; per-peer shared-secret HMAC over the raw body, constant-time; **a verified task lands in a pending inbox the owner approves out-of-band — 'A2A cannot, by construction, run anything on its own'**; signed Agent Card; a contract template (`A2A_INBOUND_CONTRACT_KIND`) with body-size and peer-id bounds; bounded 500-entry inbox. Router at agents/core/routers/a2a.py:45 (`/agent-card`).
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's inbound A2A is the stronger design on exactly the axis that matters — a peer agent's task cannot execute without a human approval, where Hermes' A2A can chain agent to agent once the toolset is enabled. Keep that invariant absolutely; it is the clearest expression of the governance thesis in the whole cluster. What is genuinely missing is the *outbound* half: Nerva can be called but cannot call, so the five client tools (discover/call/list/history/orchestrate) are worth porting — through the kernel, at a tier that treats a peer's response as untrusted input, and with the per-surface enablement gate Hermes uses.
capabilities.governance: Inbound already fails closed into the approval inbox. Outbound calls are egress plus delegation — must cross the kernel (`call.outbound` or a sibling), and peer responses must be marked tainted the way the gateway marks inbound channel text.

capabilities.name: Home Assistant as a channel (the house talks to the agent)
capabilities.hermes: A gateway adapter that turns Home Assistant into a messaging platform: event filtering with cooldown, state-change message formatting, a standalone cron sender for `deliver=homeassistant`, readiness probes, and `_TIER_MINIMAL` display defaults. Read/notify-shaped — HA state changes become agent messages. platforms-b.homeassistant-* (5 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/house/home_assistant.py — a real `HomeAssistantAdapter` with a WebSocket transport, LAN-origin validation (`_is_lan_address`, `_validated_origin`), entity/area normalization; agents/core/house/actuation.py — `HomeAssistantServiceDriver` with canonical light/climate/security commands, a payload-hash execution ledger with begin/finish/abort for idempotency; agents/core/house/ingest.py feeds presence inference; kernel kinds `house.control`, `house.security_control`, `house.recovery` (agents/core/kernel/registry.py:96-98); router at agents/core/routers/house.py.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva is decisively ahead: Hermes' HA integration reads state and narrates it into chat, while Nerva actuates the house through a kernel-mediated path with an idempotency ledger and a separate, higher-risk kind for security devices. This is one of the five areas the gap matrix already marks Nerva AHEAD and the evidence holds up. The only idea worth taking from the Hermes adapter is the inverse direction with a cooldown — letting a filtered HA event *start* a turn (a door opened while nobody is home) rather than only answering questions about state. That is a small addition to the existing ingest path, not a channel.
capabilities.governance: Already correct — actuation crosses `house.control`/`house.security_control`. An HA event that starts a turn is inbound untrusted input and must be taint-marked like any other channel ingress.

capabilities.name: Regional and enterprise-chat breadth (DingTalk, Feishu/Lark, WeCom, WeCom Callback, Yuanbao)
capabilities.hermes: Five adapters, ~60 entries: DingTalk Stream Mode with AI Cards and emoji reactions; Feishu with a 3-tier group-rules admission policy, webhook mode with signature and anomaly tracking, interactive approval cards, **document-comment intelligent reply** with its own access-control CLI, meeting-invitation events, and six agent-facing doc/drive tools; WeCom with native `msgtype: stream`, a per-chat send queue with a token bucket, and a separate Callback adapter with WXBizMsgCrypt; Yuanbao with a reverse-engineered wire protocol, SignManager auth, COS media upload, stickers, and five agent tools.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none
capabilities.rationale: Wrong audience for this product. These are corporate-suite chat platforms for a market Nerva does not serve, and each one is not a thin adapter but a vendor SDK plus a crypto/callback surface plus a tool family — Feishu alone is six agent-facing tools that read and write a document store. Bringing them in would roughly double the channel-layer surface area and the egress allowlist for capability the owner will never exercise, on a product whose thesis is a small, auditable, local-first system. The transferable ideas are already claimed by other rows: WeCom's per-chat token bucket belongs in the send limiter, Feishu's approval cards in the approvals row, DingTalk's reaction lifecycle in the feedback row. Re-open only on a signed design partner in that market, and then one platform at a time behind its own flag.
capabilities.governance: Each would add a new egress domain family and a new inbound door — the surface-area cost is the argument, not the effort.

capabilities.name: Long-tail protocol adapters (IRC, LINE, SimpleX, Mattermost, Raft, Buzz)
capabilities.hermes: Six more adapters, ~40 entries: IRC with a no-markdown platform hint; LINE with a Messaging API webhook, a bubble splitter, a tokenized media-serving endpoint and a slow-LLM postback button; SimpleX Chat with channel enumeration and DM pairing; Mattermost with a WebSocket loop, thread reply modes and 5-image batching; Raft as a wake-channel bridge with `POST /wake` and activity telemetry; Buzz on Nostr with NIP-42 signing and Blossom media URLs.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none
capabilities.rationale: Reach into audiences that overlap almost none of Nerva's — and the owner's own delta-port doc set the precedent for refusing breadth that does not serve the thesis. Each of these costs a permanent adapter, a dependency and an egress entry to serve a population of roughly zero for this product. Two named re-open paths rather than a blanket no: **SimpleX** is the one that is genuinely on-thesis (no identifiers at all, privacy-first, self-hosted) and should be reconsidered if Nerva ever markets on metadata privacy; **Raft's wake-channel shape** (`POST /wake` to rouse an idle agent) is a useful pattern for the always-on-box deployment and is cheaper to rebuild against Nerva's own scheduler than to port.
capabilities.governance: Read-only decision; no effect crosses the kernel because nothing is being built.

capabilities.name: iMessage reach (Photon/BlueBubbles sidecar)
capabilities.hermes: A Node sidecar over a loopback protocol with `hermes photon setup/status/install-sidecar/telemetry` CLI commands, access auto-configuration, sidecar directory resolution for immutable installs, a presence watchdog with health monitoring, inbound attachments/voice/rich-links/polls, tapbacks and read receipts, group mention gating, and `_TIER_LOW` display defaults because iMessage messages are permanent and uneditable. platforms-b.photon-* (~13 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: Deliberately excluded, with the reason in code: agents/core/channels/webhook_channels.py:17 — 'iMessage is intentionally excluded: it is macOS/host bound with no clean HTTP surface and belongs to a host bridge, not this layer.'
capabilities.rationale: The existing exclusion is well-reasoned and should stand. It requires a permanently-running macOS host with full-disk access to the Messages database and a Node sidecar — a second runtime, a second update path and a second trust boundary, for a channel that duplicates reach Nerva already has through Telegram and its own Expo mobile app. The gap matrix notes Nerva has 'no iMessage-class channel', and that is true, but the cost is a macOS dependency in a product that runs on a Linux box in a house. Re-open if the owner's household is Apple-only and Telegram is not acceptable — the honest version of that re-open is a host bridge exposing an HTTP surface the existing webhook-channel layer can speak to, not a port of the sidecar.

capabilities.name: Slack-native AI-app surfaces (Agent view, task cards, suggested prompts, thread titles, Block Kit)
capabilities.hermes: Slack's own AI-app UI: `chat.startStream` live typing where the streamed message is the final message; native plan/task cards with per-tool running/complete/error rows keyed by (team, channel, thread_ts); up to four one-tap suggested prompts via `assistant.threads.setSuggestedPrompts`; automatic thread titles from the first user message; `app_context_changed` telling the agent which channel the user is looking at (as a label only — 'it does not read the viewed channel's history'); Block Kit `rich_blocks` rendering; feedback buttons. platforms-a.slack-native-streaming/.native-task-cards/.suggested-prompts/.thread-titles/.agent-context/.rich-blocks/.feedback-buttons (~7 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — agents/core/channels/slack.py is 65 lines of `chat_postMessage`
capabilities.rationale: Deep, vendor-specific UI investment for a workplace surface, on a product whose current thesis is a personal/household brain — and it is gated behind Slack app-manifest features (`assistant:write`, Agent view) that assume a workspace install and admin approval. Nerva's scarce build capacity in this cluster is better spent making Slack *hear* at all (its own row) and on the governance-shaped interactive layer that works everywhere. One idea is worth lifting into the approvals row regardless of this decision: the task card's per-tool live rows are the right shape for showing a governed plan mid-execution, and Nerva already has the plan data. capabilities.name: Transport-level end-to-end encryption (Matrix E2EE, cross-signing)
capabilities.hermes: Matrix E2EE modes, cross-signing verification via `MATRIX_RECOVERY_KEY`, and a proxy mode specifically to make E2EE work on macOS. platforms-a.matrix-e2ee/.matrix-cross-signing/.matrix-proxy-mode (3 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/channels/webhook_channels.py:183-211 — MatrixChannel is an unencrypted client-server shim (`/_matrix/client/v3/rooms/{room}/send`)
capabilities.rationale: Superficially on-thesis for a privacy-first product, and on inspection it is not: the agent must read the plaintext to act on it, so the message ends up in Nerva's memory, its channel inbox and its audit chain either way. Transport E2EE protects the hop, which is the hop Nerva already controls least about — while the actual privacy guarantee the product sells is that the *processing* is local, which it already has. Buying it costs the full matrix-nio E2EE stack, device-key storage and cross-signing recovery, and it would put encrypted key material in a store the kernel does not mediate. Re-open for multi-user or group deployments where other people's messages transit rooms the owner does not control — there the hop genuinely matters.
capabilities.governance: Would introduce a key store outside the vault/secret path — a reason to do it deliberately or not at all.

capabilities.name: Agent-facing platform administration tools (act on the platform, not just chat in it)
capabilities.hermes: Tools that let the model operate the platform itself: `discord` (server participation) and `discord_admin` (server management); `feishu_doc_read`, `feishu_drive_list_comments`/`list_comment_replies`/`reply_comment`/`add_comment` plus the `hermes-feishu` toolset; `yb_query_group_info`/`yb_query_group_members`/`yb_send_dm`/`yb_search_sticker`/`yb_send_sticker`; the Teams meeting pipeline with Graph subscription lifecycle and meeting-summary delivery. (~16 entries)

The half that is genuinely useful, 'the agent can proactively send to a named channel', is already covered by the home-channel/delivery row and belongs there, behind `channel.reply`, rather than as a free-form platform tool. Re-open per-tool with a specific need; the kernel makes each one cheap to add safely once there is a reason.

capabilities.name: Drive an agent on another machine over SSH, and update that fleet
capabilities.hermes: An OpenSSH ControlMaster connection manager with classified error messages, ~/.ssh/config host suggestions, an SSH bootstrap that reuses-or-spawns a remote `hermes serve`, remote liveness revalidation, a managed SSH update transaction with a crash-recovery journal and per-profile restore lines, and an "Update all instances" fleet fan-out (16 §6, ids ssh-connection through managed-ssh-recovery; 48 gapfill managed-updates-section).

No SSH transport anywhere in agents/.

For an owner with a homelab and a laptop — which is the stated Nerva usage — "my agent runs on the GPU box, I drive it from the laptop" is a first-class use, and today the answer is a refusal string. The credential design the docstring says does not exist is exactly what the permission ledger and capability broker were built to provide.

capabilities.rationale: One-way SSE plus polling means the HUD cannot cheaply carry live per-session state, and a reconnect loses whatever streamed during the gap. Every multi-window, multi-gateway and status-bar row in this cluster is bottlenecked on this. Copy the heartbeat + replay design specifically — a resumable stream is what makes a long agent turn survivable.

capabilities.hermes: A frameless transparent always-on-top panel window with per-compositor capability detection (Wayland vs X11 vs Cocoa vs win32), click-through, native frost, edge resize handles, press-and-hold composer drag, cross-monitor drag, a game-overlay watch, Hyprland promotion, reset-layout, a move-to-pointer chord, and handoff back to the app window (16 §8 hud-* ids + 17-desktop-a.md §7, ~20 ids).

capabilities.rationale: An assistant you have to switch windows to is an app; one that floats over your work is an operating layer, which is what NERVA_VISION claims. This is the single most identity-shaping feature in the cluster. Copy the compositor-capability object wholesale — Hermes derives it once and the entries note that scattering `if (linux)` checks guarantees drift.
capabilities.governance: Window management is read-only. The one exception is Hermes's readWindowBelow (reading the window under the HUD for context) — that is screen capture and must cross desktop.step (already KERNEL, agents/core/desktop_operator.py:188) with the permission-ledger first-contact prompt, not ship as a free HUD convenience
capabilities.depends_on: Row: native app chrome; Row: real-time bidirectional wire

capabilities.name: Quick Entry — a global hotkey that captures a prompt from anywhere on the system
capabilities.hermes: A 640×168 hotkey window (default CommandOrControl+Shift+Space) with a canonicalizing accelerator validator that requires at least one modifier and forbids Escape, persisted settings, and a dumb design — it holds no gateway connection, it just hands text to the real client (16 §8, ids quick-entry, quick-entry-accelerator; 47 gapfill quick-entry-shortcut).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: frontend/src/shell.tsx:69 binds ⌘K to an in-page palette only (frontend/src/shell.tsx:244 Palette); frontend/src/panels/quickbar.tsx is a resolve-preview panel inside the console. No OS-level global shortcut anywhere; desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs registers none.
capabilities.rationale: Cheap, high-frequency, and it is the thing that makes an assistant present rather than visited. The accelerator validator is worth copying literally — the two extra rules (a modifier is mandatory, Escape cannot be the key) are the ones that stop the feature from stealing a key from every other app or becoming un-toggleable.
capabilities.governance: read-only — it captures text and hands it to the normal prompt path, which is already governed. It must not gain a submit-and-auto-approve shortcut

capabilities.name: Multi-window: peer app instances and per-session pop-outs
capabilities.hermes: "New Window" peer instances, session pop-out windows with their own webPreferences contract, popped-out Browser windows, open-session-in-terminal, and window↔connection route registration (16 §8, ids instance-window, session-window, browser-window, open-in-terminal, window-connection-route).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — frontend/src/app.tsx renders one mode at a time in a single document; desktop/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json declares exactly one window
capabilities.rationale: Product reason, not effort: Nerva's identity is one governed hub per machine, and every extra window is another surface that can render an approval card. Approval phishing across N windows — where the owner cannot tell which window's kernel is asking — would quietly damage the one thing Nerva sells. The legitimate need underneath (watch a long agent run while working) is answered by the HUD row, and "work from another device" is answered by the node mesh. Re-open path: if the owner ever needs two repos side by side, ship a saved two-pane split inside the one window, not a second app instance.
capabilities.governance: read-only

capabilities.name: Native OS notifications with action buttons that route back into the app

Nerva's governance model creates more moments where the agent needs the owner than Hermes's does, so a native "input needed" notification is worth more here than there. Copy the dedupe-returns-true detail — without it the "send test" button lies.

An action button that *approves* is not: it must post to the existing approval queue and cross the kernel like any other decision, and irreversible-tier tasks must refuse to be approvable from a notification at all — the owner has to look at the card

capabilities.name: Keep the machine awake through a turn, and be aware of power/battery state

capabilities.rationale: An always-on house brain that lets the laptop suspend mid-turn loses the turn and, worse, loses it silently. Battery-aware throttling is also a local-first virtue: it is the honest way to run a local model on a machine that is not plugged in.
capabilities.governance: A power assertion is a host effect — host.control (already KERNEL in agents/core/kernel/registry.py), default-off behind a flag per docs/FLAGS.md, and released on quit
capabilities.depends_on: Row: the shell owns the backend process
