capabilities.rationale: Deep links are how an ecosystem points at you: a docs page, a QR code from the phone, a link in a Telegram message from your own agent. Copy the dev-scheme separation too — it is the detail that stops a dev build from hijacking the owner's real links.
capabilities.governance: A link that installs an MCP server is a privileged effect and the single most obvious attack in this cluster — a URL in a hostile page that adds a tool server. It must cross the kernel as skill.install / mcp.mutating (both already KERNEL) and land in the approval queue, never in a plain confirm() dialog the way Hermes does it

What is missing is the shell half — a native "choose a folder" or "save this here" that does not go through a browser download. Add the pickers and clipboard as thin Tauri commands that hand paths to the existing governed file tools rather than doing IO themselves.
capabilities.governance: Writes, renames and trash are file.write (already KERNEL); a first-contact file root must go through the permission ledger (agents/core/permission_ledger.py) exactly as the flag docs describe. A native picker returning a path is read-only; acting on that path is not

capabilities.name: An interactive terminal inside the app
capabilities.hermes: A real node-pty host: shell resolution per platform, interactive flags per shell family, a scrubbed truecolor environment (npm_config_* stripped, TERM_PROGRAM set), remote panes that reuse the SSH ControlMaster, per-session data/exit channels, sessions kept alive while hidden, plus a terminal tab rail with Ctrl+` / Ctrl+Shift+` / Ctrl+Shift+↑↓ / Ctrl+Shift+W (16 terminal-ipc; 17 §9 terminal-rail).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/environments/execution.py + local_transport.py + terminal_contract.py + targets.py — a governed execution transport: HARDLINE denylist screened first, authorize + tamper-evident audit chain, docker by default, local host only with JARVIS_TERMINAL_LOCAL_HOST + a durable approval + terminal.exec contract + an Action-Kernel GRANT (docs/FLAGS.md:157). argv-only, cwd-jailed, output-capped, killed on timeout. No PTY, no interactive shell, no UI.
capabilities.rationale: Deliberately NOT a copy. A raw interactive PTY is an ungoverned escape hatch that would sit beside the kernel rather than behind it — the exact regression the directive's adaptation rule forbids, and it would void the audit chain that execution.py builds. Build a terminal *pane* instead: each submitted line parses to argv, crosses the contract + permission ledger + kernel, and streams output back. Slower to type in than a real shell; the only version worth shipping in this product.
capabilities.governance: terminal.exec (already KERNEL) plus the permission ledger's first-contact rule for a new target. Shell operators must stay unparseable-to-argv and therefore refused, as local_transport.py already does

capabilities.name: Git worktrees plus a full review and ship pane (stage, unstage, revert, commit, push, create PR)

The repo.sync kernel kind exists in agents/core/kernel/registry.py for GitHub-triggered pull/rebase, so the governance hook is already there.

Nerva has an approval queue for actions but nothing that shows the diff those actions produced. Worktrees are also the safe way to let a subagent work on a repo without touching the owner's checkout — which pairs with agents/core/subagents.py.

Copy Hermes's workspace-sanitize rule too: never accept a working directory inside the install tree

capabilities.name: Encrypt stored credentials with the OS keychain

For a product whose pitch is that your data never leaves the house, plaintext API keys in a dotfile is the weakest link in the story. secrets_vault.py already defines the injectable-resolver seam; an OS-keychain resolver slots in beside the vaultwarden one with no new architecture. Copy the plain-text opt-in wording too — if the owner chooses plaintext, say so in the UI.

capabilities.name: Native OAuth (system browser + loopback + PKCE) and per-connection cookie partitions
capabilities.hermes: RFC 8252 native OAuth through the system browser with a loopback redirect and PKCE, an embedded OAuth login window as the fallback, per-connection cookie partitions so two gateways cannot see each other's session, cookie-session liveness classification, an MCP OAuth loopback callback for remote backends, and Windows system-CA trust (16 §11, ids native-oauth, oauth-login-window, oauth-partition, cookie-liveness, mcp-oauth-callback, windows-system-ca).

All browser-tab flows; no system-browser + loopback + PKCE, no cookie partitioning.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva can already do OAuth in a browser tab, which is enough for a single-user local install today. It stops being enough the moment there is a native shell and more than one gateway: a shared cookie jar means signing into a remote gateway silently gives it the local one's session. Add the loopback+PKCE flow and partition per connection.
capabilities.governance: Minting or refreshing a token is privileged — already admin_guard'd; keep it there and add the audit record. The loopback listener must bind 127.0.0.1 only, matching install.sh's "never writes a bind other than 127.0.0.1"

Add those as items and adopt Hermes's item contract so contributed items are possible later.

If a lower-friction mode is ever needed, it must be a ledger widening — a durable, audited permission.grant — not a chat verb. capabilities.name: Session lifecycle: search, pin, unread watermark, rename, delete, filter, date dividers, export, branch/fork, move to project
capabilities.hermes: A session sidebar with search, a pinned section, recents/projects/worktrees grouping, per-row status dot and a persisted read-state watermark, an actions menu (rename, delete, export transcript to JSON, branch/fork with warnings, change cwd, move to project), a filter menu and date-group dividers (18 §15 + 40/41 gapfills, ~30 ids).

capabilities.hermes: Sidebar projects (create/rename/add folder), a project menu, IDEA.md idea templates with shuffle, a base-branch picker, worktree lanes under a project with add/remove, and move-a-session-to-another-project (18 sidebar-projects/-project-menu/-project-dialog/-worktree-dialog; 40 project-idea-templates, base-branch-picker, worktree-remove, move-session-to-project).

capabilities.name: User-defined scheduled jobs (cron editor, run history, delivery targets, ready-made blueprints)
capabilities.hermes: A Scheduled jobs panel: list rows, a detail metadata block, the prompt block, run history, a create/edit editor, "Deliver to" target checkboxes, Blueprints (ready-made automations), a model-impact warning and an expensive-model confirmation toast (18 §3, 10 ids + 44 gapfill day names).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/scheduler_service.py — APScheduler with a *fixed* job set (digests at 07:00/20:00, budget reset, learning-loop promotions, log scans, retention purge, optional KG sync); agents/core/routers/tools.py:73 POST /api/schedule/parse (natural-language → cron, agents/core/autonomy/nl_schedule.py); agents/core/routers/workflows.py has CRUD but no schedule attached; agents/*/HEARTBEAT.md
capabilities.rationale: Nerva can parse "every weekday at 7am" into cron and has nowhere to put the result. The owner cannot create a single scheduled job today — every recurring behaviour is hard-coded by a developer. For a house brain that is a defining gap, and the NL parser plus workflows CRUD means most of the machinery is already built.
capabilities.governance: A scheduled job is a standing grant to act unattended — the highest-stakes thing in this cluster. Creating one must cross the kernel (goal.approve is the closest existing kind) and the job's own actions must re-authorize at fire time, exactly as node_mesh.py re-authorizes at execute time rather than trusting the dispatch-time decision

capabilities.governance: Creating an inbound trigger opens an attack surface; keep it admin_guard'd and audited. The inbound request itself already fails closed without a valid token/signature

capabilities.name: Pane/zone tiling with layout presets and an agent-callable apply_layout tool

capabilities.rationale: Two product reasons. First, Nerva's HUD is a designed information surface where each mode's layout is part of the claim it makes — the LiveSourceChip, the context column, the ticker are positioned so the owner can read state without hunting; a user-tiled canvas makes "what is the HUD telling me" unstable. Second and decisively: `apply_layout` lets the agent rearrange the surface the owner uses to supervise it. That is a supervision-integrity problem, not a UI preference. Re-open path: one saved split — chat beside review — which is the only pairing this cluster's other rows actually need.
capabilities.governance: An agent-callable layout tool would be an agent effect on the owner's supervision surface; there is no kernel kind for it and there should not need to be

The only clients are the HUD (/home/user/jarvis-hub/frontend/src/gap.tsx:2904 `DecisionInboxPanel`) and mobile (/home/user/jarvis-hub/mobile/src/screens/ApprovalsScreen.tsx). Adaptation rule: the terminal renders the queued task exactly as the HUD does — tier, the exact command, the rollback plan — and POSTs to the existing admin-guarded decide route. capabilities.name: Server-side validation of a settings write
capabilities.hermes: Type coercion happens only on the CLI path (`_coerce_int`/`_coerce_float`/`_looks_structured_value`, driven by the type of the DEFAULT_CONFIG leaf) and unknown keys are written anyway with a 'did you mean' notice. `validate_config_structure` produces startup warnings for a handful of shapes (custom_providers as a dict, fallback_model missing provider) and 'any exception inside validation is swallowed (never blocks startup)'. `PUT /api/config` deep-merges whatever the form sent (22-config-b.md `config-b.core.set_value_coercion`, `config-b.core.structure_validation`).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/settings_db.py:452-495 (_validate_value / validate_category — bool excluded from the number check, select values checked against opts, tags checked element-wise, JSON-serialisability checked) and agents/core/routers/admin.py:110-118 (422 with per-key details before anything is persisted); put_category refuses keys outside the shipped spec (settings_db.py:496-528)
capabilities.rationale: A malformed value is rejected before it can be read back and trusted, which is the property Hermes explicitly does not have on its write path. Keep as is; the only worthwhile extension is min/max ranges for the numeric keys that already carry semantic bounds (money caps, quiet hours, TTLs).
capabilities.governance: read-only

capabilities.name: Credential-bearing settings encrypted at rest and never echoed back
capabilities.hermes: Secrets live in `~/.hermes/.env` as plaintext at 0600, written by an atomic dotenv editor with a name denylist (`LD_PRELOAD`, `PATH`, `HERMES_HOME`, `HERMES_YOLO_MODE`, …) so a dashboard writer cannot plant an execution- or policy-changing variable. `hermes config` masks them in the summary, but `hermes config get OPENROUTER_API_KEY` prints the value verbatim (22-config-b.md `config-b.core.dotenv_file`, `config-b.core.env_write_denylist`, `config-b.cli.config_get`).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/settings_db.py:33-108 (SECRET_KEYS envelope-encrypted at the write boundary with the `enc::v1::` marker, key held outside settings.db); agents/core/secrets.py:1-50 (SecretStore, Fernet with a PBKDF2 passphrase path and a labelled pure-Python fallback); agents/core/routers/secrets.py:29-40 (broker — 'values go in, never come back out via the API'); agents/core/routers/admin.py:90-107 (audit records changed KEY NAMES only)
capabilities.rationale: Nerva never writes a credential to disk in plaintext and never returns one through an API, where Hermes stores them in a plaintext file and has a CLI that prints them. Nerva also has no `.env` writer at all (dotenv is load-only, agents/core/plugin_manager.py:74-82), so Hermes's denylist has no attack surface to defend here — do not port it.
capabilities.governance: read-only

capabilities.name: External secret sources — resolve credentials from a vault instead of storing them
capabilities.hermes: Two source families with 15 schema keys plus a hidden reference map: Bitwarden Secrets Manager (bulk project dump, TTL cache, optional AES-GCM encrypted stale cache reusable for `max_stale_seconds` on NETWORK/TIMEOUT only — 'auth failures do not fall back', auto-installed `bws` binary, `server_url` for EU/self-hosted) and 1Password (`op://vault/item/field` refs resolved one `op read` each, pinned binary path so PATH is not consulted, service-account token env). `hermes secrets … setup|status|sync` renders a status table; mapped sources beat bulk sources and the first source to claim a var wins (22-config-b.md `config-b.secrets.bitwarden`, `config-b.secrets.onepassword`).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/secrets_vault.py:16-40 — VaultResolver(client, fallback_env, prefix) with a vault→env→default order, but the client is injected and only one call site exists: agents/core/plugins/oauth.py:103-112 resolving JARVIS_TOKEN_KEY. No cache, no TTL, no CLI, no status surface, no bulk source, no claim ordering, no settings keys.
capabilities.rationale: The seam is right and already tested (tests/test_adjacents_h21_abcd.py) — it is simply not a product capability yet. Turning it into a real source layer (registered sources, resolution order, cache with an explicit stale policy, a status view that says which source claimed which name) is what lets an owner run Nerva without a single credential on the box, which is the strongest version of the local-first pitch. Ship one source well (vaultwarden, since it is self-hostable and matches the local-first posture) rather than three shallowly.
capabilities.governance: read-only for resolution; the fetch leaves the box, so the network call rides the existing kernel-classed `plugin.egress` path rather than opening a new one
capabilities.depends_on: the layered resolution row (a vault-backed value must be visible as such in the provenance view)

capabilities.name: `${env:VAR}` interpolation inside config values
capabilities.hermes: Any string value may contain `${NAME}` or `${env:NAME}`, expanded against the process environment at load time; unresolved `env:` refs stay literal and log a WARNING naming `.env`, other `source:` prefixes warn once, `_env_ref_snapshot` invalidates the load cache when a referenced var changes, and `_preserve_env_ref_templates` writes the template (not the expanded secret) back on save (22-config-b.md `config-b.core.env_interpolation`, config.py:2871-3010).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — `rg '\$\{env:|expand_env_vars' agents/` returns nothing; settings values are stored as literal JSON in SQLite
capabilities.rationale: This capability exists in Hermes because its config plane is a plaintext YAML file that must not contain secrets — interpolation is the workaround for that shape. Nerva's config plane is a typed store with envelope-encrypted secret fields and a JIT broker, so pointing a config value at an env var would move a secret from an encrypted column into an unencrypted process environment: strictly worse. The underlying need — 'do not store this credential, fetch it' — is the external-secret-source row above. Re-open path: if the operator-pinned file layer lands, that file is plaintext on disk and will need `${env:…}` or a source reference for its own credential leaves.
capabilities.governance: read-only

capabilities.name: Surviving a corrupt or unreadable config store without silently losing policy
capabilities.hermes: A YAML parse failure warns once per `(path, mtime, size)`, snapshots the file to `config.yaml.corrupt.<ts>.bak`, and then either keeps the last successfully loaded config for a running process or falls back to defaults for a fresh one — a port of openai/codex#31188 whose stated motivation is not dropping security-critical overrides such as `approvals.deny`. `require_readable_config_before_write()` makes every writer refuse rather than overwrite an unparseable file (22-config-b.md `config-b.core.corrupt_config_recovery`, config.py:48-165, 3612-3696).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/config.py:77 — `data = yaml.safe_load(f)` with no try/except, so a malformed agents.yaml raises a raw YAMLError at boot; agents/core/settings_db.py:406-422 — `get_value` wraps everything in `except Exception: return default`; agents/core/orchestrator.py:993-994 — `load_runtime_settings` swallows every exception and logs it, leaving `_runtime_settings` at its previous value (`{}` on first boot)
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's failure mode is worse than Hermes's pre-fix one, and it is silent. If settings.db is corrupt or locked at boot, every `get_setting` call returns the caller's inline default — so an owner who set `llm.cloud_fallback: never` gets `on-demand` (the literal default at orchestrator.py:966), guardrails fall back to `guardrails_default()`, and nothing tells anyone. A governance product cannot degrade to a weaker posture without saying so. Copy the pattern: snapshot, keep last-known-good, and if neither is available refuse to start rather than run defaults.
capabilities.governance: read-only, but this is the row that protects every privileged setting — a load failure that silently restores permissive defaults is a policy downgrade with no audit record

capabilities.name: Command-line access to configuration on a box with no working server
capabilities.hermes: `hermes config show|edit|get|set|unset|path|env-path|check|migrate`. `get`/`set`/`unset` take dotted key paths with `\.` escaping, greedy literal matching for keys that contain dots (model ids, Matrix room ids), and a phantom-sibling refusal that stops a set from shadowing an existing dotted key; `set` coerces to the type of the default, refuses to overwrite a mapping section with a scalar unless `--force`, masks credential-shaped leaves in its echo, and prints a difflib 'did you mean' on an unknown key. `path`/`env-path` print the resolved files; `check` prints the schema version and which optional env vars are set (22-config-b.md §A2, config.py:5559-6255).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — pyproject.toml declares no `[project.scripts]`; `ls scripts/` has bootstrap.py, doctor.py, backup via `python -m agents.core.backup`, but no settings command; the only way to read or change a setting is `GET/PUT /api/admin/settings/{category}` behind admin_guard (agents/core/routers/admin.py:73-125), which needs a running server and a token
capabilities.rationale: This is the support story for a box that will not start, and docs/OWNER_TASKS.md says nothing in this product has run on real hardware yet. The first time a real install misbehaves, the only recovery Nerva offers is opening a SQLite file by hand. A `python -m agents.core.settings get|set|unset|list|path|check` reusing validate_category is a day of work and turns every future bug report into a paste instead of a screen-share. Scope it to the settings store plus the resolved paths — Hermes's dotted-path escaping machinery is not needed for a two-segment `category.key` namespace.
capabilities.governance: privileged — a CLI write must go through the same `config.write` mediation as the HTTP route, or it becomes the documented way to bypass the kernel
capabilities.depends_on: the settings-write mediation row below (build them together or the CLI ships as a governance hole)

capabilities.name: Config schema versioning and a migration ladder
capabilities.hermes: `_config_version: 39` in the file, a support floor at 12 ('this config predates version 12 and can no longer be auto-migrated'), and a registry of `(target_version, fn)` steps gated on the on-disk version — renames (`write_mode`→`write_approval`), re-shapes (flat `stt.model`→provider section, `custom_providers` list→`providers` dict), retirements (drop the `bfl` toolset from saved lists, remove retired plugin keys), and value corrections that only fire if the old default is untouched. Post-migration it disables MCP servers that fail validation and prompts for env vars and skill settings introduced since the old version; `_persist_migration` never materialises pure defaults (22-config-b.md `config-b.core.migrations`, config_migrations.py:53-910).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/settings_db.py:364-385 — `init_db` runs `INSERT OR IGNORE` for every DEFAULTS row on every boot (so a newly added key appears) plus one hand-written value migration, `_migrate_retired_claude_default` (settings_db.py:345-362), which replaces only the shipped retired default and preserves an owner pin; no version column, no step registry, no record of what ran
capabilities.rationale: Additive seeding solves the easy half and the retired-Claude migration shows the right instinct (preserve the owner's pin, replace only the shipped default). What is missing is the other half: renaming a key, changing its `kind`, splitting a category, or retiring one, without either orphaning the owner's value or silently ignoring it. A version stamp in `state_meta` plus a small ordered step list is enough — copy the shape, not the 27-step ladder.
capabilities.governance: read-only

capabilities.name: Reset to defaults, scoped and previewed, plus export/import of the whole configuration
capabilities.hermes: The Config page has per-tab 'Reset {scope} to defaults' that only edits the form ('changes aren't written to config.yaml until you press Save'), 'Export config as JSON', 'Import config from JSON' ('Config imported — review and save'), and a raw YAML mode; `GET /api/config/defaults` serves DEFAULT_CONFIG so a UI can show changed-vs-default (22-config-b.md `config-b.web.config_page`, `config-b.api.config_endpoints`).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/routers/admin.py:127-131 — `POST /api/admin/settings/reseed` calls `init_db(force=True)`, which is `DELETE FROM settings` followed by a re-seed (agents/core/settings_db.py:364-370): global, immediate, unscoped, no confirmation, no preview, no undo. No defaults endpoint, no export, no import; the full data-root backup (agents/core/backup.py) does capture settings.db, and agents/core/data_export.py:39-40 deliberately excludes it from the owner data export.
capabilities.rationale: 'Reseed' is a one-click irreversible wipe of every owner decision on the box — money caps, autonomy mode, posture, plugin credentials — sitting behind a plain admin_guard. That is not a smaller version of Hermes's reset, it is a worse one. Make it scoped to a category, previewed as a diff against defaults, and irreversible-tier in the approval queue; add `GET /api/admin/settings/defaults` so the UI can mark changed keys, which is also what makes a JSON export/import meaningful.
capabilities.governance: privileged and irreversible — a full reset destroys owner policy, so it belongs behind the approval queue's irreversible tier, not behind a token

capabilities.name: Per-agent / per-surface configuration overrides that persist
capabilities.hermes: `platforms.<name>.*` and `gateway.platforms.*` blocks keyed by a user-chosen platform name, accepted wholesale by the validator because `PlatformConfig` carries an open `extra` map; `display.platforms.<x>.streaming` per channel; `channel_prompts` per Discord/Slack/Telegram/Mattermost channel with forum-parent and topic inheritance; `platform_toolsets` per surface; all persisted in config.yaml and bridged at gateway/config.py:1702-1760 (22-config-b.md `config-b.hidden.absent_top_level`, `config-b.hidden.shard_open_dicts`).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/config.py:31-52 — agents.yaml gives each agent a static model, tier, llm_policy, plugins and approved_models list, editable only by hand on disk; agents/web.py:692 — `_AGENT_SETTINGS = {}` is an in-memory dict that `PUT /api/admin/agents/{agent_id}` writes into (agents/core/routers/admin.py:433-442, returns `{"saved": true}`) and `_enrich_agents` reads back at agents/web.py:761 — nothing persists it, so every override is silently lost on restart
capabilities.rationale: The route reports success for a change that does not survive a reboot; that is a defect, not a gap, and it is in the surface an owner would use to pin an agent to a model. Persist the overrides into the settings store (they are already category/key shaped), validate them against the agent's `approved_models`, and let agents.yaml stay the shipped baseline the overrides layer over — which is the same defaults ⊕ user shape as row 1.
capabilities.governance: privileged — an override can change which model an agent runs on and which plugins it may call, so it crosses the same `config.write` mediation and must not be able to widen `approved_models`
capabilities.depends_on: the layered resolution row; the settings-write mediation row

capabilities.name: Per-internal-task model and provider assignment (auxiliary models)
capabilities.hermes: 115 `auxiliary.*` schema keys over 17 helper tasks — vision, compression, skills_hub, approval, mcp, title_generation, memory_query_rewrite, tts_audio_tags, triage_specifier, kanban_decomposer, profile_describer, goal_judge, curator, monitor, background_review, moa_reference, moa_aggregator — each taking model/provider/base_url/api_key/key_env/api_mode plus hidden `fallback_chain` (ordered `{provider, model}` candidates with model-scoped vs provider-wide skip semantics and a per-task minimum context length), `max_concurrency` (per-task semaphore), and `extra_body` forwarded verbatim on every call. The desktop Settings → Model tab surfaces it as 'Helper tasks run on the main model by default. Assign a dedicated model to any task to override.' (22-config-b.md §C, auxiliary_client.py:5247-9167).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/llm/hybrid_router.py:10-20, 443-503 — routing is per-agent and heuristic (fast local slot, deep LM Studio slot via JARVIS_AUTO_DEEP/JARVIS_DEEP_MODEL, cloud escalation by token thresholds and `llm.cloud_fallback`); agents/core/llm/vlm.py:191-208 — the vision helper is configured by env alone (JARVIS_VLM_BACKEND/_MODEL/_PRESET) and refuses rather than guessing; agents/core/settings_db.py memory.compression_summarizer is a bare boolean with no model selection; agents/core/config.py:44-48 approved_models pins per agent, not per helper task
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already runs at least five distinct helper workloads — vision/grounding, context compression, review/judge, memory query, title/naming — and an owner cannot say 'run vision on the 7B VLM, compression on the tiny local model, review on Claude'. That is precisely the knob that makes a local-first box affordable and fast, and it composes with Nerva's existing per-agent `approved_models` and daily cost cap. Copy the per-task override shape and the fallback chain; skip `extra_body` (provider-routing passthrough belongs to the providers cluster) and skip 12 of the 17 tasks Nerva does not have.
capabilities.governance: read-only (model selection), but a task pinned to a cloud provider must still obey `llm.cloud_fallback` and the strict-local floor at agents/core/llm/hybrid_router.py LOCAL_ONLY_AGENTS

capabilities.name: Config-driven data lifecycle — prune, archive, vacuum on an interval-gated sweep
capabilities.hermes: 13 `sessions.*` keys plus a parallel `checkpoints.*` block: `auto_prune`/`retention_days` (90) deletes ended sessions by last activity, `auto_archive`/`auto_archive_days` (3) soft-hides them and exempts pinned ones, `vacuum_after_prune`/`min_vacuum_interval_days` (30) runs SQLite VACUUM only when a prune actually deleted rows, and `min_interval_hours` (24) gates the whole sweep through a `state_meta` row shared across processes. Motivated by 384MB databases with 68K messages (22-config-b.md §T, gateway/run.py:7745-7790).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/settings_db.py `retention` category — enabled (default False) + conversation_ttl_days 90 / audit_ttl_days 365 / ingestion_ttl_days 0, with 'a TTL of 0 means keep forever'; agents/core/data_purge.py; agents/core/backup.py (nightly local backup via memory.backup_auto_enabled/backup_keep, with a real restore drill and `PRAGMA integrity_check`)
capabilities.rationale: The dangerous half — TTL-driven deletion, off by default, with 0 meaning keep-forever — is already there and matches Hermes's reasoning. What is missing is the cheap half: a reversible archive tier before deletion, a VACUUM step so a purge actually reclaims disk (SQLite does not on DELETE), and a shared last-run marker so the sweep does not repeat per process. Small, and it is the difference between 'we deleted rows' and 'the file got smaller'.
capabilities.governance: privileged and irreversible — a retention TTL change schedules deletion of owner data, so the setting write is exactly the case for the irreversible tier; the sweep itself is internal maintenance

capabilities.name: Fail-closed boot on malformed security-critical configuration
capabilities.hermes: `validate_config_structure` emits ✗/⚠ lines for a handful of YAML shape mistakes and prints 'Run hermes doctor for fix suggestions' — but 'any exception inside validation is swallowed (never blocks startup)', and `hermes config set` writes an unrecognised key anyway with only a 'did you mean' notice. Nothing in the config plane refuses to start (22-config-b.md `config-b.core.structure_validation`, `config-b.core.key_validation`).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/boot_guards.py:39 assert_safe_bind (non-loopback bind without a token refuses), :66 assert_hardened_posture (JARVIS_HARDENED=1 without JARVIS_AUDIT_KEY refuses), :83 assert_parseable_posture_flags (a typo in a parse-critical bool, or `JARVIS_TASK_MEDIATION=enfroce`, stops the boot naming the variable and the accepted spellings but never the value); agents/core/env_config.py:56-105 — one parse home where an unrecognised spelling resolves to the flag's declared default in both directions
capabilities.rationale: This is the single best piece of config engineering in either product: Nerva refuses to run a posture the operator did not ask for, where Hermes silently warns. The env_config module also fixes the eight divergent boolean conventions its own docstring documents. Keep, and extend the parse-critical list as new posture flags land rather than adding a second parse convention.
capabilities.governance: read-only

capabilities.name: An enumerated, inspectable environment-variable surface
capabilities.hermes: `OPTIONAL_ENV_VARS` and `ENV_VARS_BY_VERSION` are real registries: `hermes config check` prints 'Required:' and 'Optional:' with '✓ NAME' or dimmed '○ NAME → tool1, tool2' so an operator sees which vars are set and what each unlocks; migrations offer to configure vars introduced since the old version; `hermes config` masks keys in its summary and warns about stale `.env` lines ('run hermes doctor --fix'); `reload_env` re-reads and removes vanished vars, but only for known names (22-config-b.md `config-b.cli.config_check`, `config-b.core.dotenv_file`, `config-b.core.migrations`).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/env_config.py provides the typed getters (env_flag/env_str/env_list/env_int/env_float/env_json_object/env_int_map) but holds no registry of names; `rg -o 'JARVIS_[A-Z0-9_]+|NERVA_[A-Z0-9_]+' agents/ scripts/ | sort -u` yields 368 distinct names; .env.example carries 76; docs/FLAGS.md documents 5 sections covering roughly a dozen flags; scripts/doctor.py:219-235 checks python/venv/locks/bind/data-root/runtimes/readyz and never inspects the env surface or settings
capabilities.rationale: 368 environment variables govern this product and there is no list of them, no way to ask a running box which are set, and no way to learn what one unlocks short of grepping. The parse discipline is excellent and the documentation of it is nearly absent — that asymmetry is the honest finding here. A declared registry (name, type, default, what it enables, whether it is parse-critical) feeding a read-only status view and new doctor rows costs little and makes every other config surface diagnosable. Never print values — env_config's own module contract forbids it.
capabilities.governance: read-only — report set/unset and purpose, never the value

capabilities.name: Settings changes as governed, mediated actions
capabilities.hermes: None. `PUT /api/config` deep-merges and writes; `hermes config set` writes; nothing is recorded anywhere. The only control is the managed-scope refusal and the package-manager install lock, and the config plane has no audit trail at all (22-config-b.md `config-b.api.config_endpoints`, `config-b.core.save_config`).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/routers/admin.py:90-125 — every accepted write emits a SecurityEventType.SETTINGS_CHANGE audit event carrying the changed key names only, deliberately never the values; but agents/core/kernel/registry.py:32-130 has no `config.write`/`settings.write` kind, so the write never reaches kernel.authorize — meaning `autonomy.cap_per_action`/`daily_ceiling` (read at agents/core/autonomy/policy.py:116-237), `llm.cloud_fallback`, `ambient.enabled`, `acquisition.enabled`, `security.guardrails_mode` and the `retention.*` TTLs can all be changed on an admin token alone
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already beats Hermes on audit and is the only one of the two that could close this properly. Today the settings plane is the one place where Nerva's own differentiator is not applied to itself: raising the money cap is a privileged act that the kernel never sees, so it escapes the kill-switch, taint escalation and the irreversible-tier queue that guard every action the cap is supposed to bound. Add a `config.write` kind classified KERNEL, route the HTTP route, the future CLI and the reset path through it, and split the tier — a reversible toggle grants, a posture/cap/retention change queues.
capabilities.governance: privileged — a new `config.write` kind in ACTION_REGISTRY, KERNEL-classed, with policy-changing and data-deleting keys pinned to the irreversible tier so a kernel GRANT cannot lift them out of the approval queue
capabilities.depends_on: agents/core/kernel/registry.py (the kernel already exists; this is a classification plus a call site)

capabilities.name: Layered configuration load with a defined precedence order
capabilities.hermes: Six ordered layers resolved at every startup: inherited shell -> ~/.hermes/.env (override=True) -> ~/.hermes/.op.env (override=False, only if the bootstrap token is unset) -> project .env (override only when no user file existed) -> external vaults -> managed /etc/hermes/.env (override=True, deliberately last), then _reapply_terminal_config_bridge() re-asserts config.yaml-owned terminal.* keys over whatever .env supplied. hermes_cli/env_loader.py:468-560; entry env-vars.precedence. Long-lived processes re-run the whole load per turn, which is why the bridge is re-applied (issues #29186, #67323). HERMES_HOME / HERMES_PROFILE / XDG_* select which files those are.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/plugin_manager.py:73-82 (repo .env then <user home>/.env, both via load_dotenv, second with default override=False); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/paths.py:130 (copies .env.example into the user home on first run); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/env_config.py:26-31 (deliberately refuses to load dotenv itself, so import-time posture reads never see .env)
capabilities.rationale: Nerva has two layers and no stated precedence, no managed layer, no re-assertion of code-owned keys, and no reload — a value changed in .env needs a process restart because HybridRouter reads keys once at construction (agents/core/llm/hybrid_router.py:325). The layering instinct is sound and the refusal to dotenv-load inside env_config is better than Hermes; what is missing is an explicit, documented, testable order plus a reload path.
capabilities.governance: read-only at load time; a reload that re-reads credentials must not widen posture flags mid-process, so posture flags stay pinned at boot and only non-posture keys hot-reload

capabilities.name: Admin-pinned managed scope an owner-level edit cannot override
capabilities.hermes: $HERMES_MANAGED_DIR/.env, default /etc/hermes/.env, root-owned, applied LAST with override=True so it beats the user's file and any shell export. managed_scope.is_env_managed(key) is a predicate every writer consults, and save_env_value() refuses with 'Cannot set {key}: it is managed by your administrator ({src}) and cannot be changed.' (hermes_cli/config.py:4556). The inventory is honest that v1 enforcement is filesystem permissions only — an agent can still mutate os.environ in-process (design section 8.1). Entry env-vars.dotenv-managed, plus HERMES_MANAGED (coarse write lock) and HERMES_MANAGED_DIR.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — grep for MANAGED_DIR / is_env_managed / managed scope across /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/, scripts/, docs/ returns only the Hermes inventory files
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's own vision is a household brain, and a household has an owner and non-owner users. Without a pinnable layer there is no way to say 'this box may never talk to a cloud model' or 'the kill switch stays armed' in a way a later edit cannot quietly undo. It is also the only clean answer for the family/second-device story in NERVA_VISION.md. Copy the layer but fix Hermes' admitted v1 hole: make the pinned mapping authoritative in-process, not just on disk.
capabilities.governance: read-only itself, but it must be the floor the kernel reads: a pinned posture key has to be unwritable by the config.write action kind, and the refusal must be an audited event
capabilities.depends_on: the layered load with a stated precedence order

capabilities.name: Configure Nerva from the product — write a key or setting and have it take effect
capabilities.hermes: One writer used by every surface (CLI setup, dashboard Keys page, MCP installer, plugin setup): save_env_value() / save_env_value_secure() / reload_env() / get_env_value() / get_env_value_prefer_dotenv() (hermes_cli/config.py:4544-4823). Writes are name-validated, CR/LF-stripped, credential-ASCII-checked, quoted, and applied by rewriting the first matching KEY= or export KEY= line atomically; reload_env() returns the count of changed vars and deletes known Hermes keys that disappeared from the file. capabilities.hermes: `tools/budget_config.py` resolves a per-tool threshold (pinned → override → `mcp_` prefix → the entry's own `max_result_size_chars` → default), then `tool_result_storage.py` **spills** an oversized result to disk and substitutes a ~1,500-char preview whose footer carries the file path. `budget_for_context_window(n)` scales the caps to the model's actual window (15% per result, 30% per turn, floors 8k/16k) instead of a constant. `PINNED_THRESHOLDS={"read_file": inf}` breaks the persist→read→persist loop. `tools/tool_output_limits.py` centralises `tool_output.max_bytes` (50k), `max_lines` (2000), `max_line_length` (2000). Rolls up 2 entries.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/environments/output_limits.py (`truncate_text` — head+tail, byte-accounted, explicitly documented as "for future execute_code transports"); agents/core/agent_runtime.py:69 (a single flat `max_result_bytes=50_000` for every tool, no per-turn budget, no spill)
capabilities.rationale: Nerva truncates and throws the rest away; Hermes spills and keeps it recoverable. For Nerva that difference is not just ergonomics — a truncated `file_read` or a truncated governed `terminal_run` transcript means the *audit* record and the model's view diverge, and the owner reviewing an approval sees less than the tool produced. Spill-to-disk with the path in the preview, plus a per-turn budget scaled to the local model's real (usually small) context window, is worth more on Nerva's local-first models than on Hermes's cloud ones.
capabilities.governance: read-only
capabilities.depends_on: a data-root path convention for spilled results + retention/GC (same gap the file-tool snapshots already have)

capabilities.name: Stop a model that is looping on the same tool call
capabilities.hermes: `agent/tool_guardrails.py` (854 lines) hashes (tool, canonical args, result) per turn: a notice fires on the 3rd consecutive identical call; from the 2nd byte-identical result, payloads ≥512 chars are replaced by a reference stub carrying a 120-char args preview — and error results are NEVER stubbed, so the model sees each fresh failure verbatim. Separate counters for exact-failure (warn 2 / stop 5), same-tool-failure (3/8) and no-progress (2/5); hard stops are opt-in so interactive sessions only get a nudge. Pollers (`process`, `*_poll`, `*_get_result`) are exempt. Rolls up 1 entry.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/iteration_budget.py (a flat consume/refund counter, itself ported from hermes-agent per its own docstring); agents/core/agent_runtime.py:78 (`max_tool_calls_per_turn`), :70 (`max_wall_seconds=120`), :221 (`tool_loop_exhausted` event). No identical-call detection, no duplicate-result stubbing, no failure-class counters
capabilities.rationale: Nerva only has blunt caps: it stops the loop after N turns without ever telling the model *why* it is stuck. On a local 7B–30B model — Nerva's default, and weaker at self-correction than the frontier models Hermes assumes — repeat-call looping is the dominant failure mode, so the fine-grained version pays off more here. It also has a governance payoff Hermes does not claim: a runaway loop that repeatedly proposes a gated action currently floods the owner's approval queue; loop detection upstream of the queue is cheaper than the kernel's loop denial downstream.
capabilities.governance: read-only (decision-only module; the runtime turns decisions into guidance or halts)

capabilities.name: Run shell commands and manage long-running processes
capabilities.hermes: `terminal` — foreground or `background=true`, optional PTY, completion notifications, per-env-type backends (local / docker / singularity / ssh / vercel_sandbox), stdout capped at `tool_output.max_bytes` (50k). `process` (`tools/process_registry.py`, 3,491 lines) then owns the background lifecycle: poll status, read logs, wait, write to stdin, kill, with `proc_<hex>` ids resolvable by any unique prefix. `read_terminal` reads the in-app terminal pane with scrollback paging; `close_terminal` drops the mirrored GUI tab without killing the process. Rolls up 4 entries.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy_coordinator.py:520 (`terminal_run`, gated + `trusted_execution=True`, requires a durable owner-accepted task — `_durable_terminal_approval` re-reads the queue rather than trusting the caller); agents/core/environments/{execution,targets,terminal_contract,local_transport}.py (named governed targets, docker transport, audit-chained policy plane); docs/FLAGS.md:346 (`JARVIS_TERMINAL_TARGETS`, default off; ssh still returns `ssh_transport_not_implemented`)
capabilities.rationale: The governance rail is genuinely better than Hermes's approval prompt — a Nerva command cannot run without a durable, human-accepted, audit-chained row, and the task id comes from a contextvar rather than the model's args. But the capability is a single fire-and-forget synchronous call: no background execution, no process registry, no log tailing, no stdin, no kill. That makes every long job (a build, a training run, a server) unusable, and it is precisely the class of work an autonomous house agent should be doing overnight. Build background+process on top of the existing governed-target rail, with one approval covering the spawn and the kill available un-approved (stopping is always safe).
capabilities.governance: privileged — `toolrpc.terminal_run` ask-tier task, Action Kernel `authorize`, audit chain. Background spawn must cross the same kind; poll/read/kill of an already-approved process should be classified INTENTIONALLY_DIRECT
capabilities.depends_on: kernel + approval queue (exist); result spill-to-disk (row 5) for log tailing

capabilities.name: Read files and search a codebase
capabilities.hermes: `read_file` — line-numbered, paginated (`offset`/`limit`, 1-indexed), auto-extracts readable text from common document formats (PDF/docx/…), per-line cap `tool_output.max_line_length`, and is the one tool pinned to an infinite spill threshold so persist→read→persist cannot loop. `search_files` — ripgrep-backed content regex OR glob file-finding, explicitly the replacement for `grep`/`rg`/`find`/`ls` in the terminal, `max_result_size_chars=100_000`. Rolls up 2 entries.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/file_tools.py:790 (`file_read`), :806 (`file_list`) — ungated inside `JARVIS_FILE_ROOTS`, no `..`, no symlink escape, secret-looking names refused, bytes/entries bounded; docs/FLAGS.md:349 (`JARVIS_FILE_TOOLS` default off, root defaults to `<data root>/workspace`)
capabilities.rationale: The containment (rooted, symlink-safe, secret-name-refusing, byte-bounded) is better than Hermes's, which just inherits the terminal backend's reach. What is missing is the workhorse: there is no content search. Without `search_files` the model's only way to find something is to list and read files one at a time, which burns the context budget Nerva's local models can least afford — or to shell out through `terminal_run`, which means an approval prompt for a read-only grep. Adding rooted ripgrep search is the highest value-per-line item in this whole cluster. Document-format extraction is the smaller half and should follow.
capabilities.governance: read-only, but the root scope IS the security boundary — search must honour the identical `JARVIS_FILE_ROOTS` / symlink / secret-name rules as file_read, not reimplement them
capabilities.depends_on: agents/core/file_tools.py path-resolution helpers (exist and must be reused, not forked)

capabilities.name: Write and precisely edit files
capabilities.hermes: `write_file` — full replacement, parent dirs auto-created. `patch` — targeted find-and-replace with fuzzy matching (`tools/fuzzy_match.py`, 49 KB, "9 strategies") so whitespace/indentation drift does not break an edit; returns a unified diff and auto-runs syntax checks after editing; a dynamic schema layers in the OpenAI-family V4A `apply_patch` dialect for models trained on it. Both are `FILE_MUTATING_TOOL_NAMES` for interrupt-resume. Rolls up 2 entries.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/file_tools.py:821 (`file_write`), :840 (`file_delete`) — both gated ask-tier (`toolrpc.file_write` / `toolrpc.file_delete`), trusted-execution only, kernel kind `file.write`, `FILE_WRITE_CONTRACT`, previous bytes snapshotted before the touch and reversible via `restore_snapshot(ref)` (manifest rollback mode `restore`); no patch/diff tool anywhere
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's write path is materially superior — snapshot-then-write with a real rollback ref and a kernel crossing is something Hermes has no equivalent of. But whole-file replacement is the wrong primitive for the work: to change one line the model must first read the entire file into context and then write the entire file back, which doubles token cost, and — worse for governance — presents the owner with a full-file diff to approve instead of the three lines that actually changed. A `file_patch` tool makes the approval card legible, which is the point of the approval card. Snapshots still have no retention/GC (per FLAGS.md); patch will multiply them, so ship GC with it.
capabilities.governance: privileged — must land as a gated ask-tier `toolrpc.file_patch` on kernel kind `file.write`, snapshotting before the edit exactly as file_write does. A patch tool that writes outside that rail would be a regression even though it is 'just an edit'

capabilities.name: Let the model write a script that orchestrates many tool calls
capabilities.hermes: `execute_code` — Python in a persistent session kernel (variables/imports/loaded data survive across calls) that imports a generated `hermes_tools` module whose stubs marshal args over an RPC socket to the real tools: `web_search`, `web_extract`, `read_file`, `write_file`, `search_files`, `patch`, `terminal`, … The stated purpose is 3+ tool calls with logic between them — filter a huge output BEFORE it enters context, branch, loop. 5-minute timeout, 50 tool calls per invocation; stdout over 50 KB spills to a file whose path rides in the result. Rolls up 1 entry.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/tool_rpc.py:1-22 (the module's own docstring names this "the biggest net capability from hermes-agent"); agents/core/tool_rpc_runtime.py (`ToolRPCSandboxRuntime` — file-RPC transport, host-serviced, `max_tool_calls=50`, deadline that never fires before the sandbox's own timeout); agents/core/sandbox.py (docker/wasm backends); agents/core/environments/file_rpc.py. Reachable ONLY from agents/core/routers/skills.py:76 `POST /sandbox/execute` — it is NOT registered as a tool on the allowlist, so the model cannot invoke it
capabilities.rationale: Nerva built the hard, security-critical two-thirds of this and then never opened the door. The governance design is better than Hermes's: inside the sandbox a gated tool cannot execute at all — it returns `approval_required` — so a script physically cannot escalate, and every response is secret-scrubbed before crossing back. What is missing is the model-facing `execute_code` tool itself, plus kernel state persistence across calls. The zero-context-cost pipeline is the biggest single multiplier for a local-model product, because it is how you avoid paying context for data the model only needs to filter.
capabilities.governance: privileged — registering `execute_code` on the allowlist must keep the existing invariant that gated tools called from inside the sandbox only ever enqueue. The tool itself is ungated only because that invariant holds; if it ever weakened, execute_code becomes an arbitrary-effect tool
capabilities.depends_on: the ToolRPC allowlist and sandbox (both exist); result spill (row 5) for stdout

capabilities.hermes: 13 tools: `browser_navigate` (returns a compact snapshot with `@e1` ref ids), `browser_snapshot` (accessibility tree), `browser_click`/`browser_type`/`browser_press`/`browser_scroll`/`browser_back` (ref-id addressed), `browser_vision` (screenshot for CAPTCHAs and layout questions the text snapshot misses), `browser_get_images` (URL+alt inventory to hand to vision_analyze), `browser_console` (console output, uncaught exceptions, and JS evaluation), `browser_dialog` (accept/dismiss a blocking alert/confirm/prompt/beforeunload), `browser_cdp` (raw Chrome DevTools Protocol escape hatch), `browser_exec` (arbitrary Python against a persistent Browser Use CLI session). Rolls up 13 entries.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/browser_agent.py:36 (`READ_ONLY={navigate, extract, screenshot, wait}`), :43 (`RISKY={click, type, submit, download, execute_js, upload}`); agents/core/browser_playwright.py:394 `observe_snapshot` (aria_snapshot with boxes → bounded ref'd elements), :347-499 (navigate/extract/screenshot/wait/click/type/submit/execute_js/upload/download); agents/core/browser_kernel.py (the Action Kernel gate for a browser step); agents/core/browser_transport.py (IP-pinned `--host-resolver-rules` so Chromium cannot escape the SSRF-validated resolution); agents/core/routers/browser.py (only `/api/browser/check` and `/api/browser/plan/preview`). capabilities.name: Look at an image or a video and answer a question about it
capabilities.hermes: `vision_analyze` — loads an image INTO the conversation so a natively-multimodal model can see it, or falls back to an auxiliary model's textual analysis when the main model has no vision; auto chain main → openrouter → nous. `video_analyze` — sends a video (URL or local path) to a video-capable multimodal model. Both ride the `{"_multimodal": True, "content": [...]}` dispatch envelope, which is what makes 'the model actually sees it' possible. Rolls up 2 entries.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/routers/multimodal.py:38 (`GET /api/vlm/status`), :72 (`POST /api/vlm/describe`), :107 (`POST /api/screen/reflex`); agents/core/screen_grounding.py (UI-TARS / Qwen3-VL via the H13.1 VLM adapter); agents/core/screen_locator.py. No model-callable tool, and agents/core/tool_rpc.py returns JSON only — there is no multimodal result envelope, so no tool can hand the model an image
capabilities.rationale: The VLM adapter is real and local-first, which is the right architecture. Two things block it from being a capability: no tool, and — the deeper one — the dispatch contract is text-only. capabilities.name: Ask the user a question and wait for the answer
capabilities.hermes: `clarify` — 1–5 questions (single-select with a '(Recommended)' first choice and an auto-appended 'Other' free-text row, multi-select, or open-ended), delivered through the platform's blocking-prompt bridge and rendered as a form on messaging platforms; blocks until answered, returning `{responses: [...]}` in question order plus `timed_out: true` if the user walked away. capabilities.rationale: Nerva's approval queue answers 'may I do this?' and has no way to ask 'which of these did you mean?'. A blocking clarify with recommended choices is the cheap upstream fix, and it composes with what already exists: the same delivery bridge as the approval card, the same channels, the same audit record. Adopt Hermes's rule that a subagent cannot call it — a background worker must not be able to block on a human.

capabilities.name: Search what was said in past sessions
capabilities.hermes: `session_search` — SQLite FTS5 over past sessions, or read/scroll inside one; results are ACTUAL DB messages with no LLM summarisation; cross-profile reads via a `profile` argument. Rolls up 1 entry.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — agents/core/routers/sessions.py exposes only `/sessions` (list) and `/sessions/resume`; agents/core/persistence/ has json_store.py + migrations.py with no full-text index; agents/core/memory/ holds semantic recall (embeddings/KG), which answers a different question
capabilities.rationale: Semantic recall and transcript search are not substitutes. capabilities.governance: read-only, but cross-session reads must respect data_spaces / retention scoping — a transcript search must not become a way around agents/core/retention.py or data_purge.py
capabilities.depends_on: a session transcript store with an FTS index (persistence/ currently json_store only)

capabilities.hermes: 15 entries: a shared kanban with `kanban_create` (fan-out, optionally as a child of the current task), `kanban_list`/`kanban_show` (orchestrators discover and re-orient, especially on retries), `kanban_comment` (durable notes outliving the run), `kanban_heartbeat` (liveness so humans can tell 'working' from 'hung' without PID checks), `kanban_block`/`kanban_unblock` (stop and route BY WHY the worker is stuck), `kanban_request_review`/`kanban_request_changes`/`kanban_complete` (a real review cycle with structured handoff), `kanban_link` (parent→child dependency edges), and `kanban_attach`/`kanban_attach_url`/`kanban_attachments` (real files under the task, not comment links) — plus shared gating and delegated-child rejection. Rolls up 15 entries.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/{executor,inbox,escalation,followups,action_approvals,company_planner,company_runtime,company_supervisor,dry_run}.py (the durable governed task queue); agents/core/routers/missions.py (create/start/pause/resume/complete/cancel + per-step finish); agents/core/routers/swarm.py + `/mission-control`; agents/core/workflows/{engine,hierarchical,pipeline,pending_queue,guardrail_node}.py; agents/core/subagents.py spawn records. capabilities.name: Compaction inside the running turn (preflight, pre-API, idle, micro, fail-closed)
capabilities.hermes: Five distinct trigger points, not one: a preflight gate at turn start when the assembled request already exceeds the threshold; a pre-API gate re-checked before EVERY model call so a turn that grew by several large tool results compacts before the provider rejects it; idle-triggered compaction when a session resumes after a long gap; post-turn micro-compaction that absorbs the oldest exchange so the cost is amortised instead of batched into one pause; and PreflightCompressionTimedOut, which fails CLOSED — an oversized turn is stopped rather than sent unchanged. Around them: compression_made_progress() as a material-progress predicate, an anti-thrash budget rearm that only restores attempts after a provider proves a compaction worked, a post-compaction reference-handoff guard, reanchor_current_turn_user_idx(), and a context-overflow-blocked warning. Entries: agent-core-a.preflight-compression, .pre-api-compression, .idle-compaction, .micro-compaction, .preflight-timeout, .compression-progress, .compression-rearm, .handoff-guard, .reanchor-user-idx, .overflow-blocked-warning, .flush-baseline, .synthetic-user-turns.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: Compression runs in exactly one place and only when assembling history for a prompt: agents/core/orchestrator.py:2305 _history_for_prompt, gated by memory.context_compression (default off). The tool loop at agents/core/agent_runtime.py:137 _run_loop appends an assistant message plus one tool message per call across up to 32 iterations (_MAX_ITERATIONS=32, agents/core/agent_runtime.py:30) and never measures or compacts that list — agent_runtime.py does not import context_compressor at all.
capabilities.rationale: This is the concrete failure the whole compaction policy was written to prevent, left open on the one path that actually grows fast. A desktop-operator or coding turn that takes twenty screenshots or twenty file reads inside one tool loop will blow a 32k local window and the provider will truncate the TAIL — the half that says what is happening now. The policy object already exists; what is missing is calling it before each model call in the loop and failing closed on timeout instead of sending an oversized payload.
capabilities.governance: read-only, but a fail-closed stop must return through the same controlled-exit seam the loop already uses (agents/core/agent_runtime.py:26 _DEADLINE_REPLY) so the owner sees a reason rather than a truncation.
capabilities.depends_on: row 5 (the policy) — the compressor exists, the trigger points do not

capabilities.name: Recovery from an empty or truncated model response
capabilities.hermes: A layered ladder rather than a single check: agent.empty_response_guard detects a deterministically-empty completion and stops re-billing for it, halving the retry budget when one attempt is expensive; post-tool empty-response recovery reuses prior-turn content, then nudges, then switches provider, then terminates with an explicit "(empty)"; a finish_reason=="length" continuation chain stitches up to four fragments together with a doubling output budget; a thinking-budget-exhaustion guard detects the case where every output token went to reasoning and stops instead of burning continuations; intent-ack continuation auto-continues a bare "I will now do X" with no tool call; plus Codex/Responses continuation nudges. Entries: agent-core-a.empty-response-guard, .empty-response-recovery, .length-continuation, .thinking-exhausted, .intent-ack-continuation, .intent-ack-detection, .codex-nudges, .stall-guards.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/llm/base.py:350 _finalize_stream and :410 _finalize_lmstudio_message DROP a truncated answer: on finish=="length" with no visible content they log a warning and return "". There is no continuation, no empty-retry budget and no intent-ack continuation anywhere in agents/core/llm/ or agents/core/agent_runtime.py. The 2026-08-28 delta-port doc deferred Hermes' empty_response_guard with the reason "Nerva's LLM layer has no empty-retry loop — the guard would protect a mechanism we don't have"; that is still true (docs/research/2026-08-28-hermes-v2026.8.27-delta-port.md:39).
capabilities.rationale: Local models hit max_tokens far more often than frontier models do, and Nerva's current answer to that is to give the owner nothing at all. Silently returning "" after spending the full output budget is the worst of both — the cost is paid and the answer is discarded. The continuation chain is the part that matters; the deferred empty-response guard becomes a mechanical port once the retry loop it protects exists.
capabilities.governance: read-only, with one rule: a provider switch inside the recovery ladder must respect the local-first policy — agents/core/llm/hybrid_router.py:456 already forbids a cloud fallback for archive/strict-local routes and the ladder must not become a way around it.
capabilities.depends_on: nothing (the repetition guard already gates the degenerate case)

capabilities.name: Repetition-loop guard on truncated output
capabilities.hermes: agent/repetition_guard.py refuses to continue or deliver a truncated response whose visible text is dominated by verbatim repeats, so a degenerate model loop cannot flood the user. Entry: agent-core-a.repetition-guard.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/llm/repetition_guard.py — a near-verbatim port (MIN_FRAGMENT_LENGTH=400, 60-char repeat window, 0.5 dominance ratio, plus a cheap line-repetition fast path Hermes does not have), wired into both finalizers at agents/core/llm/base.py:362 and :418. Recorded as a completed port in docs/research/2026-08-28-hermes-v2026.8.27-delta-port.md:32.
capabilities.rationale: Already at parity and licence-clean (LICENSES/hermes-agent-MIT.txt). The one thing to revisit is placement: once row 7 lands, the guard should also gate the continuation decision, not only the delivery decision.
capabilities.governance: read-only.

capabilities.name: Failure taxonomy with per-class recovery and a stable error surface
capabilities.hermes: FailoverReason names why an API call failed; ClassifiedError carries the reason plus the recovery hints so the retry loop never re-classifies; classify_api_error() runs the pipeline over provider exceptions against explicit pattern tables; error_surface maps the internal taxonomy onto a small stable descriptor a UI can render as "Provider error" vs "Gateway error"; TurnRetryState collapses ~16 one-shot recovery guards into one testable object; retry_utils does decorrelated jittered backoff and Retry-After parsing with a provider-specific long-backoff schedule; plus content-policy refusal handling, a billing/entitlement terminal result naming the exact billing page, a Nous-Portal rate-limit pre-call guard, an Ollama context-too-small early exit, an outer-loop error cap distinguishing a deterministic local bug from a transient API failure, and stream diagnostics recording CDN edge / bytes / chunks / transport error class. Entries: agent-core-a.failover-reason, .classified-error, .classify-api-error, .classifier-patterns, .error-surface, .error-types, .turn-retry-state, .retry-utils, .content-policy, .billing-failure, .nous-rate-guard, .ollama-context-error, .outer-error-cap, .stream-diag, .thinking-timeout.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/resilience.py:14 resilient_call (retry decorator with backoff) and :132 CircuitBreaker plus :239 ResilienceMetrics; agents/core/llm/provider_errors.py exposes only provider_http_status() and a status-only logger — deliberately no text inspection, therefore no taxonomy; agents/core/llm/hybrid_router.py:466-531 has cloud/local fallback modes but chooses by policy, not by failure class. Failures reach the user as raw strings: agents/core/orchestrator.py:2452 returns f"[{agent_id} error: {e}]" and :2436 returns "[{agent_id} timeout]".
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's status-only logging is the right privacy call and should stay, but classification and logging are different jobs: right now a rate limit, an out-of-credit account, a content refusal and a genuine bug all produce the same bracketed string and the same retry behaviour. A small taxonomy (rate-limited / overloaded / context-overflow / content-policy / entitlement / local-bug) driving both the retry policy and one structured error descriptor is what turns those into distinguishable outcomes for the HUD and mobile.
capabilities.governance: read-only. The descriptor must stay redaction-safe — it names a class, never a provider body (agents/core/llm/provider_errors.py already sets that precedent).

capabilities.name: Steering, redirecting and interrupting the live turn
capabilities.hermes: A mid-turn /steer is drained on the CURRENT iteration rather than after the next tool batch; STEER_CHANNEL_NOTE defines a trusted wrapper so the model treats the injection as a real user instruction and never re-acts on replayed copies; apply_pending_steer_to_tool_results() delivers it by appending to the last tool result of the batch; _apply_active_turn_redirect() cancels the running request, records the displayed partial as an interrupted assistant row, appends the correction as a real user message and re-runs the same logical iteration; an interrupt-while-waiting prefix lets surfaces recognise cancellation as control metadata rather than prose; request_hard_interrupt() handles the ABI. Entries: agent-core-b.subagent-steer, .subagent-stop, agent-core-a.steer-drain, .turn-redirect, .steer-marker, .post-batch-steer, .interrupt-waiting, .interrupt-compat.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: Steer/stop exist, but only for children: agents/core/subagents.py:119 SteerMessage with a declared origin, :144 SteerChannel, :482 steer(), :504 stop(), exposed at agents/core/routers/mesh.py:258 POST /api/subagents/{spawn_id}/stop. The owner's own running turn has no steer, no redirect and no interrupt — agents/core/agent_runtime.py:104 run() only exposes a wall-clock deadline, and there is no cancel route for a chat turn in agents/core/routers/.
capabilities.rationale: The child can be corrected mid-flight but the agent the owner is actually talking to cannot. On a hub whose long turns are exactly the risky ones (a desktop operator sequence, a night run), the ability to say "no, not that folder" without killing the turn is a safety feature, not an ergonomic one. The origin/never-an-approval rule is already written and tested in subagents.py and should be reused verbatim.
capabilities.governance: read-only in itself, but load-bearing for governance: agents/core/subagents.py documents that a steer message is NEVER an approval — approvals only come from a human decision on a queue row. The main-turn version must carry the same invariant, or steering becomes a side channel around the approval queue.

capabilities.name: Turn exit reasons, a completion explainer and per-turn accounting
capabilities.hermes: _turn_exit_reason records why the outer loop ended and a diagnostic line logs it at INFO — or at WARNING when the agent stopped with a pending tool result (the "it just stops" case users report). A turn-completion explainer gives the user ONE consolidated reason instead of a blank response box. A file-mutation verifier footer names the write_file/patch calls that failed this turn and were never superseded, so the model cannot over-claim "every file edited". TurnSummaryCollector renders a per-turn accounting line from the tool-progress feed, and format_token_flow() shows cumulative output tokens live. Entries: agent-core-a.turn-exit-reasons, .turn-exit-log, .turn-completion-explainer, .file-mutation-footer, .turn-summary-line, .token-flow, .turn-result-dict, .finalize-turn, .guardrail-halt, .persistence-failure.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: Telemetry is good: agents/core/cognition_trace.py builds a per-turn decision/scoring trace, agents/core/run_history.py keeps a per-agent ring, agents/core/cost_tracker.py:202 records tokens, agents/core/observability/north_star.py computes the KPIs. What is missing is the user-facing half: no consolidated stop reason and no failed-write footer. The seed exists as three fixed strings — agents/core/agent_runtime.py:26 _DEADLINE_REPLY, :25 _APPROVAL_REPLY and :215 the safety-limit message.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already computes everything needed; it just never tells the owner. The file-mutation footer is the one that matters most given this repo's own honesty debt — a ✅ that means DELIVERED-not-PROVEN is the same failure mode as a model claiming it edited files whose writes failed. Turning the three fixed strings into a small typed exit-reason enum surfaced in the HUD is a day's work.
capabilities.governance: read-only.
capabilities.depends_on: row 9 (exit reasons and error classes share a vocabulary)

capabilities.name: Tool-loop guardrails: repeated-failure detection, per-tool loop caps, identical-call stall breaker
capabilities.hermes: tool_loop_guardrails detects a turn stuck repeating the same failing or non-progressing tool call, with separate warn and halt thresholds and a controlled halt the user can distinguish from a crash; loop_caps sets hard per-turn ceilings on individual runaway-prone tools; a consecutive-streak tracker emits both a loop-breaker notice on the tool result and result-reference stubs so an identical repeat returns a pointer instead of re-sending the payload; tool-failure recovery hints turn a repeated failure into actionable next steps rather than a scold; and a classification fallback decides whether a result counts as a failure when the caller did not say. Entries: agent-core-b.tool-loop-guardrails, .loop-caps, .identical-call-guard, .tool-failure-hints, .classify-tool-failure, agent-core-a.tool-loop-guardrails, .guardrail-config, .guardrail-halt, .stall-guards.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: The tool loop's only defence is a count: agents/core/agent_runtime.py:177 IterationBudget(limit) with _DEFAULT_ITERATIONS=8 / _MAX_ITERATIONS=32, plus a per-call timeout and a byte cap. Nothing inspects whether successive calls are identical or making progress. agents/core/kernel/budget.py:165 LoopDetector does exist but it is a loop-wide circuit breaker over privileged ACTION signatures at the kernel front door — it never sees a read-only tool called nine times with the same arguments.
capabilities.rationale: An iteration cap answers "how long" but not "is this going anywhere"; on a local model the difference is a turn that burns all 32 iterations re-reading the same file and then reports a safety-limit stop. The kernel's LoopDetector is the right shape and the wrong altitude — the same idea belongs one level down, on tool-call signatures inside the loop.
capabilities.governance: read-only advisory inside the loop; when the guardrail halts, it must return through the existing controlled-exit path (agents/core/agent_runtime.py:215) rather than raising, so the halt is reported and audited like any other stop. It complements rather than replaces the kernel LoopDetector.
capabilities.depends_on: row 11 (a halt needs an exit reason to report)

capabilities.name: Untrusted tool results wrapped as data, not instructions
capabilities.hermes: Content retrieved from external sources is wrapped so a poisoned page cannot issue instructions; an upstream-elision notice warns the model when a result carries provider-side "there is more data" markers; tool-output risk metadata classifies attacker-controlled output as internal advisory metadata. Entries: agent-core-b.untrusted-wrap, .upstream-elision, .tool-output-risk.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: The engine is present and stronger than Hermes': agents/core/security/quarantine.py:74 spotlight() emits a <<UNTRUSTED source=…>> block with datamarking, an explicit "DATA, not instructions" line and injection flags; taint tracking (agents/core/security/taint.py, recall_taint.py) escalates a kernel GRANT to QUEUE when a payload is tainted (docs/FLAGS.md, agents/core/kernel/__init__.py:224). But it is not wired into the live loop: agents/core/agent_runtime.py:448 _prepare_result serialises the raw tool result straight into the message list, and the only callers of spotlight() are agents/core/routers/security.py:66.
capabilities.rationale: This is the largest security gap in the cluster and the cheapest to close, because the defence already exists and is tested — it is simply not called on the path where untrusted bytes actually enter the conversation. A ToolRPC result from a web fetch, an MCP server or a channel inbox currently reaches the model unmarked and untainted, which also means the taint escalation that protects the kernel never fires for tool-sourced content.
capabilities.governance: directly governance-bearing. Marking a tool result untrusted is what makes taint propagate into the kernel decision, so a plan assembled from a fetched page gets forced back to ASK instead of executing on a GRANT.

capabilities.name: Concurrent tool dispatch with a serialized approval gate and bounded results
capabilities.hermes: Parallel tool-batch planning decides which calls in one assistant batch may run concurrently and splits the rest; concurrent execution runs the admitted batch with ordered start gating; a concurrent-tool authorization gate serialises approval prompts so they do not interleave; an in-flight activity heartbeat keeps the turn-inactivity watchdog from abandoning a silent but working tool; cancelled and timed-out calls get synthetic results so no call is left unanswered; a tool-result persistence budget stops one oversized result from pushing the request over the limit; tool-search scope enforcement stops a restricted-toolset session unwrapping a tool it was not granted. Missing relative to Hermes: batch-level planning (which calls are safe to parallelise), an in-flight heartbeat, and a whole-turn result budget rather than a per-result cap.

The remaining deltas are performance and watchdog concerns that only bite once row 6 and row 12 land, so they should ride along with those rather than becoming their own slice.
capabilities.governance: already correct: every gated call reaches the kernel through ToolRPC (tool.rpc in agents/core/kernel/registry.py:56) and an approval_required outcome ends the loop rather than proceeding.
