capabilities.name: Delegation durability and observability: background fan-out, crash recovery, exactly-once delivery, live transcripts
capabilities.hermes: A background (async) delegation registry runs a whole fan-out detached from the turn and delivers ONE completion event; durable recovery reports honestly when the owning process died instead of leaving a phantom; delivery claims make completion exactly-once across competing consumers and processes; a stale-delegation monitor catches a batch wedged before returning; live tail -f-able transcripts stream each child's operations to cache/delegation/live/; tool_trace records what tools a child called and how big the payloads were; a timeout diagnostic dump explains what a child was doing when it hung; a summary budget with truncation and spill stops a fan-out blowing the parent's context; a cross-agent stale-file reminder tells the parent when a child modified a file it had already read. Entries: agent-core-b.async-delegation, .delegation-recovery, .delegation-delivery-claims, .delegation-status-listing, .async-stall-monitor, .live-transcripts, .tool-trace, .timeout-diagnostic, .summary-budget, .result-contract, .stale-file-reminder, .child-heartbeat, .subagent-complete-event, .delegate-events, .delegate-console, .subagent-identity-kwargs, .review-input-budget.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/subagents.py holds spawns in an in-process dict (self._spawns, :330) with an optional observability-only JSONL append behind JARVIS_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_LOG (:64, default off) and the docstring is explicit that "nothing is replayed from it". A process restart loses every running spawn; there is no delivery claim, no stale monitor, no per-child transcript and no tool_trace. Nerva's durable unit is the autonomy queue row (agents/core/autonomy/queue.py), which is a different granularity.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's night-shift and company-mode ambitions mean fan-outs that outlive a turn and sometimes a process. Today a crashed hub leaves a child's work unaccounted for and unreported, which is a worse failure than not spawning at all — the owner is told nothing. The delivery-claim and durable-recovery pieces are the ones that turn delegation from a demo into something you can run overnight; live transcripts are what make it debuggable when it goes wrong at 03:00.
capabilities.governance: read-only in itself, but it is an audit surface: a completion delivered exactly once and a child whose tool trace is recorded are what let the hash-chained log (agents/core/security/audit.py) account for work a subagent did. Children performing privileged effects already cross the kernel; this makes that crossing legible after the fact.
capabilities.depends_on: row 15 (the spawn manager) and the autonomy queue for durable rows

capabilities.name: Git-worktree isolation for delegated children
capabilities.hermes: delegation.worktree_isolation gives each delegated child its own git worktree branched from the parent's HEAD, so concurrent children editing the same repo cannot corrupt each other's tree. Entry: agent-core-b.worktree-isolation.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — agents/core/routers/swarm.py carries dev locks for coordination, and agents/core/environments/ has file-RPC scoping, but nothing branches a worktree per child. grep for worktree across agents/ returns nothing.
capabilities.rationale: Company mode's whole premise is several agents working a repo at once. Advisory dev locks stop two agents editing the same file; they do not stop two agents building on each other's half-finished tree, and the failure looks like a mysterious test failure rather than a conflict. A worktree per child makes the isolation physical instead of cooperative, and it makes a child's work reviewable as a branch — which fits the approval posture better than an in-place edit does.
capabilities.governance: creating a worktree writes to disk outside the data root, so it crosses file.write (agents/core/kernel/registry.py:118); the branch it produces is the reversible artefact the approval queue can act on.
capabilities.depends_on: row 16 (durable child lifecycle) and file.write kernel mediation

capabilities.name: Background self-improvement review after a turn
capabilities.hermes: A post-turn daemon-thread fork replays a conversation snapshot and proposes memory/skill updates. build_cache_parity_fork() makes the fork's outbound request byte-identical to the parent's so the provider cache stays warm; review-fork model routing lets it run on a cheaper model with digest replay of long history; separate memory-only / skill-only / combined prompts; a /refine focus block; a dispatch-time tool whitelist; a review action summary line; result classification and a completion log; usage attributed back to the parent session; and cancellation the moment a new user turn arrives. Entries: agent-core-b.background-review, .cache-parity-fork, .review-routing, .memory-review-prompt, .skill-review-prompt, .combined-review-prompt, .refine-focus, .review-whitelist, .review-action-summary, .review-classification, .review-usage-attribution, .review-cancellation.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/learning/background_review.py + agents/core/orchestrator.py:2087 _spawn_background_review / :2110 _background_review_task. Nerva deliberately re-implemented it as ONE strict-local structured-output call whose proposals are dispatched by audited code, not by free-form tool calls: core facts are injection-scanned, deduped and capped into the CoreMemory ring; corrections go to the learning module; new skills go to quarantine PENDING_REVIEW; skill patches land in SkillProposalStore hash-checked against drift, applied only by the curator after owner approval. Gated by cognition.review_enabled (default off) with a cadence/daily budget via reviewer.should_run().
capabilities.rationale: The governance inversion is the point and it is the right one: Hermes lets a background fork call tools with a whitelist, Nerva lets a model return JSON and lets code decide what may be done with it. That is strictly harder to abuse. Two Hermes pieces are still worth taking as a small update — cancelling an in-flight review when a new user turn arrives (Nerva's fire-and-forget task can currently compete with the next turn for a local GPU), and attributing the review's token usage to the parent session in cost_tracker.
capabilities.governance: read-only by design — the review proposes, code disposes; skill installs still hit the permanent owner floor (agents/core/kernel/registry.py:96).

capabilities.name: On-demand independent reviewer of the current work
capabilities.hermes: /review spawns a full-privilege background subagent that independently reviews whatever the session just produced, with an explicit reviewer goal and context text defining what it is told and what it must not assume. Entries: agent-core-b.review-engine, .review-task-text.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none for the on-demand adversarial form. Adjacent but different: agents/core/observability/review_queue.py is a HUMAN review queue for flagged traces; agents/core/reflection_evaluation.py is held-out lesson-proposal evaluation; agents/core/observability/quality.py scores turns automatically. No path spawns a fresh-context reviewer over the change the session just made.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already has the runtime to do it (SubAgentManager with fresh sessions and typed outputs) and the strongest reason to want it: this repo's own rule that a ✅ means DELIVERED, not PROVEN. A reviewer that starts with no memory of how the work was rationalised is the cheapest available check on a self-assessing agent, and it composes with row 20's evidence ledger — the reviewer reads what was actually proven rather than what was claimed.
capabilities.governance: a reviewer must be read-only: it inherits the child blocklist (agents/core/subagents.py:52) and must additionally be denied write and channel-send capabilities, or a critic becomes an actor.
capabilities.depends_on: row 15 (subagent runtime), and it is much more valuable after row 20

capabilities.name: Project verification: recipe detection, manifest, evidence ledger, verify-on-stop
capabilities.hermes: hermes verify detects how a project is built, tested and started (detect_recipe statically infers bootstrap/build/test commands, start command and port) or loads a saved .hermes/environment.json manifest as the user-editable source of truth. A verification evidence ledger passively records what the agent actually PROVED while working. A verify-on-stop nudge fires when the model tries to finish a turn right after editing code that has no fresh verification, and a pre_verify hook gates the round-end. An evidence ledger plus a verify-on-stop nudge converts that from a documentation discipline into a runtime one — and Nerva's evidence-receipt machinery is most of the storage layer already.

The evidence ledger itself is read-only and belongs in the hash-chained audit log so a proof cannot be back-dated.
capabilities.depends_on: terminal.exec kernel mediation (exists); pairs with row 21

capabilities.name: Coding posture: workspace snapshot, project facts, edit-format steering
capabilities.hermes: agent.coding_context shifts the agent into a senior-engineer posture: a coding operating brief, a live workspace snapshot in the system prompt (repo root, branch/upstream/ahead-behind, worktree status, dirty counts, recent commits and the project's verify loop), project-facts detection handing the model the exact test/lint/build commands instead of making it rediscover them, per-model edit-format steering toward the patch mode each family was trained on, and ContextProfile/RuntimeMode as an immutable posture seam every domain reads. Under focus mode the toolset collapses and the skill index goes names-only. Entries: agent-core-a.coding-context-mode, .coding-brief, .edit-format-guidance, .runtime-mode, .workspace-snapshot, .project-facts, .onboarding-hints, .profile-build, .plan-prompt.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/codeintel/index.py is the only code-awareness module and it is an index, not a posture. No workspace snapshot reaches any prompt (grep for branch/ahead-behind/worktree in agents/core/ returns nothing outside git tooling in scripts/). agents/core/system_profiles.py and agents/core/product_posture.py model product posture, not a coding runtime mode.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's own roadmap expects a developer that continues autonomously (docs/prompts/BACKLOG_DRIVER.md, docs/NERVA_2_ROADMAP.md), and today that developer starts every session not knowing the branch, the dirty state or the test command. The workspace snapshot is a handful of git calls and is the single highest-leverage block in the whole prompt for that lane. Take the snapshot and project-facts; leave the focus-mode toolset collapsing, which fights Nerva's capability registry.
capabilities.governance: read-only (git status/log reads). If project-facts is allowed to RUN the detected command rather than just name it, that hop is terminal.exec.
capabilities.depends_on: row 1 (the snapshot belongs in the context tier so the stable tier stays cached); feeds row 20

capabilities.name: Global emergency stop
capabilities.hermes: hermes pause engages a global ESTOP sentinel that halts NEW work only — cron dispatch and kanban workers stop, in-flight work is never killed; hermes resume lifts it; is_engaged/get_state/check_paused is a cheap cache-free predicate every dispatch loop calls each tick. Entries: agent-core-b.hermes-pause, .hermes-resume, .estop-detection.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/estop.py — a one-stat sentinel that fails SAFE on stat errors (reports engaged when unreadable, :51), per-component log-once-per-engagement, wired into agents/core/heartbeat.py and agents/core/autonomy_coordinator.py, exposed at agents/core/routers/ops.py:229/:237 and surfaced on both the web HUD (frontend/src/test/estop-card.test.tsx) and mobile (mobile/src/api/__tests__/estop.test.ts). Rescoped on purpose: it pauses autonomous work only, leaving owner chat live because that is the channel used to resume.
capabilities.rationale: The rescoping is a genuine improvement — Hermes' version can pause the very channel you would use to lift it. Nerva also fails safe where Hermes fails cheap. Recorded as a completed port in docs/research/2026-08-28-hermes-v2026.8.27-delta-port.md:31. The remaining work is tiering (pause input / kill browser context / lock operator session), which the gap matrix already tracks as its own item.
capabilities.governance: the estop is itself a governance control; engaging it via admin.kill_switch crosses the kernel while disengage deliberately does not, so a halt can always be released (agents/core/kernel/registry.py:64).

capabilities.name: User lifecycle hooks running the owner's own scripts
capabilities.hermes: A hooks: block in config.yaml runs a user's shell script on any lifecycle event with a JSON payload on stdin and a defined stdout/exit-code protocol; failures fail open by default or fail_closed by declaration; a first-use consent allowlist at ~/.hermes/shell-hooks-allowlist.json requires explicit approval per (event, command) pair; hermes hooks list/test/revoke/doctor manage them, with doctor checking exec bit, allowlist, mtime drift and JSON validity; VALID_HOOKS is the full event catalogue with documented per-event extra payload keys. Entries: agent-core-b.shell-hooks, .shell-hook-wire, .hook-fail-closed, .hook-allowlist, .hooks-list, .hooks-test, .hooks-revoke, .hooks-doctor, .hook-events, .hook-extra-keys.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: Nerva has inbound triggers, not outbound hooks: agents/core/webhooks.py is a token-authenticated POST /api/webhooks/{id} with optional HMAC signing; agents/core/plugin_gate.py and agents/core/plugin_manager.py gate Python plugins. No lifecycle event catalogue and no user-script execution path exist (grep for on_turn_start / lifecycle across agents/core/*.py returns nothing).
capabilities.rationale: This is the clearest "copy, but re-root behind the kernel" case in the cluster. The capability is genuinely useful — it is how an owner makes Nerva fit their machine without writing a plugin — but Hermes' consent model is a JSON allowlist file with a fail-OPEN default, and Nerva already has a strictly better answer to both halves: a consent ledger and an approval queue. Copy the event catalogue and the wire protocol; replace the allowlist and the fail-open default entirely.
capabilities.governance: twice privileged. Registering a hook widens what Nerva may run on the owner's box, so registration is permission.grant (agents/core/kernel/registry.py:109) written only from an approved task. Firing one executes a host process, so it crosses terminal.exec (:113) with the hardline denylist in front. Fail-closed must be the default, inverting Hermes.
capabilities.depends_on: permission.grant and terminal.exec kernel mediation (both exist)

capabilities.name: Outbound signed lifecycle webhooks
capabilities.hermes: hooks.outbound POSTs lifecycle events as JSON to external HTTP endpoints (CI systems, dashboards) with bounded retries and an explicit redirect policy; reaction detection (vibe) is a token-free signal fed to the same plane. Entries: agent-core-b.outbound-webhooks, .outbound-delivery, .reactions.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: Inbound is done and signed: agents/core/webhooks.py:36 compute_signature (HMAC-SHA256, constant-time compare) and agents/core/routers/webhooks.py. Outbound goes to channels only (agents/core/channels/webhook_channels.py) — there is no lifecycle event feed an external system can subscribe to.
capabilities.rationale: The signing code and the event vocabulary from row 23 are both already there, so this is mostly plumbing, and it is the piece that lets Nerva participate in an owner's existing automation instead of demanding they watch the HUD. Skip the vibe/reaction detector — it feeds the terminal pet, which Nerva does not ship.
capabilities.governance: an outbound POST is agent egress and already has a kind: plugin.egress crosses the kernel (agents/core/kernel/registry.py:44), so a kill-switch or budget stop must silence the feed too. Payloads must pass the redaction engine before leaving the box.
capabilities.depends_on: row 23 (shared event catalogue); plugin.egress kernel hook (exists)

capabilities.name: Universal secret redaction on every log record
capabilities.hermes: redact_sensitive_text() masks API keys, tokens and credentials before they reach logs or verbose output, backed by a vendor prefix catalogue (_PREFIX_PATTERNS), three masking policies for three audiences with a non-reusable sentinel, sensitive query-parameter and body-key catalogues for opaque tokens that match no prefix, a plugin-registered pattern API, one terminal-output redaction policy across every terminal surface, and RedactingFormatter applied to EVERY formatted log record. Entries: agent-core-b.redact-engine, .redact-prefixes, .mask-helpers, .redact-terminal, .redact-plugin-patterns, .redacting-formatter, .redact-param-catalogues.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: The scanners are strong and locale-aware in a way Hermes' are not: agents/core/security/scanner.py detects Romanian CNP and IBAN with checksum confirmation plus generic secret patterns, extensible via JARVIS_SCANNER_EXTRA_PATTERNS, with redact() at :160/:261/:324; agents/core/security/secret_broker.py:112 redacts; agents/core/security/audit.py:128 redacts a preview BEFORE hashing it into the chain; agents/core/tool_rpc.py:388 masks known secrets crossing to the sandbox. What is missing is universality: agents/core/log.py:86 installs a plain logging.Formatter, and agents/core/log_safe.py is 14 lines that strip CR/LF only. A plugin that logs a token writes it to disk unmasked.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva redacts at the boundaries it thought of and nowhere else, which is the failure mode a formatter exists to prevent — the leak always comes from the call site nobody enumerated. The engine is written and tested; wrapping the root handler with it is a small, high-value change, and the checksum-validated RO patterns mean Nerva's version stays better than Hermes' afterwards.
capabilities.governance: read-only, but it protects every other governance surface: the audit chain, the support bundle (agents/core/support_bundle.py) and the outbound feed in row 24 all inherit whatever the formatter misses.

capabilities.name: Message hygiene and wire-level recovery
capabilities.hermes: A dozen small repairs that keep a long transcript sendable: surrogate sanitisation (lone U+D800–DFFF → U+FFFD before json.dumps) applied at both the loop boundary and the transport; tool-call argument repair for truncated JSON, trailing commas and Python None/True; interrupted tool-sequence closing (a synthetic assistant turn when a transcript ends on a raw tool row); tool-call id normalisation and deduplication; image stripping when a server rejects images and image shrink-and-retry when a payload is too large; serialized_messages_bytes for byte-accurate HTTP 413 recovery; non-ASCII stripping for LANG=C hosts; replay-history sanitisation stripping broken tails before replay; stale dangerous-confirmation expiry so an old plain-text 'yes' cannot be read as consent for a new action; transcript repair and in-place row reconciliation. Entries: agent-core-b.surrogate-sanitization, .tool-arg-repair, .close-interrupted-tools, .tool-call-ids, .image-strip, .serialized-bytes, .non-ascii-strip, .replay-cleanup, .stale-confirmation-expiry, agent-core-a.surrogate-scrub, .image-shrink, .transcript-repair, .message-content, .stale-reasoning-prune.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: Nerva validates rather than repairs: agents/core/agent_runtime.py:643 _is_strict_json rejects non-conforming results, :448 _prepare_result substitutes a _non_json envelope, :705 _is_valid_unicode checks surrogates, :582 _bounded_result_envelope caps size, and MAX_PARSED_TOOL_CALLS bounds fan-out. Nothing repairs a malformed tool-call argument, closes an interrupted tool sequence, dedupes tool-call ids, strips or shrinks images on rejection, or expires a stale confirmation.
capabilities.rationale: Take the subset that local models actually trigger, not all fourteen. Tool-argument repair matters most — a 7B model emitting trailing-comma JSON currently loses the whole call to bad_tool_arguments, which on a bounded loop means the turn fails rather than retries. Interrupted-sequence closing matters second, because Nerva now HAS interruption paths (subagent stop, estop, deadline) that can leave a transcript ending on a tool row. Stale-confirmation expiry is a governance item and should come regardless of the rest.
capabilities.governance: stale-confirmation expiry is directly governance-bearing: a plain-text 'yes' left in a transcript must never be readable as approval for a later action. Everything else here is read-only, but image stripping must not silently drop evidence a taint decision depended on.

capabilities.name: Context meter and @-references for the owner
capabilities.hermes: /context shows how the next request is composed by category against the model's window, rendered as a 100-cell glyph grid plus an estimated-usage table with optional per-skill and per-toolset expansion; @ references parse and expand a file/diff/page into an --- Attached Context --- block appended to the user message so the model gets the content without a tool call; a manual /compress reports exactly what it did, distinguishing a no-op, an abort, a refusal and a fallback. Entries: agent-core-a.context-breakdown, .context-grid, .context-references, .manual-compress-feedback, .compaction-status-lines, .compaction-display.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: No context meter exists on any surface — frontend/src/panels/mission-canvas.tsx:60 records that the context-compress route is REFUSED and stays on the uncalled backlog, and that the production compression path is in-process under memory.context_compression "which no route [exposes]". No @-reference expansion in agents/core/orchestrator.py or the chat routers.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva has the better compaction policy and the owner cannot see it work. That matters more here than in Hermes: this is a product whose pitch is a 24/7 local run, and the owner has no way to know whether the session is at 40% or 84% of a 32k window until a summary appears. The meter is also the only honest way to show that image-first eviction is doing something. Ship the meter; @-references are a nice second.
capabilities.governance: read-only. The meter must read the same policy object the loop uses (agents/core/context_compressor.py:116) rather than re-deriving thresholds, or it will report a state the compressor does not share.

capabilities.name: Session auto-titling
capabilities.hermes: Two stages: an instant title taken from the user's own first words at turn start, then a background upgrade by one small-model call with a prompt that instructs the model to NAME the session rather than answer it. Fired once, for every human-facing surface. Entries: agent-core-a.auto-titling, .auto-title-at-turn-start, .title-prompt, .oneshot, .side-question.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — sessions are identified by id throughout (agents/core/session_files.py defines what counts as a session file; agents/core/memory/persistence.py lists them). No titling code exists.
capabilities.rationale: Small, but it is the difference between a session list an owner can navigate and a wall of ids — and Nerva's own restore bug history (agents/core/session_files.py documents entities.json being mistaken for 'the most recent session') shows that session identity is already a usability problem here. The two-stage design matters: the instant title means the list is never empty while a local model is busy.
capabilities.governance: read-only. The upgrade call must go through the strict-local auxiliary rail (row 29), not a cloud model — a title derived from conversation content leaving the box would contradict the local-first posture for a cosmetic feature.

capabilities.name: One auxiliary-model rail for every side task
capabilities.hermes: agent/auxiliary_client.py is a single resolution chain used by every side task (context compression, session search, titling, web summarisation) so they cannot each invent their own routing; auxiliary usage is attributed to the ambient session without threading a session id through every caller; run_oneshot() runs a stateless call that never touches history and never breaks prompt caching; /btw answers a question ABOUT the conversation without adding synthetic turns; the plugin LLM facade (ctx.llm) is the supported lane for a trusted plugin's own call. Entries: agent-core-b.auxiliary-client, .aux-accounting, .plugin-llm, .plugin-stream-hooks, agent-core-a.oneshot, .side-question.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: The rail exists for exactly one caller: agents/core/orchestrator.py:2243 _compression_summarizer builds a strict-local summarizer using router.local_backend (agents/core/llm/router.py:183, the fail-closed accessor that never falls through to cloud). Nothing generalises it — a second side task would rebuild the routing, and there is no ambient usage attribution (agents/core/cost_tracker.py:202 record() takes an explicit agent name).
capabilities.rationale: The hard part is already solved and is better than Hermes': a fail-closed local-only accessor is exactly the right default for side tasks that read raw conversation content. What is missing is making it a named rail so titling (row 28), review (row 18) and any future summariser inherit that guarantee by construction instead of by each author remembering it.
capabilities.governance: read-only, and the fail-closed local-only property IS the governance: agents/core/orchestrator.py:2243 documents that side tasks read raw conversation content and must therefore never reach a cloud backend. Generalising must preserve that, not soften it into a default.

capabilities.name: Reasoning-effort control and reasoning-aware timeouts
capabilities.hermes: One canonical effort ladder with a clamping policy so an internal level never leaks to a wire that rejects it and a stronger request never resolves weaker than a weaker one; LM Studio effort resolution mapped onto its vocabulary and clamped against the model's published allowed set so the server does not 400; reasoning stale-timeout FLOORS that stop the stale detector killing a reasoning model mid-think; thinking-timeout detection that distinguishes a proxy idle-kill from a real context overflow and gives three ranked workarounds; a reasoning-echo policy per provider family; StreamingThinkScrubber holding back partial tags at delta boundaries; reasoning-summary boundary repair; stale reasoning-item pruning after a compaction. Entries: agent-core-a.reasoning-effort, .lmstudio-reasoning, .reasoning-timeouts, .thinking-timeout, .think-scrubber, .strip-think-blocks, .reasoning-summaries, .stale-reasoning-prune, agent-core-b.reasoning-echo.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: Scrubbing is at parity: agents/core/llm/base.py:169 strip_thinking (closed and unterminated <think>, plus prose 'thinking process' blocks) and :218 a streaming filter that holds partial tags. Control is not: agents/core/llm/moe_routing.py:26 decide_thinking_mode is a binary on/off by prompt length, there is no effort ladder or clamp, and agents/core/orchestrator.py:2230 _agent_call_timeout is a flat agents.agent_timeout_seconds (default 120s) applied uniformly — so a local qwen3 or deepseek-r1 thinking for more than two minutes is recorded as "[agent timeout]" at agents/core/orchestrator.py:2436.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva runs reasoning models as its default local hot path, which is precisely the configuration Hermes' timeout floors exist for, and the current flat 120s will kill a hard question mid-think and report it as a failure. The effort ladder matters less on local backends than the timeout floor does; do the floor first, the ladder second for LM Studio where a wrong value is a 400.
capabilities.governance: read-only.

capabilities.name: Unified deadline and budget layer
capabilities.hermes: One bounded-execution primitive and one timeout resolver for the whole tree, explicitly so that every new stall report stops adding another site-local mechanism; agent.run_budget_seconds caps a whole turn's wall clock with an 80%-spent wrap-up nudge asking the model to deliver from what it has; an iteration-budget exhaustion protocol notifies the model exactly once, grants one final API call and forces a summary if that call produces no text. Entries: agent-core-a.deadline, .run-budget, .run-budget-wrapup, .iteration-budget-protocol, .api-max-retries, .turn-counter-resets.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/iteration_budget.py is a clean consume/refund counter (itself a Hermes port) used by agents/core/agent_runtime.py:177 and agents/core/subagents.py. But timeouts are exactly the scattered set Hermes' deadline layer was written to end: agents/core/orchestrator.py:2230 _agent_call_timeout, agents/core/agent_runtime.py _max_wall_seconds and _tool_timeout_seconds, agents/core/tool_rpc_runtime.py:84 its own deadline, agents/core/resilience.py:28 a per-attempt timeout, agents/core/plugin_gatherer.py:138 a per-plugin deadline. There is no wrap-up nudge and no exhaustion protocol — the loop just returns a safety-limit string (agents/core/agent_runtime.py:215).
capabilities.rationale: The 2026-08-28 delta doc already picked the shape: port Hermes' deadline as an extension of iteration_budget.py rather than as a parallel mechanism (docs/research/2026-08-28-hermes-v2026.8.27-delta-port.md:52). The user-visible half is the part worth adding beyond consolidation — an 80% wrap-up nudge turns 'it hit the limit and told you nothing' into 'here is what I have', which is the same complaint row 11 addresses from the other side.
capabilities.governance: read-only, but a deadline is a containment control: a stall that is never bounded is how an autonomous run keeps spending. It should report through the same exit-reason vocabulary as rows 11 and 12.

capabilities.name: Learning made visible: journey graph and usage insights
capabilities.hermes: A learning (journey) graph assembles what the user actually learned plus the skills produced, rendered by hermes journey as a terminal timeline with a fixed palette ported from the desktop source, and node-level delete/edit that maps an id back to its on-disk home; hermes insights analyses session history for token usage, costs, tool patterns and activity. Entries: agent-core-b.learning-graph, .hermes-journey, .journey-render-constants, .journey-mutations, .hermes-insights, .learn-prompt, .learn-authoring-standards, .knowledge-skill-standards.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: The data is all there and is richer than Hermes': agents/core/analytics_store.py (KPIs, timeseries, top paths, event counts), agents/core/run_history.py (per-agent ring with latency/cost/route), agents/core/cost_tracker.py:238 apm_summary, agents/core/observability/north_star.py (accepted actions, interrupt rate, %-local, p95), plus a bi-temporal knowledge graph under agents/core/memory/. What is missing is the owner-facing narrative view and node-level edit/delete of what was learned. No /learn flow exists and no skill-authoring standard is embedded anywhere in agents/core/skills/.
capabilities.rationale: Two different things are bundled here and only one is a gap. The analytics half is already superior — north_star.py measures things Hermes does not. The journey half is a product surface Nerva lacks: the owner cannot see what the system learned from them or delete a specific lesson, which for a memory-first product is both a trust feature and arguably a data-rights one. The /learn prompt plus the authoring standards are a cheap copy on top, since generated skills already land in quarantine.
capabilities.governance: read-only to display; node-level DELETE of a learned fact is a data-rights operation and should route through the existing purge/retention path (agents/core/data_purge.py, agents/core/retention.py) rather than mutating stores directly.

capabilities.name: Telemetry export: monitoring emitter, gateway health, OTLP traces, install id
capabilities.hermes: An in-process monitoring emitter is the single seam between producers and exporters, emitting only three event shapes (never prompts, messages or tool arguments) with one unconditional egress scrub and no knobs; a resettable pseudonymous monitoring.install_id identifies an install across exported signals; a gateway health snapshot converts runtime state into an exported metric set on a periodic schedule; an OTLP trace streamer subscribes to the emitter and exports spans; trace upload publishes a session transcript as an agent trace to Hugging Face. Entries: agent-core-b.monitoring-emitter, .monitoring-events, .monitoring-redaction, .monitoring-install-id, .gateway-health-snapshot, .gateway-health-export, .otlp-exporter, .trace-upload.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: Local observability is strong and in places superior: agents/core/security/audit.py is a Merkle hash-chained SQLite log with optional HMAC row hashing and verify_chain(); agents/core/observability/http_metrics.py, agents/core/analytics_store.py and agents/core/observability/north_star.py cover metrics; agents/core/observability/tracer.py covers traces. No exporter, no install id, no OTLP (grep for OTLP/opentelemetry across agents/ returns nothing).
capabilities.rationale: The product reason, not the effort one: Nerva's promise is that the owner's data stays on the owner's box, and a health/trace exporter's only consumer is a fleet operator Nerva does not have. Even default-off, it is a surface whose existence weakens the claim MOONSHOT.md §5 makes. The Hugging Face trace upload is the same objection with the volume turned up — it ships conversation transcripts off-box. Re-open on one specific trigger: when agents/core/node_mesh.py grows into a real multi-node install, the mesh needs cross-node health, and the right shape then is a LOCAL OTLP collector the owner runs, plus the install id, plus the unconditional-scrub rule copied verbatim.
capabilities.governance: would be egress (plugin.egress) if built; the unconditional-scrub-with-no-knobs discipline is the one piece worth adopting into row 24's outbound feed even while skipping the exporter itself.
capabilities.depends_on: node_mesh maturity (re-open condition, not a dependency)

capabilities.name: Mixture-of-Agents aggregation runtime
capabilities.hermes: /moa and provider: moa run a Mixture-of-Agents turn: several reference (advisor) models see the conversation and an aggregator synthesises their outputs; a reference system prompt reframes each advisor as an ANALYST rather than the acting agent; moa.privacy_filter stops advisor output echoing PII into the labelled aggregation; moa.save_traces records the true full turn per line; guidance is attached at the END of the aggregator prompt to keep the prompt cache safe. Entries: agent-core-b.moa-loop, .moa-reference-prompt, .moa-privacy-filter, .moa-traces, .moa-guidance-attach.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: This IS Nerva's default architecture, not a mode: agents/core/orchestrator.py:2421 _run_agent fans out to multiple cabinet agents concurrently via asyncio.gather and synthesises the responses, with agents/core/cortex_compare.py, agents/core/cortex_measured_compare.py and agents/core/arena.py comparing model outputs and agents/core/orchestrator.py:1722 _detect_handoff arbitrating.
capabilities.rationale: Skipping because the capability already exists under a different name and shape — adding /moa would be a second, parallel mechanism for what the orchestrator does on every turn, and two aggregation paths is how the routing story becomes unexplainable. One piece is worth lifting on its own merits and should be tracked as part of the fan-out rather than as a MoA port: the advisor privacy filter, which stops one agent's output echoing PII into another's context. That is a real hole in Nerva's existing fan-out.
capabilities.governance: read-only. The lifted privacy filter would compose with the existing taint and recall-admission layers (agents/core/memory/recall_admission.py).

capabilities.name: Terminal display surface: pet, spinner, tool labels, inline diffs, i18n
capabilities.hermes: The CLI's own rendering layer — KawaiiSpinner with kawaii faces and thinking verbs, the Petdex animated sprite pet with state derivation and terminal-graphics protocol negotiation (kitty/sixel/ascii), friendly tool labels, tool emoji resolution, tool-call previews, inline coloured edit diffs, tool-failure display, CJK-aware markdown table realignment, single-writer stream fences, thread-scoped stdout silencing, and agent.i18n static-string translation. Entries: agent-core-a.kawaii-spinner, .friendly-tool-labels, .tool-emoji, .tool-preview, .inline-diff, .tool-failure-display, .markdown-tables, .stream-single-writer, .thread-scoped-output, .i18n, agent-core-b.pet-engine, .pet-state, .pet-render-modes.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none, by design — Nerva's surfaces are the web HUD (frontend/src/), the Expo mobile app (mobile/src/), voice and chat channels (agents/core/channels/). There is no first-class terminal client to render into.
capabilities.rationale: A product reason, not an effort one: this is Hermes' front end, and Nerva's front end is elsewhere. Porting a terminal renderer would build a surface Nerva does not ship and would then have to maintain against three real ones. Two ideas inside it are worth stealing without the renderer and belong to other rows: friendly tool labels and tool-call previews are what row 11's accounting line should show in the HUD, and the single-writer stream fence is a correctness idea for the streaming path (agents/core/orchestrator.py:1409 _handle_input_stream) rather than a display one. Re-open only if the owner decides to ship a Nerva CLI.
capabilities.governance: read-only.

capabilities.name: Vendor-owned agent runtimes: Codex app-server, NeMo Relay, tools-as-MCP-server, transport registry
capabilities.hermes: An optional runtime where the codex app-server subprocess OWNS the agent loop, with Codex event projection back into Hermes-shaped messages, a curated subset of Hermes tools re-exposed to that subprocess over stdio MCP, and its own delegated compaction path; the NeMo Relay runtime owns profile-scoped conversation/turn lifetimes and routes LLM calls and tool executions through its pipeline; a provider transport registry normalises Anthropic Messages, Chat Completions, Codex Responses and Bedrock Converse behind one interface with normalized response types. Entries: agent-core-b.codex-app-server, .codex-event-projector, .hermes-tools-mcp-server, .relay-runtime, .relay-llm, .relay-tools, .relay-session-coordinator, .transport-registry, .transport-types, .transport-anthropic, .transport-chat-completions, .transport-codex, .transport-bedrock, agent-core-a.codex-app-server-compaction.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: The transport half exists per-provider without a registry: agents/core/llm/base.py (LM Studio / Ollama), anthropic.py, gemini.py, openrouter.py, each with its own request/response handling, coordinated by agents/core/llm/hybrid_router.py. Nerva already serves MCP (agents/core/mcp/) rather than consuming a vendor runtime.
capabilities.rationale: The transport-registry piece is real work but belongs to the providers cluster, not here. The vendor-runtime piece is skipped for a governance reason that is also a product reason: a runtime that owns the agent loop executes tools inside someone else's process, which is precisely the surface agents/core/kernel/registry.py cannot mediate. Nerva's differentiator is that every privileged effect crosses the kernel; adopting a loop the kernel cannot see would trade that away for provider convenience. This matches the standing E8.1c posture that treats an external agent runtime as a rejected execution seam, not a dependency (docs/research/2026-08-28-hermes-v2026.8.27-delta-port.md:73).

capabilities.name: Undoing what the agent did to the filesystem
