capabilities.rationale: Today the owner cannot arm a single recurring automation without editing a file in the repo and restarting. Every autonomy surface Nerva already has (queue, worker, policy, kernel, escalation) is waiting for a trigger the owner can create; this is that trigger. Adapt rather than transcribe: one SQLite store (jobs + attempts + incidents) instead of JSON + flock, exactly as Hermes' own rebuild note recommends.
capabilities.governance: Arming a recurring run is capability growth in the same sense as `permission.grant` and `goal.approve`: needs a new kernel kind `schedule.create` at the irreversible tier (a standing licence to act while nobody is watching), and each firing must re-cross the kernel for whatever effect it actually attempts — the job record must never carry a pre-granted authority.
capabilities.depends_on: nothing — agents/core/kernel/registry.py, autonomy/queue.py and autonomy/worker.py are the substrate

capabilities.name: Say when in plain words (schedule syntax)
capabilities.hermes: `parse_schedule` (cron/jobs.py:962) accepts five families in a fixed order: `every 2h` intervals, bare durations (recurring), natural weekday/time phrases (`weekdays at 9am`, `every monday, wednesday at 9am`), raw 5-field cron validated by croniter, ISO timestamps anchored to the app's configured timezone, and `in 30m` one-shots; `normalize_repeat_value` coerces `forever|once|1x|3` at a single chokepoint. Rolls up automation.cron-schedule-syntax, .cron-repeat.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/nl_schedule.py `parse_schedule` (EN + RO: weekday/weekend/named days, `every N minutes/hours`, hourly, am/pm and 24h) → 5-field cron; exposed as `POST /api/schedule/parse` at agents/core/routers/tools.py:73; tests/test_h10_27_nl_schedule.py
capabilities.rationale: The hard half (bilingual natural language → cron) already exists and is better localised than Hermes'. What is missing is the other four families — one-shot delays, ISO timestamps, repeat counts — and the fact that the parser is wired to nothing but a preview endpoint. Anchoring naive timestamps to Nerva's configured timezone rather than the host's is the one correctness rule to copy verbatim.
capabilities.governance: read-only (pure parser, no I/O)
capabilities.depends_on: row 1 (a job store for the parsed schedule to land in)

capabilities.name: See every attempt an autonomous run made, and whether the scheduler itself is alive
capabilities.hermes: `cron runs` reads a SQLite `executions` table (claimed/running/completed/failed/unknown) where an interrupted attempt is only reclassified `unknown` after a pid **plus process-start-time** ownership proof; `cron status` reports ticker heartbeat age, last success, catch-up count and last error from tiny atomic epoch files that never contend on the jobs lock; an in-flight guard fences one run per job with a machine-id+pid claim and force-releases only when the claim is stale AND no live future exists; an inactivity (not wall-clock) watchdog kills a silent run and token-keyed interruption bookkeeping stops a killed run writing a false 'ok'; per-run output is one markdown file with retention. Rolls up automation.cli-cron-runs, .cli-cron-status, .cron-inflight-guard, .cron-inactivity-watchdog, .cron-output-store.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/queue.py (SQLite state machine, retry cap, no re-entry after terminal); agents/core/autonomy/work_runs.py (per-step ledger with hard step/wall-clock/interrupt budgets); agents/core/autonomy/audit_sink.py + mediation.py (HMAC-signed, hash-chained IntentLog — strictly stronger than Hermes' plain SQLite ledger); agents/core/run_history.py (per-agent input/output previews); no per-attempt row for a scheduled job, no owner fence, no ticker-liveness surface
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's audit chain is superior and must stay the sink; what is absent is the operational half — 'did the scheduler tick, did this attempt actually own the process it claims, and did a killed run lie about its status'. The pid+start-time ownership proof and the never-force-release-without-proof rule are the two subtle pieces worth copying exactly; a bare pid check misreads a recycled pid as still-running.
capabilities.governance: read-only

capabilities.name: Repeated failures collapse into one acknowledgeable incident, and an unrunnable job pauses itself
capabilities.hermes: Incidents keyed by `sha256(job_id + normalized_error[:200])[:12]` with an eight-way failure_type classifier (rate_limit/timeout/auth/delivery/config/script/agent/unknown) and a `detected → alerted → closed` lifecycle where closed is terminal for that signature; preflight runs the same predicates as `cron doctor` before firing (provider key, delivery reachability, skills present, config shape) and routes a hard error to `_block_and_pause_job` with an auditable `paused_reason` plus an alert-once bit; a model/provider drift guard compares the resolved model against a snapshot taken at create time and skips rather than silently running an unpinned job on a different brain. Rolls up automation.cli-cron-incidents, .cli-cron-doctor, .cron-preflight, .cron-drift-guard.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/error_logger.py (problems.jsonl capped at 500, sync_problems_to_diagnostics → diagnostics.md); agents/core/autonomy/log_scanner.py (quick/hourly scans, rate-spike and first-seen-code detection); agents/core/autonomy/worker.py retry cap; no dedup signature, no auto-pause with a stored reason, no pre-fire validation, no drift guard
capabilities.rationale: Without dedup, an autonomous system that fails the same way at 03:00 pings the owner forever — which in Nerva's model burns the daily interrupt budget that the whole calm-by-default posture depends on. Auto-pausing an unrunnable job with a recorded reason is the difference between a broken automation and a broken automation the owner can see and fix.
capabilities.governance: read-only (classification and pause are state changes on the owner's own job, no external effect)

capabilities.name: Let a cheap check decide whether the expensive model runs at all
capabilities.hermes: Four mechanisms, all at $0: `--no-agent` script jobs (script IS the job, stdout delivered verbatim, empty stdout = silence — the classic watchdog); script-as-context (script runs first, stdout injected as `## Script Output`, empty output skips the AI call entirely); the wake gate, where the last stdout line `{"wakeAgent": false}` suppresses the LLM and the delivery, fail-open on anything unparseable; and monitor mode, where a script or URL is hashed byte-exactly and an unchanged tick suppresses the run while a change injects a unified diff — with the new hash persisted at detection time so a failed agent run cannot re-alert forever. Plus `[SILENT]` response suppression. Rolls up automation.cron-no-agent, .cron-script-context, .cron-wake-gate, .cron-monitor-mode, .cron-silent.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/observer.py (state-change debouncing: a probe emits only on healthy→unhealthy or unhealthy→healthy, re-sampling a still-broken service does NOT re-fire); agents/core/autonomy/watchers.py (same debounce over Gmail/Calendar/balance/health streams); both are fixed, code-authored probes — nothing lets an owner attach a script or a URL to a job as its gate
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's debounce principle is already the right one and is arguably better shaped than Hermes' byte-hash (it models recovery explicitly). The gap is that it is a closed set of developer-written probes: the owner cannot say 'check this page, and only wake the model when it changes'. This is also the cost story — polling with a model is what makes autonomy expensive, and Hermes' empty-output-means-skip rule is what makes it cheap.
capabilities.governance: A job script is host execution and must cross `terminal.exec` (already KERNEL, with the hardline denylist and TERMINAL_EXEC_CONTRACT running first); a monitor URL fetch crosses `plugin.egress`. Neither may be pre-authorised by the job record.

capabilities.name: A run remembers what the last one said (continuity, chaining, per-job notepad)
capabilities.hermes: `--continuity` injects the job's own newest output as `## Your previous run's output` with a 'do not repeat what was already reported' instruction; `context_from` chains another job's latest output ('job A collects, job B analyses'), guarded by a hex-only id whitelist before any filesystem access and silent-skipping missing outputs; the notepad is a per-job SQLite KV injected into the prompt every run with hard caps (128-char keys, 16 KB per value, 64 KB per job) precisely because it inflates every wake-up. Rolls up automation.cron-continuity, .cli-cron-notepad, .cron-prompt-assembly.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — agents/core/autonomy/work_runs.py records steps within one run only; agents/core/autonomy/digest.py rebuilds each brief from the queue with no memory of the previous brief; no per-job durable scratchpad exists anywhere under agents/core/autonomy/
capabilities.rationale: Without it a daily job re-reports the same three things every morning, which is exactly how a proactive assistant trains its owner to ignore it. The notepad (a watermark, a cursor, a watchlist that survives reboots) is what turns a scheduled prompt into an actual watcher, and Nerva has no equivalent at any layer.
capabilities.governance: read-only in itself, but the notepad is prompt-injected on every run, so the byte caps are a real control, not hygiene — and its contents are agent-written, i.e. untrusted, and must be tainted like any other injected data

capabilities.name: Choose where an autonomous result lands
capabilities.hermes: `deliver` accepts `local`, `origin` (the chat the job was created from, with a home-channel fallback), a bare platform, `platform:chat:thread`, the `all` routing token, and `bot-chat[:profile]` — which injects the output into another local agent's session as a real inbound turn (agent-to-agent, deliberately excluded from `all` because it costs a full LLM turn). Routing resolves at fire time, not create time, and records why a target was chosen (`_resolved_from`) so mirroring can tell 'the owner's own chat' from 'a broadcast channel'. Rolls up automation.cron-delivery, .cron-botchat-delivery, .cron-mirror-delivery.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/escalation.py (governed multi-channel fan-out, allowlist-gated, channel-agnostic rendering); agents/core/autonomy/presence.py (present/idle/unknown → HUD only; away → also fan out to escalation channels); agents/core/channels/{telegram,discord,slack,email,voice,webhook_channels}.py; agents/core/autonomy/inbox.py decision cards
capabilities.rationale: Nerva is genuinely ahead on the harder question — *whether* to interrupt, using desk presence and an interrupt budget — and that must be kept. What is missing is per-item routing: delivery is an installation-wide setting, there is no 'reply into the conversation that asked for this', and no way to hand a result to another cabinet agent's inbox. Resolve at fire time so an automation created before a channel was connected starts using it when it comes online.
capabilities.governance: `channel.reply` is already KERNEL (agents/core/kernel/registry.py); an agent-to-agent delivery that costs a full turn on another agent should be opt-in and metered, not a routing token

capabilities.name: Bound what an unattended agent may do
capabilities.hermes: Per-job `enabled_toolsets` resolved with a strict precedence (per-job list → per-platform `cron` tools config → full default as the legacy net), where the model-supplied allowlist is **intersected with** the operator's `agent.disabled_toolsets` and never unioned onto it; `messaging` and `clarify` are always removed (they need a live human), and `cronjob` is removed unless `cron.allow_agent_scheduling` — documented in code as loop prevention, not a security boundary. A per-job reasoning-effort pin overrides both the global setting and per-model overrides, validated at the store boundary and clamped by the transport. Rolls up automation.cron-toolsets, .cron-allow-agent-scheduling, .cron-reasoning.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/policy.py (risk-tier gate: act / notify / ask, money cap + daily ceiling); agents/core/kernel/registry.py (per-kind mediation); agents/core/data_spaces.py (least-privilege READ scoping per agent); no per-item toolset allowlist and no per-item reasoning pin
capabilities.rationale: The intersect-never-union rule is the same argument Nerva's kernel already makes about grants, applied to tools, and Nerva will need it the moment a scheduled job can name its own toolset. 'A scheduled job cannot schedule more scheduled jobs' is also the cheapest anti-runaway control in the whole cluster and costs almost nothing to implement.
capabilities.governance: The allowlist itself is policy, not an effect — but it must be enforced where the agent is constructed, and a per-job list must never widen past `agent.disabled_toolsets` or the kernel's own denials

capabilities.name: Guards specific to the unattended lane (injection, credential exfiltration, self-restart)
capabilities.hermes: Three: a two-tier prompt-injection scanner chosen by **content provenance** — strict when the prompt is just the user's text, loose (sanitize invisible Unicode, drop command-shape patterns) when runtime-loaded skills or injected data are present, because cron auto-approves tool calls but a triage feed legitimately quotes `rm -rf /`; a credential-exfiltration guard that re-validates the provider/base_url pair at *use* time as a backstop for records written outside the validating API, failing closed; and a gateway-lifecycle guard that blocks a job whose prompt or referenced script would restart/stop the gateway (command-shaped detection, data-sink masking, transparent-prefix peeling, recursive script scanning to depth 8). Rolls up automation.cron-injection-scan, .cron-credential-guard, .cron-lifecycle-guard.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/kernel/__init__.py taint escalation (tainted payload or untrusted origin escalates GRANT→QUEUE, per docs/FLAGS.md); hardline denylist + TERMINAL_EXEC_CONTRACT behind `terminal.exec`; agents/core/http_client.py egress hook; agents/core/security/recall_taint.py; nothing tiers a scan by provenance, and nothing prevents an autonomous run from restarting Nerva itself
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already has the stronger primitive (taint that forces ASK) — the port is the *provenance tiering* on top of it, so a skill body loaded from disk and a scraped web page are not treated as the same trust class. The self-restart guard is a small, concrete gap: under a supervisor with restart-on-exit, one scheduled 'restart yourself' turns the owner's box into a respawn loop.
capabilities.governance: These are kernel-adjacent controls, not new effects — the provenance tier belongs in the taint model, and the credential check belongs at both the write boundary and the use boundary

capabilities.name: One-tap automations the owner accepts instead of composing
capabilities.hermes: 16 parameterized blueprints (morning-brief, important-mail, weekly-review, price-watch, competitor-watch, habit-checkin, meal-plan, …) defined once with typed slots (time/enum/text/weekdays) and rendered four ways — a dashboard form, a pre-filled `/blueprint` slash command, a `hermes://` deep link, and a docs catalog entry — with `fill_blueprint` returning `create_job` kwargs so there is no second job engine. Plus a `/suggestions` store (consent-first, dedup_key latching, MAX_PENDING=5 so it never becomes a nag wall) seeded from a four-entry starter catalog, and `classify_items.py`, a threshold urgency classifier that prints nothing below the bar so the wrapping job stays silent. Rolls up automation.blueprints, .blueprint-slots, .cron-suggestions, .cron-suggestion-catalog, .classify-items.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/digest.py (morning brief 07:00 / evening retro 20:00 — the one blueprint Nerva ships, hard-coded); agents/core/autonomy/followups.py; agents/core/autonomy/preferences.py (approval-rate learning → suggest raising autonomy for a class, a suggestion never an automatic change — the same consent-first shape applied to a different subject); no template catalog, no accept-to-create
capabilities.rationale: This is Nerva's activation path, not a nicety: docs/research/2026-09-06-hermes-and-field-gap-matrix.md already names 'your first governed morning brief, approved in Telegram, with an audit-chain receipt, inside 30 minutes' as the killer first action. A blueprint the owner accepts with zero edits is how that 30 minutes is actually met. The one-schema-four-renderers rule prevents the HUD form and the chat command drifting apart.
capabilities.governance: Accepting a blueprint mints a real job, so it lands on row 1's `schedule.create`; the suggestion surface itself proposes only and must never auto-schedule — Hermes' consent-first rule matches Nerva's queue posture exactly

capabilities.name: Fire schedules without a live local process (pluggable scheduler provider / hosted cron)
capabilities.hermes: A `CronScheduler` provider interface splits 'when to fire' from 'what firing does' so a managed-cron integration is a ~200-line plugin; the Chronos provider lets a hosted gateway scale to zero by arming exactly one external one-shot per job with Nous NAS, which calls back at fire time via `POST /api/cron/fire` (JWKS-verified); plus `fire_overdue_jobs` with a misfire grace window and a deprecated standalone systemd unit. Rolls up automation.cron-scheduler-provider, .chronos-provider, .api-cron-fire, .kanban-systemd.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — agents/core/scheduler_service.py and agents/core/heartbeat.py both assume the long-lived server process is up
capabilities.rationale: Product reason: Nerva is a house brain on the owner's own always-on machine, and its entire claim is that the kernel, the audit chain and the local models live there. A NAS-mediated external firer moves the trigger off that machine and inserts a third party into the trust story for a scale-to-zero shape Nerva does not have and does not want. Re-open if a hosted tier ships, or on a laptop-only install where the box sleeps — and even then port only the missed-run/catch-up policy (`fire_overdue_jobs` + a grace window), which is the part that matters and needs no provider abstraction.
capabilities.governance: n/a today; if re-opened, an external fire ingress is an untrusted origin and would need a signed request crossing the kernel before it may wake anything

capabilities.name: A recurring wakeup inside the conversation you are already having
capabilities.hermes: `/loop [interval] <prompt> [--times N] [--until <cond>]` with status/pause/resume/stop, persisted per session in SessionDB so `/resume` restores it. Self-paced mode (no interval) hashes a timestamp-stripped digest of the reply and backs off exponentially while nothing changes, snapping back to the floor on any change — at zero extra model cost. Stop conditions in a fixed priority order: agent self-stop (`LOOP_COMPLETE` on its own line) → `--until` judge (fail-open) → `--times` cap → `max_ticks` backstop, which *pauses* rather than finishes. The gateway idle watcher scans persisted loops every 15 s and skips (leaving the tick due) when a turn is running, when a goal owns the boundary, or when there is no route. Rolls up automation.loop, .loop-self-paced, .loop-stop-conditions, .loop-wakeup-prompt, .loop-wakeup-watcher.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — agents/core/quickbar.py parses slash input but its grammar is HUD navigation, verb navigation and agent summon only; there is no in-session recurring wakeup on any surface
capabilities.rationale: This is the cheapest autonomy in the whole product: 'keep watching this until it is green' without arming a durable job, approving a goal, or opening a work run. Nerva's schedule_runtime.py already argues for exactly the same restraint (never poke a run that should not be running, skip without ticking, every skip reported) — /loop is that discipline applied at conversation scale. Inject the wakeup as an ordinary user message so prompt caching and role alternation survive.
capabilities.governance: read-only in itself — a wakeup is a synthetic user turn; every effect the woken turn attempts crosses the kernel exactly as a typed message would. The three deferral rules (never fire mid-turn, a goal wins, leave the tick due on skip) are the safety contract.
capabilities.depends_on: a per-session state store (agents/core/autonomy has no session-scoped meta table today)

capabilities.name: A standing instruction that re-enters this session on a cadence
capabilities.hermes: `/heartbeat every <interval> <prompt>` with pause/resume/clear/status, persisted per session, fired only when the session is idle, with the fire recorded **before** the turn runs so a long turn cannot double-fire, missed ticks coalescing into one (anchor resets to now, never to the theoretical schedule), a 60 s floor, and every DB failure degrading to 'no heartbeat' rather than a crashed input loop. Rolls up automation.heartbeat.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/heartbeat.py `HeartbeatScheduler` — reads cron expressions from agents/*/HEARTBEAT.md (with HEARTBEAT.local.md and user-souls overlays), MIN_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL 3600 s, jitter 15–30 s; it is per-agent and developer/config authored, and binds to no conversation
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already has the machinery and the guardrails (minimum interval, jitter); what it lacks is the owner being able to set one in a sentence and have it re-enter *this* conversation. Copy two rules verbatim: record the fire before the turn, and coalesce missed ticks so a backlog never stacks after a restart.
capabilities.governance: read-only (an injected user turn); effects cross the kernel normally
capabilities.depends_on: row 12 (shares the session state store and the idle-boundary rule)

capabilities.name: A goal that keeps being worked until something independent says it is done
capabilities.hermes: `/goal <text>` runs a Ralph loop: after each turn a cheap auxiliary judge returns done/continue/wait and a continuation prompt is fed back as an ordinary user message until done, a 20-turn budget expires, or the user intervenes. An optional five-field completion contract (outcome/verification/constraints/boundaries/stop_when) with a closed alias table sharpens the judge; `/subgoal` appends acceptance criteria mid-loop without resetting. The judge fails **open** (a broken judge must not wedge progress) with auto-pause after 3 parse or 5 transport failures. Rolls up automation.goal, .goal-contract, .subgoal, .goal-judge.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/goal_contract.py (a GoalDraft must carry title, scope, budget, deadline, ≥1 stop condition and ≥1 success check before it can even be proposed; `unrestricted=True` must be chosen explicitly so nobody widens a goal by leaving a field blank; proposes as an ask-tier task); agents/core/autonomy/work_runs.py (open_run refuses a GoalSpec without an `approved_by` ref — no provisional mode; steps carry the durable task_id that authorised them; budgets are hard and a stop is a one-way door); agents/core/autonomy/work_verifier.py; agents/core/autonomy/work_judge.py (fail-closed, scope is a hard boundary, a rubric can only withhold a pass, never grant one); agents/core/autonomy/company_supervisor.py (one tick one step, stop read before planning, a refusal is a step that spends budget); `goal.approve` in agents/core/kernel/registry.py
capabilities.rationale: This is the row where Nerva is straightforwardly ahead and the reason the product exists. Hermes' contract is optional and its judge fails open; Nerva's contract is mandatory, the owner's approval crosses the kernel, the verifier refuses to accept the run's own claims as evidence, and the judge fails closed with scope as a hard boundary. Do not port Hermes' loop. The only things to add on top are surface-level: there is no way to say 'goal: …' in a conversation (it goes through POST /api/company), and no mid-loop `/subgoal` to add a criterion without redrafting the whole contract.
capabilities.governance: `goal.approve` — already Mediation.KERNEL in agents/core/kernel/registry.py; each step the run later takes crosses the kernel again on its own (`delegated_execution_only`)

capabilities.name: Deterministic gates that must pass before anything may be called done
capabilities.hermes: `/goal gate add <shell command>` attaches commands that must exit 0 before the LLM judge is even consulted; gates run at the turn boundary *before* the judge, and a failure short-circuits judging and becomes the next prompt verbatim (command, exit code, 3000-char output tail, 'do not declare the goal complete while any gate fails'). A workspace fingerprint lets a gate that failed on an unchanged workspace replay its recorded failure instead of burning wall-clock re-running the same red suite; exhausting retries auto-pauses the goal. Rolls up automation.goal-gates.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/work_verifier.py — a Check carries a probe callable that goes and looks; a check with no probe is `unverifiable`, never `passed`; a probe that raises is a failure, not a skip; the run's own claims are never evidence. The principle is present and stricter than Hermes', but a probe is a Python callable fixed when the goal is drafted — the owner cannot attach `pytest -q` or `npm test` as a gate, and no failure output is fed back as the next prompt.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already wins the argument ('a check needs a probe'); the missing piece is that the owner can supply the probe as a command at approval time, and that a red gate becomes the working instruction rather than just a verdict. The unchanged-workspace replay is the non-obvious win — it is what stops a stuck run re-running the same failing suite for hours.
capabilities.governance: A gate is host execution and must cross `terminal.exec` with the hardline denylist and TERMINAL_EXEC_CONTRACT applied; a gate command supplied by a model rather than the owner must not run at all

capabilities.name: Park a run on real async work instead of poking it
capabilities.hermes: Three barrier kinds on the goal state — wait on a pid until the process exits, wait on a registered session until its own trigger fires, wait until a wall-clock deadline — and while any is active `evaluate_after_turn` short-circuits **without burning a turn or calling the judge**. The judge sees the live background-process list and can itself return a third verdict, `wait`. Any dead pid, fired trigger or elapsed deadline clears the barrier on the next check, so a stale barrier can never wedge the loop. Rolls up automation.goal-wait.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/schedule_runtime.py SKIP_REASONS — `blocked` ('waiting on the owner's decision; poking it changes nothing and adds noise') is exactly this restraint for the human case, and `budget_spent`/`stopping`/`terminal` for the others; there is no barrier for a pid, a background session or a deadline
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's supervisor already refuses to poke a run waiting on a person; it has no equivalent for a run waiting on a build, a deploy or a rate-limit cooldown, so those burn budget on 'is it done yet' turns. Since a step that spends budget is a hard bound in work_runs.py, this is not just waste — it is a run failing for lack of budget it spent on polling.
capabilities.governance: read-only (the barrier suppresses work; it never grants any)

capabilities.name: Run the self-improvement review on demand
capabilities.hermes: `/refine [focus]` forks the background memory/skill self-improvement review against a *conversation snapshot* so the live session and its prompt cache are untouched, refuses while a turn is in flight, and reports the new/updated memories and skills back into the chat. Rolls up automation.refine.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/reflection.py (nightly, idempotent per calendar day, LLM highlights/lessons promoted into the KG); agents/core/routers/self_improvement.py exposes only /status and /enable; the learning loop is scheduled by agents/core/scheduler_service.py with POST /api/learning/propose as its manual trigger
capabilities.rationale: Nerva has the review and a manual trigger for one half of it, but nothing that says 'save what we just worked out, now, with this focus'. The snapshot-and-fork mechanic is the part worth copying — running a second model pass over a live conversation any other way corrupts the session.
capabilities.governance: read-only (proposes memories/skills); a skill install still crosses `skill.install` with its permanent owner-approval floor

capabilities.name: A durable board where multi-agent work lives: dependencies, atomic claims, run history, event log
capabilities.hermes: One SQLite DB per board with nine statuses that distinguish waiting-on-dependencies (`todo`) from waiting-on-a-human (`blocked`) from waiting-on-time (`scheduled`); a tasks table carrying claim_lock/claim_expires/worker_pid/last_heartbeat/max_runtime/consecutive_failures/max_retries/model pins/skills; a `task_runs` row per dispatch attempt with a closed status and outcome domain; an append-only `task_events` log with 38 event kinds from which status can be reconstructed during recovery; link/unlink building the dependency graph that `recompute_ready` promotes automatically; boards create/switch/export/import as a scrubbed tarball; comments, attachments by absolute path, gc/repair (fail-closed, auto-repairs exactly one provably safe corruption class), stats, tail, watch, assignees. Rolls up ~26 entries: automation.kanban-group/states/task-record/runs/events/init/boards/transfer/create/list/show/assign/reclaim/claim/heartbeat/complete/block/promote/link/comment/attachments/goal-mode/observability/maintenance.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/queue.py (SQLite task queue, strict transition table, retry cap, no re-entry after terminal, hash-chained mediation receipts via mediation.py — governance Hermes has nothing like); agents/core/autonomy/missions.py (persistent workspace: goal, ordered plan, hard step/second budget, artifacts dir, append-only event log, pause/resume) + agents/core/routers/missions.py; frontend/src/panels/mission-canvas.tsx. Neither has a dependency edge between units, an assignee, an atomic claim, or a per-attempt run row. `rg -i kanban` over the repo returns zero hits outside docs/research/.
capabilities.rationale: This is what turns Nerva's cabinet of named agents (jarvis, athena, friday, pepper, oracle, …) from a routing table into a company. Company mode already has the goal contract, the ledger, the verifier and the judge; the missing piece is the shared, dependency-aware unit of work those agents claim from and hand off between. Build it *onto* queue.py's state machine and mediation receipts rather than as a second store — Hermes' own rebuild note says atomic claims via conditional UPDATE plus an append-only event log is the entire durable core, and everything else is policy.
capabilities.governance: Creating and linking cards is read-only. Claiming and dispatching one is delegated execution only: a card must never carry authority, and every privileged effect a worker attempts leaves through the queue and the kernel exactly as company_supervisor.py already enforces (`delegated_execution_only`).
capabilities.depends_on: nothing — agents/core/autonomy/queue.py and missions.py are the substrate to extend

capabilities.name: Cards get dispatched to workers in isolated workspaces, with a circuit breaker
capabilities.hermes: One dispatch pass in three phases (reclaim stale claims → promote ready → spawn workers) so promotion and claiming can never interleave into a double spawn. A worker lane is a written contract: an identity (the assignee), a spawn mechanism, an environment handed in (task id, DB path, board, workspace, run id, claim lock, profile, tenant) and exactly one terminator per run (`kanban_complete` / `kanban_request_review` / `kanban_block`, else reaped as crashed/gave_up/timed_out). Three workspace kinds — scratch, git worktree, pinned dir. A per-card `max_retries` or `kanban.failure_limit` trips a circuit breaker that auto-blocks. A turn-end stop-guard refuses to read 'the model stopped talking' as success and re-prompts a bounded number of times. Rolls up automation.kanban-dispatch, .kanban-daemon, .kanban-worker-lanes, .kanban-workspaces, .kanban-stop-nudge.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/worker.py (tick runs approved tasks through an injected executor with a retry cap); agents/core/autonomy/executor.py (kind→handler registry, longest-prefix dispatch); agents/core/subagents.py (concurrency cap, depth cap, per-spawn SteerChannel with steer/stop, typed output validation, per-spawn cost attribution) + agents/core/routers/mesh.py:215-258; agents/core/environments/execution.py GovernedTargetRunner (routes a command through the target policy plane and the Sandbox). No claim, no per-card workspace, no terminator contract, no auto-block.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's spawner is in some ways ahead — steer/stop on a live child and typed output validation are things Hermes' lane contract does not give — but it fans out with no shared work unit underneath, so nothing reclaims, retries or blocks. The stop-nudge is the small, high-value port: treating 'stopped with no tool call' as a clean exit is how a model quirk silently corrupts a board.
capabilities.governance: Spawning is `node.dispatch`/`tool.rpc` class (both already KERNEL); the worker's own effects cross the kernel individually. The steer channel must remain explicitly not-an-approval — agents/core/subagents.py already documents exactly that and it must survive the port.

capabilities.name: Review as a state, not a block (request-review / request-changes / reopen)
capabilities.hermes: `request-review` moves a card to a `review` status — explicitly not a block, because treating it as one breaks ready-queue accounting — optionally reassigning to a reviewer and recording a summary plus structured handoff metadata; `request-changes` is the reviewer's verdict, returning the run to its implementer with concrete required changes recorded as an event and a comment; `reopen-review` sends review cards back. A live-claim guard refuses to move a running claimed card without `--force`. Rolls up automation.kanban-review.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/routers/review.py is an output-quality queue (H10.25: flag / vote / add-to-dataset), not a work handoff; agents/core/autonomy/inbox.py offers approve / edit / reject / defer on a single task, which is a one-party decision, not a two-party implementer→reviewer cycle
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's thesis is that a human gates what matters, and 'send it back with the concrete changes required' is the cheapest form of that gate for work the owner does not want to approve field by field. It is also the only path by which one agent can grade another's output without either of them being able to declare itself done — which is the same argument work_judge.py already makes inside a single run.
capabilities.governance: read-only (a status change plus an event); no privileged effect

capabilities.name: Turn a one-line ask into a spec, or into a graph of routed children
capabilities.hermes: `kanban specify` calls an auxiliary model to rewrite a triage card's title and body into an actionable spec and promotes it out of triage; `kanban decompose` splits a triage card into a dependency graph of children routed to the specialist profile whose *description* best fits, and falls back to specify-style single promotion when the model judges the task not worth fanning out; the dispatcher auto-decomposes up to `kanban.auto_decompose_per_tick` triage cards per pass. Rolls up automation.kanban-specify, .kanban-decompose.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/company_planner.py — ChecklistPlanner walks the plan written when the goal was approved (fully deterministic, the default), ModelPlanner is behind scope/budget/no-repeat clamps and must be passed in explicitly; agents/core/routers/workflows.py has /api/workflows/hierarchical and /api/workflows/step/generate; nothing decomposes an inbox item into routed, linked children
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's clamp discipline ('the planner proposes, the clamp disposes'; scope enforced at proposal time; a repeat is not a plan) is better than Hermes' and must stay the frame. What is missing is the *triage* front door — accepting a messy one-line ask without polluting the ready queue — and routing children to the cabinet agent whose description fits, which Nerva's named-agent roster makes natural. Keep Hermes' 'don't fan out' fallback: forced decomposition of a simple task produces make-work children.
capabilities.governance: read-only (proposes cards); the owner still approves the goal, and each child's effects cross the kernel independently

capabilities.name: A fan-out/fan-in swarm written as a graph over the existing board
capabilities.hermes: `kanban swarm <goal> --worker P:TITLE --verifier V --synthesizer S` writes the whole shape in one command — an immediately-completed planning root, N parallel workers in ready, a verifier linked to every worker, and a synthesizer linked to the verifier — with a shared blackboard as prefixed JSON comments on the root card. Deliberately **no second scheduler**: all state stays in the existing tables so the dashboard, notifier, slash command and dispatcher keep working unchanged. Rolls up automation.kanban-swarm.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/routers/swarm.py (mission-control cockpit aggregating fleet, autonomy funnel, missions, workflow runs, spawns, A2A inbox, kill switch and the external dev swarm — read-only by design); agents/core/subagents.py fans out; agents/core/autonomy/work_verifier.py and work_judge.py already are the verify and grade stages
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already has the two hardest pieces — an evidence verifier and a fail-closed judge — plus the cockpit to watch it. What is missing is the single command that writes the shape. Hermes' constraint is the important part of the port: express a swarm as a graph over the existing kernel, because a bespoke swarm runtime duplicates claiming, retries and observability for no gain, and would sit outside Nerva's mediation receipts.
capabilities.governance: read-only (writes cards); the verifier/synthesizer stages inherit the goal's approval and each effect crosses the kernel individually

capabilities.name: The system tells the operator what is wrong and what to press
capabilities.hermes: Nine stateless, read-only rules over (task, recent events, recent runs, graph context) — hallucinated_cards, triage_aux_unavailable, prose_phantom_refs, repeated_failures, repeated_crashes, review_dependency_deadlock, stuck_in_blocked, block_unblock_cycling, stranded_in_ready — each producing a canonical kind, a severity (warning/error/critical), a one-line title, detail, and structured suggested actions (reclaim/reassign/comment/cli_hint) the UI renders as buttons. Auto-clearing: nothing to migrate, nothing to garbage-collect. Deliberately excludes transient blips. Rolls up automation.kanban-diagnostics-engine.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/error_logger.py (48-hour grouping into a checkbox diagnostics.md); agents/core/autonomy/log_scanner.py (rate spikes, first-seen error codes); frontend/src/panels/* render governance state richly but nothing computes per-item diagnostics with attached recovery actions
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's honesty rails already say the right thing everywhere else ('a red verdict now names the case that broke it'); this is that principle applied to stuck work. The design constraint is the valuable part: stateless rules with a canonical kind code and attached actions mean the HUD can render a button per action without knowing the rule, and diagnostics vanish on their own when the failure mode resolves while the audit trail stays.
capabilities.governance: read-only by construction — the rules must perform no writes, which is also what makes them safe to run on every board load

capabilities.name: Subscribe a chat to a work item's terminal events — including waking the agent
capabilities.hermes: `kanban notify-subscribe <task> --platform P --chat-id C [--thread-id T] [--delivery-mode notify|notify+wake|wake]` closes a human-in-the-loop workflow back into the conversation that asked for it; `last_event_id` is advanced transactionally per subscription so a restarted notifier never re-notifies everything; `kanban.auto_subscribe_on_create` subscribes the creating chat by default and finished subscriptions are pruned after 30 days. Rolls up automation.kanban-notify.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/inbox.py (decision cards with accept/edit/respond/ignore); agents/core/autonomy/escalation.py (governed allowlisted multi-channel fan-out); agents/core/autonomy/presence.py (away → also escalate, present → HUD is enough) — richer than Hermes on *when* to interrupt, but scoped to approval decisions rather than to 'this piece of work finished'
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's presence-aware, budget-bounded interrupt model is the better foundation; it just has no subscription for completion. The `notify+wake` mode is the idea worth taking — waking the agent so it reads the full context and answers in its own voice, rather than emitting a bare status line — and the transactional `last_event_id` claim is the mechanic that stops a restart re-notifying everything.
capabilities.governance: `channel.reply` (already KERNEL); a wake spends interrupt budget and must respect the night window in agents/core/autonomy/worker.py `is_night_window`

capabilities.name: Named multi-folder projects that give work a stable repo and branch convention
capabilities.hermes: `hermes project create/list/show/use/rename/archive/restore`, `add-folder`/`remove-folder`/`set-primary`, and `bind-board` linking a project to a kanban board so cards inherit its repo and branch convention; a project store persists folders, the active-project pointer and cached repo discovery. Rolls up automation.project-group, .project-schema, .project-create, .project-lifecycle, .project-folders, .project-bind-board.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/data_spaces.py (named spaces scoping what an agent may READ — least privilege, unrestricted until deliberately scoped); agents/core/environments/ (execution profiles and governed targets). Both are adjacent concepts; neither is a workspace grouping with folders and a primary repo.
capabilities.rationale: Product reason: Nerva's unit of context is the owner's house and their approved goal, not a checkout. A project registry is a hierarchy whose only current members would be empty — it only starts paying once there is a board underneath it and a real coding lane above it. Building it first invents structure the product does not yet have work for, and it overlaps confusingly with data_spaces.py, which already answers 'what may this agent see'. Re-open the moment row 18 ships and a card needs a stable branch name; `bind-board` is then the only half worth porting.
capabilities.governance: read-only (a registry); the folder set would feed file_tools scoping, which crosses `file.write`

capabilities.name: An isolated git worktree per parallel agent, and an attended reclaim of the leftovers
capabilities.hermes: `hermes -w` starts a session inside a fresh `.worktrees/<name>/` on branch `hermes/<name>` based on the freshly-fetched remote tip, with its own checkpoint history for rollback; `/worktree new` retargets a *running* session's terminal and file tools with no restart; `hermes worktree list|prune` classifies every tree by age, size, verdict and reason and reclaims only the safe ones — never uncommitted tracked changes, never unique unpushed commits, never in-use trees, never a protected branch — archiving untracked scratch to `~/.hermes/archive/` before removal; the cron tick runs the same safe reclaim opportunistically. Rolls up automation.worktree-flag, .worktree-slash, .worktree-group, .worktree-list, .worktree-prune, .worktree-cron-maintenance.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none as a product feature — `rg -i worktree` over agents/, frontend/src, mobile/src, scripts/ finds hits only in PARALLEL_WORKFLOW.md, AGENTS.md, STATUS.md and NERVA_VISION.md, i.e. a *developer* process for humans working this repo, never something Nerva does for its own agents
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already ships codeintel and already coordinates external coding agents through repo lock files (agents/core/routers/swarm.py reads the dev-swarm locks) — the moment two of its own agents work the same checkout they clobber each other, and Nerva's own parallel-work doc exists precisely because a human noticed this. The wider prize is the posture: classify-before-delete and archive-before-remove is the only defensible shape for anything Nerva does to the owner's working tree, and per-session checkout plus per-session checkpoint history is the pair that makes parallel agents safe — either alone is not enough.
capabilities.governance: Creating or removing a worktree moves bytes on the owner's disk → `file.write` (already KERNEL, with previous-bytes snapshotting so rollback is real); the git invocations themselves are `terminal.exec`. Automatic reclaim in particular must be a governed, reversible-tier action, never a background convenience.

capabilities.name: Federated rooms across machines: replicas, authority takeover, peer grants, target-side execution policy
capabilities.hermes: A room is a durable named multi-member conversation owned by an authority gateway with an append-only ordered event log; every other participant holds a replica with fenced primitives to take authority when the host dies; RoomLinks store routes and scoped grants with a status so the UI can show when re-authorization is needed; the **target** gateway — not the caller — decides what a remote member's turn may do (toolsets, iteration cap); policy checkpoints avoid replaying full history; a deterministic turn planner produces exactly one next driver task; a driver lease ensures one process drives a room at a time. Rolls up 9 entries: automation.hosted-room-core/replicas/links/peer/execution-policy/policy-checkpoint/discussion/driver/service.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/routers/rooms.py is a simple local chat-channel list; agents/core/a2a.py is HMAC-allowlisted peer intake that is off by default and **never auto-executes** — a verified task lands in a pending inbox the owner approves out of band; agents/core/routers/mesh.py has node/satellite registration and dispatch, with `node.dispatch` already crossing the kernel
capabilities.rationale: Product reason: replica takeover and a federated authority model mean an action authorised by another machine's policy can execute here — which is precisely what Nerva's kernel and single audit chain exist to prevent. Nerva is one owner, one house, one hash-chained log; a second authority model is not a feature gap, it is a different product. The one idea to take now is the inverse of Hermes' risk and costs almost nothing: 'the target decides what a remote member's turn may do' — port that into a2a.py as a per-peer execution policy so an admitted peer's work is bounded by *our* toolset and iteration limits, not theirs. Re-open the full room model only if a multi-house / family-fleet story is ever committed to.
capabilities.governance: `node.dispatch` for the execution-policy piece being kept; the full room model would require a second trust root, which is the reason for the skip
capabilities.depends_on: nothing (the execution-policy slice is S and depends on a2a.py only)

capabilities.name: Drive a long agent run over HTTP: start, poll, stream, steer, stop, resolve its approval
capabilities.hermes: `POST /v1/runs` returns a run_id instead of holding a connection, made safely retryable by an `Idempotency-Key` that returns the original run; `GET /v1/runs/{id}` polls state; `/events` is an SSE stream of tool-call progress, token deltas and lifecycle events that clients can attach to and detach from; `/stop` interrupts at the next safe point; `/steer` injects guidance without cancelling; `/approval` resolves a pending human decision so the run resumes. Plus `/api/sessions/*`, `/api/jobs/*` (cron over REST), and X-Hermes-Session-Key scoping long-term memory independently of the transcript. Rolls up automation.api-server, .api-runs-create/idempotency/status/events/stop/steer/approval, .api-sessions, .api-session-headers, .api-jobs.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/routers/mesh.py:215-258 (POST /api/subagents/spawn, /{id}/steer, /{id}/stop); agents/web.py:985 (SSE chat stream, text/event-stream); agents/core/routers/autonomy.py:211 (POST /autonomy/tasks/{id}/decision) and agents/core/autonomy/action_approvals.py (register an action, await_decision, dry-run preview attached); agents/core/routers/company.py (GET /api/company/runs, /{id}, POST /{id}/stop). Every piece exists; there is no single run object with an id, no idempotency key, and no per-run event stream.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already has spawn, steer, stop, approval resolution and SSE — they are just five different objects on four routers, so the HUD, mobile and an external caller cannot all watch the same thing. Unifying them behind one run id with an idempotent create is what makes a long autonomous run observable rather than merely logged, and it is the surface mobile parity will need.
capabilities.governance: Status and stream are read-only. The approval endpoint must keep routing through the existing queue rather than resolving anything itself. Steer must remain explicitly **not** an approval — agents/core/subagents.py already documents this (a steer carries a declared origin and can never lift a gate) and that rule must survive the unification.

capabilities.name: Point an external client at Nerva (OpenAI-compatible chat, and capability discovery)
capabilities.hermes: `POST /v1/chat/completions` (stateless OpenAI compat, full toolset), `POST /v1/responses` with server-side conversation state, `GET /v1/models` and a rich `/api/model/options`, per-request model/provider/reasoning overrides via `model_routes`, `GET /v1/capabilities` describing the stable surface so external UIs and orchestrators discover support without depending on private internals, `/v1/skills` + `/v1/toolsets` enumeration, `/health` + `/health/detailed`, artifact upload/download and browser-control registration. Rolls up automation.api-chat-completions, .api-responses, .api-models, .api-model-routing, .api-capabilities, .api-health, .api-discovery, .api-artifacts, .api-browser-control, .api-platform-events.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: `rg 'v1/chat/completions|v1/responses|v1/capabilities'` over agents/ finds nothing — the only `/v1/models` string is an *outbound* LM Studio probe at agents/core/routers/admin.py:448. Nerva has adjacent pieces: agents/core/capability_manifests.py, agents/core/routers/system_map.py, agents/core/routers/status.py, agents/core/browser_transport.py
capabilities.rationale: Copy the discovery half only — `/v1/capabilities`, `/v1/skills`, `/v1/toolsets`, `/health/detailed` — because that is how an external UI or a mobile client learns what Nerva can do without asking the model, and capability_manifests.py already holds the data. Deliberately do **not** copy stateless `/v1/chat/completions` as a passthrough: it bypasses session, memory, presence, the interrupt budget and the approval queue, which makes it the one surface through which an integration would obtain an ungoverned Nerva. If a chat façade ever ships it must enter the same kernel path as the HUD, and be flagged accordingly.
capabilities.governance: Discovery is read-only. Any chat façade must cross the same governed path as agents/web.py's own chat, or it is a hole in the kernel by construction.

capabilities.name: Bot-to-bot messaging between machines
capabilities.hermes: `hermes peer add/list/remove` registers another gateway and stores its API key; `hermes peer dm` delivers into the remote agent's canonical Bot Chat, runs one synchronous turn and prints the reply; `hermes peer run/status/stop` is the asynchronous pair for long turns through the peer's Runs API so no HTTP connection is held open. Rolls up automation.peer-group, .peer-add, .peer-list-remove, .peer-dm, .peer-run.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/a2a.py (off by default, allowlist + per-peer shared-secret HMAC over the raw body, constant-time verify, signed Agent Card, and a verified task lands in a pending inbox — 'A2A cannot, by construction, run anything on its own'); agents/core/routers/mesh.py (/api/nodes, /api/satellites, /{id}/dispatch) with `node.dispatch` mediated in agents/core/kernel/registry.py
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's version is governed where Hermes' is not: Hermes' `peer dm` runs a full turn on the remote machine on arrival, Nerva's parks it for the owner. Keep that posture unconditionally. The only thing worth adding is the async handle — start / status / stop for an approved remote turn — so a long peer task is not a held connection; that falls out of row 28 rather than needing its own machinery.
capabilities.governance: `node.dispatch` (already Mediation.KERNEL); the pending-inbox floor must not be lifted by any peer-side grant

capabilities.name: Named inbound webhook routes that wake the agent — or deliver without one
capabilities.hermes: `hermes webhook subscribe <name>` mints `/webhooks/<name>` with an auto-generated HMAC secret (written chmod-0600-**before** the atomic rename, so a permissive umask never exposes it), a `{dot.notation}` prompt template over the payload, an accepted-event allowlist, skills to load, a delivery target, an optional filter/transform script under the scripts dir whose empty stdout / `[SILENT]` / nonzero exit means 'ignore this webhook', and `--deliver-only` which renders the template and sends it with **zero LLM cost**; subscriptions hot-reload without a gateway restart, and `webhook test` POSTs a signed payload so the signature path itself is verified. Rolls up automation.webhook-group, .webhook-subscribe, .webhook-list, .webhook-remove, .webhook-test.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/webhooks.py (H10.8/H16.4: per-webhook token, optional `signed=True` provisioning an HMAC secret with `X-Signature-256` verified constant-time, file-backed JsonStore, extract_input from arbitrary JSON) + agents/core/routers/webhooks.py (GET/POST /api/webhooks, DELETE /{id}, POST /{id} to activate an agent or workflow). Missing: prompt templating, per-route event filter, deliver-only, filter script, a test command, hot reload.
capabilities.rationale: The security half is already there and is the half that is hard to retrofit. The missing half is what makes webhooks affordable and useful: `--deliver-only` plus a filter script means a noisy feed costs nothing, and payload templating means most real traffic never needs a model at all. Hermes' own rebuild note says exactly this: make the zero-model path the easy path.
capabilities.governance: An inbound webhook is an untrusted origin: the woken turn must be tainted so every effect it attempts escalates GRANT→QUEUE per the kernel's taint rule (docs/FLAGS.md), and a filter script is host execution crossing `terminal.exec`

capabilities.name: Send a message to any configured channel from a script, with no model call
capabilities.hermes: `hermes send [-t platform[:chat[:thread]]] [-f PATH|-] [-s SUBJECT] [-l] [--json] [message]` reuses the gateway's own platform credentials, resolves the body from argument / file / piped stdin, supports `MEDIA:<path>` attachments and `--list` target discovery, returns 0/1/2 exit codes, and needs **no running gateway** for bot-token platforms. Its own rebuild note calls it 'the single most useful automation primitive an agent framework can ship'. Rolls up automation.send.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: no console entry point exists at all — `grep -n 'console_scripts|[project.scripts]' pyproject.toml setup.py` returns nothing, and scripts/ holds only build, CI and audit tooling. The adapters exist (agents/core/channels/{telegram,discord,slack,email,voice,webhook_channels}.py) but only inside the running server process.
capabilities.rationale: This is the honest bridge to everything the owner already automates elsewhere — a NAS cron job, a CI step, a Home Assistant script — and it lets them get value from Nerva's channels before trusting it with anything autonomous. It is also the cheapest possible proof that the channel configuration works, which is the failure Hermes' preflight exists to catch. Small, self-contained, and it needs no scheduler, no board and no model.
capabilities.governance: A reply into a live conversation thread is `channel.reply` (already KERNEL). A bare outbound send to the owner's own configured home channel is the reversible tier — but it must still be recorded in the IntentLog via audit_sink.py, or a script gains an unlogged voice as Nerva.

capabilities.name: Refuse a catastrophic shell command no matter who approved it (hardline floor + risky-pattern tier + de-obfuscation)
capabilities.hermes: Three stacked layers inside `tools/approval.py` (5971 lines): 12 unconditional HARDLINE rules evaluated *above* every bypass (rm -rf /, mkfs, dd of=/dev/*, fork bomb, poweroff, kill -1...), a user-editable `approvals.deny` fnmatch list at the same level, and a 99-rule risky-but-recoverable pattern catalogue that routes to a human. Crucially every layer matches over ~15 normalized *variants* produced by `_command_detection_variants()` (:2412): NFKC + backslash strip, quote masking, $()/backtick substitution, `$HOME`/`$HERMES_HOME` folding, `sh -c`/`python -c`/`perl -e` payload extraction, quote-aware `;&&|` splitting, grep-pattern span masking. Parser limits (128k chars / 4096 separator-free / 25k segments) themselves hardline-block and save the payload to a file for manual review. Container backends skip the whole layer, and Docker stops skipping the moment a host path is bind-mounted (`_should_skip_container_guards` :4075).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/environments/terminal_contract.py (HARDLINE: 19 patterns + `_recursive_root_removal`, `_ROOT_OPERANDS`, `_CMD` command-position anchor); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/environments/execution.py (hardline screened FIRST, before authorize, for every backend incl. docker); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/kernel/registry.py:117 ("terminal.exec" → Mediation.KERNEL)
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's floor list is actually broader than Hermes' (19 vs 12 — it adds wipefs, shred /dev, crontab -r, iptables -F / ufw disable / setenforce 0 / Defender-off, /etc/passwd overwrite, Windows root wipe), and the governance around it is strictly better: hardline runs before authorize, and terminal.exec cannot execute without a durable human-accepted task at the irreversible tier. But the matching is the weak half. `_normalize()` does one shlex split, lowercase and whitespace squeeze — no variant expansion. So `sh -c 'mk'\''fs.ext4 /dev/sda'`, `$(printf mkfs).ext4 /dev/sda`, `echo bWtmcw==|base64 -d|sh`, or a `\`-escaped spelling all miss a floor whose entire promise is that it holds regardless of approval. And there is no middle tier at all: `rm -rf ~/projects` is neither hardline nor pattern-classified, so the owner's approval card says "run this argv" instead of "recursive delete". Port the variant pipeline and a ~40-rule severity/reversibility-tagged pattern table that feeds the card's description.
capabilities.governance: privileged — terminal.exec; already crosses kernel.authorize and the approval queue. The port adds refusals only, never a new effect.

capabilities.name: Remember an approval so the same class stops asking, and propose safe candidates from history
capabilities.hermes: `command_allowlist` in config.yaml holds either a dangerous-pattern key or a literal/glob command; answering `[a]lways` writes it. `_has_allowlist_shell_operator()` (:3080) is a quote-aware scanner that refuses the glob shortcut for any compound command or one carrying a re-interpreting flag (`-c`, `--eval`, `git -c alias.x='!…'`), so `cargo *` still matches `cargo bench -- '^a(b|c)$'` but never `sh -c 'rm -rf /'`. `hermes approvals suggest` mines the session DB for flagged-but-executed commands, derives narrow globs, and hard-excludes 34 destructive class descriptions and 25 root binaries regardless of frequency; nothing is written without `--apply N,M`.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/permission_ledger.py (once | session | always | never per app/site/OS-input/file-root/terminal-target, immutable default-deny list, grants applied only from the human-decided task's execution, `session` grants die with the boot id, `once` consumed by one allow)
capabilities.rationale: The permission ledger is the better *shape* — grants are a governed, durable, auditable artifact that only a human decision can create, whereas Hermes' allowlist is a config line the agent could be talked into proposing. What is missing is the grain: the ledger's terminal grants are per-*target*, not per-command-class, so an owner who wants `git push` to stop asking on their own box has no way to say that except widening the whole target. capabilities.name: Unpack an archive from another machine without letting it write outside the destination
capabilities.hermes: `hermes_cli/archive_safe.py` is deliberately the single place this logic lives so a second transfer surface cannot ship a weaker extractor. `normalize_archive_parts` folds `\` to `/` first (so a Windows-authored member cannot smuggle a separator past the POSIX parse), then rejects empty, POSIX-absolute, Windows-absolute, drive-lettered and any `..`-containing names. Extraction handles directories and regular files only — symlinks, hardlinks and device nodes RAISE rather than being skipped, so a tampered archive fails the import instead of landing a partial tree. The producing side writes to a sibling temp file and `os.replace`s, because `tarfile.open` truncates the destination the instant it opens. GNU format is chosen deliberately over PAX so macOS Archive Utility can open it. The export side skips symlinks so a planted link cannot pull an arbitrary file in.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/backup.py:401 (`_safe_extract`: regular files and dirs only, every member resolved and checked inside dest, symlinks/devices skipped by design); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/skills/marketplace.py:731-785 (a separate zip-slip rejection pass before `extractall`, plus JARVIS_REQUIRE_SIGNED_SKILLS)
capabilities.rationale: Both extractors are correct today, which is the problem — there are two of them, in different formats, written at different times, and Hermes' own note is that a second transfer surface is exactly how a weaker one ships. Consolidate into one module both call, add the two protections neither has (a total-uncompressed-size and member-count cap against zip bombs, and RAISE-on-symlink rather than skip so a tampered archive fails loudly instead of restoring a quietly incomplete tree), and add the atomic-write discipline on the producing side so a failed backup does not destroy the previous one.

capabilities.name: Catch content-level attacks in a command that pattern matching cannot see
capabilities.hermes: Tirith: an external scanner run before every terminal command for homograph/IDN URL spoofing, pipe-to-interpreter shapes and terminal-escape injection. Repeated at the WebSocket layer because FastAPI HTTP middleware does not run for upgrades, with machine-parseable rejection reasons and close code 4403. CORS is pinned to a localhost origin regex, never `*`. `dashboard.trusted_proxies` validates each entry as an IP or a BOUNDED CIDR and rejects `/0` outright, failing closed rather than widening trust. Password login is throttled per IP with an `_unknown_` bucket for unattributable traffic.

That is a real attack against exactly Nerva's default deployment shape (loopback bind, owner browsing the web on the same machine). One middleware, ~30 lines, matched against `app.state.bound_host`. No WebSocket variant is needed — Nerva has no WS routes.

capabilities.name: See who authenticated, who failed, and when
capabilities.hermes: `$HERMES_HOME/logs/dashboard-auth.log`, one JSON object per line, covering 16 event types — login start/success/failure, logout, refresh success/failure, revoke, session verify failure, ws ticket minted/rejected, token auth success/failure, and the four native-app events. A fixed `_REDACTED_FIELDS` set (access_token, refresh_token, code, code_verifier, state, ticket, cookie, Authorization) is DROPPED before serialisation so tokens never reach disk, writes are lock-serialised, and a write failure logs at WARNING but never raises — auth must not fail because the audit logger broke. Its own rebuild note asks for a hash-chained log shipped off-box.

Add a per-provider data-handling tier to the router's model choice and surface it on the security posture panel.

capabilities.name: Consent once, in writing, before a user-supplied command becomes a lifecycle hook

Without a TTY registration FAILS CLOSED unless `--accept-hooks` / `HERMES_ACCEPT_HOOKS=1` / `hooks_auto_accept` is explicitly set, and `HERMES_ACCEPT_HOOKS` is itself on the env-writer denylist so a dashboard caller cannot persist it.

Re-open path: if Nerva ever adds owner-authored automation hooks that run a command on an event, this row is the design — consent per (event, command) pair, the script mtime recorded so an edit re-prompts, `shell=False`, and a non-TTY path that fails closed — and it should ship in the same PR as the hooks, not after.

Today `media_gen._queue_cloud` calls the plain `q.enqueue` (agents/core/media_gen.py:132) with risk_tier=2, and `media.image`/`media.video` are **absent** from agents/core/kernel/registry.py, whose media entries are only `media.present` and `media.restore` (registry.py:78,81). No encoder, no ffmpeg call, no provider.

Keep video_pipeline.py as the front end and give it a real render step. Adapt: one local backend plus one cloud provider behind the same seam as image generation; drop the provider-specific edit/extend tools, which are vendor lock-in dressed as capability.

capabilities.name: Look at an image and answer questions about it, mid-conversation

It takes a URL, a local path or a data: URL plus a question, and an optional `region` crop in **original-image pixel coordinates applied before any downscaling**, so the documented workflow is 'load the full image, then re-call with a region to zoom into small text'. Two execution paths: a native fast path attaching the image directly to the main model when the provider+model can carry media in a tool result, and an auxiliary-vision path that returns text otherwise (media.computer-use-vision-routing, media.vision-tool-result-support). `agent.image_input_mode` decides how user-attached images on the current turn reach the model, and inline image references are extracted from prose so they attach automatically.

But the agent-callable tool surface is only desktop_run, terminal_run, desktop_plan, operator_plan, osint_enrich, echo, time (agents/core/autonomy_coordinator.py:433-677) plus file tools (agents/core/file_tools.py:900) — there is no `vision_analyze` the model can decide to call, no region crop, and no native-attach path.

What is missing is reach: vision is an HTTP route for the HUD, not a capability the assistant has. Add the model-callable tool (kernel-mediated like every other tool via tool_rpc) plus the region crop, which is the single highest-value detail Hermes has — it is how you read small text without shipping a 4K image.
capabilities.governance: Read-only against a loopback VLM. A cloud vision model crosses `plugin.egress`; keep the screen-reflex hard refusal for non-loopback as the model for any capture-derived image. Registration goes through agents/core/tool_rpc.py, whose kind prefix already routes tool calls through the kernel (`tool.rpc`, registry.py:55).

capabilities.name: Accept an image safely before it enters conversation history
capabilities.hermes: A layered ingest guard: SSRF checks, size caps and decode validation refuse unsafe/oversized/undecodable images *before* they reach immutable history (media.vision-ingest-guards); normalisation rasterises SVG and coerces to one of the four media types the major vision providers accept (media.vision-normalize); MIME sniffing decides the declared media_type from the bytes and transcodes to PNG when the real type is not universally supported (media.image-mime-transcode); embeds are downscaled proactively and again reactively after a provider size rejection (media.vision-sizing); a CPU-burst semaphore stops an 'analyze every frame' fan-out from starving the event loop (media.vision-cpu-cap); and under a non-local terminal backend, path-like source images reach the provider as data: URLs so a container path never leaks to a third party (media.image-source-confinement). `tools/image_source.py` is the one resolver every path shares.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/security/ssrf.py (resolve_and_validate with DNS-rebind handling, IPv4-in-IPv6 unwrapping, is_private_ip, public/lan modes, a blocked-request counter) — this is stronger than Hermes's per-call guards; agents/core/llm/vlm.py:282 encode_image_block accepts only bytes, `data:` URIs and http(s) URLs and refuses filesystem paths outright, with `_downscale(..., max_dim=1024)`; agents/core/cameras/vlm.py caps at 2 MB and pins the endpoint to loopback. Missing: decode validation, SVG rasterisation, MIME sniffing/transcode, shrink-on-reject retry, and any concurrency cap.
capabilities.rationale: The network half is already superior and should be kept as-is — Nerva's ssrf.py is a real module where Hermes has inline checks. The bytes half is the gap: without decode validation and MIME sniffing, a mislabelled or malformed image becomes a provider 400 or, worse, an unbounded decode. Shrink-on-reject is the cheap win that turns a hard failure into a retry.
capabilities.governance: Read-only, but it is the boundary that decides what enters immutable history and the audit log, so it is security-load-bearing. A remote fetch crosses `plugin.egress`.
capabilities.depends_on: shares the resolver with the in-conversation vision row

capabilities.name: Understand a video (not just its audio)
capabilities.hermes: `video_analyze` sends a video from a URL or a local path to a video-capable model (Gemini-class) for understanding, explicitly distinguished from `vision_analyze` for stills (media.tool-video-analyze), sharing the `tools/image_source.py` resolver and its SSRF/size/path guards.

No frame extraction, no visual understanding of a video file.

Adapt rather than copy the shape: sample frames locally and route them through the existing local VLM (which the camera pipeline already does for masked frames), so the default answer is local; a cloud video model stays per-agent opt-in. That inverts Hermes's default and matches the local-first non-negotiable.

capabilities.depends_on: the in-conversation vision row and the ingest-guard row

capabilities.name: Serve a generated or cached media file back to a client
capabilities.hermes: `GET /api/media?path=…` serves a generated/cached media file to the browser, backed by a delivery allowlist restricting which host directories `MEDIA:` delivery may read from, plus an inbound attachment size cap and a bound on how long a cron job may spend sending media (media.api-media-serve, media.gateway-media-limits).

POST /tts (agents/core/routers/voice.py:43) does return a FileResponse, so the pattern exists for audio only.

Copy the capability but not the shape: Hermes takes a caller-supplied `path` and defends it with an allowlist; Nerva should serve by **catalog id**, resolving the path server-side, so there is no path parameter to defend in the first place. Strictly safer and no harder to build.

capabilities.name: Speak a reply out loud with a chosen voice and backend
capabilities.hermes: `text_to_speech` is a model-callable tool returning a `MEDIA:` path the platform delivers as native audio. Eleven built-in backends with a documented resolution order: Edge TTS (default, free, 322 voices / 74 languages, no key), ElevenLabs (native Opus + streaming), OpenAI and any OpenAI-compatible server, MiniMax, Mistral Voxtral, Gemini TTS (30 voices, natural-language performance direction from a persona file, hidden audio tags), xAI (cloned voices, expressive tags), DeepInfra, and three local engines — NeuTTS (reference-audio cloning), KittenTTS (25-80 MB models) and Piper (CPU-only, 44 languages). Plus shell-command providers, a Python plugin ABC, response body limits, a `hermes setup tts` wizard section and a picker.

Dispatch is substring matching on the voice string (tts.py:161-184), there is no provider registry, no response size limit, and the default (edge-tts) is a **network** call to Microsoft — the local-first posture is not honoured in the default path.

The important adaptation is not more vendors — it is making Piper or NeuTTS the default so the flagship voice loop runs with the network down, which is a Nerva non-negotiable that the current edge-tts default quietly violates. Skip MiniMax/Gemini/xAI/DeepInfra: four more cloud keys is inventory, not capability.

capabilities.name: Refuse to speak in a cloned or persona voice without recorded owner consent
capabilities.hermes: No equivalent. xAI custom (cloned) voices, NeuTTS reference-audio cloning and ElevenLabs voices are all selected by config with no consent record — the only related control is that voice and provider are user-configured rather than model-selected.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/voice/tts.py:31-80 — PERSONA_VOICE_CONSENT_CATEGORY/KEY, PERSONA_VOICE_MARKERS = ('xtts','elevenlabs','fish'), is_persona_or_cloned_voice(), voice_persona_consent_granted() which reads persisted owner consent and **fails closed** when settings are unreadable, and voice_persona_consent_status(); tests/test_q4_voice_consent.py.

Keep it, and treat it as a constraint on the TTS row above: PERSONA_VOICE_MARKERS is a hardcoded three-item tuple, so every cloning-capable backend added later must be added here in the same commit or the gate silently stops covering it. That coupling should be a test, not a convention.

capabilities.depends_on: must be extended alongside the TTS provider row

capabilities.name: Make a spoken reply sound like speech rather than read-out markdown
capabilities.hermes: TTS text normalisation turns a Markdown chat reply into speakable prose — strips formatting, emoji, `<think>` blocks and verifier footers, expands symbols, flattens newlines (media.tts-text-normalize).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/voice/tts.py:47 strip_emotion_tags() removes only the twelve known `[emotion]` tags so non-Fish backends do not read them aloud. POST /tts (agents/core/routers/voice.py:43) passes `req.text` straight to `engine.speak()` with no cleaning. agents/core/voice/sentence_stream.py segments text but does not normalise it.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva replies are markdown — headings, bullets, code fences, bold. Spoken verbatim they are unusable, and this is the difference between a voice mode that works and one the owner turns off after a day. Pure, deterministic, offline text transformation: exactly the kind of thing this repo already does well (see dictation.py) and it ships with tests trivially.
capabilities.governance: Read-only, pure function.

capabilities.name: Start hearing the answer before it is finished, and interrupt by talking
capabilities.hermes: `stream_tts_to_speaker` speaks the assistant's reply as it is generated, sentence by sentence (media.tts-streaming). Barge-in lets you interrupt mid-sentence by talking, while refusing to be interrupted by Hermes' own voice bleeding into the microphone (media.voice-barge-in). Long-form text is split into ordered sentence-aware chunks and the encoded audio grouped under the destination platform's upload limit (media.tts-chunking-packing).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/voice/sentence_stream.py (192 lines — split_sentences + SentenceAggregator emitting complete sentences from streamed deltas, with a final flush); TTSEngine.speak_stream (agents/core/voice/tts.py:190); POST /tts/stream with a documented framed wire protocol, opt-in behind the `voice.sentence_streaming` setting (agents/core/routers/voice.py:85-113); frontend/src/api/ttsStream.ts. Barge-in exists but is labelled by the product itself: frontend/src/cockpit.tsx:244 — 'experimental — talk over the reply to interrupt; needs echo cancellation'.
capabilities.rationale: The hard, pure half (sentence aggregation from a token stream, a framed protocol) is done and done well. The missing half is the audio-engineering half Hermes solved: self-capture suppression so the assistant's own voice does not trigger barge-in. The product already admits this in a UI string, which is honest but is a permanent 'experimental' label until echo cancellation lands.
capabilities.governance: Read-only; the stream is bounded by the existing per-frame size accounting. Barge-in cancels an in-flight turn, so it must route through the existing interrupt path rather than a UI-side abort, or an interrupted action's audit record and its actual effect diverge.

capabilities.name: Deliver audio as a native voice message on a chat platform
capabilities.hermes: The `MEDIA:` path returned by `text_to_speech` is delivered as native audio — a voice bubble on Telegram for compatible providers, a regular attachment elsewhere. `audio_container.py` sniffs the real container of a produced file so voice-bubble conversion and concatenation pick the right path; container repair fixes malformed Ogg, converts to Opus for voice bubbles, and concatenates multi-chunk output (media.tts-audio-container, media.audio-container). Platform packing groups chunks under each destination's upload limit; inbound size caps and a delivery allowlist bound the whole path.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/channels/telegram.py (203 lines) exposes only `send`, `send_card`, `send_action`, `_answer_callback` — text and inline buttons. `rg -i 'sendVoice|send_voice|sendAudio|sendPhoto|sendDocument'` across agents/core/channels/*.py returns nothing. Neither discord.py, slack.py nor email.py carries a media attachment path. No ffmpeg/Opus/container handling anywhere in agents/.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva can synthesise audio (POST /tts returns an MP3) and can reach Telegram, but the two never meet — every reply on every channel is text. For a house assistant reached from a phone, a spoken reply in the chat is the whole point of having TTS at all. Adapt: one container path (Opus for voice notes, the source file otherwise), not Hermes's full repair/concat matrix.
capabilities.governance: Privileged — an outbound message to a third party. `channel.reply` already exists as a kernel kind (agents/core/kernel/registry.py:102); the audio attachment must ride that same mediated reply rather than opening a second send path, or a governed text reply and an ungoverned voice reply would coexist on the same channel.
capabilities.depends_on: the TTS provider row and the media-serving row
