capabilities.name: Transcribe a voice message or dictated speech
capabilities.hermes: `transcribe_audio` validates, preprocesses and dispatches to the active backend, returning `{success, transcript, provider, error?}` (media.stt-pipeline). Eight backends — local faster-whisper (CPU default, GPU when available), a `local_command` env-var escape hatch, Groq, OpenAI, Mistral Voxtral (13 languages, diarization, word timestamps), xAI, ElevenLabs Scribe (audio-event tagging), DeepInfra — plus shell-command providers, a `TranscriptionProvider` ABC, strict explicit selection with auto-detect only on a never-configured install, a whisper prompt-length cap, cloud silence trimming to cut upload bytes, a picker and `POST /api/audio/transcribe`.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/voice/stt.py (102 lines — faster-whisper only, model size and device from settings, `transcribe`/`transcribe_async`, HAS_WHISPER guard); POST /api/voice/stt (agents/core/routers/voice.py:187); GET /api/voice/capabilities (:286) probing engine availability; tests/test_voice_stt.py, tests/test_stt_config.py.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's single backend is the *right* one — faster-whisper local is Hermes's own local option and it matches the local-first non-negotiable, so this is not a deficit of choice. What is missing is the seam (one provider ABC so an OpenAI-compatible transcription endpoint can be added without editing stt.py) and cloud silence trimming, which is pure upload-cost reduction. Skip Groq/Mistral/xAI/ElevenLabs/DeepInfra as distinct backends: one OpenAI-compatible client covers most of them and five more keys is not capability.
capabilities.governance: Local transcription is read-only. Any cloud STT crosses `plugin.egress` and ships the owner's recorded speech off-box — the same disclosure class as cloud TTS, and it should be classified rather than a config default.

capabilities.name: Not turn a silent recording into a message
capabilities.hermes: A hallucination filter drops the canned phrases Whisper emits when it hears silence, so a quiet recording does not become a message (media.voice-hallucination-filter — a 26-phrase list per the v0.20.0 notes). Alongside it, silence-based auto-stop (VAD) ends the recording after continuous silence so the user need not press a key.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/voice/stt.py returns the raw Whisper transcript with no phrase filtering. agents/core/voice/dictation.py cleans disfluencies, stutters and spoken punctuation but has no silence-hallucination list. `rg -i 'hallucinat|vad|webrtcvad|silero'` over agents/ frontend/src/ mobile/src/ returns nothing relevant.
capabilities.rationale: Whisper hallucinating 'Thank you for watching' into an empty room is not a cosmetic bug in a hands-free house assistant — it is a spurious user turn that can trigger a real action, and with wake-word capture running it happens unattended. The fix is a phrase list and a confidence floor: hours of work, and it removes an entire class of false actuation.
capabilities.governance: Read-only filter — but it sits directly upstream of an inbound-taint boundary, since a voice-originated turn is what escalates a mutating action into the approval queue. A hallucinated turn is an un-authored instruction entering a governed system, which makes this a safety control, not a polish item.

capabilities.name: Clean up dictated text into written prose
capabilities.hermes: No equivalent. Hermes normalises text *for* speech (TTS direction) and filters Whisper hallucinations, but nothing converts a raw transcript into clean dictated text.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/voice/dictation.py (132 lines) — strips single-token disfluencies matched whole-word only ('um' dropped, 'umbrella' untouched), collapses stutter repetitions, applies opt-in spoken-punctuation conventions ('period' → '.', 'new line' → a break), bilingual RO/EN, and returns the filler and repeat counts so the cleanup is inspectable rather than a black box.
capabilities.rationale: Pure, deterministic, offline, honest about what it changed — this is the repo's discipline applied well, and it is a capability Hermes simply does not have. Keep it and wire it into the STT path so it is on by default for dictation rather than being a module tests call.
capabilities.governance: Read-only, pure function.

capabilities.name: Hold a hands-free voice conversation
capabilities.hermes: Voice mode records the mic, transcribes with the configured STT backend, submits the result as your message and optionally speaks the reply (media.voice-mode). Around it: a push-to-talk key binding normalised so the same config string works in both CLI front ends; audio cues (start/stop tones and an ambient thinking blip); stop phrases that end the conversation when spoken alone; silence-based auto-stop; audio-environment detection that works out whether the host can record at all (PortAudio, PulseAudio, Termux) and prints a platform-correct fix; and `voice_client_config.py` publishing the record key, direct-capture flag, beeps and thresholds so client and backend agree without duplicating config parsing. Server side: `GET /api/audio/voice-config`, `POST /api/audio/speak` + a speak-stream WebSocket, and an ElevenLabs voice list for settings.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/voice/pipeline.py (139 lines — VoicePipeline coordinating wake → STT → response → TTS, with a done-callback that surfaces exceptions from the fire-and-forget capture task); frontend/src/cockpit.tsx:240 hands-free/push-to-talk toggle and frontend/src/wall.tsx:101 (genuine press-to-start/release-to-stop PTT); frontend/src/voice.ts; GET /api/voice/capabilities (agents/core/routers/voice.py:286) with an engine probe; mobile/src/voice/. Missing: VAD auto-stop, stop phrases, audio cues, a normalised record-key binding, and audio-environment detection with a platform-correct fix message.
capabilities.rationale: The loop closes end to end and the browser/mobile clients exist, which is more than the gap matrix's 'behind' suggests. The missing pieces are all ergonomics that decide whether the loop is usable unattended: without VAD the user must press a key to end every turn, and without audio-env detection a host that cannot record fails silently instead of telling the owner to install PortAudio. Copy those four; skip the ElevenLabs voice-list endpoint, which is one vendor's settings page.
capabilities.governance: Read-only capture. The critical property is the existing one: a voice-initiated turn carries inbound taint, so anything above read-only lands in the decision inbox rather than executing. That must survive every ergonomics change here — a stop phrase or VAD must never become a path that submits a turn with a different origin classification.

capabilities.name: Wake the assistant hands-free with a spoken phrase
capabilities.hermes: 'Hey Hermes' is an always-on, fully on-device hotword listener that opens a fresh session and captures voice through the existing pipeline — no audio leaves the machine for detection (media.wake-word). Three engines: openWakeWord with the bundled 'hey hermes' ONNX/TFLite model shipped in-tree so it works out of the box; sherpa-onnx keyword spotting that detects **any typed phrase with no training** via a streaming zipformer; and Picovoice Porcupine for built-in keywords and custom .ppn files. Capture mode chooses whether PCM comes from PortAudio on the backend host or is streamed as int16 frames from the desktop/TUI client via `wake.feed`, and profile routing lets different profiles enroll different phrases.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/voice/wake_word.py (83 lines) — openWakeWord only, `openwakeword.OWWModel()` with no model pin, a warning if the package is absent, a listen loop and a callback into VoicePipeline._on_wake_word (agents/core/voice/pipeline.py:41). No configurable phrase, no bundled model, no client-fed capture path, no per-profile enrollment.
capabilities.rationale: Wake word is the difference between a chat app and a house assistant, and Nerva's is a stub: no bundled model means it does not work out of the box, and no configurable phrase means it cannot say 'Nerva'. Add sherpa-onnx open-vocabulary spotting (a typed phrase, no training — that is the one that makes the brand name work) and the client capture mode so the browser HUD and the Expo app can feed frames instead of requiring PortAudio on the backend host. Skip Porcupine: a commercial key for a hotword contradicts the local-first non-negotiable.
capabilities.governance: Read-only and, critically, must stay fully on-device — detection audio never leaves the machine, matching the screen-reflex loopback rule. A wake-triggered session inherits the same inbound taint as any voice turn.

capabilities.name: Have the room you spoke in become the output device
capabilities.hermes: No equivalent. Hermes has voice mode and wake word but no notion of rooms, satellites or spatial output routing — audio comes back on the surface that asked.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/voice/wyoming.py (323 lines — Wyoming protocol plus H30.6 authenticated room-aware voice context: digest-only satellite credentials, expiry/peer/transport binding, replay protection, server-owned room identity that ignores client spoofing, refusal on privacy or ambiguity); agents/core/satellite_hub.py; agents/core/rooms.py; media_director `target:"presence:auto"` resolving the owner's room default gated on a fresh presence signal plus JARVIS_MEDIA_PRESENCE_ROOM, with an honest `presence_unknown` on idle/away/stale.
capabilities.rationale: This is the AI-OS thesis expressed in code and there is nothing like it on the Hermes side. It is also the piece that makes the whole voice cluster worth more than the sum of its parts: the TTS, STT and wake-word rows above all get better when the answer comes out of the right speaker. Keep, and treat it as the destination the media rows should aim at.
capabilities.governance: Already correct — output routing lands on the kernel-mediated `media.present` kind and refuses rather than guessing when the room is ambiguous or the presence signal is stale.

capabilities.name: Play or show something on a real device with etiquette, verification and undo
capabilities.hermes: No equivalent. The closest surfaces are the Electron `desktop_preview` pane and browser session recording — Hermes has no device registry, no room model, no playback fabric and no restore semantics.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/media_director.py (1068 lines) — MediaDevice with strict identity/support validation across chromecast/spotify_connect/browser_tab/local/speaker/tv, a bounded atomic corrupt-safe DeviceRegistry with room-aware resolve_target that refuses ambiguity, content resolvers (url/local/catalog/query) that never fetch, session state with interruption etiquette, MEDIA_PRESENT_CONTRACT validated before the kernel sees a request, `verified: true` only when the driver's own status() confirms it, and restore() replaying a pre-present snapshot as machine-readable undo. Kernel kinds `media.present` and `media.restore` (agents/core/kernel/registry.py:78,81); routes in agents/core/routers/media_director.py; NullMediaDriver refuses honestly by default; LocalFileMediaDriver binds via JARVIS_MEDIA_DRIVERS=local_file.
capabilities.rationale: The strongest thing in this cluster and a genuine category difference — Hermes generates media, Nerva *presents* it, governed, verified and reversible. The honest caveat the owner needs: only the local_file driver ships, the Chromecast/Spotify constructors are owner-wired seams, and per docs/OWNER_TASKS.md the audible/visible half has never run on real hardware. Shipping one real driver (Chromecast via pychromecast) is what turns a proven fabric into a proven product.
capabilities.governance: Already the reference implementation for this repo — contract before enqueue, kernel-mediated present/restore, verified-not-asserted, snapshot-as-undo. Every media capability copied from Hermes should be held to this bar; media generation currently is not (see the image-generation row).
capabilities.depends_on: nothing for the fabric; one real driver needs owner hardware

capabilities.name: Read a document (PDF, DOCX, slides) into the conversation
capabilities.hermes: Document extraction backs `read_file`: three formats with the stdlib alone, widening to about a dozen more when the optional `firecrawl-anydoc` package is installed (media.document-extraction), with Office skills (docx/xlsx/pdf/pptx) bundled since v0.20.0. Scanned-PDF coverage detection notices that a PDF's pages carry little or no extractable text and tells the user **which page ranges are empty** so they know to run OCR rather than trusting a half-empty extraction (media.pdf-coverage).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/local_docs.py — indexes a dropped folder into memory: .md/.markdown/.txt/.text/.rst read natively, .pdf/.docx best-effort and **skipped (counted, never fatal) when the optional parser is absent**. That is an indexing path into memory, not a read-file path a turn can use. agents/core/ingestion/{normalizer,knowledge}.py handle ingestion formats. `rg -i 'tesseract|pytesseract|easyocr|paddleocr'` across the repo returns zero hits — there is no OCR anywhere.
capabilities.rationale: 'Read this PDF and tell me what it says' is a first-week request, and today Nerva can only answer it if the file was pre-indexed into memory and the optional parser happened to be installed — otherwise the file is silently skipped. The coverage-detection detail matters more than the format count: a scanned PDF that extracts to near-nothing currently produces a confident answer over empty text, which is exactly the overclaim this repo refuses everywhere else.
capabilities.governance: Read-only file access, bounded by the existing agents/core/file_tools.py path allowlist rather than a new one. No new kernel kind.
capabilities.depends_on: the chat-attachment row for the 'drop a file in' entry point

capabilities.name: Search the web and pull clean page content
capabilities.hermes: `web_search` and `web_extract` are two model-callable tools over independently-selectable backends. Eight in-tree providers behind one `WebSearchProvider` ABC — Firecrawl, Parallel.ai, Exa, SearXNG, Brave free tier, DDGS, Keenable, xAI. Resolution walks a legacy preference list, falls back to a keyless MCP ring that round-robins anonymous free tiers so a fresh install can search before configuring anything, and performs an automatic 'rescue' retry when the configured provider fails. A TTL result cache stops repeat lookups re-billing the provider; website policy and URL-safety guards block private/internal addresses and operator-disallowed sites, classifying a policy block separately from a provider failure so the rescue path never retries a deliberate refusal.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/plugins/websearch.py (175 lines — Tavily, SearXNG, and a DuckDuckGo HTML-scrape fallback; `fetch_page`; register_dynamic_domain for the configured SearXNG host); agents/core/security/ssrf.py (resolve_and_validate, is_private_ip, public/lan modes, blocked-request counter). No provider ABC, no result cache, no rescue retry, no keyless ring; the DuckDuckGo fallback needs BeautifulSoup and logs a warning when it is absent (websearch.py:103).
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's URL-safety half is stronger than Hermes's — a real SSRF module with DNS-rebind handling versus inline checks — so keep that and add the three cheap mechanics: a provider ABC, a TTL result cache, and rescue-vs-policy-block classification. That last distinction is the one with teeth: retrying a deliberate policy refusal as if it were a transient failure is how a governance boundary quietly becomes advisory. Skip the keyless anonymous ring: unattributed third-party free tiers as a default egress path is not a posture this product should adopt.
capabilities.governance: Privileged egress. `plugin.egress` already exists as a kernel kind (agents/core/kernel/registry.py:45) and the websearch plugin registers its dynamic domain through the SEC-5b path — the provider ABC must not create a second egress route around it.

capabilities.name: Drive a web page (browser automation)
capabilities.hermes: Ten built-in text-first tools rendering pages as accessibility trees with @eN refs (navigate, snapshot, click, type, scroll, back, press, get_images, vision, console) plus `browser_exec` (model-written Python in a persistent Browser Use harness), `browser_cdp` raw protocol passthrough and `browser_dialog` for blocking native dialogs. Backends: Browser Use CLI 3.0 (default), local Chromium, Camofox (Firefox fingerprint spoofing), Lightpanda (Zig, ~16x lower memory), and cloud Browserbase / Browser Use / Firecrawl. Around them: a CDP supervisor holding one persistent socket for dialog and frame detection; hybrid routing that auto-spawns a local Chromium sidecar for private/LAN URLs so the cloud provider never sees them; consent-gated real-profile browsing; credential-scrubbed subprocess env; eval SSRF guards; output redaction; session recording; snapshot spill-to-disk; inactivity reaping and suspect-session recycling; and an extension-control broker at /v1/browser-control.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/browser_playwright.py (641 lines), agents/core/browser_kernel.py, agents/core/browser_transport.py (273 lines, IP-pinned transport per SEC-B4), agents/core/browser_agent.py; kernel kind `browser.step` (agents/core/kernel/registry.py:92); agents/core/routers/browser.py; default-off behind JARVIS_PLAYWRIGHT_HOST. Per docs/research/2026-09-06-hermes-and-field-gap-matrix.md row 12: no aria-snapshot observation, no CDP tool, no real-profile snapshot, no LAN sidecar routing, no replay.
capabilities.rationale: Cross-cluster — the browser cluster owns the detail; recorded here because 45 of this file's entries are browser entries and a media ledger that ignored them would be dishonest about coverage. The media-relevant slice is `browser_vision` and `browser_get_images`: the governed browser cannot currently hand a screenshot or a page image to the vision path, which is where browser automation and this cluster actually meet. The hybrid private-URL sidecar is the other idea worth stealing outright — it is a governance pattern (the cloud provider structurally cannot see a LAN address), not a convenience.
capabilities.governance: Already kernel-mediated via `browser.step`. Any ported piece must stay behind it: `browser_exec` in particular executes model-written code and must inherit the `terminal.exec` trust level, exactly as Hermes gates it behind the terminal toolset.

capabilities.name: Control the computer (desktop control)
capabilities.hermes: The `computer_use` toolset drives macOS, Windows and Linux desktops — screenshots, mouse, keyboard, scroll, drag — background-first, without stealing the user's cursor, focus or Space, so agent and user co-work on one machine. One tool with 14 actions; approvals split always-allowed reads from gated mutations with a small hard-blocked set regardless of approval level; three permission modes map onto cua-driver's runtime modes including a private daemon with a reviewed capability manifest; binary resolution checks a runtime contract and nudges on updates; macOS refuses anything but a genuinely-signed CuaDriver.app; capture routes either to the main model as multimodal content or to an auxiliary vision model; upstream telemetry is disabled on every invocation; plus a driver-management CLI (install/status/doctor/permissions) and dashboard status/grant endpoints.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/desktop_drivers/{base,capture,keys,linux,macos,platform}.py; agents/core/desktop_operator.py (GovernedDesktop, DesktopActionExecutor, validate_desktop_run_args); agents/core/desktop_control.py allowlist/plan; agents/core/host_probe.py; kernel kind `desktop.step` (registry.py:85); POST /api/desktop/{allowlist,plan,preview,run} (agents/core/routers/multimodal.py:225-333) double-gated behind JARVIS_DESKTOP_HOST + JARVIS_DESKTOP_ISOLATED, with an UnavailableDriver that refuses each step by name and reason rather than answering 'deferred'. Shipped 2026-09-06/07; per docs/OWNER_TASKS.md it has not run on real hardware.
capabilities.rationale: Cross-cluster — the desktop/operator cluster owns this; recorded for coverage. The media-relevant slice is capture routing: Hermes decides per-screenshot whether pixels reach the main model or are pre-analysed by an auxiliary vision model, which is the token-economics decision that makes long desktop runs survivable on a local model. Nerva has the strict-local reflex (agents/core/screen_reflex.py) but no routing policy, so it has one mode where Hermes has two. The signed-binary and telemetry-off details are worth copying as posture, not as code.
capabilities.governance: Already kernel-mediated via `desktop.step`, with mutating steps routed through tool_rpc rather than executed inline (multimodal.py:322-332). Nerva's split — observe inline, mutate to approval — is the same shape as Hermes's read/gated split and should not be loosened for capture routing.

capabilities.name: Run code or commands somewhere other than this host
capabilities.hermes: `execute_code` runs Python that calls Hermes tools programmatically, with only stdout reaching the model so intermediate results never enter the context window; a seven-tool sandbox allowlist, child-environment secret scrubbing, session kernels keeping one child process alive per (task, mode, interpreter, cwd, toolset) so variables survive across calls, remote kernels speaking a file protocol inside a container, and process-group kill on shutdown. Under it, eight terminal backends behind one `BaseEnvironment` spawn-per-call contract with a re-sourced session snapshot: local, docker (cap-drop, pids-limit, bind-mount persistence), singularity, ssh (ControlMaster + transactional sync), modal, managed_modal via the Nous gateway, daytona (stop/resume preserving the filesystem), vercel_sandbox — plus an mtime+size FileSyncManager, a `TerminalEnvironmentProvider` ABC, a setup wizard section and backend list/set endpoints with live health probes.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/sandbox.py (Docker container execution with a resource-limited subprocess fallback); agents/core/environments/{execution,targets,terminal_contract,file_rpc,local_transport,output_limits}.py — targets.py:346-385 registers local-host, ssh and docker rows with a TargetAuditChain (hash-chained target decisions) and per-target allow/approval_required/deny; kernel kind `terminal.exec` (registry.py:114). Per gap-matrix row 13, execution.py wires docker only — local and ssh return explicit `local_transport_not_implemented` / `ssh_transport_not_implemented`.
capabilities.rationale: Cross-cluster; recorded for coverage. Two things here are media-load-bearing and should not be lost: Hermes's source-image confinement (under a non-local backend, path-like images reach a provider as data: URLs so a container path never leaks) and the environment probe that makes the system prompt say truthfully where commands run. Nerva has the stronger *policy* plane — a hash-chained target audit Hermes has no equivalent of — and the weaker *transport* plane. Explicitly reject Hermes's stated rule that dangerous-command checks are skipped on container/cloud backends because 'the container is the boundary'; the audit chain and taint semantics are the product here, not the sandbox.
capabilities.governance: Already kernel-mediated via `terminal.exec` with a hash-chained target audit. Any ported backend must register as a target row and inherit that classification — a new transport that bypasses targets.py would be a regression even if it runs.

capabilities.name: Drive the app's own preview pane, tours, tips and layouts
capabilities.hermes: Thirteen desktop-only tools reaching the Electron renderer through a bridge that makes each report 'desktop only' elsewhere: `desktop_preview` (open a URL, localhost dev server or file beside the chat; read the rendered visible text, paged by char offsets), `drive_preview` (log in, fill forms, click through the page the user is looking at), `annotate_preview` (lasting marks that outlive drive_preview's fading ones), `focus_pane`, `apply_layout` (default/focus/terminal-deck/quad presets), `read_terminal` and `close_terminal` (pages the in-app scrollback; closing a tab does not kill the process), `read_window_below` (metadata only, never pixels), `tour` (dim, spotlight, titled popovers — over the app's own DOM *or* any web app in the preview), `tip` (one arrow bubble), `setup_mcp` (blocking inline consent card), `react_to_message` (emoji tapback written with author='agent'), and `desktop_project`.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/canvas.py (H12.18 Agent Canvas — an agent posts typed, sanitized, whitelisted, length- and count-bounded elements to a shared canvas the HUD renders; never raw HTML/script; every element attributed to its author and inspectable, pinnable or clearable by the owner); frontend/src/artifacts.tsx; frontend/src/panels/*. There is no Electron shell, no preview pane, no in-app terminal pane, and no tour/tip machinery.
capabilities.rationale: These thirteen tools exist because Hermes ships an Electron desktop app; they are the app's own furniture, not capabilities. Nerva's product surface is a browser HUD, an Expo mobile app and chat channels, and adopting them would mean adding an Electron shell to the product in order to host tools that add nothing a governed browser plus the Agent Canvas cannot already express — canvas.py is in fact the *safer* design, since the agent emits whitelisted typed elements instead of driving a renderer. This matches the owner's own 2026-08-28 delta-port reasoning about the Electron shell. Re-open path: if Nerva ever ships a desktop shell, port `tour`, `tip` and `annotate_preview` first — guided onboarding over an arbitrary web page is the real value in this group — and leave the pane plumbing behind.
capabilities.governance: Read-only in Hermes; the one exception, `drive_preview`, actuates a real logged-in browser session and would have to land on the existing `browser.step` kernel kind rather than a renderer bridge. That requirement alone makes the port larger than it looks.
capabilities.depends_on: a desktop shell that does not exist and is not planned

capabilities.name: Run Nerva as a coding agent inside an editor (ACP)
capabilities.hermes: `hermes acp` runs an ACP JSON-RPC agent over stdio so Zed / VS Code / JetBrains drive Hermes as their coding agent: initialize advertising load_session + fork/list/resume + image prompts; session new/load/resume/fork/list (cursor, 50/page)/cancel/prompt; workspace cwd binding with Windows→WSL path translation; sessions persisted into state.db with source="acp"; a dedicated 29-tool `hermes-acp` toolset with no messaging/audio/clarify; a benign liveness-probe log filter; shipped as the `[acp]` extra with three invocation spellings and a `--check` preflight. Inventory ids acp-mcp-dev.hermes-acp, .acp-initialize, .acp-authenticate, .acp-session-new/-load/-resume/-fork/-list/-cancel, .acp-prompt, .acp-cwd, .acp-session-persistence, .acp-toolset, .acp-probe-filter, .acp-packaging (acp_adapter/entry.py, acp_adapter/server.py, acp_adapter/session.py).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — ripgrep for `acp|agent-client-protocol|session/prompt|acp_adapter` across agents/, frontend/src/, mobile/src/, scripts/ returns exactly one hit, agents/core/payments.py:5, and that is the AP2/ACP *payment* rail, not the Agent Client Protocol. Nerva's only agent entry points are HTTP: agents/web.py:892 `/chat`, :970 `/chat/stream`.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva has no presence in the place developers already sit all day, and ACP is the one protocol that puts it there without building an editor. It is also the best possible showcase for the differentiator: an approval queue and a hash-chained audit are abstract in a chat box and concrete when the editor blocks an edit and shows the diff. Everything the surface needs — orchestrator, kernel, subagent steer/stop (agents/core/subagents.py:482), context compaction (agents/core/context_compressor.py) — already exists; only the protocol adapter is missing.
capabilities.governance: The transport is read-only, but every tool reached through it performs effects. The ACP session must call the same orchestrator path so file.write, terminal.exec, browser.step and desktop.step still cross kernel.authorize; an ACP-local tool loop that talks to drivers directly would be the regression.
capabilities.depends_on: nothing — agents/core/orchestrator.py, agents/core/kernel/ and the tool surface are already in place

capabilities.name: Approve a dangerous command or a file edit from inside the editor, with the real diff shown first
capabilities.hermes: Two bridges. `acp_adapter/permissions.py` turns Hermes' blocking approval prompt into an ACP `session/request_permission` with allow_once / allow_session / allow_always / deny / deny_always, probing the installed SDK for optional option kinds, mapping answers back to Hermes' vocabulary, and returning a distinct `"timeout"` verdict after 60 s. `acp_adapter/edit_approval.py` computes the *post-edit* text before the tool runs (write_file, patch replace-mode via fuzzy_find_and_replace, V4A patch bodies), shows it as an `acp.tool_diff_content` diff, fails closed on any requester error, and applies a three-mode auto-approve policy (ask / workspace_session / session) with `.git`, `.ssh`, `.env*`, `id_rsa`, `id_ed25519` always asking. Session modes default/accept_edits/dont_ask plus `session/set_mode` and `session/set_config_option` expose that policy to the editor (acp-mcp-dev.acp-permission-bridge, .acp-edit-approval, .acp-session-modes, .acp-set-session-mode, .acp-set-config-option).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/kernel/registry.py classifies file.write and terminal.exec as KERNEL with an approval-queue floor, and agents/core/mcp/route_tools.py enforces identity → kernel → mandatory audit before a mutating call, so the *decision machinery* is stronger than Hermes'. What is absent is any client-facing request/response channel for it and any pre-execution diff: no diff is computed anywhere before a write, and there is no per-session edit-approval policy.
capabilities.rationale: The approval queue is Nerva's headline, and today the owner answers it in Nerva's own HUD. Making the editor the approval surface is what turns governance from a thing the owner tolerates into a thing they use. The diff-before-apply half is worth copying on its own merits even outside ACP — Nerva asks for approval on file.write without ever showing what the bytes will become.
capabilities.governance: This IS the governance surface. It must render kernel/approval-queue decisions, never replace them: an editor 'allow always' maps to a permission-ledger grant crossing permission.grant, not to a local bypass flag.

capabilities.name: Steer, inspect and control a running editor thread (in-thread commands + live rendering)
capabilities.hermes: Nine commands advertised as data so the editor autocompletes them (`available_commands_update`) and dispatched before the text reaches the model, each running in a fresh contextvars context pinned to the session cwd: /help /model /tools /context /reset /compress /steer /queue /version; unknown `/words` fall through to the model as prose. Alongside them the whole rendering layer: tool calls mapped to ACP kinds with bespoke per-tool titles and file locations plus ~20 per-tool result formatters and a `_POLISHED_TOOLS` raw-output suppression set; a FIFO queue of call ids per tool name so parallel calls attach to the right card; the `todo` tool projected into Zed's native plan panel; token/usage updates including cached-read tokens; `_meta.hermes.sessionProvenance` exposing compaction lineage; compaction-summary markers; and full transcript replay awaited inside session/load (acp-mcp-dev.acp-available-commands, .acp-slash-dispatch, .acp-cmd-*, .acp-set-session-model, .acp-model-state, .acp-tool-rendering, .acp-toolcall-fifo, .acp-plan-updates, .acp-usage-update, .acp-provenance, .acp-compaction-meta, .acp-history-replay).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none for the protocol projection. The underlying capabilities exist: agents/core/subagents.py:482 `steer(spawn_id, message, origin)` with STEER_MAX_CHARS, agents/core/context_compressor.py for compaction, agents/core/llm/router.py + model_setup.py for the model inventory. Nothing projects any of it onto a client protocol.
capabilities.rationale: Without command advertisement and tool-card rendering the ACP surface is a text pipe, and a text pipe is exactly the ungoverned-looking experience Nerva should not ship. Provenance markers are the piece with the most Nerva-specific value: Hermes uses them for compaction lineage, Nerva can use the same `_meta` channel to carry the audit-chain reference for the turn, so an editor can link a rendered action to its audit row.
capabilities.governance: read-only — projection and display only. /compress and /model rebuild agent state and must stay session-scoped; /steer writes into a running turn and inherits that turn's existing authorization.

capabilities.name: Let the editor hand the agent MCP servers that exist only for that session
capabilities.hermes: `session/new|load|resume|fork` accept an `mcpServers` array; each is registered off-loop via asyncio.to_thread and expands the session's toolsets with one `mcp-<name>` toolset per server on top of `hermes-acp`. A bounded join (`mcp_discovery_timeout`, default 1.5 s) means a dead server cannot block session creation, and a scheduled late refresh re-reads the registry after discovery finishes because the agent snapshots tools once at build time (acp-mcp-dev.acp-session-mcp).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — agents/core/mcp/client.py `MCPManager` holds a single process-wide server dict populated from settings persistence (agents/core/routers/mcp.py `_save_mcp_config`/`_load_mcp_config`); there is no per-session server scope anywhere.
capabilities.rationale: Per-session servers are how an editor gives Nerva project-local tools without the owner editing global config, and the session scope is itself a governance property: a tool that exists only for one workspace is far easier to reason about than one added globally. The late-refresh trick is the load-bearing detail — without it a slow server is invisible for the whole session.
capabilities.governance: read-only to register, but the tools it registers perform effects and must land behind the same outbound MCP authorization gate as any other server (see the outbound-MCP row); a per-session server must not inherit a wider trust tier than a configured one.
capabilities.depends_on: the ACP editor-agent surface; the outbound MCP tool-call authorization gate

capabilities.name: Use a third-party agent CLI (GitHub Copilot) as a model backend over ACP
capabilities.hermes: `agent/copilot_acp_client.py` drives `copilot --acp --stdio` as an OpenAI-shaped chat backend: `--help` probe cached per binary before spawn, credentials-inheriting-but-Tier-1-stripped subprocess env, a full JSON-RPC dance, permissions auto-denied (no human channel), and an fs bridge confined to the session cwd with read redaction and fail-closed writes. `agent/acp_openai_bridge.py` carries OpenAI tool schemas into the prompt as text and regex-extracts `<tool_call>` blocks back out, with an allowlist so an autonomous CLI is not re-offered overlapping tools (acp-mcp-dev.copilot-acp-client, .acp-openai-bridge).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — agents/core/llm/ has anthropic.py, gemini.py, openrouter.py, providers/, hybrid_router.py; every backend is an API, none is a subprocess agent.
capabilities.rationale: This makes Nerva a shell around somebody else's agent, which inverts the product: the whole claim is that Nerva mediates actions, and a foreign CLI that owns its own loop and auto-denies its own permission prompts is precisely the thing the kernel cannot see inside. Prompt-carried tool schemas parsed back out by regex is also a fragile contract to inherit. Re-open if a specific local agent CLI becomes a model Nerva needs and can be run tool-less, as a pure text completion backend with no fs bridge.
capabilities.governance: would be a governance hole by construction — the foreign process performs file reads/writes through its own bridge, never crossing kernel.authorize.

capabilities.name: Connect to external MCP servers and call their tools
capabilities.hermes: One long-lived asyncio task per server on a dedicated background loop, stdio and Streamable HTTP (plus legacy SSE), with the full connection key set: command/args/env, url/headers/identity_header, ssl_verify (bool or CA path), client_cert/client_key mTLS with three list arities, enabled, timeout (300 s default) and connect_timeout (60 s), protocol era negotiation (auto/stateless/legacy with handshake-first fallback logic), supports_parallel_tool_calls, skip_preflight, transport, keepalive_interval (180 s, floored at 5), idle_timeout_seconds / max_lifetime_seconds stdio recycling (acp-mcp-dev.mcp-config-root and the 18 mcp-key-* entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/mcp/client.py — `MCPServer` speaks stdio (argv-only, shell metacharacters refused at agents/core/mcp/client.py `_command_argv`) and, behind `JARVIS_MCP_HTTP_CLIENT`, Streamable HTTP via agents/core/mcp/http_transport.py; per-server cwd, env and headers; a 10 s per-call deadline with JSON-RPC id matching so a timed-out call cannot read another's reply. Absent: ssl_verify, mTLS, per-server timeouts, protocol negotiation, keepalive, parallel-call opt-in, stdio recycling. agents/core/routers/mcp.py:79 additionally rejects every transport but stdio when adding a server through the admin API, so the HTTP client is reachable only from persisted config.
capabilities.rationale: The core is genuinely sound and in two places better than Hermes — the outbound HTTP path goes through the SSRF-pinned PluginHTTPClient and the egress ledger every plugin uses (documented in agents/core/mcp/http_transport.py), and `JARVIS_MCP_STDIO_ENV_BASELINE` (agents/core/mcp/client.py `STDIO_ENV_ALLOWLIST`) is the same idea as Hermes' `_build_safe_env`. What is missing is the operational config surface real servers need: TLS options, mTLS, per-server timeouts and keepalive. The admin API's stdio-only rejection should also be lifted to match the client's real capability.
capabilities.governance: read-only to connect; the calls it enables perform effects and belong behind the outbound MCP gate.

capabilities.name: Add, test, configure and remove MCP servers as an operator
capabilities.hermes: A full command group: `mcp add` connects *before* persisting so the user sees and can curses-checklist the tool list, writes secrets to `.env` and only the `${MCP_<NAME>_API_KEY}` template into config, and refuses to save on any security finding; `mcp test` reports connect latency with credentials masked; `mcp configure` re-probes and rewrites `tools.include`; `mcp list`, `mcp remove` (with OAuth token cleanup through the manager, not the filesystem), `mcp login`/`reauth --all` (serial, verifying the token file rather than the probe); `mcp picker` as an arrow-key browser with state-dependent ENTER; `/reload-mcp` plus `mcp.auto_reload_on_config_change` and an `approvals.mcp_reload_confirm` gate; and `${VAR}` / `${env:VAR}` / `${workspaceFolder}` interpolation everywhere in an entry (acp-mcp-dev.mcp-root, .mcp-add, .mcp-remove, .mcp-list, .mcp-test, .mcp-configure, .mcp-login, .mcp-reauth, .mcp-picker, .mcp-interpolation, .mcp-reload).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/routers/mcp.py:51-176 — admin-guarded GET/POST/DELETE `/api/admin/mcp` plus `/{name}/connect` and `/{name}/disconnect`, persisted via `web._save_mcp_config()`; surfaced in the HUD's INTEROP panel (frontend/src/modes2.tsx:303-316, frontend/src/api/live.ts:397). No probe-before-save, no per-tool selection, no credential masking in output, no connect-latency reporting, no interpolation of any kind, no hot reload.
capabilities.rationale: Adding an MCP server is the moment the owner widens what Nerva can touch, and right now they do it blind: the admin POST persists a server before anything has proved it connects or shown which tools it will expose. Probe-then-persist with a tool checklist is the single highest-value change here — it converts server installation into an informed consent step, which is exactly the product's posture. Interpolation matters too: without it the owner has no way to add an authenticated server except pasting a live secret into settings storage.
capabilities.governance: read-only for list/test; add/remove/connect widen the tool surface, so treat installation as capability growth and route it through permission.grant the way skill.install already is (agents/core/kernel/registry.py).

capabilities.name: Install a vetted MCP server in one step from a catalogue
capabilities.hermes: `optional-mcps/<name>/` is a directory-as-registry of 65 reviewed entries (presence in the directory *is* approval, merged via PR review); `mcp catalog` prints them next to the user's own servers with per-entry `future_manifest`/`invalid` diagnostics, `mcp install <name>` writes the entry from the manifest, prompts for credentials, probes and offers the tool checklist, and the manifest carries transport, auth, `tools.default_enabled`, suggest keywords/hosts and `post_install` prose. A `hermes://mcp/install?name=&config=BASE64` deep link lets a vendor ship an 'Add to Hermes' button that is inert until confirmed, 32 KB-capped, scheme-restricted and never overwrites an existing name (acp-mcp-dev.mcp-catalog, .mcp-install, .mcp-deeplink).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — there is no catalogue directory, no manifest schema for MCP servers and no deep-link handler anywhere in agents/ or desktop/src-tauri. The closest analogue is the *skills* side: agents/core/skills/marketplace.py + importer.py + curator.py + signing.py, which is a real curated-install pipeline but only for skills.
capabilities.rationale: This is the adoption surface for the whole MCP ecosystem, and Nerva already proved the pattern one layer up — the signed, curated, owner-approved skill marketplace is a *better* trust model than Hermes' 'a PR merged it, therefore it is approved'. Applying the same review + signature + owner-approval pipeline to MCP servers gives Nerva a catalogue that is a governance artifact rather than a convenience. Reuse agents/core/skills/signing.py and curator.py rather than inventing a second registry.
capabilities.governance: installing a server widens capability: same posture as skill.install (KERNEL, with a permanent owner-approval floor that a kernel GRANT cannot bypass). A deep link must be inert until the owner confirms in-app.
capabilities.depends_on: the operator MCP surface (probe-then-persist and tool selection)

capabilities.name: Sign in to a remote MCP server that requires OAuth
capabilities.hermes: OAuth 2.1 + PKCE through the MCP SDK, owned by a single manager (`tools/mcp_oauth_manager.py`) that is the only place a provider is instantiated: per-server token files under `~/.hermes/mcp-tokens/`, transparent refresh with re-auth only on refresh failure, an mtime disk watch so a token refreshed by another process is picked up without restart, and in-flight-future dedup so N concurrent 401s trigger one recovery. Client identity is a published Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD) with recorded per-server rejection falling back to DCR; callback ports pinned to 27890–27894 and held as bound sockets so an exact-match redirect can work on a first login, reverting to a random port under nine documented conditions; a dashboard-mediated callback bridge relocates the two human/browser hops for headless installs without moving any crypto; and an `oauth:` sub-block overrides client_id/secret/name/auth-method/redirect and a token-endpoint-only user_agent (acp-mcp-dev.mcp-oauth, .mcp-oauth-cimd, .mcp-oauth-ports, .mcp-key-oauth-block, .mcp-dashboard-oauth, .mcp-oauth-manager).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/mcp/oauth.py is the *inverse* — an OAuth 2.1 **resource server** (RFC 9728 metadata, RFC 8707 audience binding, self-issued HMAC tokens) that protects Nerva-as-MCP-server; agents/core/routers/mcp.py:189-228 serves `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` and `/api/mcp/token`. On the client side agents/core/mcp/client.py carries only static `headers` held in memory and deliberately never persisted (`to_config` omits them). There is no authorization-code flow, no token store, no refresh.
capabilities.rationale: Without this, every commercially interesting remote MCP server — the ones behind a real account — is unreachable, and the owner's only workaround is pasting a long-lived bearer token into config. A short-lived, refreshable, per-server, audience-bound credential is strictly the better security posture and the one Nerva's own resource server already demands of its callers; not offering it as a client is an inconsistency. Skip the CIMD/pinned-port complexity in v1 and use DCR with a random loopback port.
capabilities.governance: read-only in itself, but it mints and stores durable credentials — tokens belong in the existing secret scope (agents/core/routers/secrets.py, agents/core/vault.py), never in settings storage, and each acquisition should leave an audit row.
capabilities.depends_on: the operator MCP surface; secret storage

capabilities.name: Choose which of a server's tools the model may see
capabilities.hermes: `tools.include` / `tools.exclude` accept exact names or fnmatch globs matched against the *original* MCP tool names, with include winning outright when both are set; `tools.resources` / `tools.prompts` enable or disable the four utility wrappers, additionally gated on the capability actually being advertised in the server's initialize/discover result so tools-only servers do not get four stubs that all answer -32601 (acp-mcp-dev.mcp-key-tools-filter, .mcp-key-utility-policy).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — agents/core/mcp/client.py `_list_tools` appends every tool the server reports, unconditionally, and `MCPManager.get_tools()` returns all of them. There is no per-server filter field in the config shape written by agents/core/routers/mcp.py:79.
capabilities.rationale: A single MCP server routinely exposes 40+ tools; without a filter the owner's only granularity is the whole server, which makes least-privilege impossible at exactly the boundary where it matters most. Nerva already practises allowlisting on its own server side (ROUTE_TOOL_ALLOWLIST, four entries, in agents/core/mcp/route_tools.py:82) — the client side should hold itself to the same standard rather than accepting whatever a third party advertises.
capabilities.governance: read-only mechanically, but it is the primary least-privilege control on the outbound tool surface; the filter must be evaluated at call time as well as registration time so removing a tool from the allowlist revokes it immediately.

capabilities.name: Read an MCP server's resources and prompts, not just call its tools
capabilities.hermes: Four utility tools registered per capable server — `mcp__<server>__list_resources`, `read_resource` (uri), `list_prompts`, `get_prompt` (name + arguments) — with `nextCursor` pagination capped at 50 pages, a 50 MiB single-resource cap, and binary blocks cached to disk (image/audio/embedded resource) so the model is handed a path rather than megabytes of base64 (acp-mcp-dev.mcp-tool-list-resources, .mcp-tool-read-resource, .mcp-tool-list-prompts, .mcp-tool-get-prompt, .mcp-content-blocks).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — agents/core/mcp/client.py issues exactly two methods, `initialize` and `tools/list`, and calls `tools/call`; the words resource and prompt appear nowhere in agents/core/mcp/. agents/core/mcp/server.py:293 likewise advertises only `capabilities: {"tools": {}}` on its own initialize.
capabilities.rationale: Resources are half of what MCP servers publish — documentation sets, file trees, database schemas — and a client that ignores them silently gets a worse answer from every server that leads with them. The disk-caching rule is the part worth copying carefully: handing the model a path instead of inline base64 is also what keeps a hostile server from flooding context.
capabilities.governance: read-only on the client side, but resource content is untrusted third-party text entering the model's context and must go through the same treatment as any external input (description scan, Unicode tag stripping, size cap).
capabilities.depends_on: the MCP client; the supply-chain/injection defenses row

capabilities.name: Let an MCP server ask the agent for an LLM completion or for user input mid-call
capabilities.hermes: `sampling:` gives a server `sampling/createMessage` with a per-instance handler: enabled flag, model override and `allowed_models` list, `max_tokens_cap` (4096), timeout (30 s), `max_rpm` (10) on a 60-second sliding window, `max_tool_rounds` (5), log level, and tracked request/error/token/tool-use metrics. `elicitation:` lets a server ask the user for structured input mid-tool-call and routes it through `tools.approval.prompt_dangerous_approval` so it surfaces on whichever channel owns the session; URL-mode is cleanly declined; the schema field is read under both mcp-1.x and mcp-2.0 spellings; everything fails closed to decline/cancel (acp-mcp-dev.mcp-key-sampling, .mcp-key-elicitation).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — no `sampling` or `elicitation` handler in agents/core/mcp/; the client passes no callbacks on initialize (agents/core/mcp/client.py `_initialize` sends empty params).
capabilities.rationale: Elicitation specifically, and gated: it is the one place the MCP spec lets a third-party server reach the human, and Nerva already owns the best answer to 'where does a request for the owner's decision go' — the approval queue with its reversible/irreversible split. Routing elicitation into that queue instead of inventing a second prompt channel is a small amount of code and turns a spec feature into a demonstration of the differentiator. Sampling is the weaker half (the spec deprecates it under SEP-2577) but is cheap once the plumbing exists and must carry the rate limit and token cap — a server that can make you call an LLM can make you pay for one.
capabilities.governance: sampling spends the owner's model budget on a third party's behalf: it must cross the existing budget ledger (agents/core/kernel/budget.py) and be per-server rate-limited. Elicitation must land in the approval queue, fail closed on timeout, and never auto-accept.
capabilities.depends_on: the MCP client; the approval queue

capabilities.name: Authorize an outbound MCP tool call before it runs
capabilities.hermes: `trust: untrusted` on a server makes every write-capable tool call require explicit approval first: `_annotation_read_only_hint` treats a tool as write-capable unless `annotations.readOnlyHint is True` (a missing key, a missing annotation block, or a truthy non-bool all count as write), the trust value fails closed on any unrecognised spelling, the gate calls `tools.approval.request_elicitation_consent` with a named surface, and an approval-system exception blocks rather than allows. A denial returns text that explicitly tells the model not to retry (acp-mcp-dev.mcp-key-trust).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/mcp/client.py `_tool_call_blocked` evaluates an `mcp.tool_call` ContractTemplate before every call — but that contract only checks name/args-key *shape* and whether the transport is armed; it has no notion of read vs write, no trust tier and no approval hop. The kernel is not on this path: `rg 'kernel|authorize' agents/core/mcp/client.py` returns nothing, and agents/core/kernel/registry.py's `mcp.mutating` = KERNEL covers the *inbound* server direction (agents/core/mcp/route_tools.py), not outbound. The one governed outbound write is hand-built and single-purpose: agents/core/mcp/worldview_write.py (plugin gate + Action Kernel + scoped HMAC capability token, then the stdio call).
capabilities.rationale: This is the row where Nerva's own claim is currently untrue. 'The Action Kernel mediates every privileged action' does not hold for an MCP server the owner added: its tools can send mail, move files or spend money and the only thing between the model and that effect is a regex on the argument key names. worldview_write.py proves the pattern works and that it is affordable — it just needs to be generalised into the client so every server gets a trust tier, every tool a read/write classification, and every write a kernel hop plus an audit row.
capabilities.governance: a new kernel kind — `mcp.tool_call` (outbound), classified next to the existing `mcp.mutating` in agents/core/kernel/registry.py. Write-capable calls on an untrusted server go to the approval queue; a DENY refuses before the JSON-RPC frame is written; every authorized call leaves a hash-chained audit row like agents/core/mcp/route_tools.py already does inbound.
capabilities.depends_on: nothing — kernel, contracts and the audit logger are all already wired on the inbound path

capabilities.name: Refuse a malicious MCP server config or a poisoned tool description
capabilities.hermes: Three layers. `hermes_cli/mcp_security.py` validates every entry at save time *and* at spawn time against a hardcoded IOC list (the June-2026 hermes-0day SSH key prefix and source IPs), shell-interpreter-plus-network-egress shapes, and OS-persistence shapes (authorized_keys, /etc/cron, .bashrc, pam_*.so, systemd). `_scan_mcp_description` runs ten patterns over every tool description before it reaches the model's context ('ignore previous instructions', role-tag injection, concealment, network commands, base64 decode, exec/eval, dangerous imports). Plus an OSV malware preflight on stdio packages with two nested timeouts and fail-open, `strip_unicode_tags` on descriptions and schemas so invisible tag characters cannot smuggle instructions, and a two-tier result cap (2 M-char hard truncation above a 50 K spillover threshold, 50 MiB per resource) (acp-mcp-dev.mcp-security-validator, .mcp-injection-scan, .mcp-osv-preflight, .mcp-result-caps).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/mcp/client.py refuses shell metacharacters in a stdio command and never passes it through a shell; `STDIO_ENV_ALLOWLIST` + `_SECRET_LIKE` keep hub credentials out of the subprocess; agents/core/mcp/http_transport.py caps a reply at MAX_REPLY_BYTES (4 MiB) and MAX_SSE_EVENTS (256) and pins DNS through PluginHTTPClient. Absent: any config validator (no IOC list, no egress/persistence shape detection), any tool-description injection scan (`rg 'ignore previous instructions|strip_unicode_tags' agents/` hits only agents/core/skills/loader.py:300, on the skills path), and any OSV/package preflight. Nerva does own a prompt-injection classifier elsewhere — agents/core/security/governance.py, agents/core/security/quarantine.py, agents/core/autonomy/transcript_watcher.py.
capabilities.rationale: The tool-description scan is the cheapest high-value item in this entire cluster: descriptions go straight into the model's context, a rug-pull update can change them after the owner approved the server, and Nerva already has the classifier — it is simply not pointed at this input. The config validator matters because Nerva persists MCP config to settings storage, so a hand-edited or planted config is a real path to code execution on the owner's machine, exactly the scenario Hermes' IOC list came from. Skip OSV (a network preflight on a startup path Nerva can address instead by making the catalogue the trusted install route).
capabilities.governance: read-only checks that gate a privileged effect: a validator finding must refuse the save and the spawn, not merely warn, and a description-scan hit should quarantine the server the way agents/core/security/quarantine.py handles skills.
capabilities.depends_on: the existing injection classifier in agents/core/security/

capabilities.name: Keep a flaky or slow MCP server from wedging or slowing the whole product
capabilities.hermes: Discovery starts in a daemon thread at process start with a cheap config probe so non-MCP users never import the stack, then a bounded join at the one place the tool snapshot is taken, with a retry-after-zero-connected allowance; a fingerprinted schema cache (`$HERMES_HOME/cache/mcp_schema_cache.json`, mode 0600, honouring the server's SEP-2549 ttlMs) plus lazy connect registers a server's tools with no subprocess until the first real call; reconnection is three layers — jittered exponential backoff (5 retries, 60 s ceiling, ±20 %), a per-server connect cooldown (30 s → 600 s) and a circuit breaker (3 failures, 60 s) — with a parked state that self-probes every 300 s; plus keepalive pings, stdio idle/lifetime recycling, a POSIX parent-death watchdog supervisor that kills the child's process group when Hermes dies hard, stderr redirected to a shared log so it cannot corrupt a TUI, an orphan reaper sweeping by parentage, a cross-process advisory discovery lock, and one `get_mcp_status()` feeding all four UIs (acp-mcp-dev.mcp-startup, .mcp-schema-cache, .mcp-lazy-connect, .mcp-reconnect, .mcp-shutdown, .mcp-discovery-lock, .mcp-status-api, .mcp-stderr-log, .mcp-stdio-watchdog, .mcp-key-keepalive, .mcp-key-lifecycle).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/mcp/client.py `MCPManager.connect_all()` is a serial for-loop that awaits each `connect()` and logs failures; there is no backoff, no retry, no circuit breaker, no keepalive, no watchdog, no schema cache and no lazy connect. A dead server costs the full connect path on every start; a server that dies mid-session stays dead until an admin hits `/api/admin/mcp/{name}/connect`. The only liveness signal is `is_connected()` (transport-aware) surfaced in the admin list.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva is meant to run unattended on the owner's own hardware for days, which makes this a reliability requirement rather than a nicety: one flaky remote server currently degrades every start and silently loses its tools for the rest of the process lifetime with nothing in the HUD saying so. The schema cache plus lazy connect is the highest-leverage piece — it means adding servers costs nothing at boot — and the parent-death watchdog is the one that prevents a real failure mode (orphaned stdio children racing the same upstream session after an ungraceful restart).
capabilities.governance: read-only. One caveat: a lazily-registered tool from a schema cache is advertised before the server is verified, so the fingerprint must cover every connection-defining field and the outbound authorization gate must run on the live call, not on registration.

capabilities.name: Make a third-party tool schema safe and unambiguous for every model provider
capabilities.hermes: `_normalize_mcp_input_schema` repairs a server's JSON Schema once, provider-agnostically, at registration: draft-07 `definitions` promoted to `$defs` contextually (only as a meta-keyword, never when it is a property name, because `$` in a property name 400s Anthropic and OpenAI); missing/null `type` on an object-shaped node coerced; empty `properties` added so `required` cannot dangle; `required` pruned to names that exist (Gemini 400s otherwise); Pydantic nullable `anyOf` unions collapsed to the non-null branch. Names are sanitized and prefixed to `mcp__<server>__<tool>` with everything outside [A-Za-z0-9_] replaced, matching Claude Code / Codex / OpenCode, while filters still match the original names (acp-mcp-dev.mcp-schema-normalize, .mcp-tool-naming).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/mcp/client.py `_list_tools` stores `t.get("inputSchema", {})` verbatim into `MCPTool.input_schema` with no repair, and `MCPManager.find_tool`/`call_tool` look tools up by bare name across all servers — so two servers exposing a tool with the same name collide silently and the first match wins.
capabilities.rationale: The name collision is a correctness bug today, not just a missing feature: `MCPManager.call_tool` scans servers in dict order and dispatches to whichever matched first, so adding a second server can silently redirect an existing tool call. Prefixing fixes that and is also what every other client does, so tool names stay portable. Schema normalization is the difference between an MCP server working on one of Nerva's providers and working on all of them (agents/core/llm/ has Anthropic, Gemini, OpenRouter and local backends, each with different schema tolerances).
capabilities.governance: read-only, but the prefix is a security property too: an unprefixed third-party tool can shadow a built-in tool name and intercept calls meant for a governed path.

capabilities.name: Let another MCP client (Claude Desktop, Cursor, another agent) call Nerva
capabilities.hermes: `hermes mcp serve` and `agent.transports.hermes_tools_mcp_server` expose Hermes over stdio, the latter synthesising Python signatures from Hermes' own JSON Schemas to hand a nested Codex runtime 26 curated tools. Both are full-trust: no per-tool identity gate, no kernel, no audit row — `hermes mcp serve`'s `messages_send` sends to real platforms, and `permissions_respond` answers approval requests, from any client that can start the process (acp-mcp-dev.mcp-serve, .hermes-tools-mcp).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/mcp/server.py — `JarvisMCPServer` with a transport-agnostic `handle()`, an agent allow-list (`ask_<agent>` only for exposed agents), an `agent_request_guard` and a `_agent_request_authorized` contextvar that lifecycle control re-checks before kernel authorization, and a typed `VerifiedMCPIdentity` that exists precisely so an attacker-controlled header string cannot pass as proof of OAuth validation. agents/core/mcp/route_tools.py adds allow-listed route tools with reflected-from-signature schemas and a drift-guard test; mutating tools need BOTH `JARVIS_MCP_ROUTE_TOOLS` and `JARVIS_MCP_MUTATING_TOOLS`, then an identity check, then kernel.authorize (agents/core/kernel/registry.py `mcp.mutating` = KERNEL), then a *mandatory* pre-mutation audit row — MutatingIdentityError / MutatingKernelError / MutatingAuditError / MutatingContractError are four distinct fail-closed refusals. agents/core/routers/mcp.py:230 serves it over HTTP behind an OAuth 2.1 resource server (agents/core/mcp/oauth.py, RFC 9728 + RFC 8707 audience binding); scripts/nerva_mcp_stdio.py bridges a desktop client to it without widening anything.
capabilities.rationale: This is the clearest win in the cluster and it should be advertised as such: Hermes' MCP servers are convenience surfaces, Nerva's is the only one where an external client's write crosses an identity gate, a kernel decision and a mandatory audit row before the effect happens. The honest caveat is already written into the code (agents/core/mcp/route_tools.py, the RESIDUAL GAP comment): a leaked JARVIS_USER_TOKEN drives the whole write surface, there is no rate limiting and no proxy-origin reasoning. Fix that, and grow the allow-list — four read tools and one write tool is a very small window onto a hub with 445 routes.
capabilities.governance: already correct — `mcp.mutating` crosses kernel.authorize with a mandatory audit precondition; keep the double kill-switch and the fail-closed identity default when extending the allow-list.

capabilities.name: Read conversations and answer pending approvals from an MCP client
capabilities.hermes: `hermes mcp serve` exposes ten tools over stdio: `conversations_list`, `conversation_get`, `messages_read`, `attachments_fetch`, `events_poll` (monotonic cursor), `events_wait` (long-poll, 5-minute cap), `messages_send` (platform:identifier targets, delegating to the agent's own send tool), `channels_list`, `permissions_list_open` and `permissions_respond` (allow-once / allow-always / deny) — backed by an EventBridge that turns SQLite polling into a push-shaped queue with an mtime short-circuit and waiter support (acp-mcp-dev.mcpserve-* , 11 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: The data all exists and is reachable only over HTTP: agents/core/channel_inbox.py, agents/core/channel_reply.py, agents/core/routers/sessions.py, agents/core/routers/permissions.py, agents/core/routers/actions.py. None of it is exposed as an MCP tool — agents/core/mcp/route_tools.py's read allow-list holds four entries and its write allow-list holds one (`memory_remember`).
capabilities.rationale: The approval half is the compelling part and it is Nerva-shaped: the owner already lives in an editor or an MCP client, and letting them see and answer the approval queue from there removes the main friction of graduated autonomy — that governance costs a context switch. The messaging half is a smaller win but nearly free once the route-tool allow-list grows. Build it as allow-list entries on the existing governed server, never as a second server process, so `permissions_respond` inherits the identity gate and the audit row rather than becoming the one unaudited way to approve an action.
capabilities.governance: answering an approval IS a privileged act — it must cross the same identity + kernel + audit path as any mutating route tool, and must not be able to approve an irreversible-tier action that the queue floor reserves for the owner's own surface.
capabilities.depends_on: Nerva's MCP server (extend ROUTE_TOOL_ALLOWLIST / MUTATING_ROUTE_ALLOWLIST); the residual-gap fix on per-identity tokens

capabilities.name: Point any OpenAI-compatible app at Nerva as its backend
capabilities.hermes: The api_server platform serves `POST /v1/chat/completions` (system messages flattened into an ephemeral prompt, last message as input, the rest as history, a conversation fingerprint deriving a stable session id for stateless frontends, streaming SSE plus a custom `hermes.tool.progress` event, idempotency keys, 502 with `agent_incomplete` rather than rendering a failure string as content), `POST /v1/responses` with server-side storage, `previous_response_id` chaining, named conversations and spec-compliant typed streaming events, `GET|DELETE /v1/responses/{id}`, `GET /v1/models` advertising a stable virtual model plus route aliases, and `GET /api/model/options` returning the native provider inventory (acp-mcp-dev.api-chat-completions, .api-responses, .api-get-response, .api-delete-response, .api-models, .api-model-options).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none inbound — `rg '/v1/chat/completions|/v1/responses' agents/` returns only *outbound* client code (agents/core/llm/base.py:461, agents/core/plugins/cloud_llm.py:146) and probes of local runtimes (agents/core/llm/router.py:73). agents/web.py serves `/chat` and `/chat/stream` in Nerva's own shape. This is already on the roadmap: docs/research/2026-09-06-hermes-and-field-gap-matrix.md row 37 specifies it with the exact governance design.
capabilities.rationale: Zero-cost adoption: every OpenAI-format client in existence becomes a Nerva front end without Nerva writing a client. It is also the substrate for Nerva-to-Nerva peering. The gap matrix already worked out the right posture — requests arrive origin=inbound and therefore tainted, so every mutating kind QUEUEs — which turns a compatibility shim into a demonstration that taint-based escalation is real.
capabilities.governance: inbound requests are untrusted and must be marked tainted at the boundary so the kernel's taint escalation forces mutating kinds to the approval queue; mandatory bearer key even on loopback; default-off flag; bind 127.0.0.1.
capabilities.depends_on: nothing — the orchestrator and the taint/origin plumbing (agents/core/action_origin.py) already exist

capabilities.name: Accept work from another agent over the open A2A protocol
capabilities.hermes: The full Linux-Foundation A2A v1.0 inbound surface on stdlib HTTP: a signed Agent Card at `/.well-known/agent-card.json` (plus the legacy path) with skills derived from enabled toolsets and a public URL resolved from forwarded headers; one JSON-RPC endpoint accepting both v1.0 PascalCase and pre-1.0 path-style names for SendMessage, SendStreamingMessage (JSON-RPC-enveloped SSE), GetTask, ListTasks, CancelTask, SubscribeToTask and four push-notification-config methods; eight task states with terminal-state handling; `[INPUT_REQUIRED]` replies flipping a task to INPUT_REQUIRED so the peer knows to answer; HMAC-SHA256-signed push webhooks with SSRF filtering of the callback URL; and inbound tasks injected into the *live* gateway session so a peer gets the same agent, memory and tools (acp-mcp-dev.a2a-plugin, .a2a-agent-card, .a2a-jsonrpc, .a2a-send-message, .a2a-send-streaming, .a2a-get-task, .a2a-list-tasks, .a2a-cancel-task, .a2a-subscribe-task, .a2a-push-create/-get/-list/-delete, .a2a-health, .a2a-metrics, .a2a-conversations).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/a2a.py + agents/core/routers/a2a.py — off unless `JARVIS_A2A_ENABLED`; `GET /.well-known/agent-card` serving an HMAC-signed card; `POST /api/a2a/task` authenticating by per-peer HMAC over the raw body, constant-time, with an `a2a.inbound` ContractTemplate; verified tasks land in a file-backed pending inbox (bounded at 500) that the owner approves or rejects out of band, and approval explicitly does NOT execute. Missing: the JSON-RPC method surface entirely, task states, streaming, push notifications, task get/list/cancel, and any interop with the official a2a-sdk.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's posture here is the right one and better than Hermes' — a peer cannot make this agent do anything, only ask, and the owner decides — but the wire format is bespoke, so no A2A-compliant peer can talk to it and the capability is effectively unreachable. Wrap the existing HMAC + inbox model in the real JSON-RPC method names, task states and Agent Card shape so the governance model survives contact with the ecosystem. Keep the never-auto-execute floor: express it as TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED / submitted-until-approved rather than abandoning it for parity.
capabilities.governance: inbound peer requests are external and tainted; an approved task's execution still crosses whatever kernel kind the work implies. The approval floor is the differentiator here and must not be traded away for protocol conformance.

capabilities.name: Call other agents as tools and fan work out to peers
capabilities.hermes: Five outbound tools registered independently of the inbound listener, so an agent can call peers without exposing itself: `a2a_discover` (fetch and summarise a remote Agent Card before calling), `a2a_call` (natural-language task to a configured peer name or a raw URL, returning the context id for multi-turn), `a2a_list`, `a2a_history` (recall a persisted transcript by context id, surviving compaction and restarts), and `a2a_orchestrate` (fan out by capability tag with all/first/best aggregation). Peers live in an `a2a_agents:` registry with url, bearer auth, timeout and capability tags (acp-mcp-dev.a2a-tool-discover, .a2a-tool-call, .a2a-tool-list, .a2a-tool-history, .a2a-tool-orchestrate, .a2a-agents-config).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — agents/core/a2a.py is inbound-only (`add_peer`, `verify_peer`, `receive_task`, `decide`); there is no outbound HTTP call to a peer anywhere in it, and no peer `url` field. The frontend INTEROP panel (frontend/src/api/live.ts:397-403) lists A2A peers read-only.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already has the inbound trust model, the peer registry and the signed card — outbound is the smaller half and it is what makes the capability bidirectional and therefore worth having at all. It also matters for the product's own roadmap: 'work like a company toward any goal' implies reaching another Nerva on the owner's other machine, and A2A is the interoperable way to do that rather than a private protocol.
capabilities.governance: calling a peer sends the owner's data off the box: it is egress and must cross the existing plugin.egress kernel path with the egress ledger, per-peer allowlisting, and outbound credential redaction before the text leaves.
capabilities.depends_on: the inbound A2A protocol work (shared card/registry/transcript code)

capabilities.name: Harden the A2A channel against a hostile or runaway peer
capabilities.hermes: Identity derived from the presented credential and never from the body, constant-time compared, with per-peer tokens so rate limiting and audit are meaningful; a bind-host safety rule where a token alone does not widen the bind and a wide host alone is ignored (two independent switches); an optional trusted-peer allow-list layered above authentication; inbound text defanged (eight injection patterns neutralised to `[filtered]`, never rejected) and framed with an explicit untrusted-provenance banner, applied to *every* message including ones starting with `/` so a peer can never reach operator slash commands; outbound credential redaction (eight patterns incl. JWTs and emails); 60 req/min per identity; a per-context ping-pong turn cap of 5 with a hard ceiling of 20; and a JSONL audit line per exchange (acp-mcp-dev.a2a-auth, .a2a-bind, .a2a-trusted-peers, .a2a-inbound-filter, .a2a-outbound-redaction, .a2a-rate-limit, .a2a-turn-cap, .a2a-audit, .a2a-env).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/a2a.py has the strong half: allowlist + per-peer shared secret, HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body verified constant-time, fail-closed on unknown peer or bad signature without leaking which (agents/core/routers/a2a.py returns a bare 401), a contract template bounding peer_id length and body size (_MAX_CONTRACT_BODY_BYTES 64 KB), a bounded inbox, and the approval floor. Missing: inbound injection defanging and provenance framing, outbound redaction, per-identity rate limiting, an anti-loop turn cap, and a dedicated append-only A2A audit stream (there is a hash-chained audit log in the product but this path does not write to it).
capabilities.rationale: The inbound framing is the one that must not be skipped: peer text goes straight into the model's context, and Nerva's approval floor stops the peer *executing* something but does nothing about the peer talking the agent into doing something else through a channel the owner does trust. Nerva has the classifier already (agents/core/security/governance.py, quarantine.py) — point it at this input and prepend a provenance banner. The turn cap is cheap insurance the day two Nervas talk to each other.
capabilities.governance: read-only filters guarding a privileged path; the audit line should join the existing hash-chained audit rather than a separate JSONL, so a peer exchange is provable alongside every other action.
capabilities.depends_on: the existing security classifier; the audit logger

capabilities.name: Show the agent the semantic errors its own edit just introduced
capabilities.hermes: Real language servers as background subprocesses feeding an `lsp_diagnostics` field on every successful write_file/patch: baseline the file's current diagnostics, write, re-query, subtract, report only what is new — with a freshness gate so a diagnostic counts only if the server produced it for the post-edit content, and `range_shift.py` re-anchoring baseline ranges across the edit. A 27-server registry with extension-or-basename matching and a language-id map decoupled from it; 14 install recipes across npm/go/pip plus an explicit manual tier, staged into a Hermes-owned directory that never touches a shared prefix; `hermes lsp status|list|install|install-all|restart|which` including a backend warning for the 'spawns fine but silently emits nothing' case; lazy spawn, idle reaping with a clamped timeout, a broken-pair set, and silent fallback to the syntax-only result on any failure (acp-mcp-dev.lsp-diagnostics, .lsp-root, .lsp-status, .lsp-list, .lsp-install, .lsp-install-all, .lsp-restart, .lsp-which, .lsp-registry, .lsp-install-recipes, .lsp-config, .lsp-service).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — `rg -i 'language server|pyright|gopls'` over agents/ and scripts/ returns no LSP integration. agents/core/codeintel/index.py (173 lines) is a lightweight symbol index, not a diagnostics loop, and agents/core/file_tools.py performs no post-write check beyond what the tool itself returns.
capabilities.rationale: Not because it is hard — because it is a capability for a product Nerva is not. Hermes is a coding agent whose main loop is edit-verify-edit; Nerva is a governed house/desktop/life agent whose privileged actions are locks, money, cameras and the owner's machine, and whose code edits are a side activity. Spending a multi-week subsystem plus 27 language-server binaries on the owner's box to improve the edit loop buys less than any other row here, and the always-on daemons are themselves an attack surface the kernel does not cover. Re-open the moment the ACP editor surface ships and real users edit code through Nerva daily — at that point diagnostics-on-write is what makes the editor agent competitive, and the ACP tool-result channel is already the place to put them.
capabilities.governance: read-only, but it auto-installs binaries from npm/go/pip onto the owner's machine, which would need the lazy-deps allowlist posture and a kernel hop before any install.
capabilities.depends_on: the ACP editor-agent surface, if ever re-opened

capabilities.name: Let third-party apps ride the owner's authenticated model subscription
capabilities.hermes: `hermes proxy start` runs a local OpenAI-compatible forwarder that replaces the client's Authorization header with a freshly-resolved bearer from an OAuth-authenticated provider, so any app can point at it with any token. Deliberately minimal — it never logs, transforms or rewrites bodies — with a per-adapter allowlist of forwarded paths (404 otherwise), hop-by-hop header stripping, a one-shot retry on upstream 401/429 via a credential pool, streaming preserved chunk-by-chunk, an authentication check before the port is bound, and two adapters (Nous Portal, xAI OAuth) behind a five-member ABC (acp-mcp-dev.proxy-root, .proxy-start, .proxy-status, .proxy-providers, .proxy-server, .proxy-adapter-api, .proxy-adapter-nous, .proxy-adapter-xai).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — agents/core/llm/egress.py governs Nerva's *own* outbound model calls; there is no inbound forwarder. agents/core/llm/auth_rotation.py handles credential rotation for Nerva's own use only.
capabilities.rationale: It is a credential-lending service, not an agent capability, and it inverts the product's central promise: a proxy that attaches the owner's real credentials to a request it has explicitly decided not to inspect is an ungoverned egress path with a listening socket, sitting next to a kernel whose entire job is that no privileged effect escapes unmediated. The overlap with the OpenAI-compatible inbound API is also real — that row gives external apps a Nerva-shaped front door where taint and the queue apply, which is the version of this idea that fits.
capabilities.governance: would be an unmediated egress path by design — bodies opaque, no ledger entry, no kernel hop. That is the reason to decline it.

capabilities.name: Write, install and validate a third-party extension
