capabilities.hermes: A declarative `plugin.yaml` (v1 plus an additive v2 with `manifest_version`/`api_version` as separate axes, `requires_plugins` with topological load ordering, declared-but-never-auto-installed `python_dependencies`, and a `config_schema`) discovered from bundled dirs, `~/.hermes/plugins/`, the project dir and pip entry points, with one `register(ctx)` entry point whose failure disables only that plugin. A written five-rule compatibility contract with a four-condition deprecation policy enforced by frozen behaviour fixtures. `hermes plugins doctor` runs the real registries — invalid hook names, callbacks missing `**kwargs`, declared-vs-registered drift — under a temporary HERMES_HOME with direct sockets blocked (acp-mcp-dev.plugin-manifest-v1, .plugin-manifest-v2, .plugin-compat-contract, .plugin-register, .plugin-doctor-contract, .ctx-register-tool, .ctx-register-command, .ctx-register-cli-command, .ctx-register-skill, .ctx-dispatch-tool, .plugin-context-api, .plugin-storage, .plugin-utils, .plugin-lazy-deps).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: Nerva's plugins are in-tree Python modules — agents/core/plugins/ holds 25 of them (weather.py, gmail_plugin.py, n8n.py, homebridge.py, …), each declaring a PluginManifest in code (agents/core/plugin_gate.py) with NetworkAccess/DataScope/allowed_domains/agents_served, surfaced by agents/core/routers/plugins.py. There is no manifest file format, no discovery from a user directory or pip entry point, no register(ctx), no ctx object and no doctor for plugins (scripts/doctor.py is an install health check).
capabilities.rationale: Right now nobody can extend Nerva without a PR, which caps the product at whatever its maintainers build. But copy the shape, not the trust model: Hermes states plainly that plugins are full-trust in-process Python that can monkey-patch core, and the ClawHub data in the gap matrix (341 malicious skills in weeks) is what that costs at scale. Nerva already has the better answer one layer up — agents/core/skills/{signing,curator,approval,quarantine} with `skill.install` crossing the kernel behind a permanent owner-approval floor — so the extension format should be an extension of that pipeline: signed, quarantined, owner-approved, and declaring its capabilities up front.
capabilities.governance: installing an extension is capability growth: `skill.install`-shaped (KERNEL, owner-approval floor that a GRANT cannot bypass). An extension that registers a tool performing effects must have those effects cross their own kernel kinds — a plugin must never be able to register a tool that bypasses the kernel, which means the registration API cannot expose a raw driver handle.
capabilities.depends_on: the skills signing/curation/approval pipeline as the trust substrate

capabilities.name: Run custom logic at a lifecycle event, in Python or in any language
capabilities.hermes: 37 named hook points validated loudly at registration — session start/end/reset/finalize, pre/post_llm_call, pre/post_tool_call, pre/post_api_request, api_request_error, pre/post_approval_request, pre_command, pre_gateway_dispatch, pre_verify, pre_transcription, subagent_start/stop, stream start/delta/end, the kanban family, and four `transform_*` hooks — with correlation fields (turn_id, api_request_id, task_id, session_id) on every payload, a bounded-timeout allowlist for hot-path hooks and an explicit unbounded set for gates and flushes. `pre_tool_call` can veto or escalate to human approval; `pre_llm_call` returns context injected into the *user* turn (never the cached system prefix) with a 10 K-char spill to disk. The same hook set is reachable from shell scripts: a `hooks:` config block, argv execution with shell=False, a documented JSON stdin/stdout wire protocol accepting both Hermes and Claude-Code directive spellings, exit code 2 as a block, opt-in fail-closed per entry, process-tree kill on timeout, and a first-use consent allowlist keyed on (event, command) with a file lock. Plus drop-in gateway hooks (HOOK.yaml + handler.py) for lifecycle events (acp-mcp-dev.plugin-hooks-list, .ctx-register-hook, .plugin-context-injection, .shell-hooks-schema, .shell-hooks-protocol, .shell-hooks-consent, .gateway-event-hooks).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — `rg 'register_hook|pre_tool_call|post_tool_call|register_middleware' agents/ scripts/` returns nothing. agents/core/routers/webhooks.py is inbound HTTP webhooks (a different thing), and the only extension-shaped seam is the fixed plugin manifest set in agents/core/plugin_gate.py.
capabilities.rationale: Shell hooks first, plugin hooks second. Shell hooks are the lowest-friction extension point that exists — the owner writes a script in any language, gets it approved once, and it runs on the event they care about — and the two hooks that matter most for Nerva are exactly the two Hermes made blocking: `pre_tool_call` (a policy script that can veto or escalate a call to the approval queue) and `pre_llm_call` (inject house state, calendar or presence into the turn). That turns Nerva's policy layer from something only its maintainers can change into something the owner can extend, without a Python plugin and without full-trust code in-process. Copy the three non-negotiables verbatim: argv with shell=False, per-(event, command) first-use consent, and a clamped timeout.
capabilities.governance: a hook that can BLOCK a tool call is a policy component, so it must be able to tighten and never to loosen: a hook may veto or escalate to approval, but a hook return must never be able to grant an action the kernel would have queued or denied. Registering a hook is itself capability growth (arbitrary local execution) → permission.grant plus the consent allowlist, and HERMES_SAFE_MODE's equivalent must skip hook registration entirely.
capabilities.depends_on: nothing for shell hooks; the plugin authoring row for Python hooks

capabilities.name: Rewrite a tool call or a model request before it happens
capabilities.hermes: Four middleware kinds distinct from observing hooks: `tool_request` returns `{args}` replacing the effective arguments *before* hooks, guardrails, approvals and execution see them; `llm_request` replaces the provider kwargs; `tool_execution` and `llm_execution` wrap the call with a single-use `next_call` that may be skipped to short-circuit. Request middleware chains with `original_args`/`original_request` always carrying the pre-middleware copy, payloads copied between callbacks, a `middleware_trace` handed to downstream observers, a schema version on the payload, and unknown kinds registering with a warning for forward compatibility (acp-mcp-dev.ctx-register-middleware).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — no middleware registry in agents/; the closest analogue is agents/core/automation_contracts.py, which evaluates declarative ContractTemplates over an action view and can only deny, never rewrite.
capabilities.rationale: A seam that lets third-party code silently rewrite a tool's arguments before approvals and guardrails see them is the exact inverse of Nerva's design. The approval card the owner reads would describe post-middleware arguments while the audit chain records an action the model never asked for, and 'the kernel mediates every privileged action' stops meaning anything if what it mediates can be swapped underneath it. Nerva's declarative contract layer is the right shape for this need — it can refuse, and a refusal is legible. Re-open only as a *pre-kernel, pre-approval, trace-recorded* transform whose before/after both land in the audit row, which is a different feature than what Hermes ships.
capabilities.governance: as specified by Hermes it would run before approvals and guardrails on a path that reaches privileged effects — an unmediated rewrite of a mediated action. That is the reason to decline it.

capabilities.name: Swap in a different backend for memory, models, search, browser, speech or secrets
capabilities.hermes: A published routing table mapping 'I want to add X' to the exact seam, with ~14 provider ABCs each growing through defaults so a new method never breaks an existing implementation: model-provider (`ProviderProfile` with prepare_messages / build_extra_body / fetch_models overrides, user plugins overriding bundled ones by name), platform adapter, memory provider (single-select via `memory.provider`, auto-detected as `kind: exclusive`), context engine, image-gen, video-gen, web-search, cloud browser, secret source, TTS, transcription, dashboard auth, plus config-driven TTS/STT command providers with no Python at all (acp-mcp-dev.plugin-interface-map, .plugin-context-api, .plugin-compat-contract).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: Real seams exist but none is third-party-pluggable. agents/core/llm/ has anthropic.py, gemini.py, openrouter.py, providers/, hybrid_router.py + moe_routing.py behind agents/core/llm/router.py; agents/core/memory/ has store.py, graph.py, living_recall.py; cameras, desktop_drivers/ and browser_playwright.py are driver-shaped. All are selected by config among in-tree implementations — `rg 'MemoryProvider|register_memory'` over agents/ returns nothing, so there is no ABC an external package can implement.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva has the internal seams; what it lacks is the published contract that lets someone else fill one. The two worth opening first are the two where the owner's environment is genuinely unpredictable and Nerva cannot ship every option: secret sources (the gap matrix already wants keychain/Bitwarden/1Password at row 22 — and moving secrets out of plaintext .env is a governance win, not just an integration) and desktop/house drivers, where the owner's hardware is the whole point. Publishing the routing table itself costs almost nothing and prevents the most common contributor failure — building against the wrong seam.
capabilities.governance: mixed by seam. A secret source handles credentials and must never expose them to the model (fill-by-reference only). A driver seam actuates and must be `requires_kernel`: agents/core/kernel/registry.py already encodes this for desktop.step ('a requires_kernel driver cannot use the legacy direct path') — that rule generalises to every provider that touches the world.
capabilities.depends_on: the plugin authoring row for the discovery/install half

capabilities.name: Declare what an extension is allowed to do, and consent to it once
capabilities.hermes: A canonical `CAPABILITY_REGISTRY` of seven ids (tools.override, five llm.* overrides, gateway.platform_actions), each with the legacy config gate it replaces and the risk sentence shown on the consent screen; grants stored as `granted_capabilities` plus a `capabilities_consent` recording the SHA-256 of the declared set at consent time, so an update declaring more re-asks with a diff; everything defaults OFF and any failure to read consent state means not-granted; pip-distributed plugins declare capabilities through a companion entry-point group read from installed metadata without importing the code. Documented honestly as 'a consent and audit layer over host API surfaces — NOT a sandbox'; in-process Python can still import anything and monkey-patch core (acp-mcp-dev.plugin-capabilities).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/plugin_gate.py declares NetworkAccess (none/lan/restricted/full), DataScope (local_only/processed/transmitted), allowed_domains and agents_served per plugin, and the gate *enforces* the network scope at call time rather than only recording consent — with least-privilege wildcard restriction and per-agent grants surfaced at agents/core/routers/plugins.py:70-72. agents/core/capability_manifests.py adds risk levels (read_only → irreversible_or_money) and RollbackContract, and agents/core/capability_verification.py links each to its verification. Missing: any consent *flow* — because there is no third-party install to consent at — and the hash-of-what-you-saw re-consent on update.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva is ahead on the part that matters (enforcement, not just declaration, with real egress restriction) and behind on the part it never needed (consent, because everything is in-tree). The moment third-party extensions exist, the consent hash is the piece to copy verbatim: it is the only mechanism that stops an update from silently widening what the owner already agreed to, and it composes exactly with agents/core/permission_ledger.py.
capabilities.governance: granting a capability is itself the privileged act — `permission.grant` (already KERNEL in agents/core/kernel/registry.py, with the grant written only from the approved task's execution and never by the requester). Keep that discipline: an extension must not be able to grant itself anything.

capabilities.name: Distribute and reproduce a set of extensions
capabilities.hermes: Three formats. Plugin packs (`hermes-pack.yaml`) pin every plugin to an exact 40-character commit SHA — tags and branches rejected — with optional non-secret config seeds that are refused if a key name looks like a credential, that may never touch `granted_capabilities`/`capabilities_consent`, and where installing a pack still runs the per-plugin consent flow (never bulk-granted), capped at 1 MiB. Pip distribution via the `hermes_agent.plugins` entry-point group. Portable Agent Plugins v1 directory packages (plugin.json + skills/ + mcp.json), validated locally, skipped per-component on a bad entry, namespaced deterministically, installed disabled by default, with the honest note that v1 defines no trust, permissions or sandbox (acp-mcp-dev.plugin-packs, .portable-agent-plugins, .plugin-pip-distribution, .plugin-nix-distribution).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: For *skills*, the pipeline exists and is strong: agents/core/skills/marketplace.py (SQLite registry, ZIP packaging, review_status, version archive for rollback), signing.py (content-hash / HMAC signatures, `JARVIS_REQUIRE_SIGNED_SKILLS` refusing unsigned Python), importer.py (imports from Hermes, OpenClaw and any agentskills.io-compatible repo with provenance recorded), curator.py, approval.py, proposals.py, plus agents/core/skills/hermes_pin_v1.json. There is no equivalent for plugins, no exact-SHA pinning, no pack format and no config seeding.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva does not need three formats — it needs one, and it already has most of it. Add exact-SHA pinning and the two rules that make a bundle safe (secret-shaped keys refused, capability consent never bulk-granted) to the existing marketplace so an owner can reproduce a known-good set across machines. Explicitly do not adopt Portable Agent Plugins v1: the inventory's own note is that v1 defines no trust, permissions, provenance or sandbox, which is precisely what Nerva's signing and curation exist to supply.
capabilities.governance: each item in a bundle installs through `skill.install` (KERNEL + owner-approval floor) individually — a bundle must fan out to N consents, never collapse to one.
capabilities.depends_on: the skills marketplace (present); the plugin authoring row for the plugin half

capabilities.name: Extend the desktop app and the web dashboard with custom UI
capabilities.hermes: A published Electron desktop SDK (`apps/desktop/src/sdk/index.ts`) with nine contribution areas — panes, routes, sidebar nav, status bar, title bar, palette commands, keybinds, themes, composer extensions — plus transcript directives the model can address, a host API, React Query + nanostores data layer, a full UI kit, OKLCH theming math, and a bundled agent-facing skill with a copy-ready template. Separately a web dashboard plugin manifest that can add a nav tab, replace a built-in page, or contribute only to shell slots, with a JS bundle, optional CSS and optional FastAPI routes mounted at `/api/plugins/<name>/` (acp-mcp-dev.desktop-plugin-sdk, .dashboard-plugin-manifest).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — desktop/src-tauri is a Tauri shell, not Electron, and there is no contribution-area registry; frontend/src/ has fixed panels (modes2.tsx, panels/) with no slot or manifest system.
capabilities.rationale: The desktop half is the wrong stack: Nerva chose Tauri deliberately, and docs/research/2026-09-06-hermes-and-field-gap-matrix.md already lists the Electron shell among the patterns not to copy. The dashboard half is a real capability but premature — third-party UI in the HUD is only worth building once third-party *logic* exists to surface, and shipping a slot system before an extension format means designing the surface for users who cannot yet exist. Re-open after the plugin authoring row lands, and then dashboard-first: a tab-or-slot manifest for the HUD is far more useful to a governance product than desktop chrome.
capabilities.governance: read-only chrome, but a dashboard plugin that mounts FastAPI routes at `/api/plugins/<name>/` would be adding unaudited endpoints to a hub whose route-auth matrix is snapshot-tested — that alone would need its own gate.

capabilities.name: Deploy Nerva as a container or a declarative system service
capabilities.hermes: A multi-stage Debian image with a pinned custom SQLite build, s6-overlay supervision, uv-managed Python and Node, and a stage-2 bootstrap doing UID/GID remapping (with PUID/PGID aliases for NAS users) so container-written files land owned by the host user; the CMD runs as /init's main program rather than a supervised service to preserve every invocation contract; a dashboard service that exits 125 when disabled so it reads as down rather than crash-looping, and an auth gate that engages automatically on non-loopback binds with `HERMES_DASHBOARD_INSECURE` accepted-but-ignored after the June-2026 hardening. Plus docker-compose (default and Windows variants) and a Nix flake with NixOS/Home-Manager modules mirroring the YAML config as typed options with a deep-merge escape hatch (acp-mcp-dev.docker-image, .docker-compose, .docker-compose-windows, .nix-flake, .nix-module-options).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: Dockerfile at the repo root plus docker-compose.yml, docker-compose.quickstart.yml and docker-compose.worldview.yml; install.sh, install.ps1, INSTALL.bat/START.bat/UPDATE.bat/UNINSTALL.bat; deploy/; scripts/build_exe.py, scripts/build_release.sh, scripts/gen_sbom.py, scripts/install_smoke.py; scripts/doctor.py as the post-install health check with named reasons including `bind_is_loopback` guarding exactly the non-loopback-without-token case Hermes hardened. Nix is absent.
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's packaging story is aimed at the right user — an owner installing on their own machine, with .bat/.ps1/.sh installers, an .exe build, an SBOM and a doctor that explains failures in one named reason each — whereas Hermes' is aimed at a container operator. The one idea worth stealing is s6's 'exit 125 so a disabled service reads as down rather than restarting forever', which is a legibility trick Nerva's supervisor (scripts/runtime_supervisor.py) can use. Nix is explicitly best-effort even upstream; skipping it costs nothing.
capabilities.governance: read-only, with one live constraint already enforced: agents/core/boot_guards.py refuses a non-loopback bind without a token, which is the check Hermes only added after an incident.

capabilities.name: Shell completion and native search-index extensions
capabilities.hermes: `hermes completion bash|zsh|fish` generates a completion script by walking the *live* argparse tree — canonical names only, help text stripped of quotes and backslashes, profile-name completion special-cased — so a plugin-registered subcommand appears automatically. Separately `native/fts5_cjk/` builds a `cjk_unicode61` FTS5 tokenizer (unicode61 + CJK bigrams) with vendored SQLite headers so 1–2 character CJK terms stop falling through to LIKE full-table scans in session search (acp-mcp-dev.completion, .native-fts5-cjk).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: no CLI to complete — pyproject.toml states plainly that the project is not an installable package and is run via requirements, and scripts/ holds standalone tools rather than a subcommand tree. FTS5 is used (agents/core/memory/store.py, graph.py, agents/core/permission_ledger.py, agents/core/screen_locator.py) but with the stock tokenizer.
capabilities.rationale: Completion presupposes a CLI Nerva deliberately does not have — its operator surface is the HUD and the HTTP API — so this is a downstream consequence of a product decision, not a gap. The CJK tokenizer is a real search-quality improvement but it is scoped to the memory/search cluster, requires a compiled .so on the owner's machine, and only pays off for CJK-language owners; it belongs on the memory backlog behind evidence that such an owner exists. Re-open completion if a `nerva` CLI is ever shipped, and generate it from the live parser rather than a list.
capabilities.governance: read-only.
capabilities.depends_on: a Nerva CLI, which does not exist

capabilities.name: Read the product's own per-feature manual (published docs site)
capabilities.hermes: A 52-page Docusaurus feature section (`website/docs/user-guide/features/*`) — one page per capability with verbatim promises, examples, config keys and cross-links, plus a generated index (`_category_.json` position 4) and an `overview.md` hub grouping every feature into five sections. The inventory calls it the closest thing upstream has to a complete feature list in prose (docs-features.category-json, .overview-page).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/docs/FEATURES.md, /home/user/jarvis-hub/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, /home/user/jarvis-hub/NERVA.md, /home/user/jarvis-hub/docs/HERMES_HEAD_TO_HEAD.md, /home/user/jarvis-hub/docs/FAQ.md — markdown in-repo only; no site generator anywhere (no docusaurus/mkdocs config).
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's docs are written for the owner and for AI contributors (docs/AI_CONTEXT.md, AGENTS.md), not for a stranger deciding whether to install. A page-per-capability manual is also the cheapest drift detector the repo could own: since 2026-09-07 a ✅ in BACKLOG.md means DELIVERED not PROVEN, and a public feature page forces the claim to be stated in user terms where an unshipped one is visible.
capabilities.governance: read-only

capabilities.name: Read a PDF / Office document / notebook as text from inside a tool call
capabilities.hermes: `read_file` auto-converts by extension — .ipynb/.docx/.xlsx via stdlib, .pdf/.doc/.ppt/.odt/.rtf/.epub via the optional `firecrawl-anydoc` converter — returning Markdown through read_file's normal offset/limit pager, refusing >50 MB, with lazy install gated by `security.allow_lazy_installs`. Plus a `[EXTRACTION COVERAGE WARNING: …]` prefix that uses poppler pdftotext per-page counts to name the exact scanned page ranges (fires at >20% of pages or 10+ absolute) so the agent OCRs only the gaps (docs-features.document-extraction, .pdf-coverage-warning).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/local_docs.py:32 extract_text (.md/.txt/.rst native; .pdf via pypdf, .docx best-effort, skipped+counted when the parser is missing), agents/core/knowledge_packs.py, agents/core/file_tools.py (file_read returns bytes/text only)
capabilities.rationale: local_docs is an ingestion path into memory, not something the model can call mid-turn — so Nerva's only model-facing file surface cannot see a PDF at all, and the owner's own documents are the most likely thing he points it at. The coverage warning is the genuinely clever half: it stops a 300-page scanned PDF from consuming the whole context of a local model on OCR nobody asked for.
capabilities.governance: read-only — extraction adds no new effect; it must resolve through the same FileScope roots file_read already enforces

capabilities.name: Give the current conversation one recurring instruction (session heartbeat)
capabilities.hermes: `/heartbeat every 10m <prompt>` (alias /hb) binds one recurring instruction to the *session*: when idle and the interval has elapsed it fires as an ordinary user-role turn in the same context and prompt cache. status/pause/resume/clear; 60 s floor, 5 s poller, missed ticks coalesce to one, user messages win, survives /resume and compaction; state lives at `heartbeat:{session_id}` in SessionDB. Ships with an explicit heartbeat-vs-cron decision table (docs-features.heartbeat, .heartbeat-vs-cron).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/heartbeat.py:35 HeartbeatScheduler (reads per-agent HEARTBEAT.md frontmatter, MIN_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL=3600, APScheduler+jitter), agents/core/routers/heartbeat.py (status / {agent_id}/start|stop|run-now only), agents/jarvis/HEARTBEAT.md
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's heartbeat is per-agent and file-authored: to watch something you edit a Markdown file, restart, and accept a one-hour floor. "Keep an eye on X while we work" is the most-used shape of always-on assistance and Nerva has no answer for it at conversation scope — its proactivity currently only exists at fleet scale.
capabilities.governance: read-only to create — it schedules a *turn*, not an effect. The injection point must reuse the normal turn path so every action the fired turn proposes still crosses the kernel exactly as a typed turn does; a separate privileged injection path would be the regression.

capabilities.name: Re-run a prompt on a cadence inside the session, self-paced, with stop conditions (/loop)
capabilities.hermes: `/loop [interval] <prompt> [--times N] [--until <cond>]` (alias /proactive). Two cadence modes: fixed (30s/5m/2h/1h30m, floor `loops.min_interval_seconds`=30) and self-paced exponential backoff (floor 60 s → ceiling 900 s, doubling while the reply digest is unchanged, snapping back to floor the moment it changes). Five stop conditions including a `LOOP_COMPLETE` marker and an LLM `--until` judge routed through `auxiliary.goal_judge`; an active /goal owns the session and defers wakeups; Ctrl+C pauses rather than kills (6 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — agents/core/autonomy/schedule_runtime.py wakes company-mode *work runs* on an interval (a different unit); agents/core/autonomy/nl_schedule.py only parses text→cron. No session-scoped repeat, no self-pacing, no --until judge, no digest change detection anywhere in agents/.
capabilities.rationale: The 2026-08-28 delta-port deferred this on the claim that "există /loop-echivalente în autonomy" — that claim does not survive a read of the code, and correcting it matters more than the feature. The self-paced backoff is the piece worth taking outright: it is the only polling design in either product that costs *less* when nothing is happening, which is exactly the constraint of a box running a local model on one GPU.
capabilities.governance: read-only to schedule; the woken turn's actions cross the kernel normally. The tick cap must be a hard bound like the existing interrupt budget, not advisory.

capabilities.name: Pull a file or slice of a file into a message inline (@ context references)
capabilities.hermes: Typing `@file:path` expands the content inline under an `--- Attached Context ---` section, with `#L10-40` line ranges and tab completion over reference types and filesystem paths. Guarded by size limits, sensitive-path blocking for credential material, path-traversal rejection outside the workspace root, binary-file detection, and inline warnings instead of hard failures; explicitly CLI-only (the gateway does not expand) (11 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — ripgrep for `@file:` / context_reference / attached context across agents/, frontend/src/, mobile/src/ returns nothing; the HUD composer (frontend/src/cockpit.tsx) has no reference syntax and there is no server-side expander.
capabilities.rationale: The cheapest possible "look at what I'm looking at" affordance, and Nerva's alternative today is pasting the file by hand into chat. The security half is already built and is the part most products get wrong — FileScope in file_tools.py already enforces resolved roots, no `..`, no symlink escape and secret-looking-name refusal, which is precisely the guard set the expander needs.
capabilities.governance: read-only, with two hard rules: resolve through the same FileScope as file_read, and mark the expanded content tainted (agents/core/security/taint.py) so any plan assembled from it escalates GRANT→QUEUE at the kernel

capabilities.name: Receive generated files as native chat attachments (deliverable mode)
capabilities.hermes: The gateway scans every agent reply for absolute or `~/` paths ending in one of 57 allow-listed extensions across 9 categories (`MEDIA_DELIVERY_EXTS`), ignores paths inside code blocks and backticks, removes the path from the visible message and uploads the file natively — images and video inline, audio as a voice attachment, everything else as a file. Source extensions (.py, .log) are deliberately excluded. `kanban_complete(artifacts=[…])` rides completion notifications the same way (6 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/channels/telegram.py:51 (send / send_card / send_action — text only), agents/core/channels/base.py, slack.py, discord.py, email.py (same text-only ChannelAdapter contract), agents/core/plugins/telegram_bot.py:57 send_photo / :76 send_document (never called from a reply path), agents/core/media_export.py
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already produces charts, media bundles, day reports and support bundles; today the owner receives a filesystem path he cannot open from his phone. Attachment delivery is the step that turns everything the media and reporting layers generate into something a person actually receives.
capabilities.governance: privileged — this is egress of file bytes to an external channel. It must go through the governed channel send path under `channel.reply` mediation, with an explicit extension allowlist and a FileScope check on the resolved path, so a reply that names ~/.ssh/id_rsa cannot exfiltrate it.

capabilities.name: Run a durable multi-agent task board with worker lanes (kanban)
capabilities.hermes: A SQLite board shared across profiles: boards, tasks, links, comments, workspaces (scratch | dir: | worktree), a dispatcher and tenants. A `kanban_*` worker tool surface with an enforced lifecycle terminator (a worker that calls none and exits is treated as crashed), protocol-violation stop-nudges with bounded retry, an unblock-loop breaker, per-task model override and pinned skills, goal-mode cards, `scheduled_at` starts, a respawn guard, concurrency/promotion config, a runs table (one row per attempt), a `task_events` WebSocket, a dashboard plugin with a task drawer and a Triage decomposer, notification subscriptions, multi-tenant use, plus a documented worker-lane contract (assignee → spawn → terminator) and a four-story tutorial (70 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/missions.py (durable SQLite workspace: plan, hard step/wall-clock budget, pause/resume state machine, append-only event log), agents/core/subagents.py (isolated spawns, steer/stop, typed output, blocked capabilities), agents/core/routers/swarm.py (read-only Mission Control cockpit), agents/core/routers/missions.py
capabilities.rationale: Nerva has the durable half (missions + queue + audit) and the spawn half (subagents) but not the shared artifact that makes parallel work legible to a human: no columns, no dependency links between cards, no assignee-based dispatch to a named lane, no per-card run/retry rows, no worktree-per-task isolation. And Nerva's approval queue is a strictly better dispatcher gate than Hermes's, which has none — the board is the missing view, not the missing governance.
capabilities.governance: privileged — card dispatch spawns work and must enqueue through the existing TaskQueue and cross the kernel like `node.dispatch`; the pinned workspace must resolve inside FileScope; the "external CLI worker lane" Hermes documents as an unpaved path must stay unpaved in Nerva unless it crosses `terminal.exec`

capabilities.name: Search X / Twitter from the agent (x_search)
capabilities.hermes: An `x_search` tool backed by xAI's server-side search on the Responses API (`https://api.x.ai/v1/responses`) — Grok runs the search and returns synthesized results with citations back to the originating posts. Auto-registers whenever either xAI credential path exists (OAuth token or XAI_API_KEY), toggleable in `hermes tools`, with client-side from_date/to_date validation, a documented x_search-vs-xurl decision table and a four-case troubleshooting matrix (7 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/social.py (governed X *writes* only — post/reply/DM through the approval queue with SecretBroker auth), agents/core/osint/ (open-web reading), agents/core/plugins/websearch.py (DuckDuckGo / Tavily / SearXNG) — nothing searches X
capabilities.rationale: It is one hosted vendor's search behind one vendor's key, on a platform whose API terms have repeatedly changed, and Nerva's OSINT layer already reads the open web. Adding it as a core tool would make a first-class capability depend on a single company's goodwill. Re-open path: if the owner actually wants X monitoring, it belongs as a governed plugin with its own registered egress domain under plugin_gate, not as a core tool.
capabilities.governance: read-only, but egress — would need a plugin_gate domain registration and cross `plugin.egress`

capabilities.name: Steer which upstream provider serves an OpenRouter request (provider routing)
capabilities.hermes: When routing through OpenRouter or Nous Portal, six knobs shape the underlying provider: `sort` (price/throughput/latency ranking), `only` (whitelist of provider slugs), `ignore` (blacklist), `order` (explicit priority with unlisted providers as fallbacks), `require_parameters` (refuse providers that would silently drop temperature/top_p/tools), and `data_collection: allow|deny` (keep prompts out of provider training) (9 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/llm/openrouter.py — a plain OpenAI-compatible bearer-auth backend with strip_thinking and an injectable client; no `provider` block in the request body, no sort/only/ignore/order keys anywhere; agents/core/llm/hybrid_router.py chooses a backend, not a sub-provider
capabilities.rationale: `data_collection: deny` and `require_parameters` are privacy and correctness controls, not tuning knobs — a product whose north-star metric includes %-local (docs/METRICS.md) should not, when it does route to cloud, let the request land on a provider that trains on it or silently drops the tool schema. It is a request-body dict plus a settings row.
capabilities.governance: read-only (request shaping), but it belongs in the settings surface next to the other posture controls so the owner can see that cloud routing is constrained rather than assume it

capabilities.name: Let other apps use your subscription as an OpenAI endpoint (subscription proxy)
capabilities.hermes: `hermes proxy` runs a local HTTP server presenting a managed provider subscription (`nous`, `xai`) as an OpenAI-compatible endpoint to any external app, attaching and auto-refreshing credentials through an `UpstreamAdapter` so the app never holds a static key. Restricted by an allowed-path allow-list, with documented LAN exposure and rate limits and worked recipes for OpenViking and Karakeep (7 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none — nothing in agents/ serves outbound credentials to third-party apps; agents/core/secrets_vault.py and the SecretBroker exist specifically to keep credentials from becoming ambient
capabilities.rationale: Its whole purpose is to launder a hosted subscription into other people's tools. Nerva's thesis is that the model runs on the owner's box and credentials resolve only at action time behind approval; a credential-attaching proxy would recreate exactly the ambient-credential surface the secret broker was built to remove. Re-open path: only if Nerva ever ships a hosted tier of its own.
capabilities.governance: would be privileged (credential egress to arbitrary local clients) — and that is the reason to refuse it, not merely to gate it

capabilities.name: Keep hundreds of tools reachable without paying their schema cost every turn (Tool Search)
capabilities.hermes: Opt-in progressive tool disclosure: deferrable MCP/plugin tools are replaced in the model-visible array by three bridge tools (`tool_search`, `tool_describe`, `tool_call`), retrieved with BM25 + Snowball stemming plus a literal substring fallback. Tiered disclosure 0/1/2 degrades per server against a `min(threshold_pct% of context, listing_max_tokens)` budget; core tools never defer; the bridge unwraps at dispatch so hooks, guardrails and approval prompts all run against the real tool name (8 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/tool_rpc.py:109 register_tool, agents/core/autonomy_coordinator.py:433-677 (exactly 7 registered model-loop tools: desktop_run, terminal_run, desktop_plan, operator_plan, osint_enrich, echo, time), agents/core/file_tools.py:900 (file tools behind JARVIS_FILE_TOOLS), agents/core/mcp/client.py
capabilities.rationale: Not urgent today — with 7 registered tools nothing strains the context — but it is the precondition for the MCP breadth the owner wants. The moment a real MCP server attaches, the tool array stops fitting the context of a local model, which has far less to spare than a frontier one. Building it before the breadth arrives is cheaper than retrofitting it after.
capabilities.governance: read-only, with one hard rule: `tool_call` must unwrap before mediation so kernel.authorize sees the real action kind, never a generic bridge kind — a kernel that authorizes a bridge authorizes the wrong thing
capabilities.depends_on: MCP tool exposure to the model loop (not yet wired)

capabilities.name: Paste or attach a screenshot into the conversation (vision & image paste)
capabilities.hermes: `/paste` plus layered Ctrl+V/Cmd+V reading the OS clipboard image, `/terminal-setup` for VS Code/Cursor/Windsurf, a per-platform matrix (macOS / X11 / Wayland / WSL2) with SSH limits and workarounds, content-block formatting for vision-capable models, routing that keeps text-only models from receiving images, and `vision_analyze` dual behavior (11 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/llm/vlm.py (strict-local VLM adapter over the OpenAI-vision contract — Qwen3-VL / UI-TARS class, base64 data-URI + downscale to respect the KV budget), agents/core/routers/multimodal.py (GET /api/vlm/status, POST /api/vlm/describe), agents/core/desktop_drivers/capture.py, agents/core/screen_grounding.py
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already runs the hard half — a vision model on the owner's own GPU, with no image leaving the box — and is missing the trivial half: there is no clipboard read, no drag-drop into the HUD composer wired to /api/vlm/describe, no terminal image path. "Show it what I'm seeing" is one of the most common ways a personal assistant gets used.
capabilities.governance: read-only, but a pasted image is untrusted input and must be tainted like a RAG hit so a plan derived from it escalates to ASK

capabilities.name: Get working search / images / TTS / browser without signing up for five vendors (Nous Tool Gateway)
capabilities.hermes: One paid Nous Portal subscription routes web search, image generation, text-to-speech and cloud browser automation through infrastructure Nous runs, so the user never registers with Firecrawl, FAL, OpenAI or Browser Use. `hermes setup --portal` enables all four in one command, with eligibility rules, a free tool pool, per-category mix-and-match against your own keys, documented image-model IDs, selection keys, a deprecated `use_gateway` flag and self-hosted env overrides (12 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: none by design — agents/core/plugins/websearch.py requires the owner's own Tavily/SearXNG key or falls back to keyless DuckDuckGo; agents/core/image_gen.py runs local diffusion; agents/core/voice/tts.py runs local/BYO engines
capabilities.rationale: The 2026-07-06 migration plan already named hosted pass-throughs as the anti-thesis and nothing has changed: a gateway that proxies every query, prompt and page fetch through one vendor is the exact inverse of %-local as a north-star metric. The onboarding pain it solves is real, though — the honest Nerva answer is a first-run wizard that stands up *local* backends (Ollama/LM Studio, SearXNG, Piper), not a hosted relay.
capabilities.governance: would route every query and prompt through one vendor — egress that governance can log but not undo; the disqualifying reason

capabilities.name: Run commands somewhere other than this machine (toolsets + terminal backends)
capabilities.hermes: Toolsets enabled/disabled per platform via `--toolsets` and `hermes tools`. A terminal-backend table covering local, a persistent Docker container, SSH, Singularity/Apptainer, Modal and Vercel Sandbox, with container resource keys, container security hardening, shell-startup-file handling for non-interactive commands, a `process` tool for background processes, sudo support, and tool-result annotations for signal deaths and UTF-16 transcoding (15 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/sandbox.py (Docker or resource-limited subprocess, env scrubbed via prepare_python_child_env, output bounded by truncate_text), agents/core/environments/__init__.py (EnvironmentProfile local/docker/ssh + CWD marker protocol), agents/core/environments/execution.py (GovernedTargetRunner — "docker only; local/ssh refuse honestly"), agents/core/environments/targets.py, agents/core/autonomy_coordinator.py:521 terminal_run, agents/core/kernel/registry.py (`terminal.exec`)
capabilities.rationale: The SSH backend is the one that matters and it is already half-built — the owner's homelab/NAS is exactly the "somewhere else" a house brain needs to reach, and the target policy plane exists to decide where a command may land. Modal/Vercel/Singularity are serverless cloud execution and stay out on the same local-first grounds the delta-port doc already recorded. The genuinely missing primitive is a background-process tool: today a long-running command must block a turn.
capabilities.governance: privileged — every remote target must cross `terminal.exec` with the hardline denylist and the durable-approval floor (irreversible tier), and agents/core/environments/targets.py must remain the only thing deciding the destination

capabilities.name: Run the agent over thousands of prompts to produce training / eval data (batch processing)
capabilities.hermes: `batch_runner.py` runs the agent across hundreds or thousands of prompts in parallel to emit ShareGPT-format trajectories with tool-usage statistics, aimed at fine-tuning and evaluation. Documented dataset format, four flag families (core, provider-routing, reasoning-control, advanced), toolset distribution sampling, an output directory layout, a trajectory JSON schema, content-based checkpoint resume, quality filtering and a statistics rollup (13 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/self_evolution.py:18 TrajectoryStore (ShareGPT-style scored trajectories, cap 500, best-K per agent, feeding propose_optimization), training/prepare_data.py, training/sft_grpo.py, agents/core/bench.py (latency/throughput/success harness)
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already fine-tunes (Howard runs a fine-tuned local model) and already stores scored trajectories — what is missing is the harness that generates them at volume, which is the only cheap way to keep improving a *local* model. This is a place where the local-first thesis compounds and hosted products cannot follow.
capabilities.governance: privileged per run in aggregate — each batch turn is a real agent turn, so a sweep must run with an explicitly read-only or narrowly-scoped action scope, or a thousand prompts become a thousand approval cards. Default the runner to a read-only toolset.
capabilities.depends_on: agents/core/self_evolution.py; a headless turn entry point

capabilities.name: Have an animated mascot react to what the agent is doing (pets)
capabilities.hermes: A petdex-gallery sprite that reacts to agent state (idle / running a tool / thinking / finishing / failing) across CLI, TUI and desktop, rendered with terminal graphics protocols and a half-block fallback. `hermes pets` command family, `/pet`, `/hatch` generation, desktop Cmd+K adoption, roaming, Alt+wheel resize, vibe reactions, a pop-out overlay, config keys and a `pets doctor` (14 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: frontend/src/orb.tsx, frontend/src/burst.tsx — Nerva's presence affordance is the orb/burst animation in the HUD
capabilities.rationale: Nerva already has an identity for "the agent is alive and doing something" — the orb — and two mascots is one too many: a second one dilutes the brand rather than adding a capability, and docs/BRAND_BOOK.md exists precisely to prevent that. The one idea worth keeping is the state mapping (idle / tool / thinking / failing), which the orb should express faithfully and mostly does.
capabilities.governance: read-only

capabilities.name: Restyle the CLI chrome (skins & themes)
capabilities.hermes: `/skin` swaps 9 built-in skins or a custom `~/.hermes/skins/*.yaml`: 22 color keys, 4 spinner keys (faces and verbs), 6 branding keys, plus `tool_prefix`, `tool_emojis`, `banner_logo` and `banner_hero`. A third-party visual skin editor exists (9 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: frontend/src/styles.css and frontend/src/shell.tsx (a single designed theme), docs/BRAND_BOOK.md — no skin file format, no swap surface
capabilities.rationale: The CLI is not Nerva's product surface at all — the HUD is — and Nerva has a brand book asserting one deliberate look that user-authored skins would fight. Re-open path: a HUD light/dark plus density setting if owners ask for it, which is one settings row, not a skin engine.
capabilities.governance: read-only

capabilities.name: Change who the assistant is, per session and globally (personality & SOUL.md)
capabilities.hermes: A global `SOUL.md` loaded only from HERMES_HOME (never project-local, for injection safety), 14 built-in personalities switchable mid-session with `/personality`, custom presets under `agent.personalities`, a reset path (`none|default|neutral`), a defined position in the prompt stack, and a documented SOUL-vs-AGENTS.md-vs-personality separation (11 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/jarvis/SOUL.md and one per agent; agents/core/paths.py:30 souls/<id>/SOUL.local.md gitignored personalization overlay that wins at load; agents/core/soul_versioning.py + agents/core/routers/admin.py:304 (prompt version control: history / diff / rollback / A-B); agents/core/agent_templates.py (5 archetypes rendering a SOUL.md skeleton); agents/core/routers/agents_api.py:54 (live SOUL read)
capabilities.rationale: Nerva is stronger on both axes: persona is per-agent rather than one switchable global, and it is version-controlled with diff and rollback, which Hermes's is not. The single idea worth adopting is the named-preset switcher — the owner should be able to say "be terse today" without editing a file and without losing the versioned identity underneath.
capabilities.governance: read-only; SOUL edits already pass through soul_versioning and the admin guard

capabilities.name: Give the agent a standing objective it keeps working toward (/goal)
capabilities.hermes: `/goal` sets an objective that survives turns; after each turn a lightweight judge decides satisfied/continue and auto-feeds a continuation into the same session until achieved, paused, cleared, or `goals.max_turns` runs out. Plus `/subgoal` mid-goal criteria, `/goal gate` quality gates, automatic and manual wait barriers, a documented judge verdict protocol, **fail-open** semantics, judge-model selection, a walkthrough and a "when the judge gets it wrong" section (15 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/autonomy/goal_contract.py (a draft must carry title, an explicitly chosen scope, step/wall-clock/interrupt budget, a future deadline, ≥1 stop condition and ≥1 success check before it can be proposed; propose() enqueues an ask-tier task and grants nothing), agents/core/autonomy/work_verifier.py, agents/core/autonomy/work_judge.py (fail-closed, cannot pass what the verifier failed, scope drift fails the run), agents/core/autonomy/schedule_runtime.py
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's design is strictly better where it counts: Hermes's judge is fail-*open* and its goals declare nothing verifiable, which is exactly how an agent works confidently on the wrong thing for an hour. What to take is only ergonomics — a one-line way to start a small goal in an ordinary conversation that fills the six contract fields by asking two questions, instead of requiring the full company-mode intake.
capabilities.governance: privileged already — goal approval is an ask-tier governed task and every step of the run crosses the kernel; the lightweight entry path must fill the same contract, not bypass it

capabilities.name: Have the agent pick up a project's conventions automatically (context files)
capabilities.hermes: Auto-discovers and loads context files: an AGENTS.md chain walked from the git root down to cwd, progressive subdirectory discovery as the agent moves, a defined startup load pipeline, a prompt-injection scanner over everything it loads, size limits with truncation, documented best practices, and `.cursorrules` / `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` compatibility (8 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/knowledge_packs.py and agents/core/local_docs.py (owner documents indexed into memory), agents/core/learning/core_block.py (detect_injection applied to every injected fact, flagged entries become `[BLOCKED …]` placeholders) — but no cwd/git-root convention chain: the repo's own AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md are for its AI contributors, not something a Nerva agent discovers at runtime
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's operator, governed file tools and terminal all now run inside a working directory; without convention discovery the owner has to restate the same rules every session. The hard half — the injection scanner on loaded content — already exists and is wired into the memory core block, so this is mostly a discovery walk plus a size budget.
capabilities.governance: read-only, and it must reuse detect_injection plus taint on everything it loads — a discovered file is untrusted input by definition, which is why Hermes refuses to load SOUL.md project-locally

capabilities.name: Let the model write a script that calls tools without a round trip per call (execute_code)
capabilities.hermes: `execute_code` runs model-written Python that calls Hermes tools over a local RPC — `code_execution.mode` project|strict, resource limits, documented RPC mechanics and error handling, env scrubbing as the security model, skill env passthrough, HERMES_* hardening in the child with a documented workaround, an execute_code-vs-terminal decision table and platform support notes (12 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/tool_rpc.py (allowlist — unknown tool refused; risk-gating — read-only inline while gated/external tools enqueue an ask-tier task and execute only from the approved task; recursive secret-scrub of responses; run_pipeline for N calls without an LLM round trip), agents/core/sandbox.py, agents/core/environments/output_limits.py truncate_text (wired live), agents/core/environments/file_rpc.py, agents/core/kernel/registry.py (`tool.rpc`)
capabilities.rationale: H20.1 named this the biggest net win from Hermes and Nerva's version came out ahead: Hermes's security model is "scrub the env", Nerva's is "the sandbox cannot read a secret and cannot execute a gated tool at all". The remaining gap is breadth of registered tools, not design — widen the allowlist rather than rebuild the mechanism.
capabilities.governance: privileged and already mediated — `tool.rpc` is a KERNEL kind in registry.py; a gated call crosses kernel.authorize before it can even enqueue an approval task

capabilities.name: Keep working when one API key is rate-limited (credential pools)
capabilities.hermes: Register several keys or OAuth tokens per provider and rotate on failure, with four selection strategies (round_robin / least_used / fill_first / random) and a documented error-recovery matrix: plan-limit 429 rotates immediately (a cap won't clear on retry), generic 429 retries once then rotates, 402 rotates with a 1 h cooldown, 401 refreshes the token then rotates, all exhausted → `fallback_model` on another provider. Plus `hermes auth` CLI and an interactive wizard, `custom:` endpoint pools, auto-discovery sources, sharing with subagents and a documented storage schema (9 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/llm/auth_rotation.py (multi-key pool per provider from `*_API_KEYS`, rotation on 401/403/429, exponential cooldown with later retry, single-key pool behaves exactly like the old single-key backend, injectable clock), agents/core/llm/provider_errors.py, agents/core/secrets_vault.py
capabilities.rationale: The mechanism is there and is offline-testable; what is missing are the branches that matter in practice — 402 billing failures and OAuth refresh — plus any way for the owner to see pool health before everything is cold. Keys should also resolve through the vault Nerva already has rather than living only in environment variables.
capabilities.governance: read-only routing, but key material must resolve through the SecretBroker/secrets_vault and never reach logs — the existing log_safe discipline applies

capabilities.name: See the type errors an edit just introduced (LSP semantic diagnostics)
capabilities.hermes: Runs ~27 real language servers (pyright, gopls, rust-analyzer, typescript-language-server, clangd and more) as background subprocesses and feeds their semantic diagnostics into the post-write lint check used by `write_file` and `patch`, so the agent sees type errors, undefined names, missing imports and project-wide semantic issues — not just syntax. Git-workspace gating and layering, a `hermes lsp` CLI, config keys, install locations, performance characteristics, global and per-language disabling, troubleshooting (10 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/codeintel/index.py (read-only AST symbol index over the project with build_index/search_symbols, cached), agents/core/routers/codeintel.py, frontend/src/panels/codeintel.tsx — answers "where is this symbol", not "did my edit break the types"
capabilities.rationale: Nerva now has governed file_write; a write tool with no semantic feedback is how an autonomous agent leaves a repo broken and reports success. For the "developer continues alone" lane in docs/NERVA_2_ROADMAP.md this is the single highest-leverage quality gate available, and it is the cheapest way to make the verification fabric real for code.
capabilities.governance: read-only for the diagnostics, but a language server is a long-lived child process — it must launch under the same environment/target policy as any other child, with the env scrubbing prepare_python_child_env already provides

capabilities.name: Generate an image from a prompt (image generation)
capabilities.hermes: `image_generate` via FAL.ai with 11 selectable models (FLUX 2 Klein/Pro, GPT-Image 1.5/2, Nano Banana Pro, Ideogram V3, Recraft V4 Pro, Qwen, Z-Image Turbo, Krea V2 M/L), an OpenRouter image catalog, GPT-Image quality pinning, image-to-image editing, aspect-ratio control, upscaling, a per-platform delivery matrix, a debugging section and stated limitations (11 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/image_gen.py (local diffusion — ComfyUI/diffusers Flux FP8 — with an LLM unload/reload swap so generation never contends for VRAM, and the LLM always restored even on diffusion failure), agents/core/media_gen.py (local inline; any cloud generation enqueues an ask-tier approval), agents/core/media_catalog.py, agents/core/media_export.py
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's VRAM-swap design is the better one for a single-GPU box and its local-vs-cloud approval split is exactly right. What is missing is the ordinary controls a user expects — pick a model, set an aspect ratio, edit an existing image, upscale — without which a working local backend still reads as a demo.
capabilities.governance: privileged for the cloud path only, already an ask-tier task via media_gen; local generation is a reversible host effect on the owner's own GPU and correctly stays out of the queue

capabilities.name: Answer a hard question with several models at once (Mixture of Agents)
capabilities.hermes: MoA is a virtual provider: each named preset appears as a selectable model whose aggregator writes the response and emits tool calls, while reference models run first and supply analysis. `/moa` one-shot, preset configuration, `reference_max_tokens` for advisor speed, `fanout` cadence, a privacy filter, per-slot reasoning effort, a `hermes moa` CLI, published benchmarks, prompt-caching interaction and documented constraints (12 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/arena.py (same query to 2+ models, blind A/B labels, human vote, ELO leaderboard), agents/core/llm/moe_routing.py, agents/core/cortex_compare.py + cortex_decision.py (evaluation-only shadow comparison), agents/core/llm/hybrid_router.py (complexity-based escalation to the deep slot) — nothing aggregates several models into one answer
capabilities.rationale: MoA multiplies token cost per turn by the number of advisors, and tokens on a local single-GPU box are the scarcest resource in the whole system; the hybrid router's deep-slot escalation already buys most of the quality for one inference. Re-open path: if Nerva ever routes to cloud by default, MoA's privacy filter is the piece to copy first, before the aggregation.
capabilities.governance: read-only

capabilities.name: Plug in an external memory backend (Honcho and 8 memory providers)
capabilities.hermes: Eight swappable external memory providers (Honcho, OpenViking, Mem0, Hindsight, Holographic, RetainDB, ByteRover, Supermemory), one active at a time alongside built-in memory, with profile isolation and a comparison table. Honcho itself adds dialectic reasoning and a running user model: two-layer context injection, cold/warm prompt selection, three cadence/depth knobs, multi-pass dialectic depth, session-start prewarm, query-adaptive reasoning level, self-hosted auth, 17 config keys, three recall modes, gateway identity mapping, observation modes, 5 tools and a 15-command CLI (29 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/memory/bitemporal.py, graph.py, entity.py, episodes.py, fusion.py (RRF), decay.py (ACT-R), consolidation.py, recall_admission.py, living_recall.py, profile_extractor.py, worldview_sync.py; agents/core/learning/core_block.py (bounded core rings, injection-scanned, frozen per-session snapshot so mid-session writes never break the prompt cache); agents/core/learning/background_review.py (per-turn strict-local distillation with a daily budget)
capabilities.rationale: This is Nerva's strongest area and every one of those eight providers is a hosted service that would ship the owner's life to someone else's database — adopting any is a direct regression against the product's reason to exist. The one idea worth borrowing is Honcho's cold/warm split: cheap recall by default, deep reasoning only when the query warrants it, which is a cost discipline a local box needs more than a hosted one does.
capabilities.governance: read-only for recall; externally-driven KG writes already cross `kg.write` with a mandatory capability token, while the high-frequency internal ingestion path is deliberately direct so a halt cannot freeze per-turn memory

capabilities.name: Control music playback by voice or chat (Spotify)
capabilities.hermes: Full Spotify Web API control with PKCE OAuth — 8 tools covering playback, devices, queue, search, playlists, albums and saved library, plus Home Assistant-managed speakers via Spotify Connect. One-shot and two-step setup flows, developer-app creation, OAuth over SSH/headless, a Free-vs-Premium matrix, cron recipes, sign-out and revocation, token-refresh verification, custom scopes and client IDs, a documented storage layout and a seven-case troubleshooting section (21 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/plugins/spotify_plugin.py (get_playback / play / pause / next_track / search / get_devices with token refresh, behind the plugin network-scope gate), mobile/src/screens/MediaScreen.tsx, agents/core/routers/media_director.py, agents/core/media_director.py
capabilities.rationale: Nerva has a Media Director pillar and a house brain, and music is the single most-used physical-world action in a home — yet half the tool surface (queue, playlists, albums, saved library) is missing and there is no owner-facing setup flow. The headless/SSH OAuth path matters specifically because Nerva's target deployment is a headless box the owner does not sit in front of.
capabilities.governance: privileged — playback control is actuation and belongs behind `media.present` at the CapabilityActionAPI facade; the plugin path must not become a second, unmediated route to the same effect

capabilities.name: Start the assistant hands-free by speaking to it (wake word)
capabilities.hermes: Three engines — sherpa (open vocabulary, any phrase), openWakeWord custom models, and Porcupine — with remote-desktop client capture, config keys, false-trigger reduction guidance, defined surface and listener ownership across CLI/TUI/desktop, desktop profile routing (a different phrase starts a different profile), requirements, and macOS/Windows microphone troubleshooting (13 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/voice/wake_word.py (openWakeWord + pyaudio, WAKE_WORDS = ["jarvis", "hub"] hardcoded, single callback), agents/core/voice/wyoming.py + agents/core/routers/wyoming.py (satellite path for room devices), agents/core/rooms.py
capabilities.rationale: Nerva is a house brain with room satellites, so the wake word is the front door of the entire product there — and "jarvis"/"hub" hardcoded is now a branding defect since the product renamed to Nerva. Per-phrase routing to a specific agent in the fleet is the feature that actually fits Nerva's architecture, and Hermes already shows the shape; an open-vocabulary engine is what makes it possible without training a model per phrase.
capabilities.governance: read-only for detection, but the session it opens must inherit the room's identity (agents/core/identity_manifest.py) so every downstream action is attributed to the right origin at the kernel

capabilities.name: Use the agent from inside an IDE (ACP host integration)
capabilities.hermes: `hermes acp` runs an ACP server over stdio so ACP-compatible hosts drive it — VS Code, Zed, JetBrains and Buzz Desktop, with a `hermes-acp` toolset, an `[acp]` extra, `--setup-browser` bootstrap, a Buzz channels relay bridge, a Buzz model picker, an owner-only security warning, config and credentials, `HERMES_ACP_SKIP_CONFIGURED_MCP`, session and working-directory behavior, session-scoped auto-approval and troubleshooting (16 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/mcp/server.py + scripts/nerva_mcp_stdio.py (the reverse direction: allow-listed Nerva agents exposed as MCP tools to Claude Desktop / Cursor / another Nerva, routed through the orchestrator so guardrails and the permission gate still apply), agents/core/routers/mcp.py
capabilities.rationale: MCP server mode already gets an editor talking to Nerva, over the protocol with the broader host ecosystem; a second agent protocol doubles the governed surface for one more class of host. ACP's session-scoped auto-approval is also exactly the pattern Nerva refuses on principle. Re-open path: a host the owner actually uses turns out to be ACP-only.
capabilities.governance: would be privileged, and its session-scoped auto-approval directly contradicts the approval-queue model — a reason to stay out rather than to gate

capabilities.name: Keep the skill library from rotting (curator)
capabilities.hermes: A background pass over agent-created skills that tracks view/use/patch counts in a `.usage.json` sidecar, walks active → stale → archived, and spawns a short auxiliary-model review proposing consolidations and drift patches. A tar.gz snapshot before every real pass, an append-only JSONL ledger with single-edit rollback, TTL purge that never runs automatically and captures blobs first, per-run report directories, an explicit old→new rename map in the summary, adopt/pin/restore commands and a 23-command CLI (16 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/skills/curator.py (nightly idempotent pass, active → stale 30d → archived 90d with the directory *moved* to the data-root archive and never deleted; only agent-created unpinned skills are curatable; owner-approved patches applied hash-checked against drift with a reversible backup; decisions synced into the ledger), agents/core/skills/usage.py, agents/core/skill_drift.py, agents/core/skills/proposals.py
capabilities.rationale: Same design with a stronger gate: Hermes lets the curator archive bundled built-ins by default and applies LLM-proposed patches, while Nerva requires owner approval for every patch and treats bundled/imported/pinned skills as untouchable. What is worth adding is the per-run report and the rename map — a maintenance pass the owner cannot read afterwards is a maintenance pass he cannot trust.
capabilities.governance: privileged — patch application is an owner-approved action already routed through ActionApprovalQueue; archival is reversible and correctly stays out of the queue

capabilities.name: Have the assistant remember you across sessions (persistent memory)
capabilities.hermes: Bounded, curated MEMORY.md + USER.md rendered as a frozen system-prompt snapshot; a `memory` tool with substring matching and two targets; documented what-to-save-vs-skip rules, capacity management with an explicit full-memory error, duplicate prevention and security scanning; `session_search` over past conversations; a `/journey` timeline of everything learned with a playable constellation scrubber; config keys, `memory.write_approval`, background-review notifications, reviewer model selection and an `extra_tools` allowlist (18 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/learning/core_block.py (bounded core + user rings, every entry through detect_injection, frozen per-session snapshot), agents/core/learning/background_review.py (per-turn strict-local structured review with cadence and daily budget; facts → rings, corrections → LearningModule, skills → quarantine/proposals), agents/core/memory/rag_tool.py search_memory, agents/core/memory/timeline.py build_unified_digest, agents/core/routers/memory_hud.py (list / clear / stats only)
capabilities.rationale: Nerva wins the hard part and loses the visible one: there is no model-callable search over past *conversations* (search_memory hits the vector/KG store), and no journey timeline. The timeline in particular is how a user actually sees that the thing has been learning — memory/timeline.py and build_unified_digest already exist, so this is a panel over data Nerva already has, and it is the best available demo of the product's real differentiator.
capabilities.governance: read-only; memory writes already pass the injection scanner and agent-proposed facts already go through the approval path

capabilities.name: Keep answering when a provider or model goes down (fallback providers + auxiliary routing)
capabilities.hermes: Three documented resilience layers: primary-model `fallback_providers` across a 44-row provider table plus custom endpoints with per-turn, reset-aware trigger conditions; eight auxiliary tasks with independent provider resolution, an auto-detection chain, `base_url` overrides, a capacity-error fallback ladder, per-task `fallback_chain` with per-entry timeouts, and a list of provider quota phrases that trigger it; plus compression, delegation and cron-specific overrides, summarized in a 12-row matrix (20 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/llm/hybrid_router.py (backend choice by token budget, agent policy, availability, with graceful degradation and complexity escalation to a deep slot), agents/core/llm/auth_rotation.py (key-level failover), agents/core/llm/provider_errors.py, agents/core/llm/providers/ (6 declarative provider profiles, read-only catalog)
capabilities.rationale: The strict-local pin on auxiliary tasks — background review, judge, curator all forced to `router.local_backend` after the 2026-07-06 adversarial review caught the opposite — is deliberate and correct and must not be undone. What is missing is honest degradation *within* local: a declarative chain with per-entry timeouts beats today's implicit ordering when the deep slot is loaded or LM Studio is down, and quota-phrase classification is a few lines cheaper than waiting for a timeout.
capabilities.governance: read-only, with one construction rule: a chain entry that would route a strict-local auxiliary task to cloud must be impossible, not merely discouraged by configuration

capabilities.name: Search and read the web (web_search / web_extract)
capabilities.hermes: `web_search` and `web_extract` across an 8-provider backend table with a keyless free-tier ring, free/paid tier pinning (`web.provider_tier`), an extract truncation budget, result caching, Firecrawl as the default, self-hosted SearXNG setup, Exa and Parallel, an xAI/Grok backend, documented configuration priority, an auto-detection table, a one-shot keyless rescue, a verification command and troubleshooting (16 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/plugins/websearch.py (DuckDuckGo keyless plus optional Tavily / SearXNG, with register_dynamic_domain for the configured SearXNG host), agents/core/security/ssrf.py resolve_and_validate, agents/core/plugin_gate.py, agents/core/http_client.py PluginHTTPClient (kernel-mediated egress), agents/core/security/taint.py
capabilities.rationale: Search is table stakes and Nerva's is thin — one keyless backend, no separate extract tool with a truncation budget, no cache, no tier pinning — so the agent can find a URL and then not read it well. The SSRF-validated, IP-pinned, kernel-mediated egress plumbing is the strongest part of the stack and is exactly what a broader backend set should hang off.
capabilities.governance: privileged egress — already crosses `plugin.egress` via the injected kernel hook in http_client; every new backend must register its domain through plugin_gate and fetched content must stay tainted

capabilities.name: Hand a piece of work to an isolated child agent (subagent delegation)
capabilities.hermes: `delegate_task` with context isolation, batch mode, durable background completions, child notifications, model/provider override, a `/review` command, inherited tool access with per-subagent tool blocks, max iterations, an opt-in child timeout, failure visibility, background stall detection, an `/agents` monitor, live child transcripts, mid-run steering, a depth limit for nested orchestration, worktree isolation and documented lifetime/durability properties (22 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/subagents.py (isolated session per spawn through an injectable runner, configurable concurrency cap, per-spawn SteerChannel with steer/stop whose messages carry a declared origin and are explicitly never an approval, typed output validation, per-spawn cost attribution, DELEGATE_BLOCKED_CAPABILITIES = delegate/memory_write/channel_send/skill_manage/clarify), agents/core/iteration_budget.py, agents/core/routers/swarm.py, agents/core/routers/agents_api.py
capabilities.rationale: The blocked-capability set on children is something Hermes does not have and is the difference between delegation and uncontrolled fan-out — a child that cannot delegate, write memory or send on a channel cannot quietly become a second agent. The two gaps worth closing are purely observational: stall detection and live transcripts, because a child that hangs is currently invisible until its budget expires.
capabilities.governance: privileged — spawn dispatch crosses `node.dispatch`; the blocked-capability set must stay enforced at the runner, not advertised to it

capabilities.name: Hand turns to an external coding-agent runtime (Codex app-server)
capabilities.hermes: Optionally routes `openai/*` and `openai-codex/*` turns to the Codex CLI app-server so terminal commands, file edits, sandboxing and MCP tool calls all execute inside Codex's runtime while Hermes becomes the shell (sessions DB, slash commands, gateway, memory, skill review). A built-in 5-tool set, a Hermes tool-callback MCP server, goal/kanban/cron support on that runtime, a trade-off matrix, live display bridging, `/codex-runtime`, Codex approvals surfaced in the Hermes UI, permission profiles, a managed block in `~/.codex/config.toml`, `CODEX_HOME` multi-profile isolation and MCP migration (18 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/routers/swarm.py + lock.py coordinate *external coding agents* (Claude, Codex, opencode, Antigravity) through repo lock files for the development workflow — which is a different thing: it never hands a user turn to them
capabilities.rationale: Handing turns to a vendor runtime means Nerva's kernel no longer sees the terminal command, the file write or the MCP call — every effect would execute inside a sandbox Nerva does not govern, and the approval UI would be showing decisions it did not actually mediate. This is not a feature that can be ported under governance; it is the one shape governance cannot wrap. Re-open path: only if Codex exposes a pre-execution authorization hook a kernel binding could sit in.
capabilities.governance: would bypass the kernel entirely for terminal, file and MCP effects — the disqualifying reason

capabilities.name: Get useful integrations without writing code (bundled plugins)
capabilities.hermes: Eleven opt-in in-repo plugins on the same surface as third-party ones — disk-cleanup, security-guidance, observability/langfuse, google_meet, a hermes-achievements dashboard plugin and others — with documented discovery rules, opt-in semantics and stated criteria for adding one (10 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/plugins/ — 24 in-tree modules (Gmail, Google Calendar, weather, news, stock quotes, IoT control, Homebridge, Apple Health, CRM sync, Postiz, meta ads, n8n, WhatsApp bridge, SMS alerts, Spotify, websearch, OSINT enrich, analytics, balance, degradation, honesty, oracle bridge, signal layer, telegram bot); agents/core/plugins.py NetworkAccess manifest (NONE/LAN/RESTRICTED/FULL + data scope + serving agents); agents/core/plugin_gate.py; agents/core/plugin_manager.py
capabilities.rationale: Nerva ships more than twice as many integrations as Hermes bundles, and each declares a network and data scope the core actually enforces — Hermes's bundled plugins carry no such manifest. Nothing to copy here.
capabilities.governance: privileged egress, already mediated by `plugin.egress` through the injected kernel hook in http_client

capabilities.name: Talk to the assistant and hear it answer (voice mode)
capabilities.hermes: Full voice across CLI and messaging platforms: `/voice`, VAD silence detection, spoken stop phrases (`voice.stop_phrases`), streaming TTS, desktop client-direct capture, barge-in, a Whisper hallucination filter, Telegram and Discord voice replies, live Discord voice channels, a full config reference, environment variables, and STT/TTS provider comparisons with resolution priority (16 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/voice/pipeline.py, sentence_stream.py, dictation.py, stt.py, tts.py; agents/core/voice/wake_word.py; agents/core/voice/wyoming.py + agents/core/rooms.py (room satellites); agents/core/channels/voice.py; frontend/src/orb.tsx + voice.ts; agents/core/voice/tts.py voice_persona_consent_granted (cloned/persona voices require explicit consent)
capabilities.rationale: Barge-in is the difference between a voice UI you can interrupt and one you have to wait out — on a house device that *is* the experience. The Whisper hallucination filter is a couple of hours of work that stops the assistant acting on silence it misheard, which in a governed product means a spurious approval card the owner has to reason about.
capabilities.governance: read-only for capture; the persona-consent gate on cloned voices is a governance feature Hermes has no equivalent for and must be preserved as a gate, not demoted to a setting

capabilities.name: Have the agent drive the desktop it shares with you (computer use)
capabilities.hermes: Background desktop control on macOS, Windows and Linux — clicking, typing, scrolling, dragging — without moving your cursor, stealing keyboard focus or switching Spaces, and working with any tool-capable model rather than a specific vendor's computer-use API. Install via cua-driver, permission modes, a bounded mode with a capability manifest, `computer-use doctor`, an agent cursor overlay and sessions, a cua-driver skill pack, screenshot return, provider compatibility, safety guardrails, token-efficiency notes, limitations, config and telemetry, troubleshooting (16 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/desktop_operator.py (read-only steps inline, mutating/irreversible held for approval, on-screen injection classifier reusing the H17.1 quarantine detector so a hostile UI cannot steer the agent), agents/core/desktop_control.py (canonical-key allowlist — never a binary path or shell string), agents/core/desktop_drivers/platform.py:45 DRIVER_PLATFORMS = windows/macos/linux-x11/linux-wayland, agents/core/screen_grounding.py (VLM + a11y-tree fusion), agents/core/kernel/registry.py `desktop.step`, agents/core/autonomy_coordinator.py:434 desktop_run
capabilities.rationale: Nerva has two things Hermes does not: an injection classifier on what the screen says, and a kernel that sees every step immediately before actuation. The honest caveat is that none of this has run on the owner's real machines — docs/OWNER_TASKS.md still carries it as unverified — so the gap here is production proof, not capability. The one behavioral detail worth matching is Hermes's background, non-focus-stealing input.
capabilities.governance: privileged and mediated — `desktop.step` crosses the CapabilityActionAPI facade immediately before the driver call; a requires_kernel driver cannot use the legacy direct path

capabilities.name: Choose how it sounds and how it hears (TTS / STT provider matrix)
capabilities.hermes: Eleven TTS providers — Edge (free), ElevenLabs, OpenAI, MiniMax, Mistral Voxtral, Gemini, xAI, NeuTTS, KittenTTS and Piper (44 languages), plus custom command providers and Python plugin providers — with Gemini persona prompts, audio tags, input length limits, Telegram voice bubbles via ffmpeg and xAI voice cloning; and an STT side with documented fallback behavior, command providers and Python plugin providers (17 entries).
