capabilities.rationale: Piper specifically is the right shape for this product — fully local, tiny, 44 languages including Romanian — and its absence means the privacy-first assistant currently has better voices when it phones out than when it stays home. The command-provider escape hatch is worth more than any single provider: it lets the owner wire any local engine without a code change.
capabilities.governance: read-only, except that a cloned or persona voice must keep the existing consent gate — that is governance, not configuration

capabilities.name: Point any OpenAI-compatible frontend at the agent (API server)
capabilities.hermes: An OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint so Open WebUI, LobeChat, LibreChat, NextChat, ChatBox and hundreds of others can use the agent as a backend with its full toolset: `POST /v1/chat/completions`, `POST /v1/responses` with response storage, `GET /v1/models`, `GET /v1/capabilities`, per-request model selection, health endpoints, a Runs API, a Jobs API, a Sessions API, skills/toolsets discovery, an `X-Hermes-Session-Key` memory-scoping header, system-prompt layering on top of the core prompt, bearer auth with multi-profile routing, a concurrent-run cap, security headers and CORS, and a browser-extension control protocol (20 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/routers/ + agents/web.py expose 441 routes of Nerva's own governed API behind admin_guard/user_guard (agents/core/routers/_deps.py) with agents/core/cors_policy.py and a route-auth matrix test; agents/core/mcp/server.py covers tool clients — but nothing speaks the OpenAI chat-completions contract inbound (the only /v1 reference is an outbound probe to LM Studio at agents/core/routers/admin.py:448)
capabilities.rationale: This is the cheapest distribution Nerva can buy: it makes every existing chat frontend a Nerva client without Nerva building one, and it is the honest way to let an owner keep a UI he already likes instead of forcing the HUD for chat. The adaptation that matters is that a turn arriving this way must be an ordinary identity-attributed turn — same kernel, same approval queue — never a privileged side door.
capabilities.governance: privileged — actions proposed by such a turn cross the kernel as usual, but the endpoint itself needs bearer auth bound to an identity in agents/core/identity_manifest.py, a concurrency cap, and a hard refusal to let a client-supplied system prompt widen tool scope or autonomy level

capabilities.name: Extend the agent with third-party code at lifecycle points (plugin system)
capabilities.hermes: A documented third-party plugin surface: a `ctx.*` capability API, discovery sources and sub-categories, opt-in allow-list plus deny-list, approval transports (`ctx.register_approval_transport`), 26 available hooks, 4 plugin types with a pluggable-interface map, NixOS declarative plugins, a `hermes plugins` CLI and interactive UI, one-click `hermes://` install links, capability consent, platform actions, a community plugin index with search, plugin packs (`hermes-pack.yaml`), install-time security scanning, `ctx.inject_message()` and `ctx.call_mcp()` (18 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/plugin_manager.py (24 in-tree modules built by name — no discovery, no install), agents/core/routers/plugins.py (`GET /plugins` listing only), agents/core/plugin_gate.py, agents/core/plugins.py NetworkAccess manifest; agents/core/skills/marketplace.py + signing.py + acquisition/quarantine.py are Nerva's actual extension story
capabilities.rationale: Do not import the ecosystem — the signed, quarantined skills marketplace is already a better-governed extension path than a community plugin index. What is genuinely missing is the *hook* half: an in-tree plugin cannot subscribe to a lifecycle event, so every integration is hardwired into plugin_manager.py and adding one means editing core. Add hooks plus manifest-declared capability consent; do not add a plugin marketplace.
capabilities.governance: privileged — a hook that can inject a message or call MCP is an action surface. Hook-registered effects must resolve to existing kernel kinds, and a plugin must never be able to register a new unmediated kind; that constraint is what keeps the registry's PENDING_KERNEL debt set honest.

capabilities.name: Drive a real browser to do something on the web (browser automation)
capabilities.hermes: Seven backend options — Browser Use cloud, Browserbase, the browser_exec driver, Firecrawl, Camofox local (with Docker loopback rewriting, persistent sessions, external tab adoption and a VNC live view), Lightpanda, local Chromium-family over CDP, and plain agent-browser — with hybrid routing that sends public URLs to cloud and LAN/localhost to local, real-profile browsing using your own logins plus a `browser close-profile` unlock, and 13 tools (navigate, snapshot, click, type, scroll, press, back, get_images, vision, console with JS evaluation, raw CDP passthrough, native dialog handling) with frame-tree/OOPIF visibility, WebM session recording, headed mode, stealth and session cleanup (39 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/browser_agent.py, agents/core/browser_playwright.py (chromium/firefox/webkit), agents/core/browser_transport.py (Chromium `--host-resolver-rules` pinned to the SSRF-validated IP, closing the DNS-rebind TOCTOU below Playwright's request interception — Hermes has no equivalent), agents/core/browser_kernel.py (`browser.step` consulted on the real action payload before the driver call and before the approval card is created), agents/core/kernel/registry.py

The functional gaps that block real sites are narrow: native dialog handling and console/JS evaluation are needed for ordinary flows, and real-profile browsing is what lets the agent act as the owner on sites he is already logged into, which is simultaneously the most useful and the most dangerous item on the list.
capabilities.governance: privileged and mediated — `browser.step`; real-profile mode must additionally require a per-domain grant in the consent ledger (`permission.grant`) because it borrows the owner's live authenticated sessions

capabilities.hermes: Three drop-in layers. Themes: YAML files in `~/.hermes/dashboard-themes/` with a 3-layer palette, typography plus a UI font picker, layout radius/density, `layoutVariant` (standard/cockpit/tiled), assets as CSS vars, per-component chrome overrides, colorOverrides and a raw `customCSS` escape hatch, with built-ins and a full `ocean.yaml` reference. Re-open path: the *backend* third alone (a FastAPI router under /api/plugins/<name> behind admin_guard) is defensible if the owner wants private panels.

capabilities.name: Connect the agent to external MCP tool servers, and expose it as one
capabilities.hermes: A full MCP client: `hermes mcp` command group, discovery-first `mcp add`, a curated one-click catalog with a trust model, install-time tool selection and later `mcp configure`, manifest version compatibility, runtime `${ENV_VAR}` and context-variable substitution, stdio and HTTP servers, OAuth (including remote/headless and the no-DCR pitfall), mTLS client certificates, per-user identity headers, recycling for memory-heavy stdio servers, presets, tool-name prefixing, Unicode TAG stripping on results, `_meta` passthrough with reserved-key filtering, resources/prompts wrapper tools, per-server include/exclude globs, dynamic discovery and reload, stdio env filtering, parallel tool calls, sampling (`sampling/createMessage`) and elicitation (`elicitation/create`); plus `hermes mcp serve` exposing 10 tools with an event system (37 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/mcp/client.py (stdio always; Streamable HTTP behind JARVIS_MCP_HTTP_CLIENT, deliberately refusing the deprecated HTTP+SSE pair; JARVIS_MCP_STDIO_ENV_BASELINE allow-lists what a spawned server inherits so it never sees the hub's keys), agents/core/mcp/oauth.py, agents/core/mcp/http_transport.py, agents/core/mcp/server.py + scripts/nerva_mcp_stdio.py, agents/core/mcp/route_tools.py, agents/core/kernel/registry.py `mcp.mutating`
capabilities.rationale: MCP is how Nerva gets breadth without writing 400 integrations and the governed base is already right. Two gaps are security-relevant rather than cosmetic: Unicode TAG stripping on tool results (an invisible prompt-injection vector the taint layer does not currently catch) and per-server tool include/exclude filtering, which is the difference between attaching a server and attaching three thousand of its tools. Sampling and elicitation should be refused until each has its own mediated kind — both let a remote server drive the model or the owner.
capabilities.governance: privileged and mediated — mutating MCP tools cross `mcp.mutating` after the per-identity gate; any future sampling/elicitation support needs its own kernel kind before it ships, never a reuse of `mcp.mutating`

capabilities.name: Teach the agent a new procedure and share it (skills system)
capabilities.hermes: agentskills.io-compatible SKILL.md with three-level progressive disclosure; skills as slash commands and stackable in one command; `/plan`; `/learn` to author a skill from sources plus knowledge-base skills for large ones; frontmatter format, platform-specific skills, media directives, conditional activation, `required_environment_variables` secure setup, per-skill config settings, directory structure, an advisory NVIDIA SkillEvaluator Tier-1 scan, external skill dirs, project-local skills with trust/untrust and scan-time quarantine, bundles, agent-managed `skill_manage` with write approval and a content scanner, a Skills Hub with sources and direct-URL installs, trust levels and `--force`, an update lifecycle, publishable taps with category groupings, bundled-skill reset and `/skills` commands (33 entries).

capabilities.name: Schedule work to run without you (cron / scheduled tasks)
capabilities.hermes: A single `cronjob` tool with action-style operations plus `/cron add`, `hermes cron create` and natural-language schedules. Model resolution with a drift guard, per-job reasoning effort, pre-dispatch config validation, skill-backed jobs, a per-job `workdir`, editing, lifecycle actions with name lookup, agent-managed scheduling behind a flag, a gateway scheduler tick, execution history (`cron runs`), a repeated-failure review nudge, failure incidents, a fleet `cron doctor`, delivery targets including bot-chat and routing intent `all`, Telegram topic routing, response wrapping, continuable deliveries that reattach to a session, `[SILENT]` suppression, script/cleanup/media timeouts, no-agent script-only jobs, monitor mode, a per-job notepad, chaining via `context_from`, continuity, provider recovery, missed-fire reporting, misfire catch-up, schedule formats, repeat behavior, async manual runs, per-job toolsets, a `wakeAgent` pre-run gate with recipes, storage and prompt security scanning (44 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/heartbeat.py:35 (per-agent jobs from HEARTBEAT.md frontmatter — cadence: cron, channel, do_not_disturb, checklist — APScheduler with jitter and MIN_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL=3600), agents/core/scheduler_service.py (internal jobs only: digests, budget reset, learning promotions, log scans, KG sync), agents/core/autonomy/nl_schedule.py (EN/RO text→cron, wired only to POST /api/schedule/parse at agents/core/routers/tools.py:73), agents/core/autonomy/schedule_runtime.py (company-run waking with night-window restraint), agents/core/routers/heartbeat.py (status / start / stop / run-now — no create)
capabilities.rationale: This is the widest single gap in the cluster. Everything an always-on assistant does for you between conversations is a scheduled job, and today the owner must edit a Markdown file, restart, and live with a one-hour floor — with no run history, no failure incidents, no delivery target and no way to inspect a job. Every ingredient already exists (a durable queue, a policy engine, night windows, a do-not-disturb model, an NL parser); they have simply never been assembled into a job a person can create.
capabilities.governance: privileged — creating a job is a standing authorization to act later, so creation must cross the kernel (a new `schedule.create` kind, or reuse of `permission.grant`), the job's action scope must be declared at creation the way goal_contract declares scope, each fired run's actions cross the kernel individually, and agent-created schedules must default to ask-tier

capabilities.hermes: `hermes dashboard` with multi-profile management and pages for Status, Chat (an embedded TUI over PTY), Config, API Keys, Sessions, Logs, Analytics, Cron, Profiles, Skills, MCP, Webhooks, Pairing, Channels and System; a resource-pressure banner, remote-backend connection from the desktop app, `/reload` to re-read `.env`, profile-scoped `?profile=` endpoints, a documented `/api/status` shape, and a full auth stack — gated mode with fail-closed semantics and Nous Portal / basic username-password / custom password / self-hosted OIDC (with a Keycloak worked example) / bearer-token drain providers, a public-URL override with trusted proxies, an OAuth flow with cookies, logout and an audit log, plus CORS policy and dev auto-build (37 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: 441 routes across agents/core/routers/ behind admin_guard/user_guard (agents/core/routers/_deps.py) with a route-auth matrix test; frontend/src/panels/ (approvals, permissions ledger, security-skills map, trust ops, signals governance, host readiness, LLM routing, memory consolidate, mission canvas, company room, system map, today receipt) plus modes*.tsx; agents/core/cors_policy.py; mobile/src/screens/ (Approvals, House, Media, Memory, Skills, Tasks, Ambient, Camera, Capture, Comms)

The only piece worth taking is OIDC/SSO, and only when a second human needs access; a single-owner product does not need five pluggable auth providers.

capabilities.name: Run your own code at the agent's lifecycle points (four hook systems)
capabilities.hermes: Four independent systems. Gateway event hooks (`HOOK.yaml` + `handler.py`) with an event catalog, alert/logger/webhook examples and a BOOT.md startup-checklist tutorial. Plugin hooks via `ctx.register_hook` across a 37-event catalog, including cache-safe system-prompt sections, streaming output hooks, a `pre_verify` contract and `transform_api_error_classification`. Shell hooks with a configuration schema, a JSON wire protocol, exit-code-2-means-block semantics, fail-open vs fail-closed modes, worked examples, a consent model with an allowlist, a `hermes hooks` CLI and a security model. And outbound webhooks with a signed wire format and documented delivery semantics (23 entries).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: agents/core/webhooks.py (token-authenticated *inbound* triggers, optional HMAC-signed sources via X-Signature-256), agents/core/channels/webhook_channels.py (outbound sends to WhatsApp/Signal transports), agents/core/observability/egress_monitor.py, agents/core/passive_capture.py — no user-authored hook of any kind: no pre/post-action hook, no shell hook with a blocking exit code, no signed webhook on agent lifecycle events, no consent allowlist
capabilities.rationale: Adopt exactly one of the four — the shell hook with exit-code-2-blocks — and refuse the rest for now. A blocking pre-action hook is the one extension point that makes governance *stricter* rather than looser: it lets the owner add his own refusal rule (never touch this path, never spend after midnight) alongside the kernel's. Signed outbound webhooks on approval and audit events are the second most useful, because they let the owner's existing monitoring see governance decisions without polling the API.
capabilities.governance: privileged — a hook that can block must run before the kernel decision and may only ever narrow it; a hook able to *allow* what the kernel denied would invert the entire model and must be impossible by construction. Hook scripts are themselves host execution and need an owner consent allowlist plus the same env scrubbing as any child process.
capabilities.depends_on: agents/core/kernel/__init__.py authorize path; agents/core/environments/ env scrubbing

capabilities.name: Install Nerva in one command on any supported OS, and prove the install is healthy
capabilities.hermes: One-line curl/PowerShell installers plus desktop installers; documents a per-user vs root-mode (FHS) layout, the four dependencies the installer bundles, non-sudo/system-service-user installs, install-method auto-detection (git/Docker/NixOS) and a formal Tier 1 / Tier 2 / Unsupported platform-support contract, plus `hermes uninstall` (docs-rest.installation, install-layout, install-prereqs, install-nonsudo, install-method-autodetect, platform-support, uninstall).
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/install.sh, /home/user/jarvis-hub/install.ps1, /home/user/jarvis-hub/INSTALL.bat, /home/user/jarvis-hub/scripts/bootstrap.py, /home/user/jarvis-hub/scripts/doctor.py, /home/user/jarvis-hub/scripts/install_smoke.py, /home/user/jarvis-hub/uninstall.sh, /home/user/jarvis-hub/docs/INSTALL.md, /home/user/jarvis-hub/docs/PACKAGING.md
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's bootstrap is arguably better than Hermes': a named Python-3.12 floor refusal, `pip --require-hashes` against a real lock, a loopback-only bind invariant, a real boot + /readyz + one deterministic turn as the install smoke, and scripts/doctor.py as a stdlib-only check-up that runs in a broken install. Hermes has no equivalent of the smoke or the doctor. Two Hermes pieces are worth adding on top: install-method auto-detection (so the update path can refuse correctly, see row 2) and a written platform-support tier contract in docs/COMPATIBILITY.md.
capabilities.governance: read-only — the bootstrap runs before the app boots, writes no config, and never asks for a cloud key; nothing crosses the kernel

Copy the manifest + lifecycle + doctor triad, and adapt hard: Nerva's manifest already declares network scope and data scope (plugin_gate.py), which is *better* than Hermes' capability list, and Nerva already has the trust machinery Hermes lacks — CDX-8 quarantine, signing, review queue, the skills marketplace's approve/rollback flow. So the honest port is 'Hermes' ergonomics on Nerva's trust model', not a copy. Deliberately skip from this row: the built-in tool override (a third-party plugin silently replacing a governed built-in is a governance hole no opt-in flag makes safe) and `pre_llm_call` prompt injection into the user message.
capabilities.governance: loading third-party code is the privileged act itself. It needs a kernel kind of its own (`plugin.load`, irreversible tier → approval queue) plus the existing quarantine/signature gate; every effect a plugin performs must continue through the existing kinds — plugin.egress for network, tool.rpc for tools, mcp.mutating for MCP. A plugin that reaches an effect without crossing one of those is the exact regression the directive's adaptation rule forbids.

The gateway's own OAuth flow binds its callback listener on the BACKEND machine's 127.0.0.1, which is unreachable from the user's browser when the backend is remote (SSH/Tailscale) — so MCP OAuth simply died. The fix binds an ephemeral ONE-SHOT http listener on the USER's loopback, hands its URL to the gateway as the OAuth redirect_uri (client_redirect_uri on oauth.start), and relays the redirect's code/state back via the new RPC. Security posture, verbatim: the listener closes on first callback, cancel or timeout (5 min, max 8 pending); it only ever RECEIVES code/state and forwards them — no tokens are exchanged there, and the gateway verifies state (constant-time) before redeeming anything. Entries: desktop-mcp-oauth-relay, rpc-mcp-oauth-callback.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/mcp/oauth.py (the SERVER half — RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata for Nerva's own MCP server); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/routers/oauth.py:85 POST /api/oauth/callback (third-party connect/callback for Gmail/Google, assuming the browser and backend share a host); /home/user/jarvis-hub/desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs (single file — no callback relay)
capabilities.rationale: Nerva's own deployment story is the remote-backend case: the box with the GPU sits in the house and the owner drives it from a laptop or the Tauri client. Any OAuth connect flow — Gmail, Calendar, an MCP server — therefore fails today in exactly the configuration the product recommends, and fails in the confusing way (the browser shows a dead localhost page). The security shape is the part to copy precisely: the relay carries only code/state and never redeems a token, and state verification stays server-side.
capabilities.governance: Privileged — this is credential acquisition. The relay must be incapable of redeeming; the token exchange stays behind agents/core/secrets_vault.py and the state check is constant-time on the backend.

capabilities.name: Canonical data survives a corrupt derived index, and there is a documented offline repair
capabilities.hermes: docs/state-db-recovery.md states the contract: sessions and messages are CANONICAL; the full-text index and its sync triggers are DERIVED and may be detached temporarily. On an FTS corruption error class, SessionDB records a durable fts_stale marker, removes the sync triggers in the same transaction, retries canonical writes without the derived sinks, and serves searches from canonical rows through a LIKE fallback — the failing LIVE operation never runs FTS5('rebuild'), because that turned a single message write into an unbounded full-transcript rebuild. A later open may rebuild under a cross-process admission lock; if it cannot, FTS stays detached, canonical writes stay available, and `hermes doctor` names the repair command. `hermes sessions repair [--check-only] [--no-backup]` is the explicit path, backing up first. Supporting fixes: quarantine a 0-byte truncated DB, serialize startup check/quarantine/connect/schema, cap read connections per process and per file, isolate background reads from the writer connection. The doc's operational warning: never copy state.db, -wal and -shm independently with cp — they are one live SQLite image. Entry: state-db-recovery.
capabilities.nerva_evidence: /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/backup.py:111 _sqlite_consistent_copy, :124 _integrity_check (PRAGMA integrity_check per DB), :236 backup_health ('so "we have backups" is checkable'); /home/user/jarvis-hub/agents/core/memory/store.py:278 and settings_db.py:341 and analytics_store.py:96 (WAL + synchronous=NORMAL across the stores) — but no corruption containment on the live path, no derived-vs-canonical split, and no repair command; `rg -i 'corrupt|malformed'` finds only JSON-store tolerance in persistence/json_store.py
capabilities.rationale: Nerva runs four or more SQLite databases on a box that is expected to lose power (autonomy queue, settings, analytics, memory, audit chain) and its backups already prove the owner cares. The gap is what happens BETWEEN backups: today a corrupt index in any store takes writes down with it, and the audit chain in particular must never stop accepting rows — a governance product whose log stops recording because a search index went bad has lost the thing it sells. Split canonical from derived explicitly, degrade the derived half, and ship the repair as a named command rather than as folklore.
capabilities.governance: Privileged where it touches the audit chain (agents/core/security/audit.py): a repair must preserve and re-verify the Merkle chain, never silently re-write rows, and a repair itself should be an owner-approved irreversible action.

capabilities.name: A client whose backend session died recovers instead of staying bound to a phantom
capabilities.hermes: apps/desktop/src/store/runtime-gone.ts learns a runtime is gone through two channels and routes BOTH to the same recovery lever: PUSH (a session.reclaimed event drops the cached state and unbinds the tile) and PULL (a session-scoped RPC rejected with 4001 'session not found' — the terminal verdict). Every user-initiated action already honored the pull verdict; the BACKGROUND POLLERS, the only callers that run while the user is not acting, did not — so a view could stay bound to a dead runtime for the rest of its life. Healed runtime ids are latched permanently. The push channel provably cannot cover a runtime that died with a previous app process, was reaped while disconnected, or was reaped by a gateway this client had not yet dialled — in those cases the 4001 is the ONLY notice that ever arrives. Related: a flapping no-mux SSH tunnel child now restarts within a bound instead of poisoning the whole connection and SIGTERMing a healthy backend. Also in this cluster: HUD drag geometry across mixed-DPI monitors, Bot Mode rebuilt as ~70 typed modules with a plugin-scoped i18n bundle, empty-chat slots owned by the plugin, menu labels normalized to bare verbs in sentence case, desktop composer metadata declared on the command registry (argument_mode + desktop availability) so the UI stops guessing, /busy widened beyond the CLI, a Keys-page delete that reconciles custom vs known variables correctly, and dashboard OAuth routes following the selected management profile. Entries: desktop-runtime-gone, desktop-ssh-tunnel-restart, desktop-hud-drag, bot-mode-rebuild, desktop-board-switcher-menu, desktop-preview-download, desktop-menu-sentence-case, command-desktop-metadata, busy-command-scope, web-env-delete-state, web-oauth-profile-scope.
